title: The Wargame review – Michael Gove is awful at pretending to be PM in this mind-warping reality show | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The premise is an imminent attack on Britain by Russia in a world in which Michael Gove is prime minister and Nicola Sturgeon his deputy. It’s enjoyably terrifying – and the politicians’ stiffness is huge fun
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The premise is an imminent attack on Britain by Russia in a world in which Michael Gove is prime minister and Nicola Sturgeon his deputy. It’s enjoyably terrifying – and the politicians’ stiffness is huge fun
Content: ‘The real entertainment lies in seeing who works well on camera and who doesn’t.’Photograph: Justin Downing/SkyView image in fullscreen‘The real entertainment lies in seeing who works well on camera and who doesn’t.’Photograph: Justin Downing/SkyTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewThe Wargame review – Michael Gove is awful at pretending to be PM in this mind-warping reality showThe premise is an imminent attack on Britain by Russia in a world in which Michael Gove is prime minister and Nicola Sturgeon his deputy. It’s enjoyably terrifying – and the politicians’ stiffness is huge funLucy ManganMon 21 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrigger warning: this review contains the phrase “Michael Gove cosplaying as PM.” There is no helpline.The Wargame is mind-warping. On the one hand, it posits an imminent nuclear strike on Britain by Russia. Bad! On the other, it posits this happening in a world in which the government is composed of Michael Gove cosplaying as prime minister,Nicola Sturgeonas his deputy, Harriet Harman as home secretary, Sayeeda Warsi as attorney general and Penny Mordaunt as defence secretary. So, you know, there’s a competing “Come, friendly bombs …” vibe too.How does it happen, you wonder? Is there a long process of producers wooing, cajoling and making increasingly tempting offers to their putative cast members while these sober adults thoughtfully weigh the pros and cons, and the risk to professional reputations that any foray into the entertainment sphere represents (and The Wargame is essentially a heavily scripted reality show) before eventually signing on the dotted line? Or – politics being showbusiness for ugly people and all that, and large numbers of modern politicians being BoJo-type vortices of insatiable need and ego rather than the public servants of yore shaped by ancient notions of faith and duty – did they all come running? Were they begging for parts, flashing teeth and thighs and playing coquettishly with their lapels as soon as rumours of the commission made their way down the hallowed corridors of Westminster? We may never know. We may have our deeply held suspicions. But we will never know.View image in fullscreenThe Wargame participants.Photograph: Justin Downing/SkyThe four-part double-faceted nightmare that is The Wargame is set nine months in the future. Is this a coded warning to have your affairs in order and a stockpile of beans to hand by next summer? Given Channel 4 also recently aired televisualurban prepper manual Apocalypse, we cannot rule out the possibility that somebody, somewhere is trying to tell us something.Here, we begin with a Cobra meeting, convened after the assassination of two RAF pilots and a malware attack on regional ambulance services. Which hostile force is behind them and are they linked? Hmm. The politicians all agree that they should wait for more information. The intelligence services and military brass round the table roll their eyes and go off to get it. News comes that a Russian spy ship has been found in Blighty waters, hovering over the undersea cables upon which 93% of our national infrastructure depends, and that everything can probably now be connected to Russia.The programme starts off relatively slowly: people spend a lot of time telling each other that “This is straight out of the Russian playbook!” and you can see Gove straining to appear statesmanlike when there is nothing yet to be particularly statesmanlike about, which would be endearing if it wasn’t risible. But soon the twists and turns begin. Developments start gathering pace by the end of the first episode and the momentum builds to enjoyably terrifying proportions by the end of the third (the finale, alas, was not available for review).When does a hostile act become an indisputable act of war? Can you hope for the best but prepare for the worst without giving the wrong signal to your enemies or your electorate? Can the electorate usefully be informed of anything in the social media age, or is everyone essentially a dysregulated toddler now? Can we depend on our allies? What about the one that is led by a dysregulated toddler now? Is there ever a point at which you have to stop thinking about optics and just do what you think best? Is there anyone left who can do that?All these big questions are interestingly gestured at. But of course the real entertainment – and The Wargame rapidly becomes almost too much fun for something resting on the threatened annihilation of millions – lies in seeing who works well on camera and who doesn’t, and, on that basis alone, working out who you would actually want in place when the motherfunking shit hits the motherfunking fan.Gove, Harman and Sturgeon are fabulously awful. Stiff, self-conscious, self-important, entirely unable to give any portion of themselves up to the purported reality or the flow of the thing. Sturgeon is an alternately whining and furious goblin, Harman a disappointed schoolmarm and, though I suspect he is desperate to do so, Gove cannot modulate his perma-condescending tone – whether he is addressing his fellow cabinet members, his military advisers or the nation.Meanwhile, Mordaunt, Jim Murphy (Foreign Office minister in real life 2007-08, foreign secretary here) and Gen Richard Barrons (joint forces commander IRL 2013-16, chief of defence staff in TV land) are like MGM movie stars by comparison. Swift, decisive, plain-speaking (Murphy is the first to swear and he times it beautifully) and – yes, in an uncrowded field – charismatic, these are the people I want deciding my fate. Within The Wargame, sure. But also, at this point, maybe out here, too. If this is not just a warning to us but an audition for them, consider this trio through to the next round.The Wargame aired on Sky One and is available on Now.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionMichael GovePenny MordauntNicola SturgeonHarriet HarmanSayeeda WarsireviewsShareReuse this content

title: Another day, another Reform Wales leader. Grumpy Nige seems to miss the old one | John Crace | The Guardian
description: At a low-key event, Helen Jenner replaces Dan Thomas, who was arrested on suspicion of assault and gets warm words from Farage
Author: John Crace
Headline: At a low-key event, Helen Jenner replaces Dan Thomas, who was arrested on suspicion of assault and gets warm words from Farage
Content: Reform UK members line up at the Senedd during the unveiling of the Wales leader, Helen Jenner, standing next to Nigel Farage.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenReform UK members line up at the Senedd during the unveiling of the Wales leader, Helen Jenner, standing next to Nigel Farage.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAThe politics sketchReform UKAnother day, another Reform Wales leader. Grumpy Nige seems to miss the old oneJohn CraceAt a low-key event, Helen Jenner replaces Dan Thomas, who was arrested on suspicion of assault and gets warm words from FarageMon 21 Sep 2026 13.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareTwenty-five or so Reform members of the Senedd were lined up against a wall. Almost as if they were in a police identification parade. Reform’s need to find a new leader inWalesis becoming habit-forming.First, Nathan Gill wasbanged up for 10 and a half yearson eight counts of taking £40K in bribes to make statements in support of Russia. Easily done. Who among us hasn’t been tempted by the Kremlin? And then last week, Dan Thomaschose to stand down after being arrested on suspicion of assault and coercive behaviour, leaving the Welsh leadership spot open once more. He denies the allegations.It’s almost as if there’s a pattern emerging. That the job of Reform leader in Wales is somehow cursed. Otherwise law-abiding men and women suddenly find themselves accused of all sorts of things. So much so that it’s now the job that no one really wants.Yet politics abhors a vacuum, and someone has to do the job. So it was a decidedly grumpy-lookingNigel Faragewho turned up in Cardiff on Monday morning to pretend to be interested in announcing the next Reform Senedd leader. Perhaps he reckoned he had better things to do.The event – if you can call a five-minute announcement that – was supposed to kick off at 11.45. Nige was booked on the 12.18 back to Paddington and had hoped to be in London for a late lunch. No champagne and oysters. There were no undercover reporters posing as Americans trying to make a potentially illegal donation this time. Instead, there was a 20-minute delay.Nige really was going through the motions. He was thrilled bythe results in Wales at the May elections, he began. He didn’t sound thrilled. Though that could be because Reform has been shedding support in Wales – as elsewhere – ever since. They have lost seven points in the opinion polls over the course of the summer and are looking less and less likely to challenge Plaid Cymru.“Dan Thomas has been doing a brilliant job,” Nige continued. “I am sorry for his personal difficulties.” This was just weird. Almost as if he hadn’t even considered what Thomas had been alleged to have done. Yeah, Dan. Great bloke. Brilliant Reform leader. Always buys his round in the pub. It’s just unfortunate that he’s been arrested on suspicion of assault and coercive control. But it’s no big deal. He’ll soon be sorted.Nige doubled down, calling the arrest a “bump in the road”. Not a word of sympathy or support for the person he is accused of having assaulted or subjected to coercive control. Besides, he was clear that Dan would come back soon. There would always be a welcome in the Reform valleys for Dan. We all need someone like Dan.After the Song for Dan, Nige made the briefest of introductions to the new leader. Best to skip over the bit where almost half the Reform members of the Senedd had preferred a different candidate. The party in Wales is a hotbed of backstabbing. Not literally, mind. Thejob was going to Helen Jenner, the former deputy leader and Nige’s old-time Ukip mucker. “I’ve known her for years and I trust her,” he said.Helen mumbled her thanks and said she would build on the good work done by others. It wasn’t clear if Dan would take over from her if he is cleared of the allegations, which he denies. It sounded like a possibility. In which case, I guess Dan might then only be keeping the seat warm for Nathan when he gets early release in 2031. You have to admire Reform’s loyalty.And their amnesia. Because you also can’t help wondering if Nige is beginning to lose the plot somewhat. How else do you explain his recent Substack post in which he claimed that “British politics is awash with dirty money”? I mean, he’s obviously not entirely wrong. But why would he want to draw attention to it when questions remain over money received by Reform and figures associated with the party?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWith Kemi’s new shadow chancellor, the Tories must hope for a bout of public amnesiaRead moreThere’s the £40K that went to Gill from the Russians. There was the apparent eagerness on the part of Dan Jukes and James Orr to accept overseas donations. A meeting at which Nige was present. Though not listening, apparently. There’s the dosh from Ben Delo, a man convicted of failing to comply with anti-money-laundering legislation in the US.There’s the cash from Posh George and his mum that is somewhat opaque to say the least. There are the police and parliamentary investigations. The £5m gift that went undeclared. With the best will in the world, none of this seems the model of transparency. But what do I know? And it’s good to know that Reform operates in a world where any transgressions are so readily forgiven.Explore more on these topicsReform UKThe politics sketchNigel FarageWalescommentShareReuse this content

title: Is it true that … cycling affects fertility? | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Saddling up is only likely to be an issue for elite athletes – and those with low sperm counts
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: Saddling up is only likely to be an issue for elite athletes – and those with low sperm counts
Content: Illustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianIs it true that …CyclingIs it true that … cycling affects fertility?Saddling up is only likely to be an issue for elite athletes – and those with low sperm countsKate LloydMon 21 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Cycling isn’t big on the radar of fertility doctors,” says Prof Colin Duncan, a fertility expert at the University of Edinburgh.For women, he says, the only time cycling is likely to affect fertility is when it’s done at extreme levels, such as the kind of training undertaken by elite athletes.“Doing huge amounts of physical activity can lower body fat, and that can switch off the ovaries,” he says. “Elite athletes may stop having their periods and reduce their fertility.”For men, things are a little different. Sitting on a bicycle saddle for prolonged periods can increase the temperature around the testicles, “almost incubating them”. This can affect sperm production, because sperm develop best at a cooler temperature – one reason the testicles are located outside the body.double quotation markIf you’re doing extreme cycling, it will change your sperm count a littleIs it true that … mental health is affected by inflammation?Read moreBut for most men, Duncan says, this isn’t something to worry about. “The testicles produce way more sperm than is actually required for fertility.“If you cycle a normal amount, it’s still going to make absolutely no difference at all. But if you’re doing extreme cycling, it will change your sperm count a little.”Even then, he says, the impact is more likely to matter for men whose sperm count is already borderline. “If you’ve got a really good sperm count, it probably doesn’t make an awful lot of difference. You’ve still got a lot of sperm there that are swimming.”In fertility clinics, Duncan says he’ll consider lifestyle factors when assessing a patient’s sperm sample. “If there are abnormalities I’ll get a sense of what their lifestyle is like and talk about changes,” he says. “If you’re doing certain things to excess – smoking, drinking, saunas – it’s probably worthwhile moderating that.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingIs it true that …featuresShareReuse this content

title: Sense and Sensibility review – Daisy Edgar-Jones leads sober-minded next-gen do-over of Austen romcom | Movies | The Guardian
description: With Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as the Dashwood sisters, this fresh take on a beloved classic is not to be confused with Ang Lee’s
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: With Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as the Dashwood sisters, this fresh take on a beloved classic is not to be confused with Ang Lee’s
Content: Jane again … Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles in Sense and Sensibility.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus FeaturesView image in fullscreenJane again … Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles in Sense and Sensibility.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus FeaturesMoviesReviewSense and Sensibility review – Daisy Edgar-Jones leads sober-minded next-gen do-over of Austen romcomWith Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as the Dashwood sisters, this fresh take on a beloved classic is not to be confused with Ang Lee’sPeter BradshawMon 21 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s no reason for anyone working on a new adaptation of Jane Austen’s Sense and Sensibility to be intimidated bythe celebrated 1995 movieby director Ang Lee and screenwriter Emma Thompson, any more than they should be or overawed by Austen’s original novel. Sacred cows are there to be … not slain, but re-invented. The decision to bring out a next-gen Sense and Sensibility, with a new young cast – as opposed to, say, a new Northanger Abbey ora new spin on the unfinished The Watsons– might bemuse some and at first it bemused me, like hearing about a Love Actually remake starring Millie Bobby Brown. But this turns out to be a more downbeat, ruminative version, happening in much cloudier weather than 30 years ago and without the sugar-rush final wedding scene. The mood is cooler, but interestingly austere, sober and thoughtful. There are also some strange casting decisions.The sisters at the heart of the story, Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, played in 1995 by Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet, are now played byDaisy Edgar-Jonesand Esmé Creed-Miles, and frankly don’t look and sound much like the sisters we thought we knew. They look like young women who knew each other reasonably well at uni and are now in a flatshare in London. It is a story of financial and romantic crisis. Mrs Dashwood and her three daughters, having happily occupied a handsome Sussex estate, are forced to move to humble Barton Cottage in Devon when Mrs Dashwood’s stepson John Dashwood inherits their property and effectively evicted them.Before this can happen, Elinor meets and falls for young Edward Ferrars, a shy and decent young man of a well-to-do family, reticently portrayed byGeorge MacKay. Here, in fact, it should be said that Diana Reid’s script and Georgia Oakley’s direction put into valuably sharper focus something left unstressed in 1995: that Mrs Dashwood (Caitríona Balfe) is pointedly insisting on moving away to the west country rather than endure the indignity of her daughter seeming to be a gold-digger.It is in the wilds of Devon that Elinor broods unhappily on why Edward isn’t proposing marriage, and where the headstrong, romantic Marianne twists her ankle while out for a walk and is carried back to the cottage by dishy dreamboat-cad Mr Willoughby. The latter is played by Frank Dillane with a certain amount of insidious charm, but also a sort of Uriah Heep smirk. And Marianne does not see the integrity and all-round loveliness of the gallant ex-soldier who is poignantly in love with her: Colonel Brandon, heavily and inexplicably played behind hefty facial hair by Norwegian actor Herbert Nordrum.Now, no actor would want to follow Alan Rickman from 1995 in the role of Colonel Brandon. But Nordrum, genuinely great inJoachim Trier’s Oslo-set comedy drama The Worst Person in the World, is just an eccentric, stolid outlier in this context; his line-readings feel unengaged and he doesn’t seem to be that moonstruck by Marianne, or particularly enthused by anything much at all. Of course, some of the film’s (worthwhile) intention is to push against envelopes and stereotypes and I quite enjoyed the gender-challenging casting of Eliot Sumner, icily playing Mr Palmer. But Brandon feels uncomfortable.The scene-stealer is the mischievous, gossipy and forthright Mrs Jennings, marvellously played byFiona Shaw, who brings up the voltage every time she comes on and effectively makes of it a far bigger role than Elizabeth Spriggs in the same part in 1995. Overall, the movie always looks and sounds perfectly good, though some of the sensibility is lacking.Sense and Sensibility is out on 25 September in the UK, 15 October in Australia and 16 October in the US.Explore more on these topicsFilmFilm adaptationsJane AustenRomance filmsDrama filmsDaisy Edgar-JonesGeorge MacKayreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Europe is under attack from three sides – but the EU and Nato are unfit to defend us | Nathalie Tocci | The Guardian
description: Ursula von der Leyen’s outreach to Canada and new security proposals are wise – but she may not be the right messenger, says Guardian Europe columnist Nathalie Tocci
Author: Nathalie Tocci
Headline: Ursula von der Leyen’s outreach to Canada and new security proposals are wise – but she may not be the right messenger, says Guardian Europe columnist Nathalie Tocci
Content: ‘The EU is slow and cumbersome, built for peacetime. Its membership, while large, is not wide enough, excluding key players in the wider European space.’Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The EU is slow and cumbersome, built for peacetime. Its membership, while large, is not wide enough, excluding key players in the wider European space.’Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersOpinionEuropeEurope is under attack from three sides – but the EU and Nato are unfit to defend usNathalie TocciUrsula von der Leyen’s outreach to Canada and new security proposals are wise – but she may not be the right messengerMon 21 Sep 2026 11.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 16.25 EDTShareEurope’s strategic predicament is ever clearer, and ever darker. The continent is at war, which is being fought militarily in Ukraine, but is escalating rapidly across Europe through hybrid attacks.Germany’s disclosurethat it blames Russia for the drone attack at Leipzig airport; a Russian drone strikeon a trainnear the Ukraine-Poland border; an Italian jet shooting down aRussian drone over Lithuania; flares fired from a Russian warshipat a Danish helicopter– all within the space of a couple of weeks – tell a coherent story. Whether because Russia is bogged down and unable to advance in Ukraine, or because it believes the US will not come to Europe’s rescue, Vladimir Putin’s regime is ever more bent on escalating its aggression in Europe.Canada is seeking new global neighbours – no wonder, as Trump rolls out stupidities at scale | David MoscropRead morePutin’s calculus is not irrational. Trump never misses a chance to lash out at Europe – the latest example being histhreats of further tariffson the EU if Brussels proceeds to offer Canada “associate membership”. Europeans have grown numb to Trump’s insults and threats, but these threats do underline his deep antipathy, suggesting that if a Russian attack warranted a response, Trump might look the other way. The US certainly can’t be relied on to have Europe’s back.This is the context in which Ursula von der Leyen caused surprise last week byproposing associate membershipof the EU for Canada. To bolster Europe’s defences, the European Commission president also wants a “European security council”, and a mutual solidarity mechanism to respond to hybrid attacks.While they have distinct rationales, these ideas fit into the same strategic logic: in a world of predatory powers, the “rest of the west” must huddle together.The threats are not only external. Along with Putin’s Russia and Maga America, the rise of the far right in Europe completes a triangle of threats. The far right is a threat to liberal democracy. But by instigating internal division and pushing for disintegration, it also supports the divide-and-rule designs of predatory external powers, representing a challenge to Europe’s independence and sovereignty.It has taken the earthquake of theAfD’s successesin German regional elections for von der Leyen toacknowledge openlythat Europe’s threats are also homegrown. Better late than never.European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against NatoRead moreFaced with this unprecedented convergence of threats from three sides, leaders are scrambling for a response. Nato has what it takes to defend Europe againstRussia. But if its majority shareholder – the US – is unwilling to step in, the question of its plans, structures and capacities is moot. If a hybrid attack on a European country caused civilian casualties, would Nato be bypassed if Washington signalled its unwillingness to act? Collective defence would not even be invoked if the anticipated result were the US’s betrayal of its European allies.This is where von der Leyen’s emergency protocol comes in, filling the gap between the high-water mark of mutual assistance – article 42.7 of the EU’s founding treaty, which covers armed aggression – and nothing at all. The attacked state would activate the protocol, an emergency European Council would convene, and the commission and EU high representative would propose responses, including evacuation and medical support, stockpiling and energy security, economic coercion, military mobility and more. The mechanism could extend to like-minded non-EU partners, starting with Canada, Norway, the UK and Ukraine. The proposal to offer Canada associate membership, while still undefined, can be read in this light as well.On paper, it all makes sense. In practice, it is hard to see such a mechanism operating seamlessly, let alone rapidly, given the EU’s organisational complexities, its slowness to act and its internal divisions.Hence the proposal for a European security council, consisting of those countries willing and able to contribute to the defence of Europe, without the US if need be. Some of these countries would be EU members, but not all – again, Canada, the UK, Ukraine and possibly Turkey.Both the problem and the solution are clear. To protect itself against predatory powers, what remains of the west must cooperate ever more closely. But the existing multilateral organisations –Natoand the EU – are unfit for purpose. Nato will remain anchored to the US, while the EU is slow and cumbersome, built for peacetime. Its membership, while large, is not wide enough, excluding key players in the wider European space.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDeveloping alternative forms of EU membership could be of interest not just to Canada, but to the UK, too. The ideawas first raisedby Berlin for Ukraine, in fact, but Kyiv turned down the offer, seeing it as second-class. Ukraine deserves full EU membership, but if a substantial associate membership is on the table in the short term, it should take that, while continuing to press for more.The rise of far-right nationalism means that reaching consensus within the EU will become harder, not easier – which is precisely where the proposal for a smaller, more agile European security council comes in, provided far-right governments do not simultaneously come to power across major European countries.Von der Leyen’s security proposals are sensible and urgently needed. The potential pitfall lies not in the message, but in the messenger.In her years at the helm of the commission she has grown a reputation for centralising power and overstepping boundaries, irking other EU officials in Brussels as well as European capitals. When it comes to security and defence especially, sovereignty is jealously guarded by the EU’s nation state governments. It would be tragic if European governments ended up killing off a set of good ideas because of Europe’s institutional turf wars. Rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic is the last thing Europe and its partners need right now.Nathalie Tocci is a Guardian Europe columnistExplore more on these topicsEuropeOpinionRussiaEuropean UnionVladimir PutinUrsula von der LeyenNatocommentShareReuse this content

title: What is Trump’s third-country deportation policy and who does it target? | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Key questions answered about scheme that has sent more than 25,000 people to countries that are not their own
Author: Louisa Loveluck
Headline: Key questions answered about scheme that has sent more than 25,000 people to countries that are not their own
Content: The Trump administration is deporting people to countries where they often have no connections.Composite: Guardian Design/AP/Reuters/Getty Images/ SOPA Images/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Trump administration is deporting people to countries where they often have no connections.Composite: Guardian Design/AP/Reuters/Getty Images/ SOPA Images/REX/ShutterstockUS immigrationExplainerWhat is Trump’s third-country deportation policy and who does it target?Key questions answered about scheme that has sent more than 25,000 people to countries that are not their ownBanished: Trump’s secret deportation dealsFreedom oppressed: journalists caught up in Trump crackdownLouisa LoveluckandAlice SperiMon 21 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 01.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince returning to office in 2025, Donald Trump’s administration has deported more than 25,000 migrants, refugees and asylum seekers to countries that are not their own.Human rights lawyers describe these so-called third-country national arrangements as a “show of force”, intended to make people fear the consequences of entering the US without permission.Banished to alien lands: Trump’s secret deportation dealsRead moreTo compile the most comprehensive account of a policy that has mostly operated behind closed doors, the Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Paris-based Forbidden Stories. The consortium interviewed more than 100 people affected by, or involved in, the US drive to extinguish unauthorised immigration, and reviewed documents outlining details of the agreements made by US officials with governments around the world.What are third-country deportations?The Trump administration has struck 35deals allowing it to deport migrants and asylum seekers to countries that are not their own and where they often have no connections.Human rights lawyers say the administration is using a loophole: under US law it is illegal to send people back to countries where they are likely to be persecuted, and so the Department of Homeland Security is deporting migrants and asylum seekers to third countries instead.In many cases, however, the receiving countries then deport them onwards to the very place they fled.Is this a new policy introduced by the Trump administration?While the Trump administration trialled the policy during its first term, most of the deals with foreign countries have been struck since 2025. The US has pledged at least $410m (£307m) to secure such agreements with 35 countries, almost a third of them in Africa, according to internal records reviewed by the Washington Post as part of the Deportation Project.The drive is being led by the White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, afervent opponentof most migration to the US. It is being run out of the newly created Office of Remigration, a new section within the Department of State’s Bureau of Population, Refugees and Migration. The name of the office incorporates a termadopted by the far rightto describe the forcible expulsion of minority ethnic immigrants.Who is being deported?About 20,000 people have been bussed to Mexico, while at least 5,000 more have been put on planes to countries in Latin America, Africa, central Asia and the Caribbean.The Trump administration says its deportation drive is focusing on removing criminals from the US. People interviewed by the Guardian for this project include a nurse, originally from Sierra Leone, who was her parents’ main carer in the US; an anti-government protester who fled the Iranian regime; and a gay man who fled Ghana after he was outed, and then hunted, by members of his family.The state department claims that its priority is to deport people with criminal histories, but people interviewed by the Guardian said they had none. Immigration judges had also ruled the people should be allowed to stay in the US because of credible fears they may face harm if sent home. And state department documents indicate that a majority of the 35 countries to have signed deals with the US have specified that they will not accept migrants with violent criminal records.Why would third countries agree to participate?While the fine print of most deals remains opaque, the Trump administration is paying millions of dollars to the 35 countries that have agreed to accept foreign migrants, either temporarily or long term.The state department is also using its foreign aid budget to sweeten the deals, allocating funds to UN agencies that support migrants in some of the third countries.The internal state department records, reviewed by the Washington Post, indicate $30m was earmarked for Cameroon, in order to support UN operations in the country, in return for accepting 1,000 migrants. The US has so far sent only 44. The Democratic Republic of the Congo was promised $50m towards UN operations there in return for accepting 2,000 migrants. It has only received 15, and flights to Kinshasa are on hold because of the country’s Ebola outbreak.A spokesperson for the UN agency that receives these funds, the UNHCR, said it supported “states in fulfilling their primary responsibility to protect refugees and asylum seekers on their territory by helping ensure that, irrespective of the circumstances of their arrival, they have access to asylum procedures and are not returned to places where they face a risk of harm”.chart showing Central African Republic has received the largest sum of payments from the US in deportation agreementsAre third-country deportations legal?A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that the Trump administration’s third-country removals policy was unlawful. A three-judge panel unanimously agreed that the policy violated due process by failing to give people enough notice of the decision to deport them, or the chance to legally contest it. Human rights lawyers said that meant third-country deportation flights should be grounded immediately. But the government has 90 days to appeal against the court’s decision, and is expected to do so. “The third country deportation policy continues,” James Percival, the Department of Homeland Security’s general counsel, said in a statement.The ruling relates to a March 2025 lawsuit arguing that the US was sending people to places where they could be hurt or killed. While a US district judge issued a preliminary injunction in April 2025, resulting in a pause on deportation flights,the supreme court decided two months later that the policy could resumewhile the legal case played out, and the administration then ramped up the flights.Get in touchContact our investigations teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailinvestigations.contact@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsUS immigrationDonald TrumpRefugeesMigrationHuman rightsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Trump administrationexplainersShareReuse this content

title: UK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fighters | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham seeks stability in Middle East to bring down prices at home as first meeting with Trump looms
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Andy Burnham seeks stability in Middle East to bring down prices at home as first meeting with Trump looms
Content: Inside the cockpit of an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft of the type that will help to refuel Saudi jets.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenInside the cockpit of an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft of the type that will help to refuel Saudi jets.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAAndy BurnhamUK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fightersAndy Burnham seeks stability in Middle East to bring down prices at home as first meeting with Trump loomsPippa CrerarPolitical editorMon 21 Sep 2026 17.33 EDTFirst published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK has agreed to provide defensive air support toSaudi Arabiato help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump.The prime minister said he had agreed to a request for air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets to defend energy infrastructure against the Iran-backed rebels and help keep oil flowing from the Gulf to ease global economic turmoil.Burnham also revealed he will use his first meeting with Trump on Tuesday to urge the US president to de-escalate the conflict in Iran, warning that “dark clouds of global instability” are directly affecting people’s lives all over the world.The turmoil in the Middle East has pushed up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and increasing government borrowing costs to multi-year highs just weeks before a crucial first budget for the new government.On the flight to theUnited Nationsin New York, Burnham told reporters that an RAF Voyager would help refuel Saudi jets for several weeks, in his first military deployment since taking power, after the Houthis advanced to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait.The key Gulf ally has used the waterway as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz. The RAF operational support is in addition to the UK Sky Sabre air defence system already operating.“We have received a request from Saudi Arabia for military support and … I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling. On cost of living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain, the wider region … we need to keep those pathways open,” Burnham said.The prime minister also plans to press Trump to wind down US action in Iran, which has destabilised the region, blocked key supply chains and unleashed global economic volatility, including in the UK, where the government will struggle to drive down the cost of living as a result.“Of course the message is that we want to see an end to the conflict as quickly as possible and we stand ready to play our part,” Burnham said when asked if he would raise the issue in talks with Trump.As well as the focus on the Middle East, other major international challenges, including the war in Ukraine and artificial intelligence, are expected to dominate Burnham’s meetings at the UN general assembly.The global security backdrop to the summit is bleak: European leaders have warned that Russia couldlaunch a drone or missile attack on Nato territory within monthsto test the strength of the alliance.Burnham’s speech to the UN is expected to focus on harnessing the power of AI, amid concerns at home over the safety of the rapidly advancing technology. He will be accompanied on the trip by his AI minister, Kanishka Narayan.The prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump is a significant moment, with the US president still said to be angry over the UK’s refusal to support his military action in Iran, and ongoing tensions over levels of defence spending.Burnham will attempt to highlight the importance of the security partnership after the UK and US launched a heavyweight torpedo, designed to sink ships and deep-diving submarines, in British waters last week from a Plymouth-made drone named Excalibur.Government insiders, however, are taking some solace from Trump’s low-key response to UKsanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, after weeks of diplomacy with the White House over the summer.They are also hoping to avoid a clash over energy policy. The prime minister is expected to signal to Trump that he is in favour of more drilling in the North Sea, including the Jackdaw gasfield that is likely to get the green light within weeks.Analysts believe the balance of risk for the bilateral relationship has shifted since Keir Starmer was in office, given the Republicans face a difficult set of midterm elections and the US president’s personal ratings are plummeting.Trump is also likely to be more focused on his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and his address to the UN, which comes shortly before the talks on Tuesday.Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would try to pursue a “third way” in his relationship with the US president, neither as adversarial as the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, nor as publicly fawning as Starmer’s early approach, and relying on the strength of his personality.Asked whether he felt he could trust Trump, Burnham said: “Yes, of course, we trust our allies. Of course, we do.” Pressed whether this applied to the US president personally, he repeated: “Yes.”Downing Street said the prime minister wanted to use his UN meetings – which will also include the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen – to “drive opportunity and deliver hope”, making progress on areas with the potential to deliver for people at home.Burnham has focused on domestic issues since his arrival in No 10, despite Starmer warning that it would be impossible to separate them from global affairs, given how the Ukraine war is weighing heavily on UK security and the Iran conflict on the economy.On the flight Burnham acknowledged they were inseparable. “[Starmer] was right to say it’s about how we deliver back at home and the situation in the Middle East is a very clear example of that. It is a very big driver of the cost of living pressures that we’re currently facing,” he said.Before the trip, Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “The British people at home are at the forefront of the prime minister’s mission in New York this week. Because to deliver at home, we must ensure we are leading international efforts to brighten a darkening global picture …“To give people the breathing space they need, he is clear we must work with our international partners to face up to the biggest challenges of our generation. So this week at [the UN general assembly] he will be leading the charge on the global issues that impact people’s lives at home.”Burnham will tell world leaders the UK will focus on AI and climate change when it hosts the G20 in Manchester next year, potentially causing ripples with Trump, who has previously criticised the UK’s stance on global warming.The meeting gives Burnham an opportunity, however, to host international allies on his home turf, although the location of the summit was chosen under the Starmer administration.Burnham has been accompanied on the trip by his wife, Marie-France van Heel, who No 10 said would be meeting her international counterparts and supporting the prime minister, whose father, Roy, died last week.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamDonald TrumpDefence policyMilitaryUnited NationsMiddle East and north AfricaHouthisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Martha’s rule to be expanded to every A&E in England | NHS | The Guardian
description: System gives patients, loved ones and health workers the right to ask for a second opinion on care
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: System gives patients, loved ones and health workers the right to ask for a second opinion on care
Content: The rule is named after Martha Mills, who died in 2021 from sepsis after a bicycle accident but, a coroner found, would probably have survived if she had been moved to an intensive care unit.View image in fullscreenThe rule is named after Martha Mills, who died in 2021 from sepsis after a bicycle accident but, a coroner found, would probably have survived if she had been moved to an intensive care unit.NHSMartha’s rule to be expanded to every A&E in EnglandSystem gives patients, loved ones and health workers the right to ask for a second opinion on careAndrew GregoryHealth editorMon 21 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMartha’s rule, which lets NHS patients, staff and relatives request a review of their care, is being expanded to every A&E inEngland, health officials have announced.The system gives patients, their loved ones and health workers the right to ask for a different medical team to examine the care being provided on inpatient wards and to recommend changes. It has already potentially saved hundreds of lives,official figures show.Now it will be rolled out to every emergency department in England, including waiting rooms, offering “a critical new lifeline” to improve care and save more lives,NHSEngland said.The system is named after Martha Mills, 13,who died in 2021from sepsis after a bicycle accident. A coroner found she would probably have survived if she had been moved to the intensive care unit at King’s College hospital in London when she began deteriorating.The initiative is the direct result of pressure put on politicians, NHS bosses and doctors after Martha’s parents, Merope Mills and Paul Laity,told the storyof what happened to their daughter, who would have turned 19 this month if she had lived.Mills, a senior editor at the Guardian, and Laity spent years campaigning forthe introduction of Martha’s rule, under which people can call a hospital-run helpline with their concerns and seek a “rapid review”.In the first 16 months of the scheme after its introduction in England in 2024, helplines received more than 10,000 calls, potentially saving 446 lives,figures show. Thousands of patients were either moved to intensive care, received drugs they needed or benefited from other changes as a direct result of the calls.In June this year, the initiative was expanded to every maternity and neonatal unit in England, giving women and parents the right to a second opinion about the care of a mother or baby.From this month, it will be expanded to A&E units. It means patients, loved ones and staff in busy emergency departments will be able to call a dedicated phone number to trigger an urgent review if a patient’s condition is deteriorating and they think their concerns are not being listened to.A phased rollout will be completed by March 2028, NHS England said. It follows a pilot in seven trusts which tested whether Martha’s rule could work safely in A&E.During the eight-month pilot, 69 calls were made, with some patients going on to have urgent surgery or being transferred to intensive care, NHS England said.Prof Aidan Fowler, director of patient safety at NHS England, said: “A&Es see some of our most vulnerable patients, so the ability to raise concerns about deterioration quickly and trigger a rapid review of care is essential.“Martha’s rule is already having a transformative effect in making our acute care even safer, and by expanding Martha’s rule into A&Es, we are giving even more patients, their families and NHS staff a critical new lifeline to help improve care and save more lives.“Early testing has shown that Martha’s rule can work well in busy A&Es and builds on the evidence from our adult and children’s wards, where thousands of calls have been made by patients, families and staff to date – with many leading to changes in treatment and potentially life-saving interventions.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMatthew Hopkins, acute and ambulance director at the NHS Alliance, which represents and supports the health and care system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said health bosses supported the move.“NHS leaders welcome the rollout of Martha’s rule to all hospital A&E departments and waiting rooms, following the initial pilot in seven trusts.“They support the initiative’s aim to give the most vulnerable patients, families and staff the chance to be heard and raise concerns.“This will enhance the safety of care and will provide reassurance for patients and their families if there are concerns that the patient’s condition is getting worse.”Gillian Merron, a health minister, said: “Martha’s rule is about making sure patients and their loved ones are heard when they raise concerns about their care.“Expanding it to A&E will give patients, families and staff another way to speak up when they are worried that someone’s condition is getting worse, ensuring concerns are acted on quickly. This is part of our wider efforts to put patient safety at the heart of the NHS.”The latest data for Martha’s rule calls, for July 2026, show the highest ever monthly total (1,678) since the system was introduced.Explore more on these topicsNHSEnglandHealthShareReuse this content

title: Trump set to press Zelenskyy at UN to agree energy ceasefire with Russia | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President to meet Ukrainian counterpart in New York as Ukraine steps up attacks on Russian energy sector
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: President to meet Ukrainian counterpart in New York as Ukraine steps up attacks on Russian energy sector
Content: Trump with Zelenskyy at the White House in October last year. The pair are expected to meet during a rare sitdown on the sidelines of the UN general assembly.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersView image in fullscreenTrump with Zelenskyy at the White House in October last year. The pair are expected to meet during a rare sitdown on the sidelines of the UN general assembly.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersDonald TrumpTrump set to press Zelenskyy at UN to agree energy ceasefire with RussiaPresident to meet Ukrainian counterpart in New York as Ukraine steps up attacks on Russian energy sectorAndrew Rothin WashingtonMon 21 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump is expected to press Ukrainian leaderVolodymyr Zelenskyyon an energy ceasefire during a face-to-face meeting this week during United Nations high-level week, as world diesel prices have soared due to the war in Iran, as well as Russia’s war in Ukraine.Ukraine stepped up its attacks on Russia’s energy sector over the weekend, launching its largest reported strike yet on the Moscow region in a barrage that struck a major Moscow oil refinery and killed three people.On Monday, Trump said the whole world was suffering due to an energy shortage that he said was being exacerbated by the war in Ukraine.“Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine,” Trump said in a Truths Social post on Monday morning. “A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission.”“This ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended,” Trump said. “The whole World suffers as 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are being killed each month. What a shame!”Trump had earlier blamed Kyiv for the escalating energy war even as Russia has decimated Ukraine’s economy and launched night barrages of drones and ballistic missiles against Ukrainian cities.Zelenskyy on Monday said negotiations were continuing and that that there are “ideas on the table for bringing peace closer, starting with strong de-escalation steps”.“Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part,” he said in a statement. “Solutions are possible.”The two leaders are expected to meet on Tuesday during a rare sitdown on the sidelines of the high-level week of the United Nations general assembly. Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov will also be in Washington this week, and is expected to meet with secretary of state Marco Rubio.During a trip to Ireland last week, Trump directly addressed Zelenskyy, saying he has to do “one thing: he has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia”.“Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage,” he said.Trump spoke with Zelenskyy on Sunday in a phone call that one senior Ukrainian official told the Financial Times was about “diesel, diesel, diesel”.Average diesel prices in the United States hit a record $6.50 per gallon on Monday, up from $3.19 per gallon this time last year before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran and Tehran responded by closing the Strait of Hormuz to most international trade. The rise in prices is seen as a liability for Trump’s Republican party in the US midterm elections, which will take place in November.Trump is expected to deliver a speech to the UN general assembly on Tuesday morning, and is expected to meet with major energy producers including the Gulf Cooperation Council and Venezuela’s recently installed leader Delcy Rodriguez.In a preview, Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, said Trump would speak about how he has “confronted complex problems head-on around the world. Many of the peace deals that he has driven to conclusion, or is in the process of driving to conclusion.”Trump last week prematurely announced an energy ceasefire under which Ukraine had agreed not to hit Russian energy targets and that “Russia has agreed to do likewise!” The deal had not been agreed, however, and Russian strikes against Ukrainian energy and other critical infrastructure have continued.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsVolodymyr ZelenskyyUkraineUS foreign policyShareReuse this content

title: ‘Jaw-dropping’ El Niño bursts through temperature record months before peak | El Niño southern oscillation | The Guardian
description: ‘Godzilla-level’ phenomenon is supercharging the climate crisis and will have a huge impact on communities across the world
Author: Damian Carrington
Headline: ‘Godzilla-level’ phenomenon is supercharging the climate crisis and will have a huge impact on communities across the world
Content: A firefighter at a wildfire in Ogan Ilir, Sumatra, Indonesia.Photograph: Mast Irham/EPAView image in fullscreenA firefighter at a wildfire in Ogan Ilir, Sumatra, Indonesia.Photograph: Mast Irham/EPAEl Niño southern oscillation‘Jaw-dropping’ El Niño bursts through temperature record months before peak‘Godzilla-level’ phenomenon is supercharging the climate crisis and will have a huge impact on communities across the worldDamian CarringtonEnvironment editorMon 21 Sep 2026 09.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe “jaw-dropping” El Niño currently heating up the planet has burst through the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon, several months before its expected peak.Thelatest datashows the temperature rise at the heart of El Niño in the Pacific Ocean has now reached 3.05C. That is higher than the 3.02C set in late November 2015, the previous high set in the 150 years of modern records. This temperature is measured against the average of 1991-2020.Thepreferred measureof most meteorologists uses a 30-year rolling average as a reference and so takes account of human-caused global heating. This metric, called ONI (Nino3.4), is on the brink of breaking the record, just one-hundredth of a degree below the 2015 record. Both metrics are underpinned by data from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).View image in fullscreenDamaged beachfront homes in Dana Point, California.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesThe most recent forecasts predict a peak of 4.0C in November and December, according to the average of 14 different models assessed by climate scientist Zeke Hausfather. That is a level so far above previous events that Hausfather called it “mind-blowing”, while others have described it as “Godzilla-level”. Any temperature rise above 0.5C is deemed an El Niño; above 2C is officially called a “very strong” El Niño – often referred to as a “super” El Niño.The current El Niño is likely to be the largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into an atmosphere in which temperatures are already rising rapidly due to human-caused global heating. This double whammy means 2027 is expected to “blow apart” previous records and become thehottest year ever recorded.The climate crisis, caused by pollution from fossil fuels, is alreadysuperchargingextreme weather andkilling people. The El Niño will ratchet up the impacts even further, and has already begun to affect regions across the planet as weather patterns are altered.View image in fullscreenThe Panamanian-flagged LPG tanker G. Spririt on the Panama canal.Photograph: AFP/Getty Images“Very strong El Niño events like those in 1997/1998 and 2015/2016 were associated with hundreds of billions of dollars in damages globally – this event is leaving those past ones in the dust,” said Hausfather, whose analysis ispublished by Carbon Brief.Prof Friederike Otto, at Imperial College London, said: “This event is a huge redistribution of energy in the climate system and is dangerous because it is unfolding on top of a much warmer, human-influenced climate system.“So, in many places around the world we will see never-before-experienced heat extremes, with all their consequences on health, food security and water stress,” she said. “El Niño comes and goes, but as long as we continue to burn fossil fuels it occurs on an increasingly hotter baseline, making it much more difficult for communities to deal with the consequences.”GraphHot and dry conditions in Indonesia have already spurredrecord wildfiresandfatal levels of air pollution, whileIndia has seen vital monsoon rainscurtailed. Drought conditions in Central America and the Caribbean are causingcrop lossesand a slowdown of trade due tolow water levels in the Panama canal. The World Food Programme said in August the impacts of El Niño were likely to push about 50 million peopleinto acute hungerand drive prices up.‘Forcing a reckoning’: How Asia is preparing for a ‘supersized’ El NiñoRead moreEl Niño years also see more intense rains and flooding in some regions, with Peru and Chile already suffering, and access to Machu Picchu is disrupted. The Horn of Africa is also very vulnerable to increased downpours, while the southern US is expected to experience fierce rains in the winter.The southern hemisphere summer is predicted to be hotter and drier as a result of the huge El Niño, meaning greater wildfire risk and droughts in Australia and southern Africa. Typhoons in the Pacific are expected to be more intense, but Atlantic hurricanes are suppressed by El Niño and, unusually,none has yet occurredthis year.While the usual impacts of El Niño are well known, scientists are concerned that the multiplying effect of the climate crisis could shift these patterns. This would make it harder for countries and communities to prepare. The UN World Meteorological Organization said it has launched the biggest mobilisation in its 50-year history to support national weather services to deliver “life-saving” forecasts.2:58Could ‘Godzilla’ El Niño bring the hottest year on record? – video explainer‘The physical toll is visceral’: How Indonesia’s fire haze affects millions - visual guideRead moreThe UN secretary-general António Guterres said earlier in September: “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather. The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people.”Inthe Guardian on Tuesdaymeanwhile, Prof Bill McGuire said: “What is happening in the equatorial Pacific is jaw-dropping and could well mark one of the biggest global weather upheavals in a millennium.“It will spawn a string of weather catastrophes around our world.”He said strong El Niños can have a devastating effect on the global economy: “While the great recession of 2008 resulted in global GDPreducing by around $2tn, the 1997–98 super El Niño resulted in losses of $5.7tn.” That El Niño has already been surpassed by the current one.Recent research showsglobal heating is now intensifying El Niño cycles, which then in turn intensify the impacts of the climate crisis. Data from analysis of corals, tree rings and historical documents suggest no El Niño has reached this level in the last millennium, added Hausfather.“All effects from El Niño are magnified by global climate change,” said Prof Kevin Trenberth, at the National Center of Atmospheric Research in the US. “The northern summer of excess heat and wildfires in Europe, North America and Asia are but a sample of what is to come.”Explore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationClimate crisisExtreme weatherClimate sciencenewsShareReuse this content

title: Halt super-intelligent AI with non-proliferation treaty, Ed Davey to say | Liberal Democrat conference | The Guardian
description: At Lib Dems’ conference in Brighton, leader will accuse Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and ‘tech bros’ to solve problem
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: At Lib Dems’ conference in Brighton, leader will accuse Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and ‘tech bros’ to solve problem
Content: Ed Davey on the beach at Brighton during the Lib Dems’ party conference, where he is expected to lay out plans for a new international AI safety agency.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEd Davey on the beach at Brighton during the Lib Dems’ party conference, where he is expected to lay out plans for a new international AI safety agency.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockLiberal Democrat conferenceHalt super-intelligent AI with non-proliferation treaty, Ed Davey to sayAt Lib Dems’ conference in Brighton, leader will accuse Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and ‘tech bros’ to solve problemAlexandra ToppingandPeter WalkerMon 21 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEd Davey is to call for a global nuclear-style non-proliferation treaty to halt the development of super-intelligent AI when he makes his keynote speech at theLiberal Democrat conference, accusing Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and “tech bros” to solve the problem.When he addresses the faithful on the final day of the gathering in Brighton, the party leader will call for a global pause on super-intelligent AI, comparing it to a nuclear arms race that could result in technology that could “destroy us all”.Davey is expected to lay out plans in his speech on Tuesday for a new international AI safety agency – modelled on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and headquartered in the UK, after numerous warnings from AI researchersthat artificial intelligence could wipe out humanitywithin the decade. “We didn’t leave the atom bomb to a few billionaires to police themselves,” he will say.Davey is expected to call for a new global movement to work together to protect humanity from the risks of super-intelligent AI, saying that the IAEA was built by nations “working together to control a technology that could destroy us all”, but warning that the future of AI is being decided by “a tiny number of the richest and most powerful in California and in Beijing” with no guardrails to slow down development.“As liberals – we know that something as existential as nuclear weapons or climate change cannot be left in the hands of a powerful few. And so it must be with AI. We can’t leave it to Mark Zuckerberg, to Sam Altman, or to Elon Musk to save us,” Davey will say.On Monday, the prime minister announced a new AI partnership with the US ahead of Trump’s address to the UN general assembly on Tuesday.But Davey will say the plan “doesn’t come close to meeting the scale of this threat” and “only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros”.It comes after the Lib Dems’ home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, on Monday announced thatthe party proposed a big tech levyand promised to create a new online crime agency focused on offences including child sexual abuse material, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and deepfake AI-generated pornographic images.Wilkinson said the Lib Dems would properly regulate use ofMeta’s smart glasses, which he called “perv goggles”, telling the conference that the glasses “are more than a benign piece of tech that provides a bit of fun” and that people – especially women – were being recorded without consent or warning. “This is becoming the new norm, because this government won’t stand up to big tech to protect our civil liberties,” he said.On Sunday Davey set out a proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period, as well as reducing the bus fare cap from £3 to £1 and other transport-related cost of living policies.View image in fullscreenEd Davey views the stands as he tours the exhibition hall during the conference in Brighton.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PADavey defended himself in a series of interviews on Monday about complaints his party lacks vision, saying it was pointless to try to compete with the attention-grabbing ideas of the likes of Reform UK and the Greens.“It’s a very noisy environment at the moment,” he told the BBC. “But let me tell you, some of the noise generated by the populists are things that divide our country, that are nasty, or that are just completely crazy. I don’t want to do that. I want to tell people that we have really well thought through policies that will cut their taxes.”Asked if he would propose further tax cuts in the wake of the pledge to slash 10p from fuel duty for three months, Davey replied: “Absolutely.” These would, he said, be financed by higher economic growth due to the Lib Dem proposal to seek entry to the EU’s single market.The Lib Dem leader did praise Burnham for wanting to reform adult social care, but told Sky News the “jury is out” on whether Burnham will deliver as prime minister. But Davey was positive about some of what Burnham has done.“I think it’s good when other parties start talking about Liberal Democrat priorities,” he said. “We have led the debate on social care and carers because it’s so important for our health service. We’ve led the debate on political change because we need to change our political system, and Mr Burnham seems to be up for that.”Explore more on these topicsLiberal Democrat conferenceLiberal DemocratsAI (artificial intelligence)Ed DaveyComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Young people’s Pip claims for ADHD and autism ‘rising fastest in affluent areas’ | Society | The Guardian
description: Experts say trend across England probably reflects swifter access to diagnoses as wealthier families go private
Author: Will Parman
Headline: Experts say trend across England probably reflects swifter access to diagnoses as wealthier families go private
Content: Obtaining a clinical diagnosis is likely to increase the chances of a successful Pip claim.Photograph: Johner RF/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenObtaining a clinical diagnosis is likely to increase the chances of a successful Pip claim.Photograph: Johner RF/Getty ImagesSocietyYoung people’s Pip claims for ADHD and autism ‘rising fastest in affluent areas’Experts say trend across England probably reflects swifter access to diagnoses as wealthier families go privatePatrick ButlerandWill ParmanMon 21 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome of the most affluent areas ofEnglandhave had the sharpest rises in the proportion of young people claiming disability benefits for ADHD and autism since the pandemic, according to new research.Claims for the personal independence payment (Pip) benefit for these health conditions were typically proportionally far higher in deprived areas with higher rates of poverty, low educational outcomes and insecure employment.However, the fastest growth in ADHD and autism-related Pip claims has been in some of the country’s most prosperous areas such as Wokingham, Warwick, and parts of Hampshire and Surrey.This trend probably reflects swifter access to ADHD and autism diagnoses in more affluent areas, say the researchers, in part highlighting the ability of wealthier families to skip longNHSwaiting lists and pay privately for clinical diagnoses.They say the relative gap in Pip claims between rich and poor areas is shrinking, with growth rates in wealthy places such as Runnymede in Surrey outstripping the likes of Blackpool and Stoke-on-Trent.The research also found that Pip claim rates for ADHD and autism were higher among white people than other ethnic groups. This was reflected in lower than expected claims in ethnically diverse areas such as Newham and Brent, in London, and Leicester.One of the sharpest rises was seen in leafy Surrey Heath (a 630% increase in Pip clams for autism and ADHD since 2019), while in contrast, the relatively deprived towns of Mansfield and Great Yarmouth saw 30% and 50% increases respectively.The researchers say this shift is counterintuitive and unique to ADHD and autism. There is no evidence of similar trends in learning disability, depression, anxiety or physical conditions. Records from GPs show higher rates of new ADHD diagnosis in relatively affluent areas.Sally Gainsbury, a senior policy analyst at the Nuffield Trust, which carried out the research, said the findings probably reflected “substantial inequality in access” to private and NHS diagnostic services, meaning “people with better resources and more support are often able to get to the front of the queue quicker”.It may also reflect the ability of more privileged individuals to navigate a notoriously difficult and unpredictable Pip claims process, Gainsbury said. Obtaining a clinical diagnosis is likely to increase the chances of a successful Pip claim.Pip is designed to help claimants with the extra costs of disability, such as energy, transport and food. It is not means-tested or linked to employment status and is paid to individuals whose condition impairs their ability to carry out everyday tasks.About 205,000 16- to 24-year-olds received Pip for disabilities linked to ADHD or autism in April this year, a more than threefold increase since 2019, at a cost in 2025-26 of £1.36bn. The average Pip claim for this cohort was £8,800 a year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPlan to limit NHS diagnoses of ADHD attacked as ‘rationing’ healthcareRead moreThe sharp rise in numbers of young people claiming Pip and other disability benefits, particularly since the pandemic, has been at the centre of a political debate about the sustainability of working-age disability benefits spending, which is forecast to rise from £14bn in 2019 to £34bn in 2030.The issue has become aculture war topic. Rightwing media and politicians have questioned the validity of Pip claims they say are the result of exaggerated mental health symptoms, and alleged overdiagnosis of neurodivergent conditions.The Nuffield Trust research comes in advance of a government-commissioned report on mental health, autism and ADHD diagnoses. It isexpected to recommenda “needs-based” system whereby overstretched NHS services target patients most acutely affected by ADHD, such as those who are at risk of self-harm or unable to work.Led by Prof Peter Fonagy, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst at University College London, the interim review published earlier this year concluded that the system forces children and adults to obtain a formal diagnosis in order to get support.Explore more on these topicsSocietyNeurodiversityAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderNHSAutismWelfareHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stop relying on AI chatbots for customer care, UK banks and energy firms told | Chatbots | The Guardian
description: Citizens Advice says providers of essential services such as energy, banking, phone and internet should guarantee the ‘right to talk to a human’
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Citizens Advice says providers of essential services such as energy, banking, phone and internet should guarantee the ‘right to talk to a human’
Content: Almost half of people who had to use a chatbot found them unhelpful with some concluding the chatbot seemed rigged to ‘make me give up’.Photograph: Alamy/PAView image in fullscreenAlmost half of people who had to use a chatbot found them unhelpful with some concluding the chatbot seemed rigged to ‘make me give up’.Photograph: Alamy/PAChatbotsStop relying on AI chatbots for customer care, UK banks and energy firms toldCitizens Advice says providers of essential services such as energy, banking, phone and internet should guarantee the ‘right to talk to a human’Robert BoothUK technology editorMon 21 Sep 2026 12.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStop relying on AI chatbots for customer care and guarantee the “right to talk to a human”, Citizens Advice has urged essential service providers, as research found they wasted time, caused stress and delayed problem solving for more than half of users.The spread of the AI-powered systems to provide help about the provision of vital services such as energy, banking, phones and internet, is making it harder for millions of already digitally excluded people to handle snags, according to the frontline charity that last year provided more than 2.7 million people with one-on-one help in England and Wales.The charity concluded that chatbots caused harm, saying too often they trapped humans in an “endless loop” in which nothing got resolved, and almost half of people who had to use a chatbot found them unhelpful, with some concluding the chatbot seemed rigged to “make me give up”.It called for service providers to respect a new right for customers to speak to a human after it investigated the wider impact of digital exclusion,estimatedto affect at least 14 million UK citizens. It uncovered slower and less reliable support for people who struggle with or have limited access to online systems and found the erosion of phone, face-to-face and paper communication had created a two-tier support system.“Going round in circles with a chatbot isn’t just annoying, it can be a blockade to essential services,” said Tom MacInnes, policy director at Citizens Advice. “We’ve seen organisations’ overreliance on chatbots and online forms leaving people unable to fix billing problems, sort out their debt or even access homelessness prevention services. There’s a role for chatbots, but the quiet erosion of face-to-face and telephone services is letting too many people fall through the cracks.”That erosion of traditional ways of communicating means that people without good digital access can face serious difficulties getting simple problems fixed. For example, the charity found that submitting energy meter readings to correct a wrong bill can take less than an hour online if systems are working properly. Without good digital access it takes as long as six weeks offline, putting people “at risk of further harm”. In some locations applying for low-cost social tariff broadband – itself intended to reduce digital exclusion – is being made harder by being digital only, Citizens Advice found after it took evidence from its frontline advisers and hundreds of case summaries.One adviser reported that when people struggled with digital-only applications for homelessness support they ended up “homeless for longer … they’re in danger … they’re losing money … they get into debt” and said: “It can ruin a lot of people’s lives.”The warnings come amid growing frustration with the proliferation of AI customer services. Online message boards with titles like: “I’m so sick of AI Customer ‘Support” Chat Bots” and “Has anyone ever actually had their problem solved by a company’s chatbot?” are filled with tales of woe. Several chronicle frustrated customers’ attempts to circumvent phone-based chatbots by repeatedly yelling “human!”.Only 20% of UK adults polled on behalf of Citizens Advice in July said chatbots were their preferred way to communicate, with phone calls, email and instant messaging all preferred.Gripes about other forms of digital exclusion include multifactor authentication, which requires rapid and dextrous manipulation of more than one device just to log in and time-limits to complete transactions.Of the people who found it difficult or not possible to talk to a human to resolve an issue with their essential services, 49% felt stress or frustration, 27% felt powerless, 44% experienced delays to resolution and 14% gave up trying to resolve the issue altogether.The UK government has previously said it is investing £11.9m in a digital inclusion innovation fund, supporting local projects to help people get online. About 1.7m households in the UK do not have a laptop, tablet or desktop computer.A government spokesperson said: “Businesses have a legal obligation to provide contact information in a manner which is clear and easily accessible.”Explore more on these topicsChatbotsUtilitiesBankingMobile phonesInternet, phones & broadbandConsumer affairsAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content
