title: ‘Half my day’s pay goes to filling up my car now’: diesel crisis ripples across Britain  | Petrol prices | The Guardian
description: Small traders and drivers bear the brunt of a refining shortage taking UK diesel towards £2 a litre as wars wipe out about a fifth of global supplies
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Small traders and drivers bear the brunt of a refining shortage taking UK diesel towards £2 a litre as wars wipe out about a fifth of global supplies
Content: A motorist refuels a vehicle with diesel fuel at an Esso petrol station in Lutterworth, near Rugby in central England.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA motorist refuels a vehicle with diesel fuel at an Esso petrol station in Lutterworth, near Rugby in central England.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesPetrol prices‘Half my day’s pay goes to filling up my car now’: diesel crisis ripples across BritainSmall traders and drivers bear the brunt of a refining shortage taking forecourt prices towards £2 a litre as wars wipe out about a fifth of global suppliesJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentMon 21 Sep 2026 12.29 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 18.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThesmoke rising from the Kapotnya oil refineryto the south-east of Moscow marks one of Ukraine’s biggest air raids on the Russian capital since the start of the war, and the latest salvo in an energy crisis that threatens to affect households and businesses across the globe.More than 1,500 miles away, British motorists are braced for the ripple effect from that conflict, and the US-Israel war on Iran. Average UK diesel prices are expected to reach record highs within days – while across Europeand the US, pump prices have already surpassed all-time highs.In a call on Sunday, Donald Trump pressed Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian refineries over concerns that the attacks were pushing up global fuel prices, the Financial Times reported. On Truth Social, TrumpsaidRussia has “unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry” and called for an end to “this ridiculous and never ending war”.View image in fullscreenRise in UK fuel prices have pushed the inflation rate to 3.1%. Above, a Texaco petrol station in Northwich, Cheshire, UK.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesWhile the price of Brent crude oil – which briefly fell below $100 a barel on Monday – remains in flux, already hard-pressed households and small firms face a far greater cost threat at forecourt pumps as the combined impact of Russia’s war-damaged refineries and the Middle East crisis has erased about a fifth of the world’s diesel supplies.“Around half my day’s pay goes to filling up my car now,” says Jon Barden, a former humanitarian adviser turned handyman, who says his fuel costs have doubled. His diesel Ford estate, once used for camping trips, is now used to carry heavy tools to jobs around Tottenham in north London.View image in fullscreenJonathan Barden, a handyman, says his fuel costs have doubled.Photograph: SuppliedAcross Britain’s forecourts, the average price of diesel has climbed by 54% to 196.28p a litre since the Middle East crisis began in late February. It is expected to reach a record £2 a litre within days, with some forecourts already charging above the psychologically important mark.In Europe, pump prices have already hit record highs in recent weeks,leading to unrest and growing callsfor government leaders to protect consumers from the surge in cost.While the popularity of fully electric and hybrid petrol vehicles may be on the rise in the UK and Europe amid attempts to move away from polluting fossil fuels, diesel remains the overwhelmingly dominant fuel. It is the single biggest cost for many independent traders and small business owners, powering transport, tools and services. It is also theeconomic lifeblood for farmers, and logistics and haulage businesses, layering costs on to grocery bills and consumer purchases.“I’ve had to put my prices up,” says Barden. “I don’t want to because the people around here don’t have a lot of money. But when fuel prices go up everything else follows. The things I need to buy from Wickes to do a job will cost more before I even fill up,” he says.In part, the surge in fuel prices is due to the rise in global oil prices following Iran’s effective blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital trade route for Gulf oil. The price of Brent crude has climbed to a four-year high, raising the cost of refined oil products such as diesel and gas oil.View image in fullscreenMotorists form a queue as they wait to refuel their cars at a Rosneft gas station in Moscow on July 3, 2026.Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/Getty ImagesYet the most pressing energy crisis is not a shortage of crude, but a shortage of the refining capacity to turn crude into the fuels consumers need. The Middle East crisis has severely damaged many of the region’s refineries, which once supplied 10% of the world’s fuels. What little can be produced has struggled to circumvent the blocked trade artery.Output from Russia’s war-damaged refineries has fallen by almost a third over the past year to reach a 20-year low following sustained drone attacks by Ukraine, according to the International Energy Agency. The latest strike on Kapotnya came after asimilar attackby Ukraine in June.Although Russian oil exports have been subject to toughened EU sanctions since 2022, a reduction in exports to other parts of the world,including Asia, is likely to push up global prices.In China, which hosts the world’s largest refining capacity, and had been the largest importer of Iranian crude, exports of refined oil products have been capped since March to safeguard the country’s domestic supply.The global refining slump has helped to keep oil market prices down by dampening the demand for crude. But this is cold comfort for economists who warn that the ‘crack spread’ – or the price difference between crude oil and its refined products – has climbed above $100 a barrel on the continent for the first time and is likely to rip through the economy by raising the cost of all transported goods, as well as household bills.View image in fullscreenA London Black Taxi refuels at a BP Plc petrol and refueling station in London.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesDiesel in particular is “the workhorse fuel that powers business, haulage, deliveries and rural communities”, according to Luke Bosdet, the AA spokesperson on fuel prices. “Increased fuel costs are passed on to customers, and then on to consumers, which adds to inflation.”While sales of new diesel passenger carshave plummeted over recent yearsas motorists increasingly opt for petrol, hybrids, and electric vehicles, the UK’s consumption of diesel has continued to climb because of its role as a crucial industrial fuel.UK diesel price chart“Almost everything on supermarket shelves got there on a lorry,” Richard Smith, the managing director of the Road Haulage Association said. “When diesel goes up that cost has nowhere to go but on to the price of goods.”The AA’s chief concern is for “small businesses, such as taxis and vehicle-based services, and rural communities who already do higher mileages even before diesel costs went through the roof”, Bosdet adds. “They don’t get to add diesel surcharges to invoices, like many of the big companies, for fear of losing customers.”Mehmet, from Clacton, began driving black cabs in central London 35 years ago. “When I first started, diesel cost 10 bob a gallon,” he laughs. In modern terms this would be 11p a litre, or a fraction of the looming £2 a litre average expected nationwide within days, while cab fares remain capped.Diesel taxis are easily outnumbered by EVs in London, but they still make up about a third of the black cabs. Drivers were told in February that they would be allowed to raise their fares by 4% this year. At the time, the rise was above inflation – amid concerns over an exodus of black cab drivers. However, the US-Israeli bombardment of Iran ignited a war that has caused fuel costs to surge and inflation to remain well above the Bank of England’s 2% target,at 3.1% last month.View image in fullscreenSmoke rises from an oil refinery following a Ukrainian drone strike in Moscow, Russia, on 20 September.Photograph: Reuters“We’re stuck with it,” says Mehmet. “We don’t want the meter price to go up, because then we lose custom. But we can see oil companies making billions in profit while we take home less. How can that be right?”The UK may be acutely exposed to the global squeeze on road fuel supplies. The number of refineries in the UK has dwindled since the start of the century from nine to four, causing the UK’s reliance on diesel imports to climb from 14% of the UK’s diesel consumption in the early 2000s to 54% last year, according to Fuels Industry UK.Elizabeth de Jong, chief executive of Fuel Industry UK, said: “Our latest annual statistics, published earlier this week, show that UK demand for petroleum products increased by 1% in 2025 to almost 61m tonnes, while the closure of the Grangemouth and Lindsey refineries reduced UK refining capacity by almost a quarter.“We are currently having to import about 55% of our road diesel, meaning a growing dependence on overseas supply. Global events such as the conflict in the Middle East demonstrate the vital role that UK refineries play and why they are crucial to our economy,” she said.Explore more on these topicsPetrol pricesOilCommoditiesMotoringUK cost of living crisisUS-Israel war on IranConsumer affairsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Awaab’s law is not working, say social housing tenants stuck in mouldy homes | Social housing | The Guardian
description: Residents say new legislation in England forcing landlords to fix dangerous hazards is not improving conditions
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: Residents say new legislation in England forcing landlords to fix dangerous hazards is not improving conditions
Content: Sarah Killick claims her landlord has done nothing to address the root causes of the damp in her home.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSarah Killick claims her landlord has done nothing to address the root causes of the damp in her home.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianSocial housingAwaab’s law is not working, say social housing tenants stuck in mouldy homesResidents say new legislation in England forcing landlords to fix dangerous hazards is not improving conditionsJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentMon 21 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSarah Killick has been battling problems in her social home for months, including mould and damp. She says the anxiety has been insufferable and she has permanently damaged her teeth from grinding them due to stress.She thought help would come in the form of Awaab’s law,new legislation designed to force social housing landlords in England to fix dangerous hazards, which came into effect in October last year.But it did not. Killick said her landlord, ClarionHousingAssociation – the largest social housing provider in the UK – sent contractors to do a mould wash, but claimed they did nothing to address the root causes of the damp. This was despite surveys showing outside cracks, as well as guttering and drainage problems that could be contributing to the issue.“We have to leave the mould on the walls, because if they turn up and we’ve wiped it, they say there’s no mould, so you have to start the process again. You have to leave the mould growing until it’s really furry and it’s awful,” she said.The housing ombudsman has just concluded maladministration and service failure on the part of Clarion in Killick’s case, and said the landlord “did not recognise that it failed in its duty to fully comply with Awaab’s law”. Clarion said it did not agree with the ombudsman’s conclusion and would appeal against the decision.View image in fullscreenA section of wall in Killick’s home. Clarion has been ordered to pay her £1,175 in compensation.Social housing residents living in homes managed by a number of providers, as well as campaigners, have raised concerns that Awaab’s lawis not working and people are still stuck living in mouldy, damp and dangerous homes.The law was named in memory oftwo-year-old Awaab Ishak, who died in December 2020 from a severe respiratory condition caused by prolonged exposure to black mould in his family’s social housing flat.Suzanne Muna, a co-founder of the Social Housing Action Campaign (SHAC), said that while Awaab’s law had introduced timelines for hazards to be fixed, it was difficult for tenants to enforce this.If landlords do not adhere to the law, tenants can take them to court for breach of contract, and the housing ombudsman can publicly name noncompliant landlords, order apologies, repairs and compensation.But Muna said many tenants struggled to navigate the complexities of court action, especially when up against housing associations with a team of solicitors.“We haven’t really seen any improvement, because it’s no easier now for people to enforce their legal rights than it was prior to Awaab’s law,” said Muna. “The law says landlords have to make things fit for human habitation within these timescales, but it did nothing to address the enforcement gap.”She believes some landlords would rather pay compensation than spend potentially larger amounts of money on repairs to make properties compliant with Awaab’s law.In Killick’s case, Clarion was ordered to pay her £1,175 in compensation, provide a formal written apology, and complete the full repairs by 9 November. If it does not do so, it must explain to the ombudsman why.“I just don’t think it’s going to happen, it’ll have to go to court,” said Killick, who is a full-time carer for her disabled son and also struggles with mental health issues.View image in fullscreenKillick stands in her garden next to cement that is cracking due to a void underneath.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianClarion claimed that Killick had repeatedly denied it access to the property. The ombudsman found that Killick’s temporary refusal to allow access contributed to delays, but there was no evidence “the landlord took steps to obtain access to complete any of the other outstanding repairs”.The ombudsman said that, as of 15 July 2026, it had received more than 400 cases where Awaab’s law was relevant, and there was a finding of maladministration in 97% of completed cases.Damp, mould and fungal growth accounted for the largest number of cases, and the most common failings were not realising that Awaab’s law applied, failure to investigate emergency hazards within the set timeframe, and not keeping records.Complaints to the ombudsman take an average of nine to 12 months to be resolved, although its interim head, Andrea Keenoy, has said the organisation is working hard to reduce the backlog, including hiring 77 new case workers.Muna said it was hearing multiple reports of landlords doing minor fixes, such as applying mould washes and mould-resistant paint, to meet Awaab’s law deadlines but failing to stop problems recurring.“People are still having to throw out clothes, worrying about the impact on their children – all of the things that were happening before are still happening,” she said. “Landlords might do things a bit quicker now, but that’s no comfort if they’re not solving the problem.”Khayriya*, a single mother with five children living in Sheffield, has struggled with serious problems in her council home for years, including living without a working shower and toilet.She said the mould and damp in the property was so severe that she believed it led her children to become ill with respiratory conditions, and addedthat they were bullied at school because of hygiene issues caused by the faulty shower.View image in fullscreenThe bathroom in Khayriya’s house. She says the mould and damp in her property led her children to become ill with respiratory issues.Even after Awaab’s law came into effect, she said it took months for problems to be addressed. Local campaigners at the community union Acorn confronted Sheffield council’s housing policy committee chair at a Green party event in July to spur them into action.Repair work then took place, but Khayriya said she was concerned mould had just been painted over in some places.“Awaab’s law doesn’t feel like it’s made any difference yet,” she said. “[Landlords] have still got the money, the power, the responsibility, but there’s not enough accountability. Tenants still need more protection.”A spokesperson for Clarion said: “Resident safety is our top priority, and we take all reports of damp, mould and repairs needed within properties seriously. We are sorry that Ms Killick has been experiencing issues with her home and have been working hard to provide a resolution.“Over the last nine months, five senior colleagues have been focused on Ms Killick’s case with a dedicated single point of contact liaising with her to try to resolve her concerns. We have attempted to make multiple appointments with Ms Killick to complete works, and have repeatedly been refused access. We have also paid for an independent survey and facilitated an inspection by the local authority’s environmental health team when she remained dissatisfied with our assessments.“Whilst we acknowledge that Ms Killick remains dissatisfied we do not agree with the ombudsman’s recent determination and will be taking up our right to appeal this decision. We remain confident we have complied fully with Awaab’s law, and have tried to provide a range of options for third-party support to allow Ms Killick to be confident in the safety of the approach that we are taking.”A government spokesperson said: “Everyone has a right to a safe and secure home, free of damp and mould, and it is completely unacceptable for any social landlord to ignore fixing these issues.“If social landlords fail to meet the proper safety and quality standards for their property, they can face strong punishments including an unlimited fine, and Awaab’s law aims to further empower social tenants to hold their landlords to account using the full force of the law if they fail to investigate and fix hazards on time.“We’re ensuring that these rogue landlords cannot dodge their legal responsibilities by working with councils to ensure they know how to enforce Awaab’slaw, and investing up to £50m to modernise courts so that it’s simpler to hold landlords accountable.”Sheffield city council has been contacted for comment.* Name has been changed for anonymity.Explore more on these topicsSocial housingHousingCommunitiesLocal governmentEnglandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Celia Birtwell ‘humanises’ Burberry in London fashion week closing show | London fashion week | The Guardian
description: Textile designer brings florals, vines and smiley doodles to brand’s luxury checks for one-off paired collection
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Textile designer brings florals, vines and smiley doodles to brand’s luxury checks for one-off paired collection
Content: Models showing leafy prints in the Burberry meets Birtwell spring-summer 2027 collection.Photograph: Katie Collins/ReutersView image in fullscreenModels showing leafy prints in the Burberry meets Birtwell spring-summer 2027 collection.Photograph: Katie Collins/ReutersLondon fashion weekCelia Birtwell ‘humanises’ Burberry in London fashion week closing showTextile designer brings florals, vines and smiley doodles to brand’s luxury checks for one-off paired collectionJess Cartner-MorleyMon 21 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 18.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBurberry and Celia Birtwell are both national treasures of sorts. One is Britain’s grandest luxury name, the other the textile designer who dressed bohemian 1960s London in her prints and has a place in art history as David Hockney’s favourite muse.Burberry’s designer, Daniel Lee, has always loved Birtwell’s prints. When the two met this spring, he fell for “her energy, and her zest for life”, and a one-off Burberry meets Birtwell collection that closedLondon fashion weekwas born.Burberry’s calling card is a graphic check; Birtwell is all blowsy doodled florals and psychedelic snaking vines. “The check is so dominant and so brilliant that at first I thought: what can I do here?” Birtwell said before the show. She hand-painted a less regimented version, which Lee loved. “She made the check more human. If you are buying a luxury product it’s not a necessity, it’s an emotional purchase, so it needs to feel human.” A doodle of round, Smartie-bright faces from her archive, drawn 20 years ago but never produced, became another print of the season.View image in fullscreenCelia Birtwell’s doodled smiley faces on Burberry’s spring-summer 2027 collection.Photograph: Katie Collins/ReutersThe mood of the show, held around the corner from Burberry HQ at Chelsea School of Art, was buoyant: charming prints, soft silhouettes, and the eclectic guest list that is as much a Burberry signature as the check itself: actor Fiona Shaw and footballer Djed Spence on the front row, with rapper Central Cee making a cameo on the catwalk.Burberry isbouncing backfromits crisis years, steered by its chief executive,Joshua Schulman, and designer Lee. This summer, the brand reported its first revenue growth in three years, as retail sales rose 5% year-on-year in the second quarter. Schulman’s strategy is offering “value for money in a luxury context”, which translates as pivoting from an ill-fated attempt to sell Burberry handbags at Hermès prices to more realistic price tags. Lee has brought a youthful, gen Z inflection to the Britishness that is Burberry’s calling card.View image in fullscreenCoats and more at the Burberry show.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAA successful element of its turnaround has been Burberry zeroing in on the outerwear market, where Burberry has bona fides to best every other name. British heritage is a trump card when it comes to coats, and the appeal of the Burberry name reaches from arctic explorers to football fans. For this summer collection, trenches came in slinky silk taffeta, with puffball hems and ruched collars; one model carried an embroidered umbrella, against summer showers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo amplify itsLondonfashion week message, Burberry is staging a small display in an upstairs gallery of the V&A museum in South Kensington, which will be open to the public until 3 January. The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon includes a military overcoat worn by a lieutenant colonel in the British army in 1939, designer Hardy Amies’ own Burberry trench, as well as metallic leather and gold snakeskin runway trenches from recent catwalk shows.Explore more on these topicsLondon fashion weekBurberryFashion weeksFashion industryWomen's coats and jacketsLondonLuxury goods sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Being in Madness kept some of them out of jail’: how the baggy-trousered nutty boys made a guerrilla cinema classic | Madness | The Guardian
description: From a jail-inspired light sabre fight to the moment a sax-player flew, Take It or Leave It brilliantly captured the band’s grimy origins. Will the film’s return see it finally honoured as a music movie landmark?
Author: Stevie Chick
Headline: From a jail-inspired light sabre fight to the moment a sax-player flew, Take It or Leave It brilliantly captured the band’s grimy origins. Will the film’s return see it finally honoured as a music movie landmark?
Content: ‘Like kids at school showing off’ … Madness filming the music video for Our House in 1982.Photograph: Clare Muller/RedfernsView image in fullscreen‘Like kids at school showing off’ … Madness filming the music video for Our House in 1982.Photograph: Clare Muller/RedfernsMadness‘Being in Madness kept some of them out of jail’: how the baggy-trousered nutty boys made a guerrilla cinema classicFrom a jail-inspired light sabre fight to the moment a sax-player flew, Take It or Leave It brilliantly captured the hit-makers’ grimy origins. Will the film’s return see it finally honoured as a music movie landmark?Stevie ChickMon 21 Sep 2026 09.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 15.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s March 1981 andMadnessare revisiting the haunts of their recent youth with a film crew in tow. In the 18 months since releasing their debut single, The Prince, the group have become the UK’s most beloved hit-makers, their ascent abetted by inventive music videos that have left viewers of Top of the Pops and Tiswas believing a man could fly – while blowing a sax.But this new project is something else. Instead of squandering their newfound wealth on fast cars and country piles, the seven-piece have invested in a semi-fictional big-screen telling of their origin story that tempers their trademark “nuttiness” with a kitchen-sink realism suiting their working-class roots. While Take It or Leave It sank into obscurity soon after release, a new 4K restoration has primed the film for rediscovery as a time-capsule of grimy 70s London, and perhaps cinema’s most honest depiction of the challenges involved in trying to get a band together.The movie was the brainchild of Dave Robinson, honcho of Stiff Records. Back in 1979, Robinson triumphed in the bidding war for Madness, then in their late teens and early 20s. “There was a special connection,” the charismatic Dublin-born mogul says today. “To them I was ‘Uncle Dave’.”View image in fullscreenAll naturals … Madness filming Take It or Leave It in 1981.Photograph: BFIRobinson recognised Madness as more than just prodigiously talented musicians and songwriters. “We were these different characters, jumping around and clowning about, like kids at school showing off,” says keyboardist Mike Barson. “Dave encouraged that.” Uncle Dave intuited this energy would flourish in the embryonic music-video format, hiring Chuck Statler – who’d made memorable clips forDevoand worked quick and cheap – to film Madness’s first promos. Dave took over the reins for 1980’s My Girl, working even quicker and cheaper. “I was also running a record label,” he says, “so we’d have to get the videos done in a day.”But Robinson never compromised his youthful charges’ imaginative approach. Saxophonist Lee Thompson tested the label-owner’s impressive ability to “make things happen” with 1980’s Baggy Trousers. “I told Robbo I wanted to play sax while flying through the air,” says Thompson, who arrived at the shoot to find Robinson had booked a forklift and kirby wire. The resulting stunt became part of the group’s iconography.double quotation markTracking shots were filmed by a cameraman in a trolley or on a bicycleWhen Robinson began work on Take It or Leave It, he says, “people told me it couldn’t be done, that we were mad”. He tapped the band members and manager John “Kelloggs” Kalinowski for £20,000 each (“the price of a fuckin’ two-bedroom in NW5 back then”, says Thompson), covering the rest of the budget himself. “I had planned to shoot it in a week,” he says. But when Robinson arrived on set the first day he was greeted by “50 guys staring at me, eating bacon sandwiches”. Unlike the videos, the movie was “a unionised shoot”, and Robinson sensed this crew would slow him down. “I had to get rid of them. I paid them all off and they never turned up again.”Crew purged, he returned to his “typical smash-and-grab, guerrilla-film-making methods”. Frontman Graham “Suggs” McPherson remembers tracking shots being filmed “by a cameraman in a trolley or on a bicycle”; overhead shots involved “someone hanging off a stepladder”. Robinson rarely sought permission to shoot locations, guitarist Chris Foreman describing their mindset as “do it quick enough and they can’t tell you to stop. By the time some jobsworth comes along, you’ve already finished.” It was a vibe they’d learned as teenage delinquent graffiti artists.Unsurprisingly, Madness took care of the soundtrack, covering Elvis Presley and Fats Domino tracks – often poorly, on purpose, to suggest the roughness of their first incarnations – and performing their own songs during scenes replicating early gigs. They also cut new songs such as Don’t Look Back, a funk track heard during a party scene, and co-wrote the script – what there was of it.View image in fullscreenDelinquent graffiti artists … the film’s smash-and-grab guerrilla-film-making methods harked back to the bands teenage years in Camden.Photograph: BFIBefore production began, Robinson interviewed the group about their early days, boiling his research down to 30 scenes that told the Madness story. On set, the band members would ad-lib these scenes with “great older actors” Robinson had hired to play authority figures. His cast were, he says, “all naturals”. McPherson remembers Robinson screening “Kes, Bronco Bullfrog, Mean Streets and some British kitchen-sink dramas, to get that vibe of just being ourselves”. He also took them to see Raging Bull, Thompson adds, which was “an eye-opener: black and white, grainy, gritty,real. Dave wanted that as our inspiration.”Realism was paramount. Robinson filmed scenes where they’d actually happened: shabby rehearsal rooms; legendary Camden hostelry The Dublin Castle; the Crouch End home of Mike Barson’s mum, where the group first formed. “Dave used cameramen who’d worked on documentaries,” says bassist Mark Bedford, “and the film was close to a documentary – most things had really happened.”“We’d done all these psychedelic videos,” McPherson adds, “but our aim now was to capture the dreary reality of forming a band.” The first 20 minutes of the movie are in black and white, he says, “because Londonfeltfuckin’ black and white in the late 70s”. There’s little of the manic visual invention of their music videos, although a set-piece where Thompson drives a van into a low bridge during brief, ill-fated employment on a building site is a masterpiece of comic pacing. A plan for the streets to turn into marshmallow after a wild night out was nixed due to budget – and a worry this family-friendly band shouldn’t let on that some members enjoyed psychedelics.Nevertheless, Take It or Leave It is a very funny film, much of its comedy coming from Barson. “Mike had a role he could sink his teeth into: the bad guy,” says Foreman. As the sardonic ringleader of this unruly circus, he excoriates band members for bum notes, bad attitudes and, in McPherson’s case, ditching rehearsal to go see his beloved Chelsea FC. Barson’s abrasive manner, which Bedford says was “slightly exaggerated” for the film, sees off McPherson, Thompson and vocalist/trumpeter Cathal Smyth for brief periods, although everyone agrees that without Barson’s “doggedness”, the band would never have made it. “Mike was the engine,” says Bedford.View image in fullscreen‘It’s clear the youthful Madness aren’t Brit School graduates’ … an image from Dave Robinson’s private collection.Photograph: Dave RobinsonThroughout, there is a sense that this beloved pop-cultural institution might easily have never happened, for all the everyday, low-drama reasons so many bands implode: internal ructions, the interminable juggle of creative ambitions and real-life responsibilities – and the eternal struggle to find a decent drummer. When the lineup finally coalesces and the artists formerly known as the North London Invaders rehearse as Madness for the first time, it makes for electrifying cinema.Not least because of the stakes at play. Throughout the film, it’s clear the youthful Madness aren’t Brit School graduates or posh kids slumming it before taking a job at daddy’s firm. Thompson can’t get saxophone lessons because his horn is stolen and its serial number has been rubbed off. Suggs’ chronic truancy and misbehaviour solicit the unwelcome attention of social services, looking to remove him from his mum’s care. One gig ends with an ambush by skinheads in the toilets, the band narrowly escaping a clobbering in their Morris Minors.On the commentary track for an earlier DVD release, Robinson said: “The system didn’t know what to do with young lads who weren’t nasty but were just trying to have a laugh.” Today, he reckons “being in Madness kept some of these lads out of jail”. The film reveals an edge that wasn’t obvious while the group was clowning with Tiswas’s Phantom Flan Flinger, but surfaced on grittier songs like Embarrassment, Overdone and Not Home Today.“I was at a crossroads,” nods Thompson, whose dad had been in prison multiple times. He remembers wondering, “‘Do I stick with the band, or hang around the bus stop sniffing glue?’ The pal who got me my saxophone, he was later stabbed to death in the Music Machine.”Barson’s crossroads moment is depicted in the film, although it’s played as fantasy, he and friend Si Birdsall discovering neon tube-lights, wielding them like light-sabres and evading the coppers. In reality, they actually got caught smashing lightbulbs by transport police and were sentenced to three weeks at Wormwood Scrubs. En route to prison, his police van passed Buckingham Palace, and he saw the bus he used to ride into central London.View image in fullscreenAt a crossroads … the light-sabre scene was inspired by Barson’s arrest and imprisonment for smashing neon lights.Photograph: BFI“I thought, ‘If I was free, I could get on that bus, go home and make myself a cup of tea. But now I’m wondering if they’re going to strip-search us and hose us with disinfectant when we get there.’ I was scared. After that, I pulled back from hanging out with them kids who were into wild, aggressive things and put that energy into music. Years later, in 2012, we played on the roof of Buckingham Palace and the queen waved up at us.”“We were all on a spectrum of petty criminality, growing up in an environment of violence,” says McPherson, “though none of us had that thing where you’ve been beaten into wanting to hurt other people. There was a crossroads where some in our gang were definitely going criminal, and we were the artistic side of that coin. Criminality boils down to: are you prepared to shoot someone? And no, I’m not. I don’t think I had the guts for it. The band was our way out.”Ultimately, the shoot took longer than a week: memories vary, but somewhere between a fortnight and a month. Robinson broke his foot midway through but says: “At the end, we all clapped each other on the back and said, ‘We got away with it!’ We were thinking it’d go on the art film circuit. But it played in one cinema in Camden and that was it. We didn’t get a big campaign from the distributor, which it needed.”Although the Guardian’s Derek Malcolm gave the film a positive review, and a VHS release sold well to the Madness faithful, Take It or Leave It was quickly forgotten. A couple of years later, after theirguest appearances on The Young Ones, that show’s creatives, Ben Elton and Richard Curtis,filmed a pilotfor a proposed Madness sitcom. “The premise was that we ran Britain and had to solve some big problem every week,” remembers Foreman. “ITV were interested, but we were holding out for the BBC. Then Mike left the group, so it came to nothing.”‘We met Princess Margaret and she was paralytic!’ My wild life onboard the Adam and the Ants Antmania rollercoasterRead moreLater, McPherson auditioned for Julien Temple’s Absolute Beginners, but broke his big toe while training with the choreographer. “So that was the beginning and the end of my film career,” he sighs, though he doesn’t really sound very disappointed. “Madness was always my priority,” he explains, “and I’m so glad. If I’d gone into acting, I’d never have achieved everything I did with the band. You can’t have it all.”While he never made another film, Robinson is still active, organising benefit concerts for the children of Ukraine. Madness released their 12th album in 2023 and recently completed a summer tour. The restoration has them reflecting on their movie, and the passage of time. For Barson, four-and-a-half decades have caused reality and near-reality to blur. “When I try to remember what really happened, I get stuck on how it happened in the film,” he says. “The reality has become inaccessible because that film gets in the way.”The film is now a time capsule for a bygone age: the band comment longingly on machines on the tube selling 40p tickets and the ability to park your car wherever you wanted. Other memories are more heartfelt. “Gary Dovey, who was briefly our drummer and played himself in the film, was a good friend of mine,” says Bedford. “He died a few years ago, and it’s amazing to see him on screen, speaking and being himself.”“I was so disappointed with the film when we finished it,” adds McPherson. “I thought it was prosaic and boring. But now – it’s just so charming. We were friends, most of us, before the band started, and we are good friends now. To see our story up on screen makes me very proud. I love those guys. I fuckinglovethem.”Take It or Leave It is in UK and Irish cinemas from 1 October, and on Blu-ray/DVD from 19 October.Explore more on these topicsMadnessSkaPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Shackling prisoners giving birth should be a last resort – but it’s happening around Australia anyway | Prisons | The Guardian
description: Senator Lidia Thorpe has introduced a bill to prohibit the practice in Australian prisons that advocates say violates the human rights of both mother and child
Author: Tory Shepherd
Headline: Senator Lidia Thorpe has introduced a bill to prohibit the practice in Australian prisons that advocates say violates the human rights of both mother and child
Content: Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian DesignPrisonsShackling prisoners giving birth should be a last resort – but it’s happening around Australia anywaySenator Lidia Thorpe has introduced a bill to prohibit the practice in Australian prisons that advocates say violates the human rights of both mother and childGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastTory ShepherdMon 21 Sep 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 18.01 EDTShare“She was pregnant with twins,” Tahlia Isaac says. “She was meant to be released in 10 days, but she went into labour early.”Isaac says officers handcuffed her fellow prisoner in the back of a van and took her away.In her submission to a federal inquiry into shackling during childbirth, she says many woman who have experienced it “still think about the time they gave birth to their child cuffed to the bed, years later”.“They weep when they describe wanting to cradle their newborn child but only had one available hand to do so,” says Isaac, the founder of Project:herSELF, a not-for-profit supporting formerly incarcerated women.Lidia Thorpe, the Gunnai, Gunditjmara and Djab Wurrung woman and independent senator for Victoria, has introduced a private member’s bill to prohibit shackling during childbirth.“No one giving birth is at risk of running away,” Thorpe said in her second reading of the bill. “Anyone who has given birth would agree that to be shackled whilst giving birth would be an incredibly violent and terrifying act.”There is a patchwork of state and territory laws that state shackling should only be used as a “last resort” or only when “absolutely necessary”, but critics – and Thorpe – say it’s happening anyway.Shackled, alone and scared: the grim reality for women forced to give birth in prisonRead more“People are cuffed to their hospital bed by an arm and a leg in the delivery room, their legs shackled together by a chain,” Thorpe said.As well as helping women who’ve gone through it, Isaac witnessed it herself when she was in prison. She says the woman who was taken away in the prison van was separated from her child and sent straight back.“I just remember hearing her scream, just wailing and wailing. I think every woman in that centre was left horrified,” she says.View image in fullscreenSuzzane Calgaret (centre) and Mincarlie Calgaret (right), sister and niece respectively of Heather Calgaret, who died in custody.Photograph: James Ross/AAPOn Wednesday, Thorpe told the Senate about Heather Calgaret, a Yamatji, Noongar, Wongi and Pitjantjatjara woman, and mother of four children.In 2019, she gave birth while shackled to a hospital bed in Victoria.Days after the birth, Calgaret’s baby was removed, a decision her family saidwould have “crushed” her, and her health deteriorated after that.“In November 2021, Heather died in custody after being administered a high dose of buprenorphine, a drug used to treat opioid addiction. She had no history of opiate use,” Thorpe told the Senate.“Heather should still be here with us today.“Her life was precious and her passing was preventable.”A teenage mother died in a Melbourne prison yard just days after leaving youth detention. A coroner is examining whyRead moreIn 2025, the coroner found the removal of her daughterwas “pivotal” to Calgaret’s death.According to an August report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, about one in 10 of Australia’s prisoners are women.According to the parliamentary library, between 5% and 10% of women in prison are pregnant, and at least half have a history of mental illness or childhood abuse.Almost half the female prisoners identify as Indigenous.The only data on giving birth while incarcerated was from 2017, when 25 women gave birth.Fifteen years ago, the UN general assembly adopted theBangkok Ruleson the treatment of female prisoners, which state that prison should be a last resort for pregnant women and that “instruments of restraint shall never be used on women during labour, during birth and immediately after birth”.The rules were adopted unanimously by the general assembly. But around the world, they areregularly flouted.The National Justice Project told the inquiry into Thorpe’s bill that shackling someone during labour and childbirth was “not a grey area”.“It is a clear breach of settled human rights standards and violates the rights of two people at once: the mother giving birth and the child being born,” the organisation said in its submission.View image in fullscreenIndependent senator Lidia Thorpe has introduced a private member’s bill to prohibit shackling during childbirth.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPThe Australian College of Midwives has said it was also against theMandela rules for the treatment of prisonersand shackling was “an unsafe and unnecessary practice that may result in adverse outcomes for women and newborns, perinatal mental ill-health”.The National Network of Incarcerated and Formerly IncarceratedWomenand Girls tells the story of Yannetty*, who was six months pregnant when she was handcuffed and shackled and transported in 40C heat for a medical appointment in 2013 or 2014.She said she was hot, swollen, frightened of fainting, and frightened for her baby.“I was not treated like a pregnant woman going to receive medical care. I felt like I was being treated as though I was something dangerous that needed to be bound,” she said.The chief executive of Sisters Inside, Debbie Kilroy, said shackling during childbirth was “state violence inflicted at the moment a person is most physically vulnerable and in need of care”.“Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women will be disproportionately exposed to this violence because they are disproportionately targeted, criminalised and imprisoned. The practice sits within a much longer colonial history of controlling First Nations women, separating families and denying Aboriginal mothers’ authority over their own bodies and children,” she said.The Guiding Principles for Corrections in Australiasay “instruments of restraint are not used on prisoners … during and immediately following childbirth”.The same is true for other significant medical conditions, the guidelines say, “unless an individualised assessment identifies a compelling safety risk that cannot be managed by other available means”.In the ACT, restraints are a “last resort”, and only to be used on a pregnant detainee when “all other efforts have failed”, according to the parliamentary library. In NSW, pregnant prisoners “must not be restrained unless it is absolutely necessary”.Other states and territories have similar caveats.If passed, the bill would override those exemptions.Amelia* only found out she was pregnant when she was strip-searched and put through a scanner once she got to prison. She was cuffed for all her ultrasound appointments, and struggled to roll into the right position because of the handcuffs.Officials had drawn up her birthing plan, telling her she would be cuffed during labour. She was told she could have a support person with her – then they clarified it would be a prison officer, but she could nominate them.In the end, she got out about 10 weeks before giving birth.“The birth, anyway, was traumatic because I’m so scared of needles,” she said.She was in labour for four days, had three failed epidurals, and got pre-eclampsia.“Imagine that with cuffs. I do think about it. It’s ridiculous,” she said.“I’m glad I got to do it the way I did.”In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. International helplines can be found atbefrienders.org* Names have been changed

title: Get tested and talk to your partner: how to have safer sex after age 50 | Well actually | The Guardian
description: At 51, I want many more years of a healthy, happy sex life. So I decided to compile my own guide
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: At 51, I want many more years of a healthy, happy sex life. So I decided to compile my own guide
Content: It’s important for people in their 50s and beyond to think about safer sex practices – not least because they are having more sex than ever.Photograph: Glasshouse Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIt’s important for people in their 50s and beyond to think about safer sex practices – not least because they are having more sex than ever.Photograph: Glasshouse Images/Getty ImagesWell actuallyGet tested and talk to your partner: how to have safer sex after age 50At 51, I want many more years of a healthy, happy sex life. So I decided to compile my own guideAmanda Zuckerman KlarsfeldMon 21 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I got divorced after 28 years of monogamy, I was excited to be having sex again, but had concerns. I was 48, and the last time I’d been single was in the 90s; terrified of pregnancy and hyperconscious of HIV/Aids, I hadn’t considered condomless intercourse an option back then.Now, at 51, I’ve been wondering how important barrier protection is for me. Though I haven’t hit menopause, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)says that“by 45 getting pregnant naturally is unlikely”, and HIV/Aids prevention and treatment have improved significantly in the last three decades.When I consulted with my physician, she said I should still “be careful” but didn’t provide specific guidelines.Frustrated, I started researching. I found books on safer sex for older adults, such asNever Too Late: Your Guide to Safer Sex after 60by Dr Shannon Dowler. But I wanted something more concise, like the pamphlets we saw as teens. I want many more years of a healthy, happy sex life. So I decided to compile my own guide, with expert advice about how to have safer sex as an older adult.Do older adults need to worry about safer sex?No sex is totally risk-free – at any age. This reality is reflected in the American Medical Association (AMA) using the term “safer sex” since the mid-90s, rather than “safe sex”.So it’s certainly important for people in their 50s and beyond to think about safer sex practices – not least because they are having more sex than ever.“People are living longer,” said Dr Tyler Evans, infectious disease physician and CEO of the public health organization Wellness Equity Alliance. If you add sex-enabling factors like dating apps for older adults and medical advancements in sexual longevity, you get a more sexualized older population, he said.It’s true that pregnancy becomes far less of a concern at this stage. During the years leading up to menopause, a woman’s fertility steadily diminishes. After menopause, which happens at 51 on average, according to the ACOG, natural conception is no longer possible.But sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are another matter. “While STI rates have stabilized in younger people, the rates for 55 and up are increasing,” said Dr Sarah Berg, a board-certified OB-GYN, Menopause Society-certified practitioner, and founder of Selfority, a menopause education platform. “The chlamydia rate for this age group has more than tripled the past decade, gonorrhea has gone up sixfold and syphilis has increased even more.”I’m a sex educator. Here’s what you should know about sexual incompatibilityRead more(A quick note: the term STD, or sexually transmitted disease, used to be common. Educators and healthcare providers consider “STI”a less stigmatizing term.)Older adults can contract the same STIs younger people can. But they mayoverlook infections, as symptoms can be mistaken for those of other age-related conditions like menopause, arthritis or urinary tract infections. As a result, people may delay treatment, causing STIs to fester.An age-related immune system decline can also make STIs more severe. “As adults age, their ability to mount a response to any microbial load decreases,” said Evans.“A sexually transmitted infection might increase your risk for mortality,” said Dr Renee J Flores, professor of medicine at the McGovern medical school of UTHealth Houston and a certified sexual counselor and educator, “but only if left untreated.” She emphasized that communicating with partners, using barrier protection and testing regularly can significantly decrease risk.Why are STI rates climbing in people aged 55and older?There’s a straightforward reason: more sex in the over-55 population has not coincided with an increase in preventive measures.This is partly because of a lack of information. “Many didn’t have sex education in school,” said Dr Janie Steckenrider, associate professor at Loyola Marymount University whose teaching and research focuses on gerontology, ageing and sexuality. “They don’t know the risks or the symptoms.”There’s also a misconception among sexually active older adults that their partners aren’t sexually active. “They don’t see a need to screen,” said Flores. “They think they are the rare ones having sex, though they may be having unprotected sex with multiple partners.”Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, 'Well Actually', then 'Read more on living a good life in a complex world,' then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say 'More from this section'Online dating has also contributed to increased sexual activity with less social vetting. “It’s not like you’re dating the person you grew up with or who went to your church,” explained Steckenrider. “Somebody that you’re meeting on a dating app – you get whatever information they’re willing to tell you, and a lot of people don’t feel comfortable asking.”Further, general practitioner often assume older people are not sexually active and often have “little to no medical training on sexual health and ageing”, Steckenrider said. “You fill out a questionnaire about your bowel movements and whether you havefallen, but there’s nothing about whether you’re engaging in unprotected sex.” A geriatric doctor or geriatrician may be more likely to ask or raise sexual health than a GP, said Steckenrider.It sometimes falls to the patient to bring up the subject. Steckenrider referenced aUniversity of Michigan studythat found only 17% of older adults had discussed sexual issues with their doctor in the last two years – and in 60% of those discussions, the patient initiated it.How do I have safer sex as an older adult?Get tested regularly:The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s STItesting recommendationsvary depending on age, sexual history, sexual practices, location and symptoms. If you’re over 50 and sexually active, your doctor may not recommend regular testing. “Bring it up if they don’t bring it up,” said Berg.If you and a partner want to stop using barrier protection, “get tested together before you stop using condoms, not after”, Berg added. “And know that some infections take weeks, occasionally months, to show up on a test, so one clean result on day one isn’t the finish line.”Communicate with partners:“It’s important to ask questions if you plan to get intimate with another person,” said Steckenrider. “This needs to be talked about beforehand – not in the moment.”She gave some examples: have you had unprotected sex in the last six months? How many partners have you had in the last six months, including oral sex and any kind of intercourse?Use barrier protection:According to the CDC,condomsprovide the highest level of protection against fluid-based STIs, though they only offer partial protection against those that can spread via skin-to-skin contact.Dental damsand condoms can be used during oral sex.Take prophylactic medications and get vaccines:Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV is available as a daily pill or long-acting injection. After a suspected exposure to HIV, PEP is “very effective” if taken within 72 hours,according tothe National Institutes of Health.The HPV vaccine is FDA-approved up to age 45.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAvoid sex when STI symptoms are present:Planned Parenthood recommends avoiding sexual contact, even with a condom, duringactive herpes outbreaksor when you have visiblesyphilis soresorgenital warts.How are STIs transmitted?Fluid-based infections, includingchlamydia,gonorrheaandHIV, are transmitted when infected bodily fluids (such as vaginal fluid, semen, rectal fluid or blood) come into contact with mucous membranes, according to the CDC. They can also enter the bloodstream during vaginal, anal or oral sex.STIs that spread through the blood might present a higher risk for post-menopausal women as “vaginal dryness at this age can cause bleeding, increasing the risk of sexually transmitting infections, particularly viruses”, said Evans.Infections likesyphilis,genital herpesandHPVspread primarily through direct skin-to-skin or mucous-membrane contact; fluids need not be exchanged. Transmission can occur even when an infected partner has no visible symptoms.What does STI testing entail?It depends – on whether you have symptoms or whether you are getting routine testing, and what you’re testing for.Your doctor can administer a standard STI panel via urine samples or blood draws. The makeup of the panel may differ depending on your doctor or lab – common tests include chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis and HIV. Check with your doctor if you’re not sure what’s included.For women in or beyond menopause, it is important to remain up to date with cervical cancer screenings with Pap testing, HPV testing or both. This is because they may see an unexpected rise in HPV either due to new infection or the reactivation of an old one, according to theNIH.After being dumped at 58, I realized I was not equipped for the griefRead moreGenital herpes (HSV) testing is recommendedby the CDCfor individuals with active symptoms, such as genital sores, or who know they have been exposed. It is not always included in a standard STI panel, so you may need to request it specifically.You can also request a swab in certain circumstances. “Swabbing is actually best practice for some anatomical sites,” Evans said, specifying that if you suspect vaginal, anal or oral exposure to gonorrhea or chlamydia, a swab may be more sensitive than a urine test is. You should also ask to have any active herpes or syphilis lesions swabbed; lesion swabs may detect these two infections before they show up in the bloodstream.Genital warts from HPV infection are typically diagnosed visually, rather than swabbed, per theCDC.HepatitisA,BandCcan all be passed by sexual contact, although the latter israre. The CDC recommends that adults be screened for both hepatitis B and C at least once in their lifetime, but hepatitis A testing is not recommended forasymptomatic people. Many older adults may be vaccinated againstAandB, but there is no vaccine forhepatitis C.What are common STI symptoms?STIs can result in many symptoms, perthe Mayo Clinic. For instance:Burning with urination, unusual discharge, pain with sex and testicular pain are common signs of both chlamydia and gonorrhea.Gonorrhea may cause spotting between periods (premenopausal women) or spotting (post-menopausal women).Syphilis may present as a firm, round and painless sore at the site of infection.Genital herpes can cause painful fluid-filled blisters and flu-like symptoms if it’s your first outbreak.HPV is typically symptomless but can eventually cause genital warts or precancerous cell changes.HIV often causes a temporary flu-like illness within two to four weeks of exposure, according to theNIH. Because HIV symptoms can be nonspecific and clinicians may not consider HIV in older patients, infection maybe diagnosed late, perHIV.gov.Many STIs can be asymptomatic, according tothe Mayo Clinic; for instance, chlamydia in women is commonly asymptomatic. This is why getting your and your partner’s test results before engaging in unprotected sex is important.Is there any good news?Prevention and testing have improved significantly in the past three decades.Many STIs are highly manageable and often curable if treated early.Gonorrhea, chlamydiaandsyphilisare treatable with antibiotics. For viral STIs, early intervention is very effective, according to the CDC:antiretroviral therapy(ART) for HIV makes the virus untransmittable once undetectable,suppressive therapycan reduce the transmission of genital herpes and earlyscreening for HPVallows infected individuals to remove precancerous cells before they become cancer.“There are risks, but the good news is there are a lot of prevention and treatment options,” said Evans. “The most important thing is to get educated, to become informed and talk to your medical provider.”Amanda Zuckerman Klarsfeld is a freelance writer in New York CityExplore more on these topicsWell actuallySexAgeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘My whole identity was wrapped up in Ally McBeal’ – Calista Flockhart on her smash hit 90s comedy rollercoaster | Television | The Guardian
description: ‘In the street or at restaurants, people still come up to me and say, “I became a lawyer because of you.” But I just went to work and said my lines!’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘In the street or at restaurants, people still come up to me and say, “I became a lawyer because of you.” But I just went to work and said my lines!’
Content: ‘When I moved to LA, I was too scared to get on the freeway for a year’ … Calista Flockhart with Jesse L Martin in season one of Ally McBeal.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘When I moved to LA, I was too scared to get on the freeway for a year’ … Calista Flockhart with Jesse L Martin in season one of Ally McBeal.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/Everett/ShutterstockHow we madeTelevision‘My whole identity was wrapped up in Ally McBeal’ – Calista Flockhart on her smash hit 90s comedy rollercoaster‘In the street or at restaurants, people still come up to me and say, “I became a lawyer because of you.” But I just went to work and said my lines!’Interviews by Lee CampbellMon 21 Sep 2026 08.12 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 18.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCalista Flockhart, played Ally McBealI was doing a play in New York, Three Sisters by Chekhov. We regularly got scripts sent to us. One going around was written by David E Kelley. I flew out to Los Angeles to screen test, and I got the part right in the moment. It was a difficult transition as I felt very much settled and happy in New York and I had only been to LA briefly, to shoot The Birdcage. I was such a bad driver that I didn’t get on the freeway there for a year. I was afraid of it.Playing Ally McBeal was exciting and I was up for the challenge, but it was daunting. It was also very collaborative. Everybody fed each other and we all worked it out together. We started shooting in July and were on air in September, so there was this beautiful brief time when it was just ours. I remember that very well. Then, very quickly, it became popular.David is a genius. What I love about his writing is his imagination – there’s no ceiling on it. At first, I thought the dancing baby was really weird. David was so excited about it but I really did not get it. Then, of course, I realised it was quite brilliant. Ally’s biological clock is ticking, and she’s being haunted by some weird, spooky dancing baby. It’s awesome. By nature, I’m a little on the shy side, so I had to find a place in myself to forget about being embarrassed. I just danced crazy and wild because it was sort of reflective of Ally’s inner life.double quotation markWhen Al Green guest starred I had the good fortune of dancing with him. It was magicalIn one episode – Seeing Green – I was having hallucinations ofAl Green. He guest-starred and I had the good fortune of dancing with him. It was filmed very late at night, with rain on the street, and it was so magical. He showed Ally the moves and I tried to do them. Then he flew away and Ally was left standing there alone. It was beautifully written. He is such a kind, sweet soul.In terms of the music, I wouldn’t even say that it was part of the show – the musicwasthe show. The minute you heard Searchin’ My Soul, you wanted to live in this life. I really identified with Vonda Shepard’s music and it was very reflective of what Ally was feeling. It was a way for characters to communicate with each other.At the end of most days shooting, I was emotionally raw – I was pretty much there all day, every day. I was just so totally spent from the rollercoaster of Ally McBeal’s life and where I had to go to get there. In the end, after five seasons, it had sort of run its course and done what it set out to do, but my whole identity was wrapped up in Ally McBeal for five years. My son was about one then and I was really happy to have the time with him, but it was sad to say goodbye to everybody. There’s such a strong bond between us that will never go, even though our lives have gone in many, many different directions.Sometimes at a restaurant or on the street, people come up to me and say: “I became a lawyer because of you.” Then I say: “No, you became a lawyer because of David Kelley.” It had nothing to do with me. I just went to work and said the lines. He had the hard job.Vonda Shepard,musicianI had made two albums, but then I got dropped. I was struggling. I was lugging my keyboard to gigs in the rain, playing in tiny clubs. I have been friends with Michelle Pfeiffer since I was 18, before she was married to David Kelley. The two of them came to see me play one evening, which turned out to be the turning point of my life.About a week later, I got a call from David. The songs that I was playing were from my albumIt’s Good, Eveand they resonated with the character he was writing about, he told me. David wanted me to singTell Him by the Excitersas the theme song, but my manager and I really wanted one of my own songs. So, we played them five of them, including Searchin’ My Soul, and David said: “If you can squeeze that song into one minute, that can be the theme song.” So, we just sped it up and they loved it.‘Such a water-cooler show!’ Jane Krakowski on Ally McBeal – and life as the world’s biggest scene-stealerRead moreOvernight, I went from playing for 30 people to 5,000 people. We won a Golden Globe, we won an Emmy. It changed my life. But I don’t care about being famous – I just want to be able to play music for people who like it and share that with them, and the show gave me that gift.I went on to produce more than 500 songs during its five years. It was more like a musical. It was very fulfilling, watching the music come together. When I was 16, one of my favourite albums was The Belle Album by Al Green. At the end of one track, he laughs. It’s so solidly locked into my memory. We were in the studio with him recording his vocals for an episode and all of a sudden, Al Green sings a take, and he does the laugh. I thought, “Oh, my God, I’ve really made it.”Searchin’ My Soul had the struggle and the challenge and then the breakthrough of the positive ending, the uplifting side of it. The show was a magical experience. I think back on it with such appreciation. You feel that connection and emotion, and it’s genuine.Vonda Shepardtoursthe UKand Irelandfrom 1 October. Her new album,Nine Songs, is out on25 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTelevisionHow we madeDramaTV comedyAl GreenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Britain loves its underdogs. We should be celebrating our Eurovision flops, not investigating them | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: The digital, culture, media and sport select committee is to explore why the UK’s entrants are frequently ‘dismal’. Surely such a trifling matter is not worthy of the House of Commons, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The digital, culture, media and sport select committee is to explore why the UK’s entrants are frequently ‘dismal’. Surely such a trifling matter is not worthy of the House of Commons, writes Zoe Williams
Content: Best of Britain … Sam Battle, AKA Look Mum No Computer, at Eurovision 2026.Photograph: Radek Miča/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBest of Britain … Sam Battle, AKA Look Mum No Computer, at Eurovision 2026.Photograph: Radek Miča/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionEurovisionBritain loves its underdogs. We should be celebrating our Eurovision flops, not investigating themZoe WilliamsThe digital, culture, media and sport select committee is to explore why the UK’s entrants are frequently ‘dismal’. Surely such a trifling matter is not worthy of the House of CommonsMon 21 Sep 2026 12.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTShareThe State of Play inquiry, which is run by the UK House of Commons’ digital, culture, media and sport select committee, recently announced the five areas on which it will focus in 2026-27. One of these is: why are our Eurovision entries so bad? The word used by the chair, Dame Caroline Dinenage,was “dismal”, which is parliamentary speak for “shit”.The evidence is all around. With the exceptions ofSam Ryder(second in 2022) and Jade Ewen (fifth in 2009), the UK has bumped along the bottom of the table in recent years, coming last in 2021 and 2026, second last in 2023 and 19th and 18th in 2025 and 2024 respectively. In four of those cases, the artist received no public votes at all.Mindful that parliamentary inquiries always take roughly 10 times longer than seems reasonable and cost whatever number of pounds they ought to multiplied by a million, I’m going to suggest a couple of sub-categories. Why do all the other countries hate us, irrespective of the entry?And why do we seem to enjoy it so much that they do? Some of this is about core British values and some of it is about geopolitical orientation. Sometimes those things interact in such a white-hot and contradictory way that it’s amazing no one has devised a way to give us minus points.A national underdog fetish drives the selection. Whomever we send, they cannot take themselves too seriously; they have to be self-mocking. But that’s not enough: they have to be so absurd that they can’t generate the level of ridicule required alone. Our entry this year – by Sam Battle, AKALook Mum No Computer– was no less catchy and flamboyant than many Scandinavian entries past, but some combination of trying too hard for the laugh (which was knowing and ironic) and trying too hard to speak German (“look, Mum, I – a Briton – can count to three in a foreign language”) did not translate into popularity. While we love an underdog, we also hate sincerity, which presents confusingly. Come on, Britain, do you think you’re inferior or superior? Make your mind up!Our refusal to pick a lane on this matter is another core British value. But however you articulate that – a love of ambiguity for its own sake? A reflexive, historical rebellion against being asked to emote sincerely? – other people don’t like it. Ryder is an interesting counterpoint. He slipped through the net by which we typically exclude anyone who can hold a tune, having garnered fame on the socials with his acoustic balladeering during Covid. The year in which he competed, 2022, was the tail end of a poignant time during which we briefly admitted to the experience of real feeling – loved each other, loved the NHS, loved society. That didn’t last, unfortunately.Leaving aside the music, the UK is often awardednul pointsto signal disapproval of its foreign policy. This seemingly began in 2003, because we had jettisoned European values (looking for evidence, considering consequences) in favour of American ones (going to war because, heck, we could). In 2008, our next brush with the dreadful zero, bestowed by 38 of the 42 voting countries, the objection was to the “big four” – the UK, Germany, France and Spain – getting automatic entry into the final stage of the contest.Eurovisionwas being used to symbolise the arrogance of these dominant countries after the financial crash. (No, I don’t have to prove that. It’s obvious.)I want to say that the more recent low scores may be down to Brexit, but that would raise the question of why we did so badly in the years directly before it (17th in 2014 and 24th in 2015). It may just be collective muscle memory: “Hey, I remember these guys! They’re the ones we always givenul points.”If I were involved in Eurovision, I would put together a counterinquiry to ask why the digital, culture, media and sport committee is so dismal. Alongside the cultural crises worthy of its attention this year – the structure of the football academy system, the role and funding of arts centres, the protection of journalists in conflict zones and inclusion in football management – it has chosen this matter of no consequence, this trifle, this contest we actuallyenjoybeing bad at. It has managed to produce the inquiry equivalent of one of the UK’s Eurovision entries, which is, now I think about it, quite a British thing to do.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
