title: The hill I will die on: Private karaoke is the death of socialism – only a pub singalong is good enough for the people | Kelli Blanchett | The Guardian
description: Community, camaraderie, connection: I learned about all these things while hosting pub karaoke nights. Sticky private booths are their absolute antithesis, says freelance writer Kelli Blanchett
Author: Kelli Blanchett
Headline: Community, camaraderie, connection: I learned about all these things while hosting pub karaoke nights. Sticky private booths are their absolute antithesis, says freelance writer Kelli Blanchett
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onClass issuesThe hill I will die on: Private karaoke is the death of socialism – only a pub singalong is good enough for the peopleKelli BlanchettCommunity, camaraderie, connection: I learned about all these things while hosting pub karaoke nights. Sticky private booths are their absolute antithesisMon 21 Sep 2026 09.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTShareOn a gloomy Wednesday evening, my best friend and I decided we wanted to scratch our singing itch. We searched for a pub that was hosting karaoke but couldn’t find anything in our area. So we headed to the local branch of a well-known private-booth karaoke bar instead. But it wasn’t just the astounding £18 per hour (per person!) charge or the poor sound quality that made the whole experience so profoundly sad.Private karaoke booths are sticky little cubicles for people who like singing but don’t want to be seen. They’re places where you pay a premium to avoid rubbing shoulders with strangers or making new connections. The whole point is to avoid exposure to the real world, which fundamentally misunderstands the power of karaoke.I grew up in a former steel town. Twice a week, my mum hosted karaoke at a local pub, and because we couldn’t afford a babysitter, my sister and I went with her. When Mum’s caring responsibilities for my dad increased, she passed on the mantle to me, aged 17, to earn a bit of cash and keep the family business alive. Sitting with strangers across generations, hearing the stories behind their song choices, sharing rounds of drinks and political opinions, I felt like a sponge, soaking up different walks of life.This is why when I talk about karaoke I’m not picturing these private, pay-by-the-hour cells. I’m thinking about the working-class pubs and clubs of Britain, where coming face to face with your community was more than half the point.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: Games are the opposite of fun, and I’d ban them for anyone over 12 | Emily WatkinsRead morePub karaoke is social cohesion in action. The root of socialism is to be supportive of your fellow man, to uphold them and work collectively. Whiletraditional performance art is often expensive, formal and ringfenced by wealth, private education and elite tastes, karaoke was always for the people.The death of these spaces alongside the rise in private-hire karaoke booths is denying us this cohesion. Unionism was born in the pub – collective thinking comes from being with people, exchanging ideas and belting out the classics. When you hear a plumber from Kettering sing Careless Whisper by George Michael, an angel gains its wings. When an audience comes together to support a person they don’t know, the seeds of collectivism are sown.We all crave connection, and this can’t be achieved in the cramped confinement of a beer-drenched booth in front of a tiny, curated audience of people we already know. Don’t succumb to the isolationism these corporations are foisting on us – instead, let’s get back to the pub, hand in hand, singing Sweet Caroline and hyping up our fellow strangers.Kelli Blanchett is a freelance writer, disabled activist and musicianExplore more on these topicsClass issuesThe hill I will die onSocialismcommentShareReuse this content

title: If you really hate it when music and film stars do politics, here’s the answer: give us politics that works | Nesrine Malik | The Guardian
description: The problem is not famous people speaking out, as they always have. It is the feeling that leaders have failed, obliging celebrities to fill the vacuum, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: The problem is not famous people speaking out, as they always have. It is the feeling that leaders have failed, obliging celebrities to fill the vacuum, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Content: Ed Sheeran performing at the O2 Arena in London on 6 December 2025.Photograph: Matt Crossick/Shutterstock for GlobalView image in fullscreenEd Sheeran performing at the O2 Arena in London on 6 December 2025.Photograph: Matt Crossick/Shutterstock for GlobalOpinionActivismIf you really hate it when music and film stars do politics, here’s the answer: give us politics that worksNesrine MalikThe problem is not famous people speaking out, as they always have. It is the feeling that leaders have failed, obliging celebrities to fill the vacuumMon 21 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 06.29 EDTShareEvery time a public figure in entertainment speaks up about politics in a way deemed “controversial”, it is as if it’s the first time that has ever happened. The outrage is fresh; critics rediscover and announce, as if they have just captured an elusive, profound notion, that art should be separate from politics. A form of disciplining is dispensed. Please, Mr or Miss Moneybags, with your preening notions that you have anything intelligent or informed to say aboutimmigration policyor Palestine. Stick to football. Stick to pop music. Stick to acting. Stick to children’s shows.Even at a time when a political moment has engulfed everything, this response continues to be born again, without regard for history or ability to confront rupture. The horror of Gaza hasbroken the art world, roiledHollywood,fractured literary institutions. And still, as Ed Sheeran stands alone on stage following the withdrawal of all his support acts (in solidarity with Macklemore, who was removed from the tour due to a pro-Palestinian speech), he told his audience that he wants his music to be “about unity, not division”. The speed at which his tour unravelled is not evidence of the incompatibility of music and politics, necessitating that they remain separate to avoid that “division”. It is a study in how it is becoming increasingly unnatural to separate them.View image in fullscreenEd Sheeran delivers a speech to his fans after support acts pulled out of his tour.Photograph: Ed Sheeran InstagramAgain, this is not new. The enmeshment of entertainment and politics is organic and part of many conflicts and political outrages in recent memory. Vietnam, South Africa, Darfur – all had a cohort of celebrities involved in objecting, lobbying and raising awareness. Figures such as Macklemore orGary LinekerorMark RuffaloorMs Rachelare not breaking with convention and plunging industries into turmoil and controversy, but partaking in a long legacy of activism that includes, to name a few, Nina Simone,Donald Sutherland,Kurt Vonnegut,Marlon Brando, Mia Farrow,George Michaeland George Clooney.You can disagree with the stances they have taken. But the belief that they are somehow not qualified to take and express them, and that art and entertainment are sacrosanct, is ignorant at best, disingenuous at worst. Public figures are people who have the same passions that everybody else has, and they have politics that they wish to advance with the tools at their disposal. Some people go on protests, give money, write to their representatives; others have a public forum and a profile they can leverage.They don’t have a responsibility to do so, but absolutely have the right to. And I suspect the reason they are met with such belittlement and outrage by their opponents is that there is an understanding that once politics spills over into entertainment, an uncontainable sort of trouble starts. This is where the separation of art and politics becomes a denial of the role the former plays in our psyches. Artists, writers, entertainers and sportspeople provide escapism, yes, if that’s what you want to get out of their work, but they also channel an expansiveness of the soul. They are fundamentally a collectivising force, one trained on a talent that stirs feeling. That is why you pick up a book or listen to a song or watch a movie or follow a team, to feel something. It is an exercise in being human, often in communion with others.View image in fullscreenMarlon Brando marches with members of the Congress of Racial Equality to protest an all-white housing area in Torrance, California on 1 January 1963.Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann ArchiveOnce politics enters that relationship, it becomes ungovernable. It can move the parameters of public opinion and discourse in ways that are hard to mediate, so direct is the relationship between the artists and their audience. Which is why the main criterion that renders this activism laudable or not is how much it is blessed by political and economic establishments.Often it is not a problem in itself; sometimes it is even rewarded. Sheeran himselfheadlineda concert for Ukraine. Don Cheadle and George Clooney receivedaccoladesfor their Sudan activism. But when artists’ politics clashes with powerful sponsors, as it did when Gillette Stadium owner Robert KraftremovedMacklemore from the Sheeran lineup, it all becomes less straightforward, so complicated, so bedevilled by nuance that could not possibly be litigated adequately by dilettantes.These collisions are an automatic feature of societies in which politics is failing. The outrage in Palestine is roiling culture because it has been so smothered in politics, because the pain and fury resulting from what the world is witnessing has not been appropriately channelled or responded to by a representative leadership – in fact, it has beenpoliced and criminalised. The spillover into every other part of our lives is inevitable. A healthy political culture should view these spillovers not as crude transgressions into private spaces of consumption, but democracy by other means, because electoral democracy has not squared up to the task.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs long as that remains the case, any demands that politics stay out of – you can insert any industry here – are summoning a world that does not exist, cannot exist and has never existed. In fact, they are asking for a sort of bovine state in which we are shepherded from trough to trough, chewing for momentary satiation on a cultural diet that must remain disconnected from feeling, connection and relation to other human beings. This can be a resonant message in a world in which there is so much duress. But it is an entirely unnatural state that keeps being disrupted by many people looking up from their moments of apportioned relief to be confronted with suffering of such magnitude that its acceptance can only be achieved through a sort of excising of humanity.The problem is not the outspoken artists and entertainers; the problem is what they are speaking about. I wish that the enduring agony of Palestinians were not litigated by the sound and fury and discursive froth of high entertainment, but this is where the politics has brought us. If you want to leave politics out of it, then demand that the politics do the work. Until then, it will be in your music and literature and film, fighting the coercion and bullying that hides behind concern for purity of art, but is really in the business of making you lose your soul.Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsActivismOpinionEd SheeranMacklemoreIsrael-Gaza warCelebritycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Washington press corps needs to boycott White House events  | Margaret Sullivan | The Guardian
description: CNN, MS Now and Politico accurately call last week’s sudden lockout ‘a direct assault on the first amendment’. That’s right
Author: Margaret Sullivan
Headline: CNN, MS Now and Politico accurately call last week’s sudden lockout ‘a direct assault on the first amendment’. That’s right
Content: ‘The White House press corps often talks a good game about solidarity and press rights.’Photograph: Andrew Leyden/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘The White House press corps often talks a good game about solidarity and press rights.’Photograph: Andrew Leyden/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionUS constitution and civil libertiesThe Washington press corps needs to boycott White House eventsMargaret SullivanCNN, MS Now and Politico accurately call last week’s sudden lockout ‘a direct assault on the first amendment’. That’s rightMon 21 Sep 2026 11.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.49 EDTShareOn Monday, the three news organizations that had been kicked out of the White House because ofDonald Trump’s latest fit of pique sued the president and three top advisers.An accompanying statement by CNN,MS Nowand Politico accurately calls last week’s sudden lockout “a direct assault on the first amendment”.The legal action is the right move, of course, and one that may prevail since the ban seems to be a clear case of what press-rights lawyers call “viewpoint discrimination”. In other words, Trump didn’t like their stories so he removed their access.CNN, MS Now and Politico to sue Trump after being blocked from White HouseRead moreThe president has been in a bad mood lately, for obvious reasons. Retaliating against the press is his favorite way to let off steam.But something else, beyond legal action, is necessary, too.“Time for the New York Times, Washington Post and Wall Street Journal to report on the White House from off campus,” wrote Richard J Tofel, an attorney and the longtime president of the investigative news organization ProPublica, who writes a press-relatednewsletter,Second Rough Draft.In other words, the biggest and most influential “print” news organizations – along with the major broadcast TV networks – should take collective action by boycotting that briefing room and similar White House events until their journalistic colleagues get their credentials back.The major TV networks took a commendable step in that direction on Monday by deciding to suspend “pool coverage” of presidential events, sinceCNNwas assigned to the duty of recording events and sharing them with the broader “pool” of news organizations.“There will be no replacement pool put in place,” stated Bryan Boughton, the Fox News Washington bureau chief and chair of the TV pool in a memo to the White House press corps.It’s especially good to see because the White House press corps often talks a good game about solidarity and press rights, but they’ve mostly kept doing what they’ve always done – treating Trump like any other president.He can ban the Associated Press from the briefing room for refusing to use the term “Gulf of America” instead of “Gulf of Mexico”. He can respond to a reporter’s question with the disrespectful command “Quiet, piggy.” He can (through his defense secretary) try to revoke journalistic access to the Pentagon and fire top staffers at Stars and Stripes, the military newspaper. His weaponized justice department can subpoena New York Times reporters or show up at a Washington Post reporter’s home and seize her devices.He can even trash as the “worst” his loyal rightwing media outlet, Fox News, for its recent polling that showed Americans’ deep dissatisfaction with his handling of the economy. He’s an equal opportunity media-basher.But, no matter, Trump still gets that annual invitation to the White House Correspondents’ Association’s fancy DC dinner, where he can insult the press and make personal attacks on reporters whom he finds displeasing or those he simply wants to single out for abuse.He still gets treated with deference.And the reporters who are not in particular disfavor continue to go to White House briefings and press gaggles.In other words, he mostly gets away with it.double quotation markTrump is a bully. And bullies will keep bullying until they get a punch in the noseThis most recent ban is one of the most serious actions yet, as the scholar of authoritarianism, Ruth Ben-Ghiat,declared,calling it “a moment of reckoning for America”.It’s not only, she said, “part of the autocratic playbook, but the timing is no coincidence. Trump is well into the autocratic backfire process, thus entire media outlets he sees as threats must be banished.”To put it bluntly, Trump is a bully. And bullies will keep bullying until they get a punch in the nose.As much as he professes to hate the mainstream media, Trump depends on it. He wants the constant attention. He loves being in the spotlight, where his every utterance – no matter how unhinged or false – is blasted out to the public.It will get through to him if that kind of attention is withdrawn, as it was on Monday with the pool suspension.Back when the AP was banned last year, a former Washington bureau chief at the news service, Ron Fournier, had some broader advice for the press corps.“No self-respecting journalist should attend a White House briefing while the White House bans the AP for not accepting state-mandated language,” hewroteon social media, using the hashtag #BoycottTheBriefing.Yes, media organizations may issue strongly worded statements, and may join in lawsuits, but solidarity is too often a theoretical thing, not a practical action with real-life consequences.They offer a rationale, of course. It’s of utmost importance, journalists and their bosses will tell you, to cover the president. Not doing so would be a dereliction of duty and would stoop to the president’s level. It would be, God forbid,unprofessional.But here’s the thing: reporters do not need to do their journalistic duty from inside the White House, or in an impromptu gaggle with Trump.“We don’t need our journalistic watchdogs to have ‘access’ to Trump,” as former CBS News justice correspondent Scott MacFarlaneput it. (He is now the chief Washington correspondent at MeidasTouch, the progressive media company.) “Everyone in the press room should walk out in protest … and source up.”In other words, don’t abandon the job. Report aggressively from “off campus”.It is a matter of principle at this point.And principle should trump access. Especially at a time when American democracy is teetering on the brink.Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and cultureExplore more on these topicsUS constitution and civil libertiesOpinionPress freedomDonald TrumpMS NowCNNTrump administrationNewspapers & magazinescommentShareReuse this content

title: All the signs say another financial crisis is coming. Here’s why we need to prepare for it now | Larry Elliott | The Guardian
description: War, AI disruption and markets in turmoil: the warnings are all there. But lessons from the 2008 crash could help us, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Author: Larry Elliott
Headline: War, AI disruption and markets in turmoil: the warnings are all there. But lessons from the 2008 crash could help us, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Content: A broker at the Frankfurt stock exchange, Germany, on 16 September 2008.Photograph: Daniel Roland/APView image in fullscreenA broker at the Frankfurt stock exchange, Germany, on 16 September 2008.Photograph: Daniel Roland/APOpinionMarket turmoilAll the signs say another financial crisis is coming. Here’s why we need to prepare for it nowLarry ElliottWar, AI disruption and markets in turmoil: the warnings are all there. But lessons from the 2008 crash could help usMon 21 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.14 EDTShareBad stuff happens in September. For some reason, it is a month that has had more than its fair share of financial crises, perhaps because problems that have been bubbling away come into sharper focus once the summer holidays are over. Britaincame off the Gold Standardin September 1931. The pound was turfed out of Europe’s Exchange Rate Mechanism in September 1992. And 18 years ago this week, the collapse of Lehman Brothers plunged the global economy into deep recession.This September, there are again reasons to be nervous. There are soaring oil prices, which are feeding through intohigher petrol and diesel prices, adding to cost of living pressures. There is asell-off in government bondsaround the world. There is thewarning from AI bossesthat it would be wise to slow the pace of development in their industry. Mixed together, they are the ingredients for another troubled September.Of course, it may all be a false alarm. It is now more than six months since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran and so far the impact of closing the strait of Hormuz has been far less severe than was expected back in the spring. It is possible the fear currently gripping bond markets will quickly pass, especially if the wars in Ukraine and Iran end soon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAre global stock markets heading for a crash?Read moreThe constant refrain from Donald Trump that oil tankers will soon be passing unhindered once again through the strait of Hormuz has limited the rise in crude prices. Growth has not been hit that much, and in both the US and the UK,AI has been part of that story.There are, though, signs that the war in Iran is having an effect, albeit with a longer lag than originally expected. Markets no longer believe Trump when he says a deal with Iran is about to be clinched. As a result, the rise in oil prices to more than $100 a barrel in recent weeks has heightened fears of persistent inflation and of higher interest rates from central banks. And despite crude prices not escalating,the cost of petrol and dieselremains high, thanks to a shortage of refining capacity.For months, share prices have been underpinned by the belief that there is no ceiling on the growth of technology stocks, particularly those involved in AI. That theory is now being tested and as far as Wall Street is concerned, the recent intervention by the AI bosses was spectacularly ill-timed.Trump’s rejection of the need for tighter regulation on the AI industry speaks volumes. This is only partly to do with the US-China battle to win the technology war. Financial markets now look as fragile as they have been at any time since September 2008, and with US midterm elections looming, the president needs to prevent the AI-led stock market bubble from popping.History never repeats itself exactly. There are similarities between September 2026 and September 2008, but there are differences too. The crash of 2008 was the result of banks over-reaching themselves to finance US real estate. The banks seem to be far less exposed this time, and while some of the investment in technology stocks may have been predicated on unrealistic assumptions about future profits, AI is clearly going to have a positive long-term economic impact in a way that the investment in housing pre-2008 did not. It is wrong to think all bubbles are the same.That said, there are lessons to be learned from the events of 2008. One is that if a financial crisis morphs into an economic slump – as it did 18 years ago – then orthodoxy goes out of the window. There will be no more talk of interest-rate increases from central banks or of the need for finance ministries to slash budget deficits.Indeed, therecent bond buybacksby the US treasury, which were designed to reduce the upward pressure on mortgage interest rates, car loans and credit card debt, were both an indication of how nervous the Trump administration is about the current state of financial markets and a taste of the more vigorous intervention that a full-blown financial crisis would prompt.An even bigger lesson is the need to control what happens after a crash. Last time, the left was caught unawares and allowed the right to seize the initiative. Already there are signs in Britain of the same dynamic, with the chancellor, John Healey, coming under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending in next month’s budget.This would be self-defeating, not least because it would run counter to Andy Burnham’s (to my mind, entirely correct) argument that 40 years of neoliberalism was a mistake that needs rectifying. It would also come at a time when – as this week’s TUC conference in Brighton showed – there is genuine support on the left for a comprehensive strategy to re-industrialise Britain.A range of trade unions – Unite, RMT, CWU, GMB and Equity – made it clear at the conference that they wanted a much more interventionist approach, and acollection of essays, to which I contributed, has just been published, fleshing out what Burnham would need to do to make good on his re-industrialisation pledge.If not now, then sooner or later there will be another financial crisis. People forget. They become complacent. They overlook the strains in financial markets that have been allowed to become too big and too powerful. So while recent events may blow over, it would also be sensible to plan for another September meltdown. Just in case.Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsMarket turmoilOpinionGlobal economyEconomicsFinancial crisisStock marketsBondscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Houthis’ offensive is the latest spillover from Trump’s Iran disaster | Mohamad Bazzi | The Guardian
description: Trump’s mess has rekindled Yemen’s civil war and a years-long conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia
Author: Mohamad Bazzi
Headline: Trump’s mess has rekindled Yemen’s civil war and a years-long conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia
Content: ‘The Houthis led a rapid advance along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, seizing a strategic port city and several islands that gave the militia control over the Bab al-Mandab strait.’Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAView image in fullscreen‘The Houthis led a rapid advance along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, seizing a strategic port city and several islands that gave the militia control over the Bab al-Mandab strait.’Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAOpinionUS-Israel war on IranThe Houthis’ offensive is the latest spillover from Trump’s Iran disasterMohamad BazziTrump’s mess has rekindled Yemen’s civil war and a years-long conflict between the Houthis and Saudi ArabiaMon 21 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTShareWhen the US and Israel launched a war of aggression against Iran in late February, Tehran’s allies in the Middle East jumped into the fray. Lebanon’s Hezbollah militiafired rocketsat Israel, while Shia militias in Iraqattacked US basesand diplomatic outposts. But the Houthis, who control large parts of Yemen, mostly stayed on the sidelines.Over the past few weeks, however, the Houthis have changed their tactics and have entered the conflict in full force. They led arapid advancealong Yemen’s Red Sea coast, seizing a strategic port city and several islands that gave the militia control over the Bab al-Mandab strait, a vital waterway for energy shipments and other global trade. Thanks to Donald Trump’s war, Iran and its allies now dominate the Middle East’s two major regional energy chokepoints: Bab al-Mandab and the strait of Hormuz.And Trump’s misadventure in Iran has unleashed other unintended consequences: it has rekindled Yemen’s civil war, and a related years-long conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia. In recent days, the Houthis haveexpanded their offensivebeyond the Red Sea coastline, targeting two provinces in Yemen’s eastern region, which is home to the country’s largest oil and gas fields. Those areas, including the resource-rich Marib province, are under the control of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which is supported by Saudi Arabia. If the Houthis can capture those regions, it would be their biggest territorial advance in more than a decade.The situation in Iran is dangerously escalating – but whatever you do, don’t call it a war | Arwa MahdawiRead moreThe renewed fightinghas displacedmore than 100,000 people inside Yemen, and forced thousands of others to flee across the Red Sea into Djibouti. Even before the latest escalation, Yemen was facing one of the world’sworst humanitarian crises, with nearly half the population – about 22 million people – needing relief aid and protection, according to the United Nations.The Houthi-Saudi conflict will also impact global energy supplies and prices: the militia hasattacked oil facilitiesand other infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia, in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes on Houthi-ruled areas of Yemen. After the two sides agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022, there were occasional skirmishes but the truce largely held until mid-July. That’s when Saudi airstrikesstruck the main airportin Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, which is under Houthi control. The Saudi-aligned Yemeni government claimed the attack was intended to stop an Iranian plane from landing at the airport, and to enforce an air and naval blockade that Saudi Arabia had imposed years ago against Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. The Iranian plane was carrying a delegation of Houthi officials on their way home from the funeral of Iran’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, who was assassinated by US-Israeli airstrikes in the war’s early hours.On 20 July, the Houthisdeclared a siegeon Saudi ships transiting the Red Sea through the Bab al-Mandab strait, saying it would only be lifted when the kingdom removed its own blockade on Houthi territory. After Iran shut down the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s energy supplies transited before the recent war, Saudi Arabia was forced to move much of its oil shipments via itseast-west pipelineto Saudi ports along the Red Sea. That exposed Saudi dependence on both the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab waterways.After announcing their blockade in July, the Houthis fired on several Saudi vessels in the Red Sea, forcing the kingdom to reroute a significant portion of its oil exports to Asia through a far longer and more expensive journey. Thatalternative routecan take ships more than 30 days, and it involves transiting through the Suez Canal, the Mediterranean Sea, and around the southern tip of Africa, before finally reaching customers in Asia, who buy the bulk of Saudi oil.To make matters worse for the Saudis – and global oil prices – the east-west pipeline was struck recently by a drone attack blamed on Iranian-backed Shia militias in Iraq. Saudi officials were forced to shut down the nearly 750-mile-long pipeline on 11 September, and it’s unclear how long repairs will take. If the network is offline for a month, it couldreduce global oil supplyby 120m barrels and raise crude prices as high as $120 a barrel.As the Houthis carried out their lightning offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince and de facto ruler, Mohammed bin Salman,reportedly called Trumptwice on 10 September, urging him to order US airstrikes against the Yemeni rebels. For now, Trump has ruled out direct US attacks against the Houthis, despite the appeals from his ally and benefactor Prince Mohammed. (After a mob of Trump supporters stormed the US Capitol in January 2021, several US banks and large companiesdistanced themselvesfrom the president’s family business, the Trump Organization. But Saudi Arabia and its crown prince becamea crucial sourceof new real estate and other deals for the family firm while Trump was out of power.)Trump’s decision to keep the US out of the Houthi-Saudi conflict is one of the best foreign policy choices of his second term so far, although it’s dwarfed by his catastrophic decision to launch a war against Iran. Trump seems to realize that neither the US,Saudi Arabianor other Arab states have been able to bomb the Houthis into submission – despite trying for more than a decade.Yemen’s civil war has been a complex conflict for decades, with Saudi Arabia, Iran and the US supporting different factions at various times. TheHouthis, who are officially known as Ansar Allah (the Partisans of God), emerged in the 1990s as a Shia tribal movement based in northern Yemen that fought multiple battles against the central Yemeni government and other tribes aligned with Saudi Arabia. The conflict escalated significantly in September 2014, when the Houthis overran Sana’a, and within a few months forced the internationally recognized government to flee to the kingdom, which shares a long border with Yemen.The Guardian view on the Houthi advance in Yemen: another vital Middle East artery becomes a battlefield | EditorialRead moreIn early 2015, Saudi Arabia led a coalition of Sunni Arab states to intervene in the war, trying to push the Houthis out of the capital and restore Yemen’s Saudi-backed government into power. Barack Obama and his administrationsupported the Saudisand their allies, especially the United Arab Emirates, with US weapons and extensive intelligence sharing.Despite thousands of airstrikes and a Saudi-led blockade, the Houthis survived the onslaught.Yemenwas effectively divided into two states, with the Houthis in control of Sana’a and large parts of the north, while the Yemeni government controlled much of the south and a competing capital in the port city of Aden. After seven years of stalemate, Saudi Arabia decided to cut its losses and agreed to a ceasefire with the Houthis in 2022, after which the group stopped its attacks on Saudi territory until resuming them this summer.Negotiations over a permanent peace agreement in Yemen stalled for several years, mainly over economic incentives for the Houthis and recognizing the militia’s rule over parts of Yemen. In recent weeks, the Houthis sensed an advantage in the regional chaos and global economic turmoil unleashed by Trump’s war onIran.The Houthis are trying to gain new leverage by taking control of their own regional energy chokepoint and capturing more territory from their enemies in Yemen. For now, no one seems to be able to stop them.Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York UniversityExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranOpinionIranYemenHouthisSaudi ArabiaUS foreign policyMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on rape courts: ministers know that victims deserve better | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: New facilities for witnesses who have been sexually assaulted are a step towards halving violence against girls and women
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: New facilities for witnesses who have been sexually assaulted are a step towards halving violence against girls and women
Content: The statue of Lady Justice on top of the central criminal court building in London.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenThe statue of Lady Justice on top of the central criminal court building in London.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAOpinionRape and sexual assaultThe Guardian view on rape courts: ministers know that victims deserve betterEditorialNew facilities for witnesses who have been sexually assaulted are a step towards halving violence against girls and womenMon 21 Sep 2026 13.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe creation ofspecialist courtsto try rape and serious sexual offences in England and Wales is a welcome recognition from the government that the status quo is unacceptable. Victims, the vast majority of whom are women and girls, are being failed by a system that too often appears blind to the obstacles in the way of anyone who wants to see a perpetrator brought to justice. In 2025, rape cases took an average of424 days after they had reached the crown court. Added to pre‑trial delays, this means thousands of lives being placed on hold for years.Long waits are simply unendurable in many cases; arape reviewordered by Conservative ministers in 2021 found that the proportion of complainants dropping out of cases had risen from 25% to 43% in five years. As well as the harm caused to individuals, there is an obvious impact on public safety when perpetrators go unpunished, and chances to rehabilitate them are missed.Plans for clearer scheduling, so that rape trial dates are fixed in advance, ought to make the whole experience easier to manage. A funding boost for victim support services, and commitment to greater continuity, will strengthen the framework around them. This follows other recent changes, including an extension of the period during which a sentence can be reviewed, included in the Victims and Courts Act.View image in fullscreenThe justice secretary, Alex Norris.Photograph: Ian Davidson/SOPA Images/ShutterstockMinisters have already committed, in theirviolence against women and girls strategy, to specialist units in every police force. This week’s announcement signals that an important argument has been won, about the need for dedicated training and tailored approaches in the courts as well. But implementation of both commitments will be a huge challenge. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has set an ambitious timetable. Specialist police units are due to be in place by the end of next year, with the courts given slightly longer to prepare facilities including separate waiting rooms for victims and links to observe sentencing hearings remotely.Two new taskforces have been unveiled in recent days. One will bring together experts to focus on rape justice. The other, chaired byBridget Phillipson, the women and equalities minister, will focus onmisogynistic attitudes. This twin-track approach is promising in that it addresses the underlying causes of violence against women and girls, as well as the criminal justice response. But having pledged to halve such violence in a decade, ministers will need results to convince the public that they are on track. This is all the more important given past failures, and the eagerness of rightwing parties toexploit the issue of violence against womenat every chance.The backlog in the courts is a problem that goes wider than sexual offences.Restricting jury trialswas the wrong solution, but a bigger role for magistrates has the potential to bring down waiting times. Court hours should be increased where this is feasible. Scrutiny of the Crown Prosecution Service’sdecisions on rape casesmust also continue, along with efforts to tackle the disturbing rise in online sexual offences, includingimage-sharing. Thecriminalisationof pornography featuring strangulation should be viewed as a step on a journey towards making the internet a safer place. This is a daunting agenda that stretches across government. But with concrete changes to the courts and victim support, ministers have shown an intention to grasp it.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Friedrich Merz: Germany’s chancellor must change course to halt the rise of the AfD | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A failure to address widespread economic insecurity, and a crisis in living standards, is allowing the far right the harness a growing protest vote
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A failure to address widespread economic insecurity, and a crisis in living standards, is allowing the far right the harness a growing protest vote
Content: ‘Friedrich Merz is already looking like a lame duck leader.’Photograph: Filip Singer/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Friedrich Merz is already looking like a lame duck leader.’Photograph: Filip Singer/EPAOpinionGermanyThe Guardian view on Friedrich Merz: Germany’s chancellor must change course to halt the rise of the AfDEditorialA failure to address widespread economic insecurity, and a crisis in living standards, is allowing the far right the harness a growing protest voteMon 21 Sep 2026 13.34 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareAfter less than a year and a half in office, Germany’s beleaguered chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is already looking like a lame duck leader. Anticipating dire results in two state elections which were held on Sunday, Mr Merzcancelleda planned speech at this week’s United Nations general assembly in order to plot an emergency response. A night of extraordinaryhumiliationfor his conservative Christian Democratic Union party (CDU) must have confounded even his own low expectations.In the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the far-right Alternative für Deutschland party (AfD) won its second regional election this month with 38% of the vote. The CDU meanwhile recorded its worst result since the second world war, failing even to meet the 5% threshold for representation in the state parliament. Mr Merz took over the leadership of the CDU promising to see off the threat of the AfD. Instead it has ascended to a menacing and unprecedented position of electoral strength, and enjoys a comfortableleadin national polls.View image in fullscreenElif Eralp of the Left party.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAIn the other regional contest, the CDU ceded control of the mayoralty in Berlin and finished second behind the radical Left party, which campaigned on a platform to address the capital’s soaring housingcrisis. These were seminal reverses, but Mr Merz shows no sign of learning the lessons from either defeat. Defiantly dismissing speculation over his future, he insisted that his coalition government was “determined to live up to the historic responsibilities our country is facing”.Without a change of political direction that seems improbable. Suffering from depopulation and persistent inequalities relative to the west, Germany’s eastern regions have been particularly vulnerable to the rise of one of Europe’s most extreme far-right movements. But as the continent’s powerhouse economystruggleswith Chinese competition, US protectionism, and a cost of livingcrisis, there is nationwide disillusionment with the chancellor’s abrasive style and “tough love” prescriptions. Mr Merz’s personal poll ratings hover at a recordlowof around 13%.Doubling down on a programme which includes raising the retirement age, cutting health insurance benefits, and making it much more difficult to claim sick leave, is hardly likely to turn those numbers around. The Social Democratic party (SPD), as the junior coalition partner, has attempted to act as a partial brake on the chancellor’s pro-austerity instincts. But as one of its despairing MPs acidlyobservedof Mr Merz: “He constantly asks people to work more, while tens of thousands of jobs are currently being cut in German industry!”The constitutionalobstaclesto removing a chancellor – and the reality that neither the CDU nor the SPD want a new election given the state of their respective polling – mean that Mr Merz is likely to stay in post. But if the government’s fortunes are to revive, a radical rethink is required. The chancellor’s unsuccessful strategy for spiking the AfD’s guns has been to ape its draconian positions on immigration. But it is the failure to address a crisis in living standards and widespread economic insecurity which allows the far right to channel a growing protest vote.That is deeply worrying. On Monday, Mr Merz emphasised that Germany’s “democratic future” must be defended. He was right to emphasise how much is at stake. But it is becoming increasingly and alarmingly clear how ill-suited he is for that task.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Lucy Letby, the NHS and the rise of managerialism  | Lucy Letby | The Guardian
description: Letters: Pete Dorey believes most public services are thoroughly over-managed, Michael Barrett says whistleblowing policies are essential. Plus letters from Frances Kirkham and Jenny Webb
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Pete Dorey believes most public services are thoroughly over-managed, Michael Barrett says whistleblowing policies are essential. Plus letters from Frances Kirkham and Jenny Webb
Content: ‘Hospital board members do have responsibility for their overall management, but how well they exercise their responsibilities depends very much on leadership.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Hospital board members do have responsibility for their overall management, but how well they exercise their responsibilities depends very much on leadership.’Photograph: AlamyLucy LetbyLettersLucy Letby, the NHS and the rise of managerialismPete Doreybelievesmost public services are thoroughly over-managed,Michael Barrettsays whistleblowing policies are essential. Plus letters fromFrances KirkhamandJenny WebbMon 21 Sep 2026 11.06 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.43 EDTShareTom Dolphin’s excellent article on the failings of NHS management made sombre reading (The Letby inquiry report makes one thing crystal clear: too much NHS management is scandalously poor, 16 September). Yet I believe that most of our public services are thoroughly over-managed, with frontline professionals neither listened to nor respected by their institutional superiors, and at risk of damaging their careers if they speak out about poor decisions, excessive workloads and impossible targets or “performance indicators”.Like so many of our current woes, the rise of managerialism can be traced back to the public service reforms of the Thatcher governments in the 1980s, and the mantra of “management’s right to manage”. As professionals were supposedly self-serving vested interests, the transfer of power to managers was supposed to increase efficiency and responsiveness to service users.Yet, in many cases, the long-term result has been the rise of excessive, remote and unlistening senior management, and the parallel marginalisation or exclusion of professionals from decision-making in their spheres of expertise, coupled with plummeting morale.Pete DoreyBathDr Tom Dolphin’s article on the failings ofNHSmanagement raises some important points about whistleblowing and the regulation of non-medical managers. Hospital board members do have responsibility for their overall management, but how well they exercise their responsibilities depends very much on leadership and the creation of a culture committed to patient care, as well as excellence throughout all the systems delivering that care.One of the essential assurance measures along with risk management and clinical governance is the promotion of a whistleblowing policy that encourages reporting of concerns to board level without fear of repercussions and with certainty that action will be taken if necessary. If there are still any hospital management teams out there without a clear protocol for raising and pursuing problems, confidentially if appropriate, that should be a matter for urgent action.Michael BarrettLondonYvette Cooper states: “This must be a turning point for the NHS”. The cry always goes up: “Lessons must be learned”. But the carefully considered, evidence‑based recommendations made by those who have conducted public inquiries or by coroners are invariably ignored. There is a shelf in government that’s high up – in other words, fairly inaccessible – on which every such report is placed to gather dust. So the lessons are not learned.Frances KirkhamBirminghamIn the wake of theLucy Letbyinquiry, the NHS will no doubt face a barrage of criticism. But we must also remember what a wonderful institution it still is. Earlier this month, after two agonising days and nights, my daughter died in the intensive treatment unit at Leeds general infirmary.Throughout, the service we received was wonderful – not just the medical expertise, but the kindness and loving consideration of all staff, from the consultant to the ward clerk. We were always kept fully informed about what was happening, and in the end we were consulted on the final decision to turn off the life support.By all means, criticise the NHS for its shortcomings. But let us also treasure its strengths, and its potential to help us through some of the most difficult times of our lives.Jenny WebbChichester, West SussexHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: To minimise the risks to young football players we should ban agents recruiting under-18s | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Letters: Phil Murray responds to articles about the precarious path talented young athletes face
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Phil Murray responds to articles about the precarious path talented young athletes face
Content: ‘For those such as Raheem Sterling, Max Dowman (above) and JJ Gabriel, who do achieve their ambitions, the pressures, from coaches, fans, sponsors and social media must be immense.’Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘For those such as Raheem Sterling, Max Dowman (above) and JJ Gabriel, who do achieve their ambitions, the pressures, from coaches, fans, sponsors and social media must be immense.’Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersSoccerLettersTo minimise the risks to young football players we should ban agents recruiting under-18sPhil Murrayresponds to articles about the precarious path talented young athletes faceMon 21 Sep 2026 11.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.43 EDTShareJonathan Liew’s piece (Raheem Sterling’s bleak tale a reminder of absurd path young footballers face, 17 September) is informative and timely, particularly when set against Jacob Steinberg’s report (‘They are very similar’: Arsenal’s Dowman reminds Merino of Lamine Yamal, 16 September) .The tiny proportion of young footballers originally “signed” by top flight clubs at a ludicrously young age, who then achieve their dreams of aPremier Leaguecareer, rather than being summarily dismissed at the age of 16 or 17 with the vast majority of their contemporaries, should be a reality check for parents/guardians of all aspiring young athletes.For those such asRaheem Sterling, Max Dowman and JJ Gabriel, who do achieve their ambitions, the pressures, from coaches, fans, sponsors and social media must be immense. To navigate such pressures requires an exceptional degree of individual maturity way beyond their years, ideally alongside a trusted safeguarding mentor, to guide them through the many pitfalls in their path, rather than relying on cliched verbal assurances from their clubs regarding their welfare. To help minimise the many risks to such young talents, I would also suggest that the football authorities ban any agent recruiting/negotiating on behalf of any player under the age of 18, none of whom need to be exposed to such malign influences in the early stages of their careers.Without such measures being put in place, I have no doubt that in years to come there will be regular reports of young athletes, similarly lauded in their mid-teens as the next “big thing”, only to succumb to the pressures associated with success in their chosen sport – a bleak prospect indeed.Phil MurrayLinlithgow, West LothianHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Best guest or the host with the most? | Social etiquette | The Guardian
description: Letters: Polly Hudson has sparked debate among readers over which camp they fall into
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Polly Hudson has sparked debate among readers over which camp they fall into
Content: ‘The skills of hosting can be learned, and you can make things more relaxing by buying in a few readymade dishes, or asking friends to bring one.’Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreen‘The skills of hosting can be learned, and you can make things more relaxing by buying in a few readymade dishes, or asking friends to bring one.’Photograph: GettySocial etiquetteLettersBest guest or the host with the most?Polly Hudson has sparked debate among readers over which camp they fall intoMon 21 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.43 EDTShareI realised as a teenager doing exchanges with European fellow teens many years ago that it’s always easier to be guest rather than host (There are two kinds of people in this world: hosts and guests. Nobody can be both, 15 September).The skills of hosting can be learned, and you can make things more relaxing by buying in a few readymade dishes, or asking friends to bring one. So as someone who is often host, yes the failure to reciprocate will lead to resentment.Dinah RobertsonLymm, CheshireJudging by the amount of people in my house on a weekly basis, I’m either 100% host or just have the fullest fridge. No resentment at all to all our lovely guests, we love having you. But I will admit that once in a while it is a thrill to let someone else worry about running out of wine or crisps. As long as it’s back at ours the following week.Kim ThorntonCoulsdon, LondonI am definitely a host and enjoy planning, cooking and presenting meals at our place. We have some friends who always enjoy dinner with us but rarely invite us because they enjoy being guests more and claim not to be “good cooks”. When we go out for dinner with them, they pay. Suits all of us well!Alison HumphreysFlynn, AustraliaHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The AfD thrives in the absence of mainstream parties that speak to people’s daily lives | Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Carolin Würfel’s article on the reasons behind Alternative für Deutschland’s recent electoral success in Germany
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Carolin Würfel’s article on the reasons behind Alternative für Deutschland’s recent electoral success in Germany
Content: The AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund at a campaign rally in Schwerin ahead of the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state election, 19 September 2026.Photograph: Somaya Abdelrahman/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund at a campaign rally in Schwerin ahead of the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state election, 19 September 2026.Photograph: Somaya Abdelrahman/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)LettersThe AfD thrives in the absence of mainstream parties that speak to people’s daily livesReaders respond to Carolin Würfel’s article on the reasons behind Alternative für Deutschland’s recent electoral success in GermanyMon 21 Sep 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.01 EDTShareCarolin Würfel is right to see the success of AfD in the eastern states of Germany as a way to protest against west German dominance (I know why many east Germans vote AfD. And no, it’s not an inherited longing for dictatorship, 15 September).But she overlooks the fact that the “takeover” of 1990 could not have been done much differently. Any path more resembling those of other east European nations would have led to mass migration to WestGermany. In that sense the current situation is not the fault of western politicians and industrialists. One thing could and should have been done differently, though. An attempt to build a conservative-centrist party representing the east would have been important, instead of just transferring the western parties. Die Linke fulfilled such a role for some time, but from the left, not the centre. Now AfD fulfils this role from the right.In Bavaria, the Christian Social Union has exactly such a role and has helped to keep that state a stable member of the federal republic. A similar “Ost-Union” would have been important, but for that the 5% threshold in the federal voting laws would have had to be replaced by a state-based threshold. A new local party in one state, “Thüringen.Gerecht”, formed by former members of BSW, a split from Linke, could develop into such a role, but without federal representation it will be a very long road.Jürgen SchwarzBerlinCarolin Würfel’s article highlights a dynamic that is not confined to Germany. The same forces are reshaping politics acrossEuropeand the US, and they all begin with a widening gap between political leaders and the people they are meant to represent.In much of Europe, that gap produces cynicism. Many citizens feel that leaders are driven by party interests, media pressures and broad national narratives rather than the realities of daily life. When people sense that distance, they become receptive to parties like the AfD, which present themselves as the only ones willing to listen.In the US, the emotional response is different. What I see is not just cynicism but a deeper hopelessness – a belief that no leader or institution can address the problems people face. This is the environment in which Donald Trump rose to power. Like the AfD, his appeal comes from exploiting the disconnect between political rhetoric and lived experience.Across democracies, people are responding to the same underlying pressures: deindustrialisation, rapid technological change, climate‑driven disruption and large migration flows from countries experiencing severe poverty, state fragility and deep social fragmentation. These are human problems, not ideological talking points. When leaders fail to engage directly with individuals, frustration and hopelessness become political fuel for movements whose primary interest is power, not solutions.Mickey WrightUtah, USExplore more on these topicsAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)GermanyEuropeThe far rightlettersShareReuse this content

title: Come back soon Premier League, the endlessly moreish mega-product | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Brighton have impressed in a goal-laden start to the season, in a league that remains a brutally strong attraction
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Brighton have impressed in a goal-laden start to the season, in a league that remains a brutally strong attraction
Content: Brighton outskilled and outmuscled Arsenal on their way to a 3-0 victory last weekend.Photograph: Daniel Weir/Sports Press Photo/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBrighton outskilled and outmuscled Arsenal on their way to a 3-0 victory last weekend.Photograph: Daniel Weir/Sports Press Photo/ShutterstockPremier LeagueCome back soon Premier League, the endlessly moreish mega-productBrighton have impressed in a goal-laden start to the season, in a league that remains a brutally strong attractionBarney RonayMon 21 Sep 2026 16.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGet ready for the dopamine crash. And this one really is a proper autumn nosedive. The past 17 days up to and including Sunday’s cut-off gave us 30Premier Leaguegames and 79 goals. Which, if you take Spurs out of it – and this is fair because Spurs are now post‑goal, an entertainment concept unrelated to goals or even football itself – is really quite a lot.Are your pathways stimulated? Are the neural connectors flickering? Well get ready for cold turkey, for 19 blank days of shivers and shakes until the Premier League show resumes in October. Maybe it really is time to buy one of those powders off the internet.The last two seasons were grim for Spurs. This is as bad as it’s ever been | Jonathan WilsonRead moreThe international break will provide its own intrigue. There will be discussions about whether Thomas Tuchel is or isn’t responsible for the inherited cultural weaknesses of English football. There will be rage at Tuchel’s inability to coach the players to keep the ball as never before via his few short hours on the training pitch. And yet more rage at the real issues, basically the fact he continues to be German and looks like a scurvy-ridden Napoleonic naval commander powered solely by ship’s biscuits and morphine.This is unlikely to fill the hole. There will be an unavoidable “contrast effect”, the rush of adrenaline that only serves to deepen the low when it is gone. But there are also some familiar autumn rituals to help us through. One of these is the state‑of‑the‑nation Premier League address, pegged out around key questions such as “where are we?”, “what are we?” and “where is it all going?”. This time around these are relatively easy to answer.Five rounds into the Premier League season this is pretty much a cut-and-paste job. The big news: there is no big news. Events continue to happen at great volume. But in terms of teams, style, stars, energies and potential outcomes, not much has changed. Roll back one year and this was the broad situation. A powerful team with a bald, irascible manager had won all five games, but also looked defensively fragile. The team that would win the league was second. That team was also Arsenal.View image in fullscreenAre Tottenham doomed? Probably not. They have enough semi-interested players to retain a solid hold on 17th place.Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThe middle classes were the most interesting story, those functional, well-run teams beginning with B, an entity you might call Brightonmouth. Erling Haaland was scoring goals. Bruno Fernandes was generating hair‑tearing anguish, like a young Elvis, but based more around shithousery and risky attacking passes.As ever there are still some key questions doing the rounds, but luckily these can all be answered easily. Is Michael Carrick the man to take Manchester United to the next level? No. Is Michael Carrick the reasonUnited are not at that level, but in a state where they must now employ Michael Carrick? Also no.The reality for United is that there are no other levels. This is the level, a club that instead acts as a grand, angst-ridden but very accurate metaphor for modern‑day Britain, furiously retailing its own heritage, run by fill-ins and opportunists, a mobile waxwork museum living on tourism and memories.Are Tottenham doomed? Probably not. They have enough semi-interested players to retain a solid hold on 17th place. Although frustratingly for Premier League content addicts, even this has been degraded by repetition. Spurs could get relegated now and you would just keep scrolling.Are Liverpool on the verge of a renaissance? Probably not. The Jürgen Klopp golden era is beginning to look quite distant, surrounded on all sides by something a bit like the present. And, yes, Florian Wirtz is a very good footballer. He just can’t resist contact very well, which is non‑negotiable in the Premier League. He is going to be really good at Paris Saint-Gemain/Bayern Munich/Inter.View image in fullscreenManchester United have had a difficult start to the season under Michael Carrick.Photograph: Dennis Goodwin/ProSports/ShutterstockOtherwise, it is a case of stasis and a reliable, entertaining, homogenised product. Tactically, we can still get excited about small changes. If you analyse it deeply you may find a little more counterattack, Anthony Elanga running fast, an inverted winger discovering almost by accident he can also cross with his strong foot.It is a mark of how standardised the game has become that these are deemed things worth getting excited about. There is still only one elite level style, the Omniball template of the Cruyff-Michels-Guardiola-Gegenpressing school.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis is skewed towards physicality over control in England, but it still produces football that can feel at times a bit like driving a brand new electric car: fun, high‑grade, but also endlessly repeatable. It seems possible some time soon that a robotic bait‑the‑press system will meet a robotic bait-averse system and in that moment football will just cease to exist, reduced to two banks of human units staring at each other across a strip of empty grass.There are two things the Premier League could really do with in the remaining 87% of its season. The nudge into greater physicality is exciting and distinct. It is notable how many games have been decided by duels, collisions, a sense of greater wanting-it. Or perhaps not so surprising when the players are at roughly the same technical level, where the only real point of difference is sustained physical power and competitive will.This is one reason whyBrighton’s defeat of Arsenal on Saturdayseemed so interesting. It is rare to see any reigning champions not just beaten, but outskilled and outmuscled. For 90 minutes, only one of these teams looked like genuine contenders for every trophy on offer.This is the second thing the league could really do with. Is it possible for one of the well-run middle class to sustain this level over a season and give us another Leicester or something close? Can Brighton just play like that every week?Long-range hits and goals galore: inside the Premier League’s return to chaos | Andrew BeasleyRead moreThere are obvious answers why not. One very good game against an ambushed Arsenal is not a 38-game slog. Brighton have a good squad, but also regular midweek football. Other teams will react and nullify your strengths. Also, and this is not a throwaway detail, Fabian Hürzeler is going to be on TalkSport for an hour on Tuesday just chatting football, which will now include how did you beat the champs and why are you third in the league.Nothing wrong with this. But it is an indicator of where we are. Hürzeler is 33. The entire job is essentially reinventing himself, just as all of the very good players at those middleweight clubs are auditioning for bigger clubs rather than dreaming of hauling them in, playing for the life-changing money a Champions League-level club will throw at them, motivated by a breezy and entirely logical collective individualism.Perhaps this is why one of the themes of the season has been a suspicion among fans of bigger clubs that their players don’t want it enough, that being outrun or outworked is a sign of soul sickness or debauched management. But it is also what keeps the league brutally strong, state of the art, and endlessly moreish for all its repeated story arcs. Come back soon Premier League mega-product. The comedown is already hitting.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ten lessons from Jakob Ingebrigtsen, one of the world’s most beguiling athletes | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Jakob Ingebrigtsen is meticulous in his training regime – ‘if there’s anything that’s out of my control, then I’ve not done my job properly’
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Jakob Ingebrigtsen is meticulous in his training regime – ‘if there’s anything that’s out of my control, then I’ve not done my job properly’
Content: Jakob Ingebrigtsen loves running on his treadmill at home – ‘I put it on a certain speed, at a certain incline, and it’s always the same.’Photograph: Marie von Krogh/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJakob Ingebrigtsen loves running on his treadmill at home – ‘I put it on a certain speed, at a certain incline, and it’s always the same.’Photograph: Marie von Krogh/The GuardianAthleticsTen lessons from Jakob Ingebrigtsen, one of the world’s most beguiling athletesSean IngleNorwegian is meticulous in his training regime – ‘if there’s anything that’s out of my control, then I’ve not done my job properly’Mon 21 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareOn a snowy Norwegian morning in January, Jakob Ingebrigtsen was on his treadmill, shooting the breeze about his running philosophy before our more formal interview. I should write something on this, I told him. Sure, came the reply.In recent weeks, the 26‑year‑old has added to his legacy witha European 5,000m gold, theWorld Ultimate 5,000m titleand a world road silver medal despite achilles surgery in February and a flu that lingered through May and June. So now seems as good a time as any.Some of Ingebrigtsen’s opinions were a little hardcore. Others reiterated basic truths. But whether you are a runner or not, there are certainly some life lessons from one of the most beguiling athletes around.At home with Jakob Ingebrigtsen: ‘I’ve fed my obsession my whole life’Read more1) To be the best it helps to be a control freakIngebrigtsen runs a lot, around 175-180km in a typical week. Apart from his family, that is his sole focus. “I prioritise the absolute crucial,” he says. “That is to wake up, to eat, to train.” It is, he concedes, not a life most would enjoy. “A lot of people could never be in my shoes, having my responsibility. They just wouldn’t handle it. But that’s how I want to be. If there’s anything that’s out of my control, then I’ve not done my job properly.”2) No days off“If you have a day off, you lose 20-25km of running,” he says. Counterintuitively, perhaps, he believes the risk of injury goes up too and tries to run even when he is moderately poorly.“Having one week off if you are sick, injured or travelling, or even just doing easier training, that’s probably the worst thing you can do in terms of risk of injury. Because you are taking your body out of a consistent load. When you get back again, you will have sore legs because your body is not adapted to that load and when you compensate, or just change symmetry a little bit, that’s when something snaps.”3) Consistency is kingIngebrigtsen runs twice a day, in the morning and afternoon, with hills on a Saturday and a longish run of 20km on a Sunday. He supplements this with drills, mobility and core work on Monday and Wednesday and weights every Friday and Sunday. He does this week after week after week unless he is injured. Consistency, and gradually increasing load, is a lesson he says amateur runners should apply.4) Be prepared to work very hardIngebrigtsen is famous for his double threshold runs on Tuesday and Thursdays – two runs each day that aim for the sweet spot between hard, but not brutal, fatigue, but sustainable. A morning session, for instance, might involve 5x6 minutes effort with a one‑minute jog for recovery between repetitions. In the afternoon it could be 25 times around a 400m track at 5km-10km pace with 30 seconds recovery.Ingebrigtsen says that while he runs more miles than his 1500m competitors, “the biggest difference is how often we train and the size of our sessions – we very rarely do more than 10km-12km of quality in one session”. He adds: “With having more sessions you can spread the volume out a lot more without having spikes and peaks in load.”5) No slacking even on Christmas Day“Last year, I ran twice and did 22k. I think that counts as an easy day,” he says, although he had to watch for digestion problems. “Christmas dinner in Norway is very rich in fat because we have pork ribs. I just had to be a little bit careful with the amount because we have different sausages, sheep and meat cakes too.”6) The treadmill is your friend,whatever time of year“I’ve always used treadmills, not only because of the conditions in Norway, but also to control a lot of the variables,” he says. “I put it on a certain speed, at a certain incline, and it’s always the same. It doesn’t matter if the wind is from the north or if it’s raining or cold.” He also does a morning threshold session on his treadmill, even in the height of summer, with punk and rock bands Green Day, Blink-182 and Black Sabbath topping his playlist.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJakob Ingebrigtsen wins the 5,000m final at the Ultimate Championships in Budapest.Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock7) Fast shoes help with recovery tooIngebrigtsen wears speedy and bouncy shoes for most of his running, with the Nike Zoom Fly 6 among his favourites. “You can decrease the load and impact by the amount of cushioning that’s now available in shoes,” he says. “So if I can get out of my Monday to Sunday programme 95% fatigued, that is enabling me to do the same the next week with the same amount of quality … just with 5% extra intensity.”8) Training in mud is a waste of timeIngebrigtsen sneers at the old-school approach of lots of running on trails and cross-country. “It is pointless. Training in mud or grass is not something I believe in. Let’s say I was going into a field and all of a sudden I’m doing 1k reps in mud and stones. Think about the extra risk that I’m taking, not only in terms of load and training but also tripping and snapping my ankle? Why would I risk it?”9) Always question what coaches can teach youPerhaps this is explained by Ingebrigtsen’s relationship with his father and former coach Gjert, whohe ended up facing in court in 2025. But he is adamant that discussing everything with his brothers Henrik and Filip is better than a top-down approach.“With a lot of coaches, it’s more like a priest. You can get really attached to them and it’s almost dangerous in the way it takes away responsibility from the athlete. If you have an ex-professional runner as a coach, it is always going to be ‘I did this, I did that, this is what worked for me, this is something new and revolutionary’. I don’t believe in it.”10) You always have to keep yourself accountableSome truths are universal when it comes to running and life. “You have to take responsibility for yourself,” he says. “Each individual and every athlete needs to build their own toolbox regarding their qualities and maybe lack of qualities. Responsibility, I think that’s the key word. And accountability.”Explore more on these topicsAthleticsRunningTraining programmesDistance runningcommentShareReuse this content

title: Infantino proposes an ‘independent external review’ of Fifa governance | Fifa | The Guardian
description: The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, has agreed to commission an independent governance review, in the wake of the World Cup sale debacle
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, has agreed to commission an independent governance review, in the wake of the World Cup sale debacle
Content: Gianni Infantino acknowledged to members that Fifa’s handling of a now-abandoned investment plan has caused concern.Photograph: Jarek Praszkiewicz/EPAView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino acknowledged to members that Fifa’s handling of a now-abandoned investment plan has caused concern.Photograph: Jarek Praszkiewicz/EPAFifaInfantino proposes an ‘independent external review’ of Fifa governancePresident writes to council and member nationsInfantino says he is ‘fully committed to leading Fifa’Matt HughesMon 21 Sep 2026 17.05 EDTFirst published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 16.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Fifa president,Gianni Infantino, has agreed to commission an independent governance review after coming under mounting pressure to do so in the wake of the World Cup sale debacle.The Guardian revealed last month that several members of the Fifa council had been lobbying for an external review of both the proposed Fifa Forward Enterprise sell-off and the Folarin Balogun controversy – with the Football Association chair, Debbie Hewitt, increasing the pressure last week by writing to Infantinodemanding the release of all documents relating to both issues.Uefa and Concacaf ask Gianni Infantino to give Fifa’s billions to its member associationsRead moreInfantino opted not to engage with the disgruntled members of the council, but in a letter sent to all 211 of Fifa’s member associations he has indicated his willingness to submit to external scrutiny for the first time.In addition, Infantino also invited proposals to review Fifa’s internal decision-making processes, which he said would be discussed at the next Fifa council meeting in Zurich on 15 October.“First, I will ask the council whether it wishes to commission an independent external review of Fifa’s current governance framework for major strategic initiatives and recommend potential improvements,” Infantino wrote.“Second, I will propose that the council establish a direct, structured and time-limited consultation with confederations, member associations and relevant stakeholders on how Fifa’s decision-making can be further strengthened.“The consultation would invite specific proposals on earlier institutional involvement, the respective roles of the president, the bureau, the council and the congress, and practical ways to strengthen transparency, participation and accountability in major strategic initiatives.”The Fifa Council, which comprises 28 representatives of the six confederations, eight vice-presidents and Infantino, is certain to approve the commissioning of an external review, although its terms of reference will be crucial in determining whether the world governing body is open to significant change or whether this represents the latest attempt by Infantino to shore up his power base before the presidential election in March next year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAll the presidents’ meddling: the Balogun scandal shows how Fifa can break football | Barney RonayRead moreIn his letter to the member associations, Infantino does not commit to reviewing FFE and Balogun specifically, however, so has stopped short of bowing to Hewitt’s demands.Infantino is also under pressure to release money from Fifa’s $6bn (£4.5bn) cash reserves to its members, with the presidents of Uefa, and north and central American confederation Concacaf, Aleksander Ceferin and Victor Montagliani last week making a formal request for a payout of at least $10m for each national association.The Asian Football Confederation president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, sent a similar letter on Monday with the issue of funding also to be on the agenda at the Fifa Council meeting next month.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The last two seasons were grim for Spurs. This is as bad as it’s ever been | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Pre-season thoughts of European qualification are already beginning to look bafflingly optimistic for Roberto De Zerbi’s team
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: Pre-season thoughts of European qualification are already beginning to look bafflingly optimistic for Roberto De Zerbi’s team
Content: Andy Robertson, Roberto De Zerbi and James Maddison were left disappointed on Saturday after another Spurs defeat.Composite: Shutterstock, GettyView image in fullscreenAndy Robertson, Roberto De Zerbi and James Maddison were left disappointed on Saturday after another Spurs defeat.Composite: Shutterstock, GettySoccer with Jonathan WilsonPremier LeagueThe last two seasons were grim for Spurs.
