This is as bad as it’s ever beenPre-season thoughts of European qualification are already beginning to look bafflingly optimistic for Roberto De Zerbi’s teamSign up for our free newsletter hereJonathan WilsonMon 21 Sep 2026 11.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn March, Tottenham, fearing possible relegation, spent big to bring in Roberto De Zerbi, who will probably never go into a negotiation with a stronger hand. There was obvious improvement and they stayed up on the final day of the season. Since then, Spurs have spent a net £175m ($234m) on improving the squad. The message seemed clear: the fiscal caution of the Daniel Levy era was over and this was a club willing to spend. Yet Spurs go into the first international breakbottom of the Premier League table.To an extent, the issue is confidence. On the opening weekend at Brentford, with a weird mishmash of a side, a team that was clearly undercooked, they were hammered 3-0 by much better-prepared opponents. That was not hugely surprising given how sensible Brentford’s transfer dealing had been and how early they had done it. More worrying was what happened the following week as Spurs, starting well before fading, lost 2-0 at home to Newcastle.Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s actionRead moreGoalless draws against Nottingham Forest and Everton seemed to have steadied the ship. Their biggest problem seemed to be a lack of confidence. They were tentative in possession, indecisive when chances did come. The two goals they managed in their3-2 defeat to Aston Villaon Saturday mean Spurs climbed above Coventry to second-bottom of the goal-scoring charts, but they are ninth for shots. That should be reason for frustration rather than panic; the goals will come eventually.But there are more concerning things to have come out of Saturday’s game. The lack of confidence in front of goal seems to have curdled into something worse, a more general mental degeneration. Again, they started well. The Villa keeper Zion Suzuki made a string of saves. And then just before half-time Villa scored a shambolic goal. Micky van de Ven was off the pitch receiving treatment. Andy Robertson, in preventing the ball running out for a corner, gifted possession to John McGinn. A cut-back, a scuffed shot and Johan Manzambi was unmarked in the six-yard box to score. It was a horrible goal to concede.The second goal they conceded was just as bad. A long punt not dealt with, Nicolas Jackson bringing the ball down, Van de Ven not getting tight enough, a shot that bounced in off Antonin Kinsky’s hand. The third Villa goal was whipped brilliantly into the top corner by Emi Buendía, but he had space to line it up before James Maddison, who had been marking João Gomes, got out to him. Perhaps Maddison could have been more aggressive, and the slight turn of his back as Buendía struck his shot is never a good sign, but this was at least as much a failure of structure.To an extent Spurs were unfortunate. Robertson might have cleared that ball for a throw-in, or at least got distance down the line, and Boubacar Kamara’s mishit cross could have gone anywhere. Jackson will not always be so deft in taking down a chest-high ball. Buendía, enormously technically gifted as he is, will not always pick out the top corner. But equally, each goal followed some sort of error: thePremier Leagueis full of high-class players who will take advantage of any slip.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy Tottenham are misfiring … and it’s not just down to the lack of goalsRead moreDe Zerbi spoke of Spurs being “too fragile”, by which he seemed to be talking both of their physicality and mentality. They have players returning from injury. Like so many clubs, they brought in players late. Preseasons have been curtailed, perhaps inadequate.Where the initial instinct was to be impressed by the numbers and the change of policy, doubts are now emerging about the nature of those summer signings. Is Sandro Tonali really worth £100m? Mateus Fernandes played for a relegated side. Jan Paul van Hecke wouldn’t be the first player to leave Brighton and find his level dip outside that precisely configured environment. Sávio and Omar Marmoush struggled to get into the team at Manchester City. Sávio’s finishing brought just two league goals in two seasons at City and the evidence of Saturday is that it has not improved.The sense had been that this season couldn’t be as bad as the last two for Spurs. There is no Europe to distract them. The injury crises couldn’t be as bad again. De Zerbi has proved his worth in the Premier League before. They have spent money. And yet this is as bad as it’s ever been. Once a club of Tottenham’s stature could have dismissed this as a blip, the kind of thing that would inevitably sort itself out as the season went on. After the last two seasons, nobody can be quite that confident again.It’s still implausible Spurs could be relegated, unlikely even that they’ll be in another fight, but those preseason thoughts of European qualification are already beginning to look bafflingly optimistic – and that will inevitably slow the rebuilding of the club.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueSoccer with Jonathan WilsonTottenham HotspurnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Paper trail of protests: José Mourinho plays the hits in Madrid derby defeat | La Liga | The Guardian
description: Facing Diego Simeone 13 years on, José Mourinho brought a print-out and paranoia. Some things don’t change. Some people don’t change much, either
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: Facing Diego Simeone 13 years on, José Mourinho brought a print-out and paranoia. Some things don’t change. Some people don’t change much, either
Content: José Mourinho holding up an A4 paper showing two moments he thought were red cards in the Madrid derby.Photograph: SkyJosé Mourinho holding up an A4 paper showing two moments he thought were red cards in the Madrid derby.Photograph: SkyLa LigaPaper trail of protests: José Mourinho plays the hits in Madrid derby defeatFacing Diego Simeone 13 years on, José Mourinho brought a print-out and paranoia. Some things don’t change. Some people don’t, eitherSid LoweMon 21 Sep 2026 11.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere were many questions to emerge from the Madrid derby, whichAtlético won 2-1in front of 70,514 very, very noisy people at the Metropolitano on Sunday afternoon, even if not the one José Mourinho was asking. Like: what year is this? Or: what was Dean Huijsen thinking? Why always Arda? And whatever happened to Vinícius Júnior? How come Koke isstillthe best? And how long before Giuliano Simeoneactuallybursts, hisatléticoinsides exploding across the pitch? Above all though, you were left wondering: where did Real Madrid’s manager get a printer from? And how did he get the bloody thing to work?You could still hear the singing outside when Mourinho turned up in the press room, laid down his glasses and sat. In his hand was a piece of paper. Thirteen years after his last derby, on the Santiago Bernabéu night whenMadrid lost the Copa del Rey finaland a13-yearunbeaten run against their neighbours, Diego Simeone had defeated him again. The stage was new –this stadium didn’t exist then– but his adversary was somehow still the same man, still dressed in black, and the scene was a bit like old times, a classic. Mourinho unfolded the paper and held it up. “We can save ourselves the bother of the press conference,” he said, “because the story is right here.”Printed on the back side of an Atlético info sheet were two screen grabs from the first half, one on top of the other. Someone had been sent to run off a copy, some footballing Natalie Harp or the manager himself coming back with a couple of gory, freeze-framed, full-colour closeups of tackles. The first showed Cuti Romero’s studs catching Jude Bellingham’s knee; the second showed Kang-in Lee on Fede Valverde’s ankle. Both should have been red, Mourinho insisted, and he was probably right, but neither was. It should have been nine against 11, he said; instead, it was 11 against 10 because early in the second half Huijsen dragged Giuliano Simeone down for the penalty that gave Atlético the lead and got him sent off. And that, Mourinho said, was that. End of story.View image in fullscreenReal Madrid’s Dean Huijsen was sent off after conceding a penalty to Atlético’s Giuliano Simeone during the derby.Photograph: Juan Carlos Lucas/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockAt which point he could have got up and gone, saved everyone the bother of the press conference like he promised, but no one wants that,least of all his president, and that’s the bit he does best so he carried on. Five questions he faced. Four of them were about the referee; so was the answer to the one that was not about the referee. And when he had finished, leaving the paper there for Diego Simeone to have a look at, most agreed:nowMourinho is back, and he’s playing the greatest hits, a hint of the nostalgia that had brought him “home” in the first place, a hint of the conspiratorial mindset too, echoes of him reading out13 “errors” made by the referee Clos Gómez16years earlier.Ghosts of 2023 quelled after Dortmund return to the Bundesliga summit | Andy BrassellRead moreThe “poor ref” – just 41, not an international, and named in advance rather than 24 hours before kick-off – couldn’t handle the pressure, which was “like the 1980s”, Mourinho claimed. The coach, who had already revived his famous “porqué” (why?) line after they lost at Betis, also ran through a list of decisions made by the referee in the VAR room, Daniel Trujillo Suárez – a man supposedly with history – which “make you laugh”. There was talk of “strange things” happening. He insisted he didn’twantto think ill of officials, didn’twantto say the league has been “set up” for others to win, didn’twantto think that these were anything other than honest mistakes –of course not. Hecongratulatedthe referees’ committee and vowed to fight for the title despite being six points behind already –ifthey let us. “I thought I would come back to find a different league to the one I left, but [at Madrid] they told me not and explained why not,” he said.What Mourinho didn’t say was anything really about the actual football, which might be because there wasn’t much football. The cards might have conditioned the game – of course they might – and he was entitled to insist on the reds, although you could debate Romero’s. But it was hard to avoid the feeling that Mourinho purposely missed a deeper point and revealed a deeper reality, that there could be no escaping the reality he sought to escape: that Madrid are just not very good. That too many questions were avoided and another could be asked:is that it? There was little evidence to back his brief claim that they played well in the first half and were set up to win it in the second – how? – and even if true, it pointed to something limited: wait, counter and it will come.With the players Madrid have, often it will, but Atlético were aware of that, planned for it; they were aware too of where the damage could be done, overloading Madrid’s left. Simeone’s side took more than twice as many shots and had two-thirds of the possession. They had done so cautiously, it is true, but they, not Madrid, had exercised control. Mourinho’s team had offered little before the potential reds, their first shot on target coming on 39 minutes and from 25 yards, and even less after the actual red, Atlético’s half unoccupied for most of the period except by a pigeon. With Guler withdrawn, their reaction didn’t exist. It’s not easy with 10 men, but there was barely a spark. Even the goal they did get in the 89th minute was an isolated moment and, for all the nerves at the Metropolitano, was followed by more chances for Atlético.Quick GuideLa Liga resultsShowEspanyol 1-3 Elche, Sevilla 1-3 Barcelona, Celta Vigo 5-0 Real Santander, Athletic Bilbao 0-0 Alavés, Osasuna 1-1 Rayo Vallecano, Valencia 2-3 Real Sociedad, Villarreal 3-1 Levante, Deportivo A Coruña 1-1 Real Betis, Atlético 2-1 Real Madrid, Getafe 1-0 MálagaWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.None of which would matter so much as a one-off, but these flaws were familiar. Madrid needed last-minute Carlos Espí goals tobeat Espanyoland Elcheand they’re still six points off the top already. It’s not even close to definitive just seven weeks in and Madrid’s rebuilding process has only just begun, but basic issues they have faced for the last two years remain unaddressed; Fabio Capello’s implausible2006-07 league title winis the only time Barcelona have ever had a lead that big at the top of the table and lost it. Hansi Flick’s team are flying; and right now you wouldn’t trust Madrid to take advantage even if they did slip up. Claude Makélélé summed them up as: “Nothing, nothing, nothing.” Which leaves only this: a print-out and paranoia, a campaign. Some things don’t change. Some people don’t change much, either.View image in fullscreenJonathan David (right) score the winner in a Madrid derby which Atlético dominated.Photograph: Alberto Gardin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockSome, though, do. The last time these two coaches met in a derby,Simeone’s son Giulianowas told he was too little to go to the final so he hung scarves around the living room and watched it from home with his brothers instead. It was late, it was a school night, and he was only 10. He is 23 now and these days he plays for them, a bundle of intensity going at it the way a fan would, and on the day these two “colleagues of war” – as Mourinho called them – met again 13 years later he decided the derby, forcing the penalty for the first and setting up the second. There is some footage somewhere of Giuliano as a ballboy racing up the touchline and leaping into his father’s arms, celebrating wildly whenAtlético scored against Madrid. A decade on, another derby day, and it happened again, only this time it was his dad sprinting up the line towards him.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTalking points“We give him the ball, he scores the goals,” Fermín López said. Over and over and over again. Raphinha, who isfilling in at centre forward, has now scored 12 league goals in just seven games, plus two more in the Champions League. He is five ahead of anyone else already. On Saturday night he scored an outrageously good hat-trick, the movement every inch the No 9, the touch and finishing at ridiculous speed all his, as Barcelona beat Sevilla 3-1. Sevilla went a goal up and were as good as anyone against Flick’s side so far this season but in the end just couldn’t live with them, coach Luis García calling them “stratospheric”. That’s seven wins from seven (eight from eight in all competitions), and31goals already, the captain leading the way. And not just with the goals, but with everything, taking everyone on a wild intense ride with him. Raphinha says thatLamine Yamal should win the Ballon d’Orbut right now there’s no one quite like him anywhere. That said, Lamine Yamal wasabsurdat the Pizjuan.At the end of their 0-0 draw with Athletic, Alavés goalkeeper Antonio Sivera walked off saying: “At last, at last!” His record was, he said, “ridiculous” but now at last he had done it. A European champion at U21 level, he is 30 now, and he had just saved the first penalty of his entire career.“When I played football as a kid in Croatia, everyone wants to play in one of Europe’s top five leagues and on my list Spain was bottom, but in the end it seems like Osasuna and La Ligaismy place: God’s path is different to mine,”said Ante Budimiron Saturday, after a lovely chest-and-volley goal took him to 100 in Spain.Speaking of which, what a way to celebratethe 100th birthdayof your home.PosTeamPGDPts1Barcelona724212Atletico Madrid79163Real Betis72164Real Madrid710155Sevilla71136Alaves75117Deportivo A Coruna72108Real Sociedad7-4109Villarreal71810Athletic Bilbao61811Getafe7-3812Rayo Vallecano7-5813Osasuna7-7814Celta Vigo72715Espanyol70716Racing Santander7-10717Levante6-4518Elche7-6519Valencia7-9420Malaga7-93Explore more on these topicsLa LigaReal MadridJosé MourinhoDiego SimeoneRefereesEuropean club footballAtlético MadridfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Thomas Tuchel rocked by five key withdrawals from England squad | England | The Guardian
description: Cole Palmer, Declan Rice, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento are all out because of injury issues
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Cole Palmer, Declan Rice, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento are all out because of injury issues
Content: Cole Palmer has made only three England appearances under Thomas Tuchel and again has been ruled out of contention.Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCole Palmer has made only three England appearances under Thomas Tuchel and again has been ruled out of contention.Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockEnglandThomas Tuchel rocked by five key withdrawals from England squadPalmer, Rice, Mainoo, Rashford and Livramento injuredJames Garner and Morgan Gibbs-White called-up as coverDavid HytnerMon 21 Sep 2026 09.39 EDTFirst published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 07.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel has been rocked by a host of withdrawals from his England squad, with Cole Palmer, Declan Rice, Kobbie Mainoo,Marcus Rashfordand Tino Livramento all out because of injury. The head coach has called up James Garner and Morgan Gibbs‑White to boost his options for the upcoming Nations League programme.Tuchel gave Palmer a high-profile recall on Friday for the beginning of the two-year international cycle that he hopes will end in glory at Euro 2028. England are back in the top division of theNations Leagueand they kick off against Spain at Wembley on Saturday. They then play Czechia and Croatia away before returning to Wembley to face Czechia.Palmer has felt a minor muscle issue and, not for the first time under Tuchel, has been forced to make himself unavailable. The Chelsea midfielder, who has started the season in fine form, has made only three appearances under Tuchel. He was left out of the World Cup squad after his form ebbed last season and the head coach spoke at his squad announcement of a fresh opportunity for Palmer. That will have to wait. The 24-year-old has been a virtual ever‑present for Chelsea this season, contributing four goals and two assists in all competitions.‘Embrace the chaos’: Tuchel aims to harness England’s football cultureRead moreRice’s withdrawal is not a complete surprise given his workload for a number of seasons. He needed to manage a nerve issue in a hamstring in the second half of last season which also affected his lower back and caused the midfielder discomfort at the World Cup. He has started all of Arsenal’s Premier League matches so far this season – plus their Champions League opener against Napoli. It has been decided that a rest at this point is the wisest course of action.Mainoo was taken off after 80 minutes ofManchester United’s game at Fulham on Sunday; a move from the manager, Michael Carrick, that led to boos from the travelling support. The midfielder was in the World Cup squad but he was the only outfield player not to get a single minute on the pitch. Tuchel has said Mainoo’s lack of involvement was no slight on him, his ability or application levels. It was, instead, purely down to decisions that Tuchel took for technical reasons. The head coach had promised to give Mainoo minutes over the coming fortnight or so.Mainoo’s United teammate Rashford was substituted in the 77th minute of the Fulham game and was seen holding the area by the front of his hip and groin as he slowly walked off.Tuchel has always championed Rashford; he called him up when he named his first squad in March of last year when the player was struggling for form. Tuchel wanted to show Rashford that he believed in him and he has always included the 28‑year‑old when he has been available.Tuchel seemed to lose a bit of faith after Rashford played poorly against the Democratic Republic of the Congo in thelast 32 of the World Cup finalstournament over the summer. Thereafter, Tuchel barely used him until England’s semi-final exit against Argentina, giving him a couple of minutes as a stoppage-time substitute in that game but nothing more. He did play him for the first 45 minutes of the third-place playoff against France.Livramento was named in the World Cup squad only to sustain a calf injury in training on the eve of the tournament. The Newcastle full‑back had to fly home. He underwent surgery and returned for his club as a substitute against Bournemouth at the start of the month. He had a setback in training beforeNewcastle’s win against Hull on Saturdayand was not in the matchday squad. The 23-year-old is yet to start a game this season.Garner comes in as a central midfield replacement for Rice and Mainoo while Gibbs-White adds to Tuchel’s options in the No 10 position in the absence of Palmer. Tuchel also has Jude Bellingham, Morgan Rogers and Eberechi Eze as No 10s. The players are due to report on Tuesday to St George’s Park.Explore more on these topicsEnglandThomas TuchelMarcus RashfordNations LeagueSpainnewsShareReuse this content

title: Granit Xhaka admits to receiving fake Covid vaccination certificate in 2022 | Switzerland | The Guardian
description: Granit Xhaka has been withdrawn from Switzerland’s squad after he admitted receiving a fake Covid vaccination certificate in 2022
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Granit Xhaka has been withdrawn from Switzerland’s squad after he admitted receiving a fake Covid vaccination certificate in 2022
Content: Granit Xhaka has described obtaining a fake Covid vaccination certificate, at a time when he was still at Arsenal, as a ‘mistake’.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenGranit Xhaka has described obtaining a fake Covid vaccination certificate, at a time when he was still at Arsenal, as a ‘mistake’.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PASwitzerlandGranit Xhaka admits to receiving fake Covid vaccination certificate in 2022Sunderland captain withdrawn from Switzerland squadHe will be questioned by prosecutor’s office in LucerneLouise TaylorMon 21 Sep 2026 07.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGranit Xhaka has been withdrawn from Switzerland’s squad after he admitted receiving a fake Covid vaccination certificate in 2022. The Sunderland andSwitzerlandcaptain – who was an Arsenal player at the time – has apologised for this “mistake” and will sit out his country’s forthcoming four Nations League matches.Xhaka is poised to be questioned by the prosecutor’s office in Lucerne next week as it decides whether any criminal proceedings will be initiated regarding the alleged issue of a series of false Covid certificates by a doctor based in the Swiss city during the pandemic. The doctor, who was first investigated in 2023, has denied the allegations.In a statement issued via Instagram, Xhaka acknowledged he had decided not to be inoculated against the virus. “In recent days there has been much reporting about a matter from my past. I would like to address this personally,” he wrote. “At the time, I was personally very uncertain and had serious concerns regarding the Covid-19 vaccination. I felt deep distrust of the vaccine and was plagued by fear and uncertainty.“In this turbulent emotional state, I obtained a vaccination certificate instead of clarifying my open questions through the proper channels. Today I clearly see this was not the right course of action. It was a mistake. I am sorry. I take responsibility for this decision, am committed to investigating the matter and am co-operating with the relevant authorities.”Xhaka tested positive for Covid in September 2022 and the 33-year-old – he turns 34 on Sunday – did not feature in Switzerland’s internationals that month.A spokesperson for the Lucerne cantonal prosector’s office said: “The aim [of the inquiries] is to clarify whether there has been conduct relevant under criminal law in connection with the possible fraudulent obtaining of a false certification and/or document forgery.”Should charges be brought, Xhaka could face a heavy fine or, theoretically, a five-year prison sentence. However, the imposition of the latter sanction – or any sort of custodial punishment – is understood to be extremely unlikely.Given that Xhaka was with Arsenal in 2022, Sunderland have told the Guardian they are not commenting on the matter. The midfielder left north London to join Bayer Leverkusen in 2023 and arrived at the Stadium of Light two years later.Xhaka, who has been capped 152 times by Switzerland, will now miss the Nations League matches away to North Macedonia and Scotland and at home against Slovenia and North Macedonia.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe president of the Swiss Football Association, Peter Knabel, said: “Granit Xhaka approached us about the situation last [Sunday] night and told us he would admit it publicly and take responsibility. We welcome Granit taking this step and facing the consequences. We jointly concluded that it is in the team’s interests to complete the entire camp without him. Our priority now is to calm the situation.”Although the Swiss FA possess the power to hit Xhaka with a suspension from football – something they could ask Fifa to apply worldwide – that scenario is regarded as highly unlikely.Explore more on these topicsSwitzerlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Harry Brook says Brydon Carse ‘just needs time away from the international scene’ | Cricket | The Guardian
description: England’s white-ball captain has said the fast bowler Brydon Carse ‘is working on a few things’, on the eve of the one-day international series against Sri Lanka
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: England’s white-ball captain has said the fast bowler Brydon Carse ‘is working on a few things’, on the eve of the one-day international series against Sri Lanka
Content: The England bowler Brydon Carse is still under investigation by cricket’s authorities.Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/PAView image in fullscreenThe England bowler Brydon Carse is still under investigation by cricket’s authorities.Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/PACricketHarry Brook says Brydon Carse ‘just needs time away from the international scene’Bowler ‘is working on a few things’England v Sri Lanka ODIs come a year before World CupAli MartinMon 21 Sep 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 15.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarry Brook is hopeful that Brydon Carse will break back into his England white-ball teams once the fast bowler is clear of his disciplinary proceedings, describing him as a “very good mate” who is “working on a few things behind the scenes”.Carse discovered recently he willnot face a criminal chargefor thelate-night incident in Derbylast month that led to him being briefly handcuffed. But while technically available for selection, the 31‑year‑old has not featured in England’s squads since that night as he awaits the outcome of an investigation by the Cricket Regulator.McCullum hails Brook’s captaincy as England move top of T20 world rankingsRead moreAsked before Tuesday’s first one‑day international against Sri Lanka at Chester-le-Street about the prospect of Carse returning down the line, Brook, England’s white-ball captain, replied: “He’s a very good cricketer. He’s been bowling extremely well for Durham. When his time for selection is up, that will be a debate.“I’m very good mates with Carsey. I’ve spoken a lot with him. Those conversations are private. I think he just needs time away from the international scene. He’s working on a few things behind the scenes and hopefully he’ll be ready at some point in the future.”More broadly, Brook believes the call for greater off-field professionalism has permeated through the England squads, both from Brendon McCullum, the white-ball head coach, and Stephen Fleming ahead of his new role with the Test side.Brook, who fell short of standards himselfwhen punched by a nightclub bouncer in New Zealand last winter, said: “The words Baz [McCullum] saidthe other day[were that] we want to be one of the fittest and strongest teams in the world. And to be able to do that we need to be preparing well on and off the field.”On top of Carse’s absence, England are missing Jacob Bethell and Sam Curran because of injury. Adil Rashid, another first-choice pick, will also miss the first match – and potentially the series – as he awaits scan results on an issue with his bowling hand sustained during the whitewash-sealing T20 winat Old Trafford on Saturday.View image in fullscreenAs well as captaining the white-ball teams, Harry Brook (centre) is a key figure in the Test team now under the direction of the new head coach, Stephen Fleming (right),Photograph: Matt West/ShutterstockIn come Tom Banton to open and Jamie Overton with the ball, while Rehan Ahmed, 16 years younger than Rashid at 22, gets his chance as the team’s wrist-spinner. Will Jacks, the new vice-captain, and Joe Root will provide finger-spin options.England go into the series opener with momentum from the 3-0 sweep of Sri Lanka that took themto No 1 in the T20 rankings. However their ODI ranking of seventh – one spot below the tourists – shows there is work to be done in 50-over cricket, despite having come from 1-0 down to win both their series this year.Brook said: “We’ve gone undefeated in the T20s and I think we can take a hell of a lot of confidence from that going into this ODI series. It’s more of the same. As a squad and a unit, we’re trying to play a higher-octane style of cricket and we’re really trying to put them under pressure with bat and ball.”The continued deployment of Jofra Archer and Josh Tongue at the end of a long, all-format summer for the pair is also notable. The next 12 months are about building towards the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa, meaning full-strength ODI XIs where possible and T20 series likely to involve more squad rotation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs an all-format player but one who limits his franchise cricket to the Hundred, Brook intends to plough through. His stated aim in this ODI series is improved strike-rotation during middle overs and playing against spin in particular, having enjoyed the input of Kevin Pietersen asthe team’s new white-ball mentor.View image in fullscreenTom Banton will be Ben Duckett’s sixth ODI opening partner since the start of 2025.Photograph: MI News/NurPhoto/ShutterstockAsked if Pietersen has also helped him to deal with criticism over shot selection and some of his brain fades in the past, Brook replied: “I haven’t had those conversations with him yet, but I’m sure it will come up at some point.“I think the way I’ve performed in my career so far, it’s almost a compliment to get those opinions. I’ll be trying my hardest to be the best player I can possibly be.”While Pietersen is with the senior white-ball side, his former England teammate Jonathan Trott has been named as head coach of the England Lions for tours of the Caribbean, South Africa and Sri Lanka this winter. Trott, who previously coached Afghanistan, replacesAndrew Flintoff after he stood down last month.Explore more on these topicsCricketHarry BrookEngland cricket teamSri Lanka cricket teamKevin PietersennewsShareReuse this content

title: The Joy of Six: epic sporting grudge matches | Sport | The Guardian
description: From F1 feuds to tennis’s soap opera love triangle, we run through half a dozen rivalries that have defined (not so) sporting culture
Author: Alex Reid
Headline: From F1 feuds to tennis’s soap opera love triangle, we run through half a dozen rivalries that have defined (not so) sporting culture
Content: Maria Sharapova, Cliff Thorburn, Pep Guardiola had their fair share of rivalries.Composite: Getty Images; Toronto Star/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMaria Sharapova, Cliff Thorburn, Pep Guardiola had their fair share of rivalries.Composite: Getty Images; Toronto Star/Getty ImagesThe joy of sixSportThe Joy of Six: epic sporting grudge matchesFrom F1 feuds to tennis’s soap opera love triangle, we run through half a dozen rivalries that have defined (not so) sporting cultureAlex ReidMon 21 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1Chris Eubank v Nigel BennA boxing rivalry so intense thattheir sons got to copycat it35 years later, yet the original is simply the best. That the preening, poetry-spouting, monocle-sporting, Jodhpur-wearing Eubank would irritate the rough-and-ready ex-squaddie Benn was hardly surprising. But the depth of the animosity was remarkable.“I personally do hate him,” intoned Benn, exuding malevolence at the contract signing for their 1990 middleweight fight,shown live on ITV. Eubank, who refused to even look at his foe, demanded “some parliamentary procedure” – but there would be none shown in the ring on fight night. Benn’s ferocity forced the unbeaten but untested underdog to fight fire with fire. Eubank, swallowing blood from a badly cut tongue, rose from a knockdown in the eighth round to stop Benn in the ninth and take his WBO title.In truth, the two Britons, who came from tough upbringings, had more in common than they cared to admit. But Eubank’s disdain for his profession – “a mug’s game” – antagonised Benn. Their 1993 rematch, which drew 43,000 people to Old Trafford and 16.5 million viewers on UK television, ended in a draw. It was their final in-ring fight but the two have made up, then fallen out again, several times since. We wouldn’t have it any other way.View image in fullscreenChris Eubank (left) irked Nigel Benn by describing boxing as a ‘mug’s game’.Photograph: Mirrorpix/Alamy2Nigel Mansell v Nelson PiquetDrive to Survive would give its right axle for a modern-day Formula One feud this bitter. The motor-mouthed, hot-tempered Piquet once referred to his fellow Brazilian Ayrton Senna as “a São Paulo taxi driver”. Yet Piquet’s dislike of his 1986-87 teammate Mansell raised his insults to the Shakespearean. “An uneducated blockhead,” was his view of his Williams partner, before Piquet tumbled into the gutter when referring to the British driver’s “stupid and ugly wife”.Mansell understandably bristled at such appalling language and the pair focused so much on their own battles throughout the 1986 season that Alain Prost snuck in to claim the drivers’ championship. In 1987, the moustachioed Mansell won six races to Piquet’s three, yet the latter was rarely off the podium and lifted his third world title. It was their final season as teammates but bridges have been built in retirement. After several TV appearances together, Piquet conceded that in terms of titles: “I should have won in 86, he should have won in 87.”View image in fullscreenNigel Mansell (right) savours his 1986 British Grand Prix victory at Silverstone as he shakes hands with his second-placed teammate Nelson Piquet.Photograph: Neville Marriner/ANL/Shutterstock3Pep Guardiola v José MourinhoSir Alex Ferguson v Arsène Wenger, Brian Clough v Don Revie, Diego Simeone v anyone – manager rivalries are a rich tapestry. But few burned with such intensity as Guardiola v Mourinho, particularly during their two years in La Liga. Real Madrid brought in Mourinho in 2010; the ultimate win-at-all-costs pragmatist to dismantle Barcelona’s tiki-taka idealists. Familiarity quickly resulted in contempt between the pair, who had spent four years together at Barça when Guardiola was a player and Mourinho an interpreter and assistant coach.“I hope one day he has the chance of winning a brilliant, clean championship with no scandal,” sneered Mourinho in 2011, as he accused Uefa of favouring Guardiola after a Champions League triumph. Cuttingly, he would later claim Guardiola’s baldness was a sign he “doesn’t enjoy football”. Barcelona won most of the head-to-head battles – includinga 5-0 league thrashing– but the sniping exasperated Guardiola who called Mourinho “the fucking boss” of the press room, adding: “I try to learn from José on the pitch, but I prefer to learn as little as possible from him off the pitch.” In 2012, Madrid won La Liga with 100 points and a burned-out Guardiola stepped away from management for a year.View image in fullscreenJosé Mourinho for once takes the higher ground against Pep Guardiola before el clásico.Photograph: Javier Soriano/AFP/Getty ImagesYet the toll was just as great for Mourinho, who left Madrid in 2013. The anticipated rematch in Manchester failed to spark, despite Mourinho’s gripes at City’s “financial sharks” and unfair league titles. Their feud has mellowed in the years since, but it is doubtful the two will be chuckling away on their own Iberian football podcast (‘Pep Talk’?) in retirement.4Serena Williams v Maria Sharapova“I think Serena hated me for being the skinny kid who beat her,” Sharapova wrote in her autobiography, recalling her breakthrough2004 Wimbledon final win at age 17. Well, Williams definitely hated that experience enough to win the next 19 matches against Sharapova, ending their rivalry with a staggering 20-2 win-loss record.The American’s relentless dominance, raising her game to new heights against one foe in particular, seemed fuelled by something beyond on-court competition. That they reportedly dated the same player, Grigor Dimitrov, added personal heat. “Hey, if she wants to be with the guy with a black heart, go for it,” said Williams in 2013, while labelling Sharapova “so boring”.Maria returned serve: “If she wants to talk about something personal, maybe she should talk about her relationship and her boyfriend that was married and is getting a divorce.” But Williams v Sharapova was bigger than any soap opera love triangle. It was a battle between the world’s best player and its most marketable; as if Williams – irked by the media attention paid to her 6ft, blond Russian adversary – had to remind everyone who the real era-defining athlete was. Happily, the two have actually become friends in retirement, with Sharapova asking Williams to induct her into the tennis hall of fame in 2025.View image in fullscreenSerena Williams and Maria Sharapova have made up off the court in recent years. Boo …Photograph: Reba Saldanha/Reuters5Ian Botham v Ian ChappellCricket’s ultimate ‘Ian-off’ first began with a bar brawl in Melbourne in 1977, when England’s 21-year-old rising star Botham got into it with Australia’s former Test captain Chappell. The details have been vehemently disputed ever since. Beefy’s version is him punching Chappell to end his vile pommie-bashing. Chappell’s take is a hysterical young Botham lost the plot and pushed him off his chair, then threatened him with a glass.They later clashed on the pitch – sledging, bouncers and send-offs – but it is away from the sporting arena that the rage has spilled over. More than 30 years of trading insults came to a head during the 2010-11 Ashes in Australia. Unable to walk past one another in a car park without some sly verbals, the two grandpas – combined age of 127 – went for each other and had to be restrained by their media colleagues. Three years ago a TV documentary, The Longest Feud: Chappell v Botham, brought no resolution with Chappell calling Botham “a coward”, while Sir Loin labelled his adversary “sad and lonely”. Sensational longevity.View image in fullscreenThis would not have helped relations between the two Ians – during January 1980’s second Test between Australia and England in Sydney, Ian Chappell was caught for nine runs by Ian Botham.Photograph: Patrick Eagar/Popperfoto/Getty Images6Alex Higgins v Cliff ThorburnWho didn’t the mercurial genius Higgins view as a loathed nemesis? Steve Davis (“I hate him”), Dennis Taylor (“I’ll have you shot”), Stephen Hendry (“Up your arse, you [c-word]”). Yet the greatest vitriol was saved for his polar opposite: snooker’s Canadian grinder, Thorburn. They played for money on Thorburn’s first day in England, which ended, Cliff recalled, with the Northern Irishman “at the top of the stairs with a ball in his hand about to throw it at me”.Higgins won most of their matches but lost the biggest: the 1980 world championship final, when ‘the Hurricane’ blew a 9-5 lead to lose 18-16. Away from the table, during the 1983 Irish Open, Thorburn lamped Higgins and kicked him in the groin after being told he was “a Canadian [c-bomb] who is shit at snooker”. Five years later, the (ahem) famously clean-living Higgins accused Thorburn of utilising “bags of white powder”, ruining Cliff’s reputation.View image in fullscreenNo smiles: before the final of the 1980 World Snooker Championship, posing with the trophy are Cliff Thorburn (left) and Alex Higgins (right) flanking referee John Street.Photograph: PAFor all the fallouts, a trace of respect endured. In 2009, a year before Higgins’ death, Thorburn won an embarrassingly one-sided legends match and was so upset at seeing his rival diminished thathe shed a tearas they embraced afterwards.Explore more on these topicsSportThe joy of sixPep GuardiolaJosé MourinhoSerena WilliamsMaria SharapovaIan BothamAlex HigginsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Banished to alien lands: Trump’s secret deportation deals | US immigration | The Guardian
description: After a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is one of thousands deported from the US on the back of shadowy deals made with dozens of countries. An in-depth investigation reveals the ‘show of force’ costing American taxpayers millions
Author: Louisa Loveluck
Headline: After a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is one of thousands deported from the US on the back of shadowy deals made with dozens of countries. An in-depth investigation reveals the ‘show of force’ costing American taxpayers millions
Content: Human rights lawyers say so-called third country national arrangements are part of a ‘show of force’ to discourage asylum seekers.Composite: Guardian Design/ReutersView image in fullscreenHuman rights lawyers say so-called third country national arrangements are part of a ‘show of force’ to discourage asylum seekers.Composite: Guardian Design/ReutersUS immigrationBanished to alien lands: Trump’s secret deportation dealsAfter a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is one of thousands deported from the US on the back of shadowy deals made with dozens of countries. An in-depth investigation reveals the ‘show of force’ costing American taxpayers millionsLouisa LoveluckMon 21 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 15.12 EDTShareNika’s storyView image in fullscreenNo one would tell the shackled detainees onboard theUS immigrationplane where they were going. The officers in charge would taunt them when they asked, they said. It was only when the seat-back video screens finally showed a map that the 18 migrants worked it out.Their destination wasCentral African Republic(CAR), a country few of them had even heard of.Nika, a 32-year-old Iranian woman, recalled how the handcuffs dug into her wrists. She begged the officers to loosen them, but they did not. Other passengers had it worse, she said. Some of the men were restrained in black and yellow body wraps, as if mummified, after resisting orders to get on the plane.Nika, who had fled Iran 18 months earlier after protesting against its regime, had imagined the US as a place of sanctuary. Iran was already one of the most repressive countries in the world when she left, and its horrors had only deepened since then: security forces gunned down thousands of other demonstrators this year, then Donald Trump’s administration launched the war there.After more than a year locked up in a US immigration detention centre, Nika, whose name the Guardian has changed to protect her family in Iran, was granted legal protections and freed on a judge’s orders. Within two weeks, the Department of Homeland Security had rearrested her, and days later she was on the plane heading 7,000 miles east.“They never told me they were going to deport me [to] this country,” she told the Guardian. “I don’t know anything aboutAfrica.”The Department of State warns US citizens not to travel to CAR because it says it is too dangerous. Nika spends most of her days there under a form of self-imprisonment, too scared to venture out from her small bedroom as she waits for an answer to the question on which her life depends: will she be sent back to Iran, and to a regime that could kill her?Nika is one of more than 25,000 peopledeported by the Trump administration to countries that are not their own. About 20,000 people have been bussed to Mexico, according to a count by Refugees International and Human Rights First. And more than 5,000 others have been put on flights to countries in Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean and central Asia to which they have no connection, and then, often, returned to the countries where US immigration judges had ruled their lives or liberty were at risk.Human rights lawyers describe these so-called third-country national arrangements as part of a “show of force” by the US intended to discourage migrants and asylum seekers from entering. People from Peru and Colombia have been sent to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). On 20 August, four Cubans, a Brazilian and a Cameroonianrefused to disembark in Liberia, and were sent to Equatorial Guinea instead.What is Trump’s third-country deportation policy and who does it target?Read moreIn order to compile the most comprehensive account of a policy that has mostly operated behind closed doors, the Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Paris-based Forbidden Stories. The consortium interviewed more than 100 people affected by, or involved in, the US drive to extinguish unauthorised immigration, and reviewed documents outlining details of the agreements made by US officials with governments around the world.It has tracked more than 100 flights that have carried migrants and asylum seekers to 28 different countries. This is likely to be an undercount as the consortium’s dataset only includes flights it was able to independently verify.The pace of flights is increasing. After an initial wave during the opening months of the second Trump administration, the number of deportations spiked in August again when, according to a count by Human Rights First, a record 16 flights carried people to 13 different countries that were not their own.A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that third-country removals were unlawful, arguing that they violated due process because people are not notified with enough time to mount a legal challenge to the decision to send them to another country. Human rights lawyers suggested this should immediately ground third-country deportation flights. The government is expected to appeal against the judgment, and to press ahead with its policy.A state department spokesperson said implementing the Trump administration’s immigration policies was a “top priority” and “we are unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America’s border security”. They added: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”The Trump administration has said the people it deports are criminals. Yet documents obtained by the Washington Post as part of this project show that a majority of the 35 countries that have signed deals with the US have said they will not accept migrants with violent criminal records.Map of the countries that have agreements with the US to accept people deported from the US as of 31 August 2026The people forced on to planes include those who spent most of their lives in the US, parents detained on the school run, the adult children of elderly relatives who depend on them for care.Many are people whose fear of returning home was deemed so credible that immigration judges barred their removal from the US. Nika had been granted “withholding of removal”, a protection for individuals who may face severe harm in their country of origin but are ineligible for asylum. On 28 May, not only was she released from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s custody, but she was eligible to find a job, to work, and to stay.Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/ReutersThe rug pullView image in fullscreenTrump’s deportation drive is being led by Stephen Miller (left)Nika’s lawyer, Sahar Jalili, is Iranian and, like her client, studied in Tehran. She took the case when she was pregnant, and often worked past the point of exhaustion. “That could be me,” she said of Nika.Combing through the case file, Jalili was shocked to learn ICE had officially decided to send Nika to CAR’s capital, Bangui, just eight days before a judge ordered her release from the detention centre. Her uncle’s family had prepared a room for her in Los Angeles. It took her two days to get there, and she spent a week with them, unfurling, after 18 months of hell.Her re-arrest on 8 June, during what ICE officers had presented as a routine check-in, felt like cruelty for cruelty’s sake, Jalili said.Nika said she had finished her appointment and left when an officer called her uncle and asked him to drive her back to pick up some papers.This time there were new questions. A man took Nika’s fingerprints, then her photograph, Jalili said. “Then he came back accompanied by a female ICE officer, and they said put your hands above your head.” She said she was arrested, handcuffed and led to the basement.Nika felt numb, she said, as she was transferred out of the detention facility that evening. Anti-ICE demonstrators smacked their palms on the side of the van as she passed through protests that had become a regular feature in LA.For Jalili, the previous two days had already been a blur, as she and her colleagues battled to save two other Iranian women from being put on the same plane for Bangui. The lawyers managed to get the other two women off the plane, but not Nika. The only difference between them was that Nika was detained last, so by the time a network of immigration lawyers had learned of her case, there was not enough time before the flight departed.Jalili said she begged every ICE officer: “Give me two days. Just two days.” She recalled: “They told me that they had respected the judge’s order to release her. But they’d never promised not to send her to a third country.”Image credit: Guardian Design/AP/ReutersAfrican dealsView image in fullscreenWhen Rabbiatu Kuyateh, 58, learned that the country she had been sent to, Ghana, was deporting her to her childhood homeland, she was so scared it took a scrum of people to force her into the waiting van.A video captured the moment last November when she was dragged, shoeless and distraught, by her hair. She still remembers the crack of her head on the stone steps as she begged not to be returned to Sierra Leone, screaming: “I’m not going.”Rabbiatu Kuyateh being forcibly removed from her temporary accommodation in GhanaKuyateh was a nurse and had spent most of her life in the US with her parents, after fleeing Sierra Leone. She cared for American coronavirus patients during the pandemic and had looked after disabled adults and children in the years since.She had scrapped hard for the life she built, she said. She had raised her son, Mohamed, alone and they had bought a house together. By the time Trump was re-elected in 2024, her parents were so frail she began each day by checking on them before her shift, and then returning to make sure they were ready for bed.In order to accelerate its expulsion of people such as Kuyateh, the Trump administration has remade the very institutions that were once intended to protect migrants who fled persecution.“I would describe [this] as the Trump administration’s way of trying to undermine the concept of asylum and refugee protection,” said Alma David, one of the leading immigration lawyers tracking the policy. “While the US understands that they can’t deport them to their home country legally, what they can do is basically send them through this third country that perceives itself as a transit hub.”Chart of monthly total number of people deported from the US by airThe drive is being led by Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, who has been open about his desire toend mostmigration to the US. In interviews with the Washington Post as part of the Deportation Project, current and former US officials said Miller had rolled out the third-country removals policy by pushing key appointments inside the state department that have allowed him to overrule other foreign policy objectives in service of his agenda.Among them is Christian Ehrhardt, a career state department official who heads the newly formed Office of Remigration – its nameincorporating a term adopted by the far rightto describe the forcible expulsion of minority ethnic immigrants. Ehrhardt has helped secure at least 13 third-country deportation agreements in Africa, after diplomatic tours through the continent.Internal records reviewed by the Washington Post show the Trump administration has pledged at least $410m (£307m) to secure such agreements with 35 different countries, almost a third of them in Africa.They indicate that $30m was earmarked for Cameroon, in order to support UN operations in the country, in return for accepting 1,000 migrants. The US has so far sent only 44. The DRC was promised $75m towards UN operations there, in return for accepting 2,000 migrants. It has only received 15, and flights to Kinshasa are on hold due to the country’s Ebola outbreak.The arrangements differ from country to country. A handful, including Eswatini, have agreed to accept people with violent criminal histories. But many have said they will not take anyone with a record of violence or other types of serious crimes. The state department did not respond to questions about details of these agreements.Ghana will only take people from west Africa; CAR did not specify nationalities, and the passengers on Nika’s plane were from places including Afghanistan, Iraq and Kyrgyzstan. Most of them had no ties to Africa at all, she said.On 1 July 2025, Kuyateh’s son, Mohamed, had accompanied her to a routine ICE check-in, as her immigration status required. He remembered his mother feeling anxious that the cuffs on an officer’s belt were for her. “I doubt it,” Mohamed told her. But when they called Kuyateh into an interrogation room, he was told to wait outside.“That’s the last time I saw her,” he said.During Kuyateh’s four months in ICE custody, Mohamed spoke to her often. He had not heard from her on the day in November when he said he was called by another detainee who told him she had been sent to Texas. “And I was just like, why is she going to Texas?”Two days later Kuyateh called him in tears. She was in Ghana, about to be sent to Sierra Leone.The footage of her being dragged into a bus, beginning the onward deportation, appeared to anger the Ghanaian authorities when it spread across social media, according to Malick, the Senegalese man, also deported from the US, who filmed it. The Guardian has given him a pseudonym out of concern for his safety. “They got angry,” Malick said. “They came in the evening, at night, with two trucks full of soldiers.”He said the troops drove his group to a remote military camp with faltering electricity and little contact with the outside world. The Ghanaian government did not respond to questions from the Guardian.One woman sent to the camp said she grew so scared of what might happen if she was returned to her native Senegal that she attempted suicide by drinking bleach. She was treated in hospital, then sent back to Senegal anyway. “I drank the bleach because I wanted to die,” she said. “Because they wanted to force me to go back to my country.”Image credit: Guardian Design/Rabbiatu KuyatehMalariaView image in fullscreenOnboard Nika’s flight on 11 June this year, the inflight video showed Ghana as its initial destination, so the passengers assumed that was where they were going. But their stop in the capital, Accra, was brief. The 18 passengers then landed in Bangui at 9.45pm, flight monitors said. The officers onboard removed their cuffs, but did not get off the plane.Deportation plane arriving in Bangui on 11 JuneFor several hours, the group did not meet anyone who spoke English. “They were communicating with hand gestures, like, get on a bus, and then they put us on a bus. And then they took us to give us some vaccinations, and I didn’t know what they were going to inject me with,” Nika said. It turned out to be for yellow fever.Her room was in an apartment block. She was told she could stay for three months. But the idea of returning to Iran was unfathomable.US-based Iranian rights groups say they have been unable to determine the fates of hundreds of other Iranian nationals deported back home during the course of the US-Israeli war on Iran. A recent lawsuit filed against ICE alleges the administration has shared the records of Iranian asylum-seekers with the very regime they had fled, further elevating the risk for those sent back.When a headache started clouding her brain, Nika thought it was a migraine. She felt sick, her body hurt. She had been bitten by so many mosquitoes that her skin looked bruised, she said. A medical report, seen by the Guardian, confirmed she had malaria. Speaking by phone, Nika said: “I didn’t even know what that was.”Map of nationalities of people deported to Central African RepublicBack in Los Angeles, Jalili waited anxiously on updates about Nika’s situation. There were injections every 12 hours to clear her bloodstream of parasites. The bad news did not stop when she was well enough to return to her accommodation. Jalili was horrified to learn Nika had been deported from the US without her passport, meaning she had neither identification documents, nor a visa, and on trips to the hospital and vegetable market, police officers used her lack of papers to make threats.The CAR government did not respond to a request for comment.The second time she was stopped, Nika said, the police officer mimed the action of putting cuffs on her. The message, she said, was: “I can take you in, unless you pay us.”Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/ReutersOld tools to grease the wheelsView image in fullscreenAs the Trump administration accelerates its third-country deportations, CAR is one of 13 host countries where the deported are being supported by the International Organization forMigration(IOM), a UN agency, which provides them with food, lodgings and psychological counsel upon their arrival.Although the Trump administration has announced sweeping cuts to its funding for UN agencies, there seem to be exceptions where the funds enable this deportation programme.In March last year, the state department spelled out the logic. From now on, it said, humanitarian funding would be used to “reduce mass and illegal immigration, such as funding voluntary returns of illegal aliens, incentivising governments to implement safe third-country agreements, and building the migration management capacity of other countries”.According to a federal government database that tracks spending, more than 60% of US grants to the IOM during the second Trump administration have gone to programmes in countries that accept deported migrants. In CAR, that meant an allocation of $85m. The highest US contribution to IOM in CAR under the Biden administration, according to the database, was $14m.Chart which shows US commitments made to Central African   Republic via the International Organization for MigrationNika said she had been treated well by the agency. “The people here are doing their best,” she said. The accommodation was secure and transport was provided when needed. “But at the same time, it’s not living. I’m breathing here, I’m not dying. But I can’t leave the house without a driver they provide here. I can’t find jobs. I don’t speak their language.”The potential for a negative perception of its involvement in the programme is something the IOM has grappled with. An internal risk assessment for a programme supporting third-country nationals sent from the US to one African country, seen by the Guardian, warns it could lead the agency to be “perceived as complicit”.An IOM spokesperson said in a statement that such assessments were conducted in order to ascertain whether host nations were able to commit to safeguards for the migrants, but added: “We are fully cognisant that states use financial assistance to advance their national priorities. However, IOM’s decisions to accept funding, provide post-arrival assistance, or support assisted voluntary return are guided by our own mandate and principles, and rest on a single question: whether our engagement will improve the lives of the migrants affected. In these instances, we believe strongly it does.”Many in the human rights field are uncomfortable the UN is easing the process for governments that agree to cooperate with the Trump administration.“It just feels very incongruous for IOM to be the organisation in charge of these men and women,” said Alma David. “These aren’t migrants in your typical sense. These aren’t people who chose to migrate,” she said. “These are people who were kidnapped, essentially.”Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AlamyLife in the shadowsView image in fullscreenPeople who had been returned from third countries to the places they were born describe a life now lived in the shadows. Kuyateh left Sierra Leone within days of being sent back there. The Guardian is not naming her location. “I don’t sleep at night,” she said. “Sometimes I just wake up. I’ll be sitting down like, what am I doing here? Why am I here?”She called her family every day. Sometimes, she said, she felt too sad to turn on the video and see their faces. She could get through the conversation with her mother without tears, she said, “but whenever I talk to my daddy, I’ll be crying. And when I sit here, I think about them. It hurts so much.”She was not sure what scared her more: the thought of dying alone in a foreign country, or knowing that her parents might die without her at their bedside.Freedom oppressed: the journalists caught up in Trump’s ICE crackdownRead moreAnnan, a gay man who fled Ghana after he was outed, and then hunted, by members of his family, said he was terrified when he touched back down in Accra. He had refused to disembark during his initial deportation from the US to Sierra Leone, and had to be forcibly removed from the plane, he said. He later begged authorities not to return him, he said, but they did not listen.In a statement, the Sierra Leonean government said it took its “international obligations seriously” but that questions relating to immigration protections afforded by an American court were for the US government to address.It added: “So far, no individual returned to Sierra Leone under the TCNA [third-country national arrangement] has requested to remain in Sierra Leone or not to be returned to his or her country of choice either in west Africa or beyond.”Annan’s mother had used her savings to pay for his escape to the US. She was distraught when he called to say he was back. “She knew she couldn’t protect me,” he said.He shared footage of where he lived now: an abandoned building with no electricity or running water in a neighbouring country, he said. He spent his daylight hours hiding, and walked almost an hour to find food when darkness fell. His bed was a blanket on the floor, although he barely slept, he said, too scared of being infected by one of the insects that crawled or buzzed around him. He said the loneliness felt crippling.In recent weeks, someone had texted him anonymously, saying that his survival, as a gay man, would not be tolerated. The message made him feel hopeless: he could run, it said, but he could not hide for ever.Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Rabbiatu KuyatehExhaustionView image in fullscreenIn Los Angeles, Jalili is getting more calls about clients bound for deportation flights. In June, a 30-year-old Iranian woman with a blood disorder that made her so weak she needed a walker was told she would be sent to the landlocked south African nation of Eswatini.Another client was “going crazy”, Jalili said. “They’re coming up with a new country for her every week.”Immigration lawyers said that while their jobs had always been hard, the scale of the efforts to obstruct those opposing the Trump administration’s drive to quash all types of irregular migration was unprecedented.When a client is detained, avenues of accountability have largely been shut, including the office of an independent ombudsman for immigration detention, which was responsible for investigating abuses and misconduct.In court, immigration lawyers can face hostile judges after the Trump administration purged some of those deemed insufficiently loyal to the deportation agenda. Meanwhile, the cost of even filing a case has risen steeply, under the terms of a bill passed through Congress in July last year.Jalili, like many others, spent much of the first Trump administration mounting legal challenges against a policy ofseparating children from their parents at the US-Mexico border. Knowing that what would follow might be worse, she decided on the eve of Trump’s re-election to start her own firm to fight the coming stormIt was not uncommon for calls from the desperate families of new ICE detainees to wake her in the night.One of the biggest challenges, said Erica Reilly, an immigration attorney based in Washington DC, was basic communication with ICE officers.“You send all these emails to deportation officers, and you’re like: ‘Hi, just following up again on the email I sent you last week, and the week before that, and the week before that, and the week before that, that you haven’t responded to,’” she said. “And they know they don’t have to because there’s no accountability.”Get in touchContact our investigations teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailinvestigations.contact@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreThe worst thing, she said, was the powerlessness. But the cruelty and the lack of access, she had come to believe, “that’s all the point”.“I think that the administration is doing what they can to get enough people to say, well, the alternative is too scary or too uncertain or too bad. I’ll just leave on my own.”Getting through the day meant reformulating the wins, Reilly said. “Getting a call back from a deportation officer shouldn’t be a win, but in this environment it is.”Jalili said she did her best to focus on the battles she could win. When she heard Nika’s flight had left for Bangui, she sank to the floor, called her mother, and began to cry. “It’s not a situation where you can just say: ‘Oh, I did my best.’”Nika had lost the life she knew in Iran. The US offered little better. Jalili listed the cost.“Being detained for 17 months. Being released from the federal judge’s order for 10 days. Being stripped away from her uncle’s hands. Being put in a car and then on a flight in shackles, and for 24 hours, sitting on that flight. She must have felt so lonely.”Image credit: Guardian Design/Alamy/AP/EPAAdditional reporting by Alice Speri

title: Black Tesla employees accuse company of fostering racial discrimination in major trial | Technology | The Guardian
description: Lawyers say Black employees at Tesla experienced ‘rampant racism’ that was left unchecked for years at their flagship factory in California
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: Lawyers say Black employees at Tesla experienced ‘rampant racism’ that was left unchecked for years at their flagship factory in California
Content: Brett Watson started by showing the court photographs taken throughout Tesla’s Fremont factory, including the N-word, swastikas, the Confederate flag, white supremacist logos and more scratched on to walls.Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBrett Watson started by showing the court photographs taken throughout Tesla’s Fremont factory, including the N-word, swastikas, the Confederate flag, white supremacist logos and more scratched on to walls.Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesTechnologyBlack Tesla employees accuse company of fostering racial discrimination in major trialLawyers say Black employees at Tesla experienced ‘rampant racism’ that was left unchecked for years at their flagship factory in CaliforniaDara Kerrin Oakland, CaliforniaMon 21 Sep 2026 19.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDozens of Black employees at Tesla’s flagship plant inCaliforniasaid they were subject to racist slurs, unequal pay and promotions, and bullying by supervisors on a daily basis, a situation management did little to nothing to fix.Their complaints form the basis of a lawsuit brought against the Elon Musk-owned electric car company by the state of California, which began trial with opening statements on Monday.Brett Watson, a lawyer for the California Civil Rights Department, started by showing the court a series of photographs taken throughout Tesla’s Fremont factory. There was the N-word scratched on to a grey-blue metal surface and written in black marker on a wall. “KKK”, swastikas, the Confederate flag, a white supremacist logo and “go back to Africa” had also been found scrawled in bathrooms, lockers, workplace benches and lunch tables, according to court documents.Watson listed a long string of racial epithets workers said were directed personally at them, including one incident where a Black worker said he was asked: “You want to hang from a tree?”“Despite what Tesla might argue, you will hear Black workers were deeply offended,” Watson said. “These experiences cannot be dismissed as a few bad apples … hundreds of complaints to Tesla and [the Civil Rights Department] will show these experiences were not isolated.”Watson said Black employees at Tesla experienced “rampant racism” that was left unchecked for years, and that workers referred to the factory as a “slaveship”, “the plantation” and “The Elon Slave Labor Association” – spelling out TESLA. One Black worker told state lawyers that he heard racial slurs as often as 50-100 times a day.The lawsuit was filed against Tesla in February 2022 and alleges that the company did not comply with the law, violating California’s Fair Employment and Housing Act. It alleges that the factory was racially segregated and Black workers were paid less, promoted less and terminated more frequently than their white counterparts.The state is seeking financial damages and injunctive relief, which could force Tesla to change its labor practices and internal policies. Judge Peter Borkon will make the final ruling in the bench trial, which proceeds without a jury.It’s the first such lawsuit brought against Tesla by a government agency on behalf of dozens of workers to go to trial. Legal experts say the outcome of the trial could have sweeping consequences for the company since the state is not bound by the same arbitration agreements as employees. The trial is expected to continue through the end of October.The car manufacturer has denied any wrongdoing andcalled the lawsuit“misguided”, saying it has “always disciplined and terminated employees who engage in misconduct, including those who use racial slurs or harass others in different ways”. Tesla said its Fremont factory has a majority-minority workforce and provides “the best paying jobs in the automotive industry” to tens of thousands of Californians.Tyree Jones, the lead lawyer for Tesla, began his opening statements repeatedly saying the N-word in a familiar tone. “What’s up my [N-word], my [N-word] …,” Jones said, adding that “none of which is used as a racial slur.”“By this action, the state of California attacks the way many Black people greet each other,” Jones said. “It’s offensive.”Jones touted Tesla’s accomplishments as an innovative electric car manufacturer and reiterated that the company provides thousands of jobs in the state. “The most prolific employer of California is on trial and under attack by the state,” Jones said. Referring to the racist graffiti around the factory, Jones said: “The state is blaming the employer, when it’s the victim.”After both sides presented opening arguments, the state called three witnesses. All were former Black employees at Tesla who said they either witnessed or were subject to racism at the company. The first witness worked at Tesla from 2021 to 2024 and said he was repeatedly bullied for being Black. In one incident, he alleged he was called the N-word by another employee, and the company gave him a write-up on the situation instead of the instigator.The second witness was a senior security manager who worked at Tesla for six years. He said he habitually worked with human resources when complaints of discrimination came in, and that he witnessed Black employees treated differently than workers of other races. In one incident, he alleged Musk got involved when white employees were caught drinking alcohol on site and the CEO directed management to override company policy and not terminate the workers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNadia Clark, who previously worked as a police officer and an army officer for decades, was employed as a security manager at Tesla’s Fremont facility from 2020 to 2022. She testified about an incident where a white employee called her the N-word more than ten times in a row in front of other workers.“I likened Tesla to some experiences I had on the street and in the military. It was like a pressure cooker,” Clark said. “These words have a violent landing.”She said the incident shook her and she immediately reported it to human resources, but never got a response. Clark decided to leave Tesla that day. “There were these continuous patterns that were never addressed,” Clark said. “The work environment was unsafe, hostile, and I never returned.”This lawsuit is one of dozens of discrimination suits brought against Tesla, including a case brought by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, a federal agency. The suits allege the company has routinely ignored complaints of repeated racial harassment. In 2022, a federal jury awarded Owen Diaz, a former Tesla employee, $137m for these claims – one of the largest awards given in a discrimination lawsuit brought by a single worker, although a judge later reduced that sum.Similar suits have beenfiled by female employees, who allege they experienced physical assaults, harassment and catcalling at Tesla facilities across the country.Tesla has denied wrongdoing in all cases, and has said it implemented various policies in recent years to prevent racist and sexist conduct and punish it when it does occur.Musk, who joined Tesla in 2004 and became the CEO in 2008, has also been accused of racist behavior, includingpromoting white supremacist conspiracy theorieslike “white genocide”. The CEO also tends to broadcast his thoughts on X, a social media platform he owns,fixating on anti-immigrant contentand theories that the white race is under threat.Musk is not expected to be called as a witness in the trial. He hasn’t publicly addressed the legal proceedings under way and did not return a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyTeslaElon MuskCaliforniaWest CoastDiscrimination at workRacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Chancellor vows to stay on for Germany’s ‘democratic future’ after latest loss to far-right AfD | Germany | The Guardian
description: Merz seeks to shore up support after CDU loses two state elections and is ejected from Mecklenburg parliament
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Merz seeks to shore up support after CDU loses two state elections and is ejected from Mecklenburg parliament
