Content: Merz described the results as a ‘disaster’.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersView image in fullscreenMerz described the results as a ‘disaster’.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersGermanyChancellor vows to stay on for Germany’s ‘democratic future’ after latest loss to far-right AfDMerz seeks to shore up support after CDU loses two state elections and is ejected from Mecklenburg parliamentLatest German election humiliation puts Merz on borrowed time as CDU unrest growsKate Connollyin BerlinMon 21 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTFirst published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 08.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGermany’s beleaguered leader,Friedrich Merz, has vowed to keep his fractious coalition government together for the good of the country’s “democratic future” after his conservative party suffered a drubbing at the polls in two state elections.Merz, who has vowed to plough ahead with an unpopular reform agenda, dismissed speculation over his position, saying it was vital that he and his coalition government remained in place.10:54Rise of the far right in Germany: how worried should we be? – The LatestLatest German election humiliation puts Merz on borrowed time as CDU unrest growsRead more“We are determined to live up to the historic responsibilities our country is facing,” Merz said on Monday. “It is about nothing less, and nothing more, than the democratic future of our country.”Germany faces political uncertainty in the aftermath of three hefty defeats for Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) this month, which saw it ousted from a state parliament for the first time, and the far right and far left making strong gains at its expense.Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state election 2026 resultsOn Sunday the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) emerged victorious in the coastal northern state ofMecklenburg-Western Pomerania for the third time in a German state, securing 38%. The anti-immigration, pro-Russia AfD party’s leaders predicted Merz would be out of office in months, as they set their sights on securing victory at the next federal election in 2029.“The chancellor certainly won’t make it to the end of the year,” Leif-Erik Holm, the AfD’s top candidate in Mecklenburg, said. “I think the twilight of the chancellor’s era has begun.”View image in fullscreenThe AfD’s Leif-Erik Holm, Kristin Brinker, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla after the state election results.Photograph: snapshot/Future Image/B Elmenthaler/ShutterstockMerz described the results as a “disaster”, in particular the CDU’s ejection from Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s state parliament, where it failed to reach the 5% barrier needed after losing more than half of its voters to the far-right AfD and centre-left Social Democrats. The result was all the more shocking as Mecklenburg was once a CDU stronghold.In Berlin on Sunday, the CDU fell to second place behind the far-left Linke party, which is on track to lead the next government in the city-state and could give Berlin its first Turkish-born mayor in its lead candidate, Elif Eralp.Berlin results chartIn Mecklenburg, the SPD under its existing state leader, Manuela Schwesig, is expected to lead a three-party coalition government. Her campaign had focused almost wholly on presenting herself as a buttress against the AfD, as well as distancing herself from the federal government’s reform agenda. The SPD is Merz’s coalition partner in the federal government.Although the CDU’s poor performance had been predicted, Sunday’s outcomes only added to the extreme pressure on Merz already afterthe CDU’s crushing defeat to the AfD in the state of Saxony-Anhalttwo weeks ago, which triggered the first serious speculation over his future as leader.Last week, the CDU’s powerful regional leaders governing in eight states gave their backing to Merz, but questions remain as to how sustained their support will be. At the same time there appear to be few candidates willing to step up to the post, which is increasingly being viewed as a poisoned chalice.On Monday, Merz dismissed the idea that the outcome was a personal rebuke. “The reasons for these election results go far beyond my own person,” he said. “We are witnessing a profound transformation of the political party system in Germany as well as in many other countries around the world.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKarin Prien, the CDU’s deputy leader, listening to Friedrich Merz in Berlin a week before the latest state elections.Photograph: Nadja Wohlleben/ReutersKarin Prien, the education minister and deputy CDU leader, accepted accusations that the government was failing to take voters’ fears seriously enough. But she said the government had no choice other than to continue trying to reform Germany from within, at a time of chronic economic weakness and global instability.“Without support and steadfastness we will not be able to achieve the necessary reforms, which are by no means a given. Nevertheless, not everything can remain as it is,” she told the broadcaster Deutschlandfunk.“The chancellor knows he will have to change, at least in how he addresses the people … We are a strong country, we have every chance of mastering this challenge together, but I believe that cooperating with each other will be crucial for this, and for the party it means we must broaden our appeal.”Doubts over the efficacy and fairness of the government’s agenda – which includes an overhaul of the pension system, a reduction in overbearing bureaucracy and cuts to income tax for the less well-off – played heavily into both election campaigns.On Monday, SPD leaders said they remained confident in their coalition with the CDU, but said that changes to the agenda were necessary.View image in fullscreenThe SPD’s Lars Klingbeil flanked by his party co-leader Baerbel Bas (left), and Manuela Schwesig, the state leader in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.Photograph: Christoph Rutenkolk/EPALars Klingbeil, the deputy chancellor and finance minister, said: “Saying we will ignore what the voters said to us in three state polls won’t work.”While the country needed reforms, he said, they “must be fair and they need support in the population”. The labour minister, Bärbel Bas, also of the SPD, said the plans needed a “reality check”, but said “nothing would be more lethal than letting this coalition break apart over some technicality”.Rubbing salt into Merz’s wounds, the Kremlin on Monday waded into the election analysis, calling the AfD’s win in Mecklenburg a response to Berlin’s refusal to buy cheap Russian gas, which has jolted the economy and caused prices to soar, contributing to voter dissatisfaction.The Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said: “Naturally, Germans, ​or at ​least some of them, are looking for an alternative to the current authorities in order to improve their situation. That is a natural process.”Explore more on these topicsGermanyFriedrich MerzEuropeAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)The far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Venezuelan shot by ICE seeks medical care as lawyer says bullet lodged in back  | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: Sshooting of Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez comes months after increased federal immigration enforcement in Austin
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sshooting of Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez comes months after increased federal immigration enforcement in Austin
Content: Flowers and candles are seen near the site where a Venezuelan man was shot in his vehicle by an ICE officer in Austin, Texas.Photograph: Eric Gay/APView image in fullscreenFlowers and candles are seen near the site where a Venezuelan man was shot in his vehicle by an ICE officer in Austin, Texas.Photograph: Eric Gay/APICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Venezuelan shot by ICE seeks medical care as lawyer says bullet lodged in backShooting of Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez comes months after increased federal immigration enforcement in AustinEmiliano Tahui Gomez in AustinMon 21 Sep 2026 19.13 EDTFirst published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 14.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Venezuelan man who was shot by a federal immigration officer in Texas on Sunday spoke out from detention on Monday afternoon when he was able to call his lawyer, in the middle of a press conference, and plead for better medical care.ICE agent shoots and wounds Venezuelan man at traffic stop in Austin, TexasRead moreWilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was taken from a hospital inAustininto Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, even though he apparently still has a bullet lodged near his spine and is in much discomfort.“I haven’t received any medical attention. I’m in a lot of pain,” Garcés Pérez said, in a phone call to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. “I have expressed my pain [to the guards].”He recounted that he had spent the night sleeping on the floor of a cold room in a detention center about 140 miles from Austin, where he was taken hours after being shot by an ICE officer after a traffic stop on Sunday afternoon.Lincoln-Goldfinch had told the Guardian earlier on Monday that the federal officer’s bullet was still inside her client. Garcés Pérez said he had been told it is too close to his spine to operate on to remove at this time.The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), whichoverseesICE, has not responded to requests for more information and comment. Inan initial statementissued shortly before midnight on Sunday night, DHS said Garcés Pérez was in stable condition and that he was “in federal custody pending removal” out of the US.Theshootingdid not come out of the blue, amid an immigration enforcement surge in Austin.ICE had already been active in theTexascapital of late, but then matters escalated dramatically on Sunday as shots rang out.Garcés Pérez was in the process of delivering a DoorDash food order on the city’s north side when ICE encountered him shortly before 1pm on Sunday. Video posted online appears to show an ICE officer getting out of his car and shooting at Garcés Pérez’s car three times.His car, as later visible at the scene, had a large dent on the front passenger side. Garcés Pérez, who was hit once in the back between his shoulder blades, is a Venezuelan national who has lived in the United States for two years, according to his lawyer, but had been ordered removed from the US. Garcés Pérez told onlookers who rushed to the scene that he had been shot because he hadn’t stopped.1:34Protesters gather in Austin after ICE agent shoots and wounds man – videoGarcés Pérez was taken to a downtown hospital for treatment but, according to lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, was whisked away from there by ICE late Sunday afternoon.For a few hours, his partner and the lawyer could not locate him, then on Monday morning Lincoln-Goldfinch told the Guardian he’d been located at the South Texas ICE Processing Center, in Pearsall.“Bullet still lodged in his back. No pain meds,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said by text on Monday.Garcés Pérez said when he called the attorney on Monday that what appeared to be a normal car had pulled up next to him before veering in his direction. When he eventually stopped and spoke to what turned out to be an ICE officer, he said he asked to move his vehicle to a nearby parking lot because he wanted his car to be there if he was arrested. He was told he could not and when he drove further the ICE vehicle crashed into him and then he was shot, he said.Austin, the politically liberal capital city of conservative Texas, has repeatedly found itself at the crossfire of the immigration debate.The state’s Republican leadership has often sought to make an example out of the city, forcing local leaders to weaken Austin’s policy of not collaborating with ICE.Local leaders said this summer has marked a low-profile but aggressive surge in immigration enforcement in the region, spurred by a jump in ICE acting alone, relying less on state troopers to stop people and hand them over.“As mayor of the city of Austin, I’m very angry about this,” Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said on Sunday. “A person being shot on the streets of Austin by someone purporting to be law enforcement, particularly when it’s ICE, is something that causes me to be unhappy and angry..”TDHS said that it was leading the investigation into the shooting, alongside the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). However Austin leaders have called for local and state involvement, citing public distrust of ICE.The exact details leading up to the shooting remained unclear on Monday.Video posted on social mediashows a man running out of the black SUV and shooting at Garcés Pérez’s almost stationary blue sedan from behind it. Three gunshots ring out. A witness, Nedavia Bolaños, got closest to the scene andshared videowith the Guardian of ICE officers standing next to the car as the man clutched his chest, before Austin police officers arrived and were the ones to render first aid.Within an hour, more than a hundred protesters had gathered at the site, chanting expletives against ICE and waving Mexican, American and Guatemalan flags. Several protesters could be seen washing their eyes and mouths in pain, after they were sprayed with what they said was teargas or chemical spray.The shooting came after several months of increased immigration enforcement, particularly in immigrant-heavy neighborhoods, suburbs and exurbs.Austin city council member José “Chito” Vela, who represents the neighborhood where Garcés Pérez was shot, said that he has heard constituents describe an enforcement bump driven by a rise in unilateral action by ICE. While ICE was largely seen making immigration arrests after Texas Department of Public Safety traffic stops for the first year or so of the secondTrump administration, they have begun to act increasingly on their own, Vela said.City leaders had previously raised concerns over the increased action. Congressman Greg Casar, an Austin Democrat who leads the Congressional Progressive Caucus, has sent a letter to DHS demanding cooperation in an “immediate, independent investigation” into the shooting, the full release of any footage the federal authorities have of the shooting, and “accountability for any wrongdoing by the agent responsible”.Later on Monday, lawyers representing Garcés Pérez filed both a writ of habeas corpus and an injunction motion in court, hoping to stave off any attempt to deport him before an investigation is complete. In the application for the habeas petition requesting his release, Garcés Pérez’s lawyers argued that he qualified for a type of visa given to victims of crimes.Explore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US immigrationAustinTexasProtest (US)Trump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rwandan man charged with crimes linked to 1994 genocide in first case brought in UK | Crime | The Guardian
description: Dr Vincent Brown will appear at Westminster magistrates court charged with seven offences
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Dr Vincent Brown will appear at Westminster magistrates court charged with seven offences
Content: A dossier on Vincent Bajinya, now Vincent Brown, from 2006.Photograph: José Cendón/AFPView image in fullscreenA dossier on Vincent Bajinya, now Vincent Brown, from 2006.Photograph: José Cendón/AFPCrimeRwandan man charged with crimes linked to 1994 genocide in first case brought in UKDr Vincent Brown will appear at Westminster magistrates court charged with seven offencesPress AssociationMon 21 Sep 2026 13.38 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has been charged with crimes linked to the genocide in Rwanda in 1994 in the first case of its kind to be brought in the UK.Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, who used to live in Kigali, the capital of Rwanda but now lives in Islington, north London, will appear at Westminster magistrates court on Tuesday charged with seven offences.The charges are one of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said.Frank Ferguson, the head of the CPS special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “The charges relate to allegations that Dr Brown took part in the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda in 1994.“He is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others.“The Crown Prosecution Service made its decision after reviewing a file of evidence submitted by the war crimes team at the Metropolitan police.“We concluded that our legal test for bringing criminal charges had been met.“The Crown Prosecution Service makes prosecution decisions independently of police and government, on the evidence available and in accordance with the law. Criminal proceedings against Dr Brown are now active.“The defendant has the right to a fair trial, and it is extremely important that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online that could prejudice those proceedings.”The charges arose after an investigation by the Metropolitan police war crimes team, which began in September 2019 after a request from the Rwandan government.This was to investigate those allegedly involved in a genocide in the Rugenge district of Kigali in April 1994.Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of counter-terrorism policing London, said: “To secure the first-ever UK charges related to a genocide has involved a huge amount of work and determination from officers in the war crimes team.“This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes.“The war crimes teams remains committed to ensuring those suspected of involvement in genocide and other atrocity crimes are held accountable through due legal process.“A number of other investigations remain ongoing into other individuals in the UK for similar offences related to the genocide in Rwanda.“Our thoughts remain with the people of Rwanda, particularly those who lost family members and loved ones during the genocide against the Tutsi.”Explore more on these topicsCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Planetary boundaries’ necessary for flourishing of life have been massively breached, scientists warn | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: New report shows key indicators of Earth’s health are ‘outside the safe operating space’ as climate disaster looms
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: New report shows key indicators of Earth’s health are ‘outside the safe operating space’ as climate disaster looms
Content: Trucks carry wood from a deforested area in Para state, Brazil, during the Cop30 UN climate change conference in November 2025,.Photograph: Mauro Pimentel/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrucks carry wood from a deforested area in Para state, Brazil, during the Cop30 UN climate change conference in November 2025,.Photograph: Mauro Pimentel/AFP/Getty ImagesClimate crisis‘Planetary boundaries’ necessary for flourishing of life have been massively breached, scientists warnNew report shows key indicators of Earth’s health are ‘outside the safe operating space’ as climate disaster loomsOliver MilmanMon 21 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe planetary life support systems relied upon by humans have deteriorated to their worst levels ever recorded amid ongoing pollution and habitat destruction, according to a key yet grim annual update by scientists.Of the nine “planetary boundaries” that help determine whether life can flourish on Earth, seven are being breached at their highest ever levels of transgression, according to the latest planetary health check, a process that was established in 2009.The seven key indicators in the danger zone include climate change, change in biosphere integrity, land system change, freshwater change, modification of biogeochemical flows, introduction of novel entities and,for the first time last year, ocean acidification.Climate ‘feedback loops’ could worsen global warming by 30%, study findsRead moreOnly two of the assessed areas, stratospheric ozone depletion and atmospheric aerosol loading, have shown improvement over the last decade, although researchers warn that atmospheric aerosols, which can form air pollution, are still a problem in several regions of the world.The coalition of 60 scientists who conducted the analysis of the key guardrails for human life under the auspices of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research warned that the consequences of breaching these planetary boundaries is “becoming increasingly clear all around us”.“The diagnosis is unambiguous – pressure is rising across every planetary boundary already outside the safe operating space,” said Boris Sakschewski, lead author of the report. “It means that the risk of large-scale, persistent and potentially irreversible change is increasing, while our margin for error in tackling these problems is shrinking.”While there is little time to reverse this parlous situation, humanity does still possess the knowledge and capacity to do so, according to Johan Rockström, a climate scientist and report co-author. “Accelerating action to return to the safe operating space across all planetary boundaries is essential to protect lives and livelihoods, and to deliver on the promise of shared future prosperity,” he said.The assessment, which pored over the latest scientific data, seeks to establish the state of the defined areas that provide a “safe operating space for humanity”. Human civilization has developed in the past 10,000 years due to a relatively stable climate and natural resources that sustainably provide us with food, shelter and a safe living environment.These conditions are being badly warped, however, by the ongoing release of huge amounts of planet-heating pollution, from the burning of fossil fuels, and the mass disposal of other pollution, such as plastic into our environment. Habitats such as forests and wetlands are being torn apart, fragmented and flattened to make way for agriculture and urban areas, imperiling animal species and natural systems upon which we depend.The ability of landscapes and bodies of water to cope with this and act as a buffer to the worsening climate crisis is “weakening and may be significantly overestimated”, the new report warns. While forests and oceans have sucked up a vast amount of the carbon dioxide we have emitted, there are signs that these natural systems are faltering.For example, there is a chance that the Amazon rainforest, a huge carbon store, could reach a tipping point where it becomes a savannah, which would have “serious implications for climate stability, food and water security, and human health around the world”, the report states.The report comes on the heels of a series of extreme events around the world in the past year that scientists say have been made far more likely by the upending of our environment.Huge floods hit Pakistan last year, while this year has seen record heat and wildfires across Europe, the hottest ever summer in the US, anda disastrous flood on the Tibet-Nepal border. The oceans, which are absorbing much of this extra generated heat, have hit new temperature records.“These are not separate emergencies; the planet is telling us, in every region at once, that it is out of balance,” said Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim, chair of Planetary Guardians, a coalition of scientists, business leaders and activists.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I hear this same story wherever I go, whether from a pastoralist watching the rains fail season after season or a coastal community watching the sea rise. The 2026 planetary health check puts data behind what communities on the frontlines already know from living it. We do not have the luxury of treating these as separate crises any longer.”Private jets pollute up to 14 times as much as commercial planes and are undertaxed in US, report saysRead moreThe report was released on Monday shortly after the start ofClimate Week, a major gathering of politicians, business leaders and activists in New York City that leads up to the UN general assembly.Members of the Planetary Guardians – including Mary Robinson, the former Irish president; Juan Manuel Santos, the Nobel laureate and ex-president of Colombia; and oceanographer Sylvia Earle – attended the launch of the report. They are part of more than 100,000 attenders expected at Climate Week, which organizers said was set to be the largest ever.Despite the record numbers attending talks, announcements and other events aimed at tackling the climate crisis, however, the head of the week’s non-profit organizer acknowledged a general reticence to talk about global heating.Helen Clarkson, chief executive of theClimate Group, said that even though the world had been visibly racked by recent climate-fueled disasters, “I’ve not seen this level of ‘green-hushing’ before. Many companies tell us they will be here, but not very visibly.“But after a summer like this when we saw so much tragedy driven by climate change, this is the time to be loud,” she added. “The world is standing on the edge of the abyss, and people are seeking change.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisGreenhouse gas emissionsPlasticsWaterOceansWetlandsPollutionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Colombia declares public calamity as wildfire threatens popular tourist area | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Wildfire forces evacuations and burns through mountains surrounding Villa de Leyva in the north-east
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Wildfire forces evacuations and burns through mountains surrounding Villa de Leyva in the north-east
Content: A volunteer looks on as a forest fire burns on San Marcos Hill in the municipality of Villa de Leyva, Colombia, on 20 September 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA volunteer looks on as a forest fire burns on San Marcos Hill in the municipality of Villa de Leyva, Colombia, on 20 September 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesColombiaColombia declares public calamity as wildfire threatens popular tourist areaWildfire forces evacuations and burns through mountains surrounding Villa de Leyva in the north-eastAssociated Press in BogotáMon 21 Sep 2026 13.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleColombian authorities declared a public calamity as a wildfire burned through mountains surrounding one of the country’s best-known colonial towns in the north-east, scorching large swaths of vegetation and forcing evacuations.Nearly 20 active fires are burning across the South American country. Dry conditions have increased fire danger in Colombia as it braces for the effects of El Niño, which can help wildfires spread.The fire in Villa de Leyva, a popular tourist destination about 160km (100 miles) north-east of the capital, Bogotá, began Saturday on a mountain overlooking the town. By Sunday evening, authorities said about 290 hectares (717 acres) had been affected – an area roughly equivalent to 400 soccer fields – and the blaze was about 50% under control.Strong winds have complicated efforts to contain the flames, which at times advanced toward populated areas. Local authorities declared an emergency, suspended in-person classes Monday and carried out preventive evacuations, including at hotels near the fire.View image in fullscreenFlames and smoke rise from a wildfire in Villa de Leyva, Colombia, on 20 September 2026.Photograph: Sebastian Arguello/ReutersMore than 400 firefighters, emergency workers, residents and volunteers took part in the response, while four helicopters dropped water on the flames. Carlos Amaya, the governor of Boyaca, where Villa de Leyva is located, said aircraft carried out about 170 water drops Sunday, releasing 240,000 liters (63,400 gallons).Fabio Arjona, Colombia’s environment minister, said preliminary information from the disaster management agency suggested it may have been deliberately started, but authorities were still investigating.Abelardo de la Espriella, the Colombian president, said Sunday on X the Villa de Leyva fire was about 50% controlled and contained on the ground.Colombia’s national disaster management agency said in its latest nationwide update that authorities were monitoring 27 forest fires, with 19 still active and eight under control. Nine of the active fires were in Tolima, a mountainous region south-west of Bogotá, while others were burning across several parts of the country’s Andean region.The weather agency said last week that 279 municipalities were under some level of wildfire warning, including 36 under its highest, red-alert level, with much of the risk concentrated in the Andean and Caribbean regions.Between 16 June 16 and 6 August, Colombia recorded 438 forest fires in 191 municipalities, affecting about 7,153 hectares of vegetation, according to government figures.NeighboringEcuadoris also battling a wave of wildfires. Ecuador’s national risk management agency said Sunday that 12 fires remained active across the country, while more than 21,800 hectares of vegetation have burned so far this year.High temperatures and strong winds have helped flames spread rapidly in some areas. A fire on the slopes of Ecuador’s Imbabura volcano burned about 300 hectares before being brought under control Sunday after three days of firefighting.El Niño is a periodic warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean that can reduce rainfall and raise temperatures in parts of the country, creating conditions that allow wildfires to spread more easily.Disaster officials have said the period of greatest risk across the region from the developing El Niño is expected between October and April, with wildfires and water shortages among the main concerns.Explore more on these topicsColombiaWildfiresAmericasEl Niño southern oscillationEcuadornewsShareReuse this content

title: How Saudi oil scientists ended up working on the world’s most important climate reports | Fossil fuels | The Guardian
description: Guardian investigation reveals fossil fuel links of IPCC authors, with experts declaring the body’s conflict of interest policy ‘not fit for purpose’
Author: Damian Carrington
Headline: Guardian investigation reveals fossil fuel links of IPCC authors, with experts declaring the body’s conflict of interest policy ‘not fit for purpose’
Content: Gas fires light the sky at a Saudi Aramco plant in Ras Tanura.Photograph: Thomas J Abercrombie/National Geographic/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGas fires light the sky at a Saudi Aramco plant in Ras Tanura.Photograph: Thomas J Abercrombie/National Geographic/Getty ImagesFossil fuelsHow Saudi oil scientists ended up working on the world’s most important climate reportsGuardian investigation reveals fossil fuel links of IPCC authors, with experts declaring the body’s conflict of interest policy ‘not fit for purpose’Damian Carrington,Eoghan Gilmartin, Silvia Lazzaris, Rita Cruz, Simon Guichard and David HaasMon 21 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 15.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn her first day as an expert author on the world’s most important climate reports, Prof Julia Steinberger knew nobody else, so she sat down at a stranger’s table for breakfast.“Hi, I’m Julia. I’m from the University of Lausanne,” she said. The man across the table replied: “I’m Mustafa Babiker. I work with SaudiAramco.”Aramco, Saudi Arabia’s state oil company, isresponsible formore of the carbon emissions driving the escalating climate crisis than any other company in history, and the kingdom has long been amajor blocker of climate action.Wasn’t that a conflict of interest, Steinberger asked. The UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), on which they both now sat, produces the reports that underpin UN climate negotiations andinformnational climate policy around the world. No, Steinberger recalls Babiker saying: he had declared the relationship on the IPCC’s conflict of interest form. “That didn’t seem to me a very good answer, but he was friendly and we had a very nice breakfast.”Dr Babiker has worked for Aramco for 20 years. His appointment as a coordinating lead author for the IPCC’s coming Seventh Assessment Reportsparked controversyin the climate science community last year. But a Guardian investigation, carried out in partnership with a team of international journalists, has now revealed that Babiker is far from an isolated case.At least a dozen IPCC lead authors are employed by or linked to Saudi Aramco, Saudi institutions and other oil and gas interests, the investigation found. One IPCC vice-chair, part of the body’s leadership group, also represents the kingdom at global climate negotiations as a government employee.View image in fullscreenSaudi Aramco’s Ras Tanura oil refinery and oil terminal.Photograph: Ahmed Jadallah/ReutersThe IPCC is the world’s most authoritative organisation on climate science, with its reports approved by 195 countries. They are produced by hundreds of lead authors from around the world with expertise ranging from atmospheric physics to the impacts of extreme weather.The Guardian examined the 223 lead authors inworking group III, the part of the IPCC that assesses how emissions can be reduced or removed from the atmosphere. Its work evaluates emissions-cutting policies and technologies and so is directly relevant to the economic interests of countries and companies. Working groups I and II cover the science of climate change and its impacts.The investigation identified 20 cases with strong conflict of interest concerns. More than half involved authors linked to Saudi institutions, a concentration that raises broader questions about the kingdom’s influence on how the reports are produced.The IPCC’s conflict of interest policy has been described as “not fit for purpose” by experts who have reviewed the Guardian’s investigation.‘It’s the first time we have so many Saudi-linked authors’Another Aramco employee selected as an IPCC lead author is DrDiego Armando Moya Pinta, whohas workedas an energy and sustainability scientist at the company since 2022. The IPCClistshis affiliation only as Imperial College London, where he is an honorary senior research fellow.As one of 14 lead authors for the chapter on energy systems, Moya Pinta will assess options for reducing emissions across the energy sector, an area with direct implications for Aramco’s business. “I don’t think there would be any question that a case like this would fit under the IPCC’s conflict of interest policy,” said Prof Kevin Elliott, an academic at Michigan State University specialising in research ethics.Yet in March 2026, the IPCC’s conflict of interest committeereported finding no conflicts of interestamong any of the authors selected for the Seventh Assessment Report, the next edition of its biggest and most influential publication.The disconnect between the committee’s conclusion and the presence of authors from the world’s largest petroleum company “raises questions about whether the IPCC conflict of interest policy is fit for purpose or being properly applied”, said Rachel Kennerley, a senior campaigner at the Center for International Environmental Law.Alongside the two Aramco employees, working group III includesfive authorsfrom the King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center (KAPSARC), a Saudi government-funded thinktank chaired by the country’s energy minister and whosestated missionis to “advance Saudi Arabia’s energy sector”.View image in fullscreenSaudi Arabia’s energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, speaking at the Future Investment Initiative in Riyadh in 2024.Photograph: Hamad I Mohammed/ReutersLittle-known outside energy policy circles, KAPSARC has the same number of authors in working group III as Imperial College London and Vienna’s International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis,makingthe three institutions the most represented in the group.Another energy systems lead author, Prof Zain Yamani, at King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals, was conductingjoint researchwith Aramco’s New Energies Research Division during the past year while also serving in his IPCC role. Theresulting paper, co-authored with two Aramco scientists, was published in July. A further IPCC lead author, DrSyed Masiur Rahman, works at the same university, which advertisesits proximityto Saudi Aramco as offering “countless opportunities for collaboration and innovation” between the organisations.A lead author on the chapter on carbon dioxide removal technologies, ProfHussein Hoteitat the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, was finalisingresearchbased on a demonstration project for underground carbon storage at the time of his appointment to the IPCC. Saudi Aramco conceived the project and provided substantial financial support.“It’s the first time we have so many Saudi-linked authors in the IPCC, above all in working group III,” says Dr Kari De Pryck, a political scientist at the University of Geneva, who is an expert in the organisation’s governance.De Pryck sees the growing presence of Saudi-linked authors in the context of a broader shift in the kingdom’s climate diplomacy. Itslongstanding opposition to cutting fossil fuel burningin UN climate negotiations is increasingly complemented bythe promotionof technological climate solutions. “When it comes to the IPCC, the Saudi strategy now focuses onadvocatingtechnologies like carbon capture that would limit the impact on its fossil fuel economy,” says De Pryck.View image in fullscreenSaudi Aramco’s Manifa oilfield.Photograph: ReutersThere is alsoan overlapbetween the kingdom’s government and the IPCC’s scientific leadership. Dr Malak Al-Nory, one of working group III’s seven vice-chairs, is asenior adviserto the Saudi energy ministry. Vice-chairs help oversee the assessment process and guide its scientific and technical work. They also evaluate authors’ conflict of interest disclosures and can refer cases to the IPCC’s conflict of interest committee.The IPCC does not preclude government-employed scientists working on its reports. Unusually however, Al-Nory has continued to represent Saudi Arabia in UN climate negotiations while serving as a vice-chair. She waspart of the kingdom’s delegationto the Bonn Climate Change Conference in June 2026, underscoring concerns about the compatibility of her dual roles.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Conflict of interest rules aren’t an accusation that someone has done something wrong,” said Tzeporah Berman, chair of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty. “They exist to protect an institution’s integrity by ensuring professional, financial or governmental interests that could reasonably be perceived to influence its work are disclosed and appropriately managed.”“If the IPCC’s conflict of interest system can look at an IPCC vice-chair working for the Saudi energy ministry, Aramco employees serving as lead authors, and this concentration of authors from Saudi state-linked institutions and find nothing that needs to be managed, then the policy is clearly not fit for purpose,” she said.A ‘gap’ between policy and realityUntil 2011, the IPCC had no institution-wide conflict of interest policy.That changed after a bruising credibility crisis in 2010, when mistakes in its major reports andallegations of financial conflictsinvolving its then-chair promptedan independent reviewof the organisation’s procedures.The resultingpolicystates that its purpose is “to protect the legitimacy, integrity, trust, and credibility of the IPCC”. It adds: “It is essential that the work of the IPCC is not compromised by any conflict of interest for those who execute it.”Kennerley said there was a gap between the IPCC’s written criteria and how it operated in practice. She said national representatives had raised questions over a lack of guidelines on how the policy was enforced, adding that another major problem was transparency. Authors’ conflict of interest declarations are not made public, and the conflict of interest committee provides no detail about its deliberations.A spokesperson for the IPCC said no authors had been referred to its conflict of interest committee as all potential conflicts of interest reported could be resolved by the working group vice-chairs. “The strength of the IPCC lies in its commitment to diverse leadership and author teams, multiple expert and government review processes, and the inclusive nature of its assessments,” the spokesperson said. “These safeguards collectively support the objectivity, integrity, authority and credibility of IPCC reports.”They said details of the review of conflict of interest declarations were confidential due to data protection legislation. “The public can judge whether relevant interests have been adequately assessed and managed [by the] assessment reports themselves, which go through robust, multistage reviews which are [publicly] documented.”Regarding the high number of experts linked toSaudi Arabia, the spokesperson said: “No individual author, institution, sector or country determines the conclusions of an IPCC report. Conclusions are developed collectively by large, internationally and scientifically diverse author teams.” They said IPCC authors were leading experts in their fields and deliberately drawn from a wide range of backgrounds, including government and the private sector.View image in fullscreenEngineers and journalists at a Saudi Aramco plant in Hawiyah in 2021.Photograph: Amr Nabil/APHoteit, at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, said: “There is no conflict of interest. My research and contributions related to the IPCC work were fully funded and supported by my employer, which is acknowledged in thereferenced paper.” The multi-author paper also states: “We thank Saudi Aramco for conceiving and conducting this pilot project and for providing substantial financial support.”Aramco declined to comment, and none of the other individuals or institutions responded to requests for comment.Eleven of the 20 cases of strong potential conflicts of interest identified by the Guardian investigation were Saudi-linked, with the rest spread across other nations and linked to issues including industry collaboration, fossil-fuel sponsorship of academic institutions’ research, environmental campaigning and sustainable finance.Dr Jeroen Oomen, a climate governance researcher at Utrecht University, said: “The IPCC’s mandate as the arbiter of climate science has always been based on its independence and neutrality. The conflicts [reported in this investigation] risk damaging such a reputation.”Dr Adam Standring, a researcher at the Lisbon School of Economics and Management, said the IPCC was created to bridge science and politics, and it “straddles those two worlds”. That hybrid role was fundamental to its success, he said, but also a source of problems.Berman said: “At a time when fossil fuel interests and some governments are fighting to delay the transition away from fossil fuels, the IPCC should be fiercely protecting its independence. That means strong disclosure requirements, meaningful conflict of interest rules and safeguards capable of addressing both actual conflicts and reasonable perceptions of conflict.”The IPCC said there was no process currently under way to amend its conflict of interest policy.This investigation was developed with the support ofJournalismfund Europeand is also being published in L’Humanité in France, Lucy sui mondi in Italy,Visão in Portugaland Nano (3Sat) in Germany, Austria and Switzerland.Explore more on these topicsFossil fuelsIntergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)Climate crisisClimate scienceSaudi ArabiaOilAramcofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tree vaccines and gene-edited butterflies among biotechnology projects funded by UK ‘invention agency’ | Conservation | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: The tax-funded brainchild of Dominic Cummings hopes to find ways to speed up wild species’ evolution
Author: Matthew Ponsford
Headline: Exclusive: The tax-funded brainchild of Dominic Cummings hopes to find ways to speed up wild species’ evolution
Content: The swallowtail butterfly will be gene-edited by researchers at the University of Exeter.Photograph: Allan Drewitt/Natural England/PAView image in fullscreenThe swallowtail butterfly will be gene-edited by researchers at the University of Exeter.Photograph: Allan Drewitt/Natural England/PAConservationTree vaccines and gene-edited butterflies among biotechnology projects funded by UK ‘invention agency’Exclusive: The tax-funded brainchild of Dominic Cummings hopes to find ways to speed up wild species’ evolutionMatthew PonsfordMon 21 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVaccines for ash trees, skin treatments for newts and gene-edited swallowtail butterflies are among 14 tax-funded projects from the UK’s “invention agency” aiming to accelerate nature’s ability to adapt to the climate crisis.The £54m accelerated adaptation programme from the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency (Aria) – a public body that funds high-risk, high-reward tech projects – aims to investigate applications of biotechnology that can speed up wild species’ evolution and help them to adapt to new threats such as global warming and disease.The 14 teams announced on Monday will receive a share of an initial £30m in grants over the next two years. They will develop tools to protect native British wildlife species, including the English oak tree and critical pollinators such as the buff-tailed bumblebee, said Yannick Wurm, the director of the accelerated adaptation programme at Aria.View image in fullscreenA buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) on Marlborough Downs in Wiltshire, England.Photograph: Nick Upton/AlamyThe world’s natural environments are changing so rapidly owing to the climate crisis and human pressures that many species can no longer adapt quickly enough, said Wurm, a professor of evolutionary genomics at Queen Mary University, London. “This cohort is a first exploration of how we can harness some of the powers of biotechnology to responsibly help wild animals and plants to overcome challenges they face,” he added.The projects aim to work alongside conventional nature conservation measures, such as protected reserves, to give environmentalists a new set of “precision tools” that Wurm compares to mRNA vaccines for humans.Aria is the brainchild ofDominic Cummings, the former chief adviser to Boris Johnson, who said it would fund “crazy” ideas that could “restore Britain’s place as a scientific superpower”.The publicly funded body has attracted criticism for its research into controversialgeoengineeringtechniques and grants that have given millions in UK taxpayer moneyto US tech companies and venture capital firms. Matt Clifford, Aria’s chair, was forced to stand down this month over what one senior MP called a “clear conflict of interest” after taking a job with Anthropic, the developer of the AI chatbot Claude.One team announced on Monday, led by researchers at the University of Exeter, will use Crispr-Cas9 gene-editing on the swallowtail, a butterfly onBritain’s red list of endangered species, to increase its resistance to insecticides used widely on farms. Another project developed by Rothamsted Research, the 180-year-old agricultural research facility in Hertfordshire, will edit the genes of long-lived tree species such as oaks to reproduce in months rather than decades, meaning they can rapidly develop adaptive responses to drought and invasive pathogens.New cat species identified for first time in more than a century in BoliviaRead moreEnvironmentalists across the planet have debated using increasingly powerful biotechnology and gene-editing techniquesto aid conservation. At the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s (IUCN) world conservation congress last October, more than 90 NGOs raised concerns that these technologies will irreversibly alter natural systems with unpredictable effects.The ban was narrowly rejected after 250 scientists signed an open letter to highlight the potential benefits of synthetic biology, which could allow small islands to eliminate invasive mice that threaten more than 100birds and reptiles. Instead, the IUCN adopted its firstglobal policy on synthetic biology, including a set of stringent criteria for proposed solutions.This IUCN policy has been one foundation of Aria’s ethical policy, said Marie-Claire Cordonier Segger, the chair of the programme’s ethical and social responsibility advisory committee. Although the projects are intended for the wild, none of the experimental solutions will be released during the programme, which will last until 2030, said Cordonier Segger, a professor of international law at the University of Cambridge. “The decision was made early to have the strongest possible code,” she said, adding that all grantees will work in secure labs.Chris Thomas, founding director of the Leverhulme Centre for AnthropoceneBiodiversityat the University of York, said the projects that Aria is funding offer potentially valuable tools at a time when many species and ecosystems face drought, pathogens and other threats.Skin-eating chytrid fungal infections, which have caused population declines in more than 500 amphibian species, seems a “particularly worthy target” for these new approaches, said Thomas, who is not involved in the Aria programme.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBiologists have so far had few options to prevent the spread in the wild, leading the Boston-based research lab Cultivarium to propose their project in partnership with Imperial College and Queen Mary University, London. It would genetically engineer a bacteria that lives on amphibians’ skin to produce proteins that “bind and stop” the infection, said Henry Lee, Cultivarium’s co-founder. “We’re not genetically engineering the amphibian; rather what we’re trying to do is we’re trying to give them a shield,” he said.View image in fullscreenSymptoms of ash dieback on a young ash coppice in Wayland Wood, Norfolk. Scientists at Aria believe they can give the trees a ‘vaccination’ against the disease.Photograph: David Mark/AlamyAnother project aims to prevent ash dieback –a fungal disease that is expected to kill half of Britain’s ash trees– by injecting the tree with RNA molecules that interfere with the fungus’s ability to infect. “So it is like giving the tree a vaccination,” said project lead Sarah Christofides, a mycologist at Cardiff University.But Thomas cautions that the impact of these solutions will probably be “modest” and difficult to assess. While 90 amphibian species have gone extinct owing to chytrid infection, others show signs of adaptive resistance, he said. Making certain species within a pond more resistant will inevitably affect the species not targeted, he added.To think that these interventions have an important role to play in preventing biodiversity loss “is probably pretty naive”, he said. To be deployed in the field, solutions will not only have to prove they are effective in the lab but win approval from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, which has tightly controlled the releases of genetically modified organisms.A further £24m will be allotted to projects that have shown success over the initial two years. Wurm said he hoped that a handful of successes would be “world-changing”.Ultimately, our “most urgent challenge” is to halt and reverse human-controlled drivers of environmental change, he said, but these projects aim to offer solutions in the places where we cannot.Explore more on these topicsConservationScience policyGene editingSynthetic biologyBiodiversityAsh diebackButterfliesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Airlines urge action after UK flights delayed and cancelled again | Transport | The Guardian
description: Nats says fault at Prestwick has been ‘fixed’ after airports in Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland are hit
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Nats says fault at Prestwick has been ‘fixed’ after airports in Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland are hit
Content: An affected passenger at George Best Belfast City airport.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAView image in fullscreenAn affected passenger at George Best Belfast City airport.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PATransportAirlines urge action after UK flights delayed and cancelled againNats says fault at Prestwick has been ‘fixed’ after airports in Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland are hitGwyn TophamTransport correspondentMon 21 Sep 2026 16.45 EDTFirst published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 05.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAirlines have called for “action and accountability” over the UK’s air traffic control services after a technical issue led to flights being disrupted for the second time in a fortnight.Dozens were cancelled and others severely delayed after a fault on Monday morning at National Air Traffic Services (Nats), this time at its second control centre at Prestwick in South Ayrshire.The fault, predominantly affecting Scotland,Northern Irelandand northern England, was fixed by about 10.30am, but only after airlines including British Airways and easyJet were forced to make cancellations.Flight chaos for hundreds of thousands was caused in ‘millisecond’ by software errorRead moreA Nats spokesperson said it had been “working with airports and airlines to safely lift air traffic regulations as quickly as we can to minimise any further disruption”, and apologised for the disruption. They said the problem was “unrelated to the issue two weeks ago”.Despite the relatively quick fix, at least 200 flights in and out of UK airports were expected to be cancelled by the end of Monday, according to the analysts Cirium.The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, posted on X just after 10.30am, notifying that the latest technical issue had been resolved.She wrote: “I know this will be deeply frustrating for passengers after the previous issue. There may be some delays as things reset.”The incident came less than two weeks after a serious problem at the Nats control centre in Englanddisrupted travel for hundreds of thousandsof passengers, and only three days after the companyreleased an initial reportthat promised to “continually improve the critical service we provide”.Nats said Monday’s incident had been caused by a connectivity issue at its Prestwick centre.Among the stranded passengers at Glasgow were a bride and groom who had expected to fly to their Las Vegas wedding with family and friends. Their BA flight to Heathrow was cancelled, meaning they would miss their connection to the US on Monday, and they rebooked for Tuesday.The bride-to-be, Barbara Ann Stoddart, said: “I’m completely stressed out. I have still to go to the county court in Vegas to go and get the marriage licence, and I’ve got to be there three days in advance … If there’s any hiccups I might not be getting married on Saturday now.”View image in fullscreenBarbara Ann Stoddart and her fiance, Andrew Lithgow.Photograph: Lucinda Cameron/PAThe Civil Aviation Authority said it had reminded airlines of their responsibilities to look after passengers whose flights were delayed or cancelled, but that passengers were unlikely to receive compensation for delayed or cancelled flights.“We consider that disruption caused by the technical issue at Nats Prestwick centre inScotlandon 21 September is likely to be considered the result of ‘extraordinary circumstances’ under passenger rights rules.“This means that although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident,” a CAA spokesperson said.Airlines called for action to address repeated failures, with Ryanair reiterating its calls for the Nats chief executive, Martin Rolfe, to resign.EasyJet, one of the most-affected airlines on Monday, said the latest flight disruption “once again calls into question the resilience of Nats’s systems and demonstrates the need for firm actions to prevent these repeated failures”.BA described it as “yet another technical fault with Nats” and said it was disappointing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJet2’s chief executive, Steve Heapy, said it was “simply not good enough for this critical national infrastructure to keep letting customers down”.“What customers and airlines need now is action, accountability and proper resilience, and we need it urgently,” he said.Ryanair’s chief operations officer, Neal McMahon, said: “Just three days after Nats assured airlines and passengers that it had introduced robust ‘mitigation plans’, its flight data processing system has failed again.“More than 25,000 Ryanair passengers have already suffered disruption, with more than 140 Ryanair flights delayed.“Enough is enough. Martin Rolfe should resign today.”Rolfe, who was paid £1.4m last year including bonuses, has come under increasing pressure since the major outage on 8 September, the third high-profile incident in just over three years. Rolfe apologised and said he took full responsibility, but Nats has denied that the incidents are related.A “radar-related issue” in July 2025 a caused an air traffic control failure that disrupted the journeys of thousands of passengers and forced the cancellation of more than 160 flights.The biggest incident, in August 2023, affected more than 700,000 passengers when flights were grounded across the UK after a “rogue flight plan” sparked a system failure.Alexander has commissioned the CAA to conduct an independent review of Nats and check the findings of its initial report into the 8 September breakdown. She said the government still needed “to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos”.Andy Burnham, asked whether the head of Nats should be sacked, said Alexander would have to “get to the bottom” of the problems.“These are clearly serious issues and they need to be fully investigated, and I know the transport secretary is taking these issues extremely seriously,” said the prime minister.“Further issues today do cause even greater concern, but initially this is a matter for the transport secretary to get to the bottom of what is behind this and why there has been a recurrence.”Explore more on these topicsTransportAir transportAirline industryScotlandNorth of EnglandNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Inquest into British aid workers killed in Gaza may call on Israeli and UK military chiefs | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Lawyer tells review hearing that families wish to know whether weaponry involved in the deaths was made in UK
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Lawyer tells review hearing that families wish to know whether weaponry involved in the deaths was made in UK
Content: John Chapman, Jim Henderson and James Kirby, three British workers who were killed in an air strike in Gaza.Composite: World Central Kitchen/PAView image in fullscreenJohn Chapman, Jim Henderson and James Kirby, three British workers who were killed in an air strike in Gaza.Composite: World Central Kitchen/PAGazaInquest into British aid workers killed in Gaza may call on Israeli and UK military chiefsLawyer tells hearing that families wish to know whether weaponry involved in deaths was made in BritainSteven MorrisandGeneva AbdulMon 21 Sep 2026 14.49 EDTFirst published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli and UK military commanders could be requested to give evidence to an inquest concerning three British workers killed in Gaza when aid vehicles they were travelling in were hit by an airstrike.It is also possible that the inquest into the deaths ofJohn Chapman, 57, Jim Henderson, 33, and James Kirby, 47, may examine whether the weaponry that killed the men was made in the UK.Until now, the focus of the inquest has been on the role played by the aid organisation in charge of the convoy and the security firm that was protecting it. But at a pre-inquest review, Maria Voisin, the senior coroner for Avon, indicated that the scope of the final hearing would probably be widened to include the role of Israeli authorities in the deaths.The coroner said she was “minded” to designate the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and the colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, as“interested parties”for the inquest. Interested parties are often relatives of the person who died or an organisation or individual believed to be closely involved in what happened.Israeli military authorities last monthsaid they would not open criminal investigations into the strikewhich, along with the three Britons, also killed the Australian aidworker Zomi Frankcom, and one each from Poland,Palestineand the US. The UK, Australian and Canadian governments called the Israeli decision “shameful”.View image in fullscreenOne of the vehicles in which employees of the World Central Kitchen were killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza in 2024.Photograph: ReutersMap showing sequence of events that led to aid workers being killed in GazaIn a written submission to the court, Pete Weatherby KC, for Henderson, compared the case to that of the novichok attack by the Russian state in Salisbury,in which the British woman Dawn Sturgess was killed.In that case, the high court in London ruled the lack of any criminal investigation by the Russian authorities and the strong public concern surrounding the circumstances of Sturgess’s death necessitated the expansion of the scope of the investigation.Ed Sheeran says situation in Gaza ‘unjustifiable’ in first show since tour plunged into turmoilRead moreLawyers for the three men accepted that it was possible Israel would not cooperate with the inquest but called for UK ministers to try to apply pressure if needed. Another element the families are keen to have investigated is the role the British military may have played in the incident in April 2024.Weatherby’s submission says that a Royal Air Force surveillance plane spent about five hours aboveGazaon the day of the attack, seemingly returning to base minutes before the airstrikes were launched. The families want to know what, if any, surveillance the plane gathered about the convoy – and what was shared with the Israeli authorities.The barrister also told the review hearing in Flax Bourton, near Bristol, it was a “matter of public concern” and “great importance to the family” to find out if the weaponry that killed the men was made in the UK.Voisin said she was open minded about which issues the inquest would consider and would keep some under review. “It’s very much a case of throwing the net wide at the moment,” she said.Henderson’s father, Neil Henderson, said in a statement: “We hope the coroner will carry out a thorough investigation into the attack that killed Jim and the others [including] an exploration of all the issues relevant to his death, encompassing the decisions and policies leading to the attack, and what role, if any, UK authorities or military equipment originating from the UK may have played.”Tayab Ali, who is representing the Kirby family, said: “On behalf of the Kirby family they are very pleased that the coroner took onboard their concerns and extended the scope of the inquiry to include those actors that actually caused James’s death.”The scope of the inquiry has also been widened to include inquiries of the IDF and the Israeli defence ministry. It is understood that inquiries will be made of the UK Foreign Office, Ministry of Defence (MoD) and the Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems as well.Ali said after Monday’s hearing: “In order for the inquiry to establish the real circumstances of James’s death it’s crucial that information is provided by the Israeli authorities including the IDF and MoD there, that’s the only way we’ll get to the bottom of how and why he was killed.”A further pre-inquest review will take place in March. No date for the final hearing has been set.Explore more on these topicsGazaMilitaryPalestineIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Helen Jenner unveiled as Reform UK’s new leader in Wales after arrest of Dan Thomas | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Nigel Farage dismisses loss of previous leader as ‘bump in the road’ and says party will ‘carry on as if nothing has happened’
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Nigel Farage dismisses loss of previous leader as ‘bump in the road’ and says party will ‘carry on as if nothing has happened’
Content: Nigel Farage with Helen Jenner, the new leader of Reform in Wales, at the Senedd in Cardiff on Monday.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenNigel Farage with Helen Jenner, the new leader of Reform in Wales, at the Senedd in Cardiff on Monday.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAReform UKHelen Jenner unveiled as Reform UK’s new leader in Wales after arrest of Dan ThomasNigel Farage dismisses loss of previous leader as ‘bump in the road’ and says party will ‘carry on as if nothing has happened’Ben QuinnPolitical correspondentMon 21 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTFirst published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 09.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage dismissed the loss of Reform UK’s leader in Wales last week as a “bump in the road” as the party unveiled a replacement.Helen Jenner replaces Dan Thomas, who stood down last Tuesday after he was arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviours.Jenner, who was previously the party’s deputy leader inWales, narrowly beat her rival, Jason O’Connell, in a poll of its 33 Senedd members.She joined Farage on the steps of the Senedd, where he said Reform would “carry on as if nothing has happened”.Thomas announced last week that he was standing down after his arrest. He has been bailed and insists he has done nothing wrong.The former Tory councillor, who remains a member of the Welsh parliament, was only announced as Reform’s Welsh leader in February.Jenner is from Neath, near Port Talbot in south Wales, and represents Bangor Conwy Môn in the Senedd.Farage said of Thomas: “I am sorry for his personal difficulties that he is going through. No one’s life is ever seamless and I am quite sure he will come out of these before too long.“But it was pretty much untenable for him to continue as leader while he had these domestic disputes, so we very quickly and rapidly have moved to electing a new leader.”Farage confirmed that a new deputy leader in Wales would be elected, and said: “We will carry on as if nothing has happened, waiting for Dan who is going to stay a member of this place, to come back more actively with us.“We could have done without this bump in the road. But it has happened, we are making the best of it.”Thomas issued a statement last Tuesday after intense speculation about his future, saying that he had been reported to the police the previous weekend and was released without charge.“I stress that I have done nothing wrong, but I do not want the coming headlines to be a distraction from the fantastic work our Senedd team is doing in holding this government to account,” he said.Gwent police said a 45-year-old man from the Aberbargoed area had been arrested on 13 September “on suspicion of assault and engaging in controlling/coercive behaviour. He has been bailed pending further inquiries”.Thomas was perceived by some as having been parachuted in from Reform headquarters in London, which caused tensions, but Jenner is a Welsh speaker who has a track record of involvement with Farage’s parties and was elected to her new role by colleagues.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe was a general election candidate for the Brexit party in 2019, and before that was a member of Ukip under Farage’s leadership.She takes charge at a time when Reform is hoping to consolidate and build on its gains in Senedd elections earlier this year. It emerged as the second largest party, largely at the expense of the Conservatives and Labour.She also takes charge after the party was rocked not only by the loss of Thomas but also the defection of another of its Senedd members, Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, to Plaid Cymru, which holds power.Her departure sparked fury in Reform, with the party’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, accusing her of lying to them about her political beliefs.Plaid Cymru said Cooper-Lesadd had been “honest about her political beliefs” and that her views had changed.Reform UK activists squabble over Farage’s plan for £72m donationsRead moreCooper-Lesadd, who was elected to the Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg constituency, claimed thatReform UKwas “far more interested in division, opposition and headlines than in finding solutions”.Before Thomas took up the post, Nathan Gill, who briefly led Reform UK in Wales in 2021, was jailed for 10 and a half years in 2025 for taking bribes tomake statements in favour of Russiawhen he was an MEP.Explore more on these topicsReform UKWalesNigel FaragenewsShareReuse this content

title: Edward Colston’s remains likely to stay at Bristol church that could become community space | Bristol | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Slave trader is interred at All Saints, which may be given a change of use after being closed for years
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Exclusive: Slave trader is interred at All Saints, which may be given a change of use after being closed for years
Content: Edward Colston made headlines around the world in 2020 when his statue was thrown into the harbour in Bristol.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenEdward Colston made headlines around the world in 2020 when his statue was thrown into the harbour in Bristol.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PABristolEdward Colston’s remains likely to stay at Bristol church that could become community spaceExclusive: Slave trader is interred at All Saints, which may be given a change of use after being closed for yearsSteven MorrisMon 21 Sep 2026 10.43 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBones of the enslaver Edward Colston are likely to remain interred in a church inBristolif and when the currently unused building is given a new lease of life as a community resource, it has emerged.Thedean of Bristol, the Very Rev Mandy Ford,said Colston’s remains would probably stay where they were in All Saints church on one of Bristol’s busiest streets.Colston, who died in 1721, made headlines around the world in 2020 when his statue in the city centrewas toppled during a Black Lives Matter protest and thrown into the harbour.The diocese of Bristol has been consulting with Bristolians over what to do with All Saints on Corn Street, which has been closed since 1984.While no final decision has yet been made, it seems likely it will be used as a space to reflect on the port’s connections with the slave trade – and Colston’s remains will stay where they are.Ford said: “There is very, very clear guidance which assumes that you don’t disturb remains that have been given Christian burial, except in exceptional circumstances and so the presumption is that they will stay where they are.”The dean said that if there was to be a radical rebuilding of the space there could be an argument to inter the remains elsewhere. “Otherwise the assumption is that Christian burial is permanent and that’s where they stay.”View image in fullscreenAll Saints church in Bristol, where the remains of Edward Colston are interred.Photograph: Diocese of BristolFord brings deep expertise to the job of helping decide what happens to Colston’s bones, as when she worked in Leicester she was closely involved inthe reinterment of Richard III’s remains after they were found in a car park there.She acknowledged people had different understandings of the theological or spiritual significance of human remains. “But it’s a Christian place of burial and we are a Christian church trying to do the right thing. This is the burial place of a human being who was involved in a practice which we recognise to be utterly sinful and wrong.”The question of what to do about sites connected to Colston in Bristol is a thorny one.After the Colston statue was thrown into the harbour, windows celebrating him wereremoved from two Bristol churchesas the diocese declared the fall of the statue was a “signal” for it to take action. In the same year,Bristol’s concert hall was renamed Bristol Beacon,having previously been called Colston Hall.It is likely to be many months before a final decision is made over the fate of All Saints.But the dean said: “I think people do see that it has potential as a place of learning and also a place of reconciliation. From the work that we’ve been doing in the cathedral and the relationships and the conversations that we have, I think there’s a strong sense that there’s huge potential in Bristol to have difficult conversations and to build a better future on the basis of truth-telling about the past.”She added that work carried out at a new All Saints had the potential to sit alongside projects on Bristol’s history being done by institutions including theUniversity of BristolandBristol Old Vic.Ford said: “I think one can see it as part of a much bigger picture, which I think is really important if Bristol’s going to have a peaceful and flourishing future as a civic space and as a city.”The Rev Anjali Kanagaratnam, who is leading the All Saints consultation, has been taking groups into the church.She said there had been a huge range of views. “Each extreme was covered from: ‘I never want to come back into this building’ to ‘Why haven’t I been told that this building is here? I need to bring my children.’ Some people find it a hard space to be in. Some were annoyed by the fact that they didn’t know it was there.”Kanagaratnam said it had been vital to hear the voices of people in Bristol that had been affected by transatlantic slavery but the church had also made sure it heard what people from other communities, such as white working-class areas in south Bristol.Kanagaratnam said there was great potential for All Saints to be a place of “truth-telling”. She added: “I think people do see that it has potential as a place of learning and also a place of reconciliation.”Explore more on these topicsBristolSlaveryAnglicanismHeritageBlack British cultureEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Race to be next UN secretary general could rest on US and China trade-offs | United Nations | The Guardian
description: Numerous possible last-minute entrants being discussed as current field of seven candidates struggle to garner support
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Numerous possible last-minute entrants being discussed as current field of seven candidates struggle to garner support
Content: The successful candidate must win support from nine current members of the 15-strong security council with no veto by any of the five permanent members.Photograph: David Dee Delgado/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe successful candidate must win support from nine current members of the 15-strong security council with no veto by any of the five permanent members.Photograph: David Dee Delgado/ReutersUnited NationsAnalysisRace to be next UN secretary general could rest on US and China trade-offsPatrick WintourDiplomatic editor, in New YorkNumerous possible last-minute entrants being discussed as current field of seven candidates struggle to garner supportMon 21 Sep 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 17.32 EDTShareNumerous last-minute entrants in the race to become the new UN secretary general are being discussed amid concerns that the world powers may not be able to agree a successor toAntónio Guterresfrom the current field of seven candidates.Three rounds of secret ballots have so far not produced an obvious frontrunner, with probably only three candidates regarded as still having a realistic chance of gathering the required support.The new leader, due to take office in January, will face an organisation at the start of a cost-cutting overhaul programme and seen as marginal to the major global conflicts.In a world of wars and climate crisis, a new leader could save the UN. But would Trump allow it? | Steve BloomfieldRead moreBut surveys still show strong international support for the institution among a public that blames world leaders as much as the UN itself for its recent failing.Asurvey by GeoPoll for the UN Foundationpublished last week found six out of 10 people trust the UN to deliver on the issues that matter to them, but 85% said they had heard nothing or little about the process to choose a new secretary general.The successful candidate must win the support of nine current members of the 15-strong security council with no veto by any of the five permanent members of the council – France, the UK,China, Russia and the US.Achieving consensus among the permanent five is fraught given the breadth of political divisions. Guterres’s term ends on 31 December.Names being mentioned as potential late drafts include Lana Nusseibeh, the minister of state at the United Arab Emirates and a former UAE ambassador to the UN, and Sigrid Kaag, a former UN under secretary general and Dutch centrist politician.
