She was briefly the senior humanitarian and reconstruction coordinator for Gaza before joining the advisory committee to Donald Trump’s Board of Peace.Other candidates mentioned include Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, the polyglot president of Kazakhstan, and, in deference to the US, Viktor Orbán, the former prime minister of Hungary, who is still much admired by Trump but reviled as a disruptive populist by many European leaders.Vuk Jeremić, a Serbian former president of the UN general assembly who came second behind Guterres in the 2016 race, has also been mentioned.View image in fullscreenDutch politician Sigrid Kaag has been mentioned as a possible late entrant into the contest.Photograph: Geert Vanden Wijngaert/APNone of the speculated candidates have given any public indication they wish to be drafted.A communique at the end of this month’s Brics summit attended by 21 countries, of which 10 are full members, said: “We note that no woman has ever been elected for the role of secretary general, and only one national from Latin America and Caribbean, and only two nationals from Africa and Asia each have ever occupied this position.”Some would also resent a late candidate, regardless of their origin, entering the field since strenuous efforts have been made to democratise the selection process by holding regional and global hustings. The last general assembly president, Annalena Baerbock, has helped spearhead the attempt to open the selection process.But the need to avoid alienating any of the five, internally divided, veto-wielding security council members inevitably incentivises the candidates to issue slightly bland consensus-seeking statements at a time when the organisation needs firm leadership. All the candidates have said they would like to see the UN return to an active role as a peacemaker – a task often demanded by amateur US diplomats close to Trump.In the third and last straw poll of the 15 security council members on Friday, Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica regained the lead after receiving nine “encourage” votes from the security council. She got five “discourage” votes and one “no opinion”. Her fear is that the discourage votes came from Russia and China, an opposition she would need to overcome.In the second straw poll on 21 August she had dropped behindCarolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, a Guyanese politician who then came first – receiving eight encourage votes, three discourage and four no opinions.Last Friday, Rodrigues-Birkett maintained the eight encourage votes, but her discourage votes had risen from three to six.A third candidate, the Ecuadorian former finance minister María Fernanda Espinosa, is just about still a viable contender despite the numbers discouraging her reaching six last week, up from three in August. She has been calling for an early warning system inside the UN to help prevent wars, and for a secretary general more willing to take risks in mediation.View image in fullscreenRebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica regained the lead in the last poll but received five ‘discourage’ votes.Photograph: Santiago Mazzarovich/AFP/Getty ImagesIt will not be until later in the process – when colour-coded balloting reveals if a vote is from a permanent member of the security council or not – that it will be clear whether a candidate faces an insurmountable barrier.In reality the decision may turn on the horse-trading between the US president and the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and whether Trump accepts that China cares more about the UN’s future than him, and that may mean accepting a candidate that China wants and the US can tolerate.The Trump administration appears to have softened some of its scepticism towards the UN under the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz. The US not only provided $1.8bn (£1.35bn) in additional humanitarian funding in March but also recently sent $827m in dues, admittedly less than a quarter of what it owes the cash-strapped organisation.Michelle Bachelet, a former president of Chile and a human rights campaigner,became the first candidate to drop out of the race at the weekendafter she received only one encouragement in last week’s poll.Explore more on these topicsUnited NationsAntónio GuterresUS foreign policyChinaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Pakistan jails sisters of Imran Khan before protest seeking his release | Pakistan | The Guardian
description: Police crack down on family and political supporters of former PM who say authorities are ‘slowly killing’ him in prison
Author: Shah Meer Baloch
Headline: Police crack down on family and political supporters of former PM who say authorities are ‘slowly killing’ him in prison
Content: Khan’s sisters Aleema Khanum, Uzma Khanum and Noreen Niazi among supporters of the former Pakistan PM in Rawalpindi last December.Photograph: Salahuddin/ReutersView image in fullscreenKhan’s sisters Aleema Khanum, Uzma Khanum and Noreen Niazi among supporters of the former Pakistan PM in Rawalpindi last December.Photograph: Salahuddin/ReutersPakistanPakistan jails sisters of Imran Khan before protest seeking his releasePolice crack down on family and political supporters of former PM who say authorities are ‘slowly killing’ him in prisonShah Meer Balochin Islamabad andHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiMon 21 Sep 2026 10.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree sisters of Pakistan’s incarcerated former prime ministerImran Khanhave been arrested amid a heavy-handed government crackdown on plans for a nationwide protest to demand Khan’s release.The lawyer for the three sisters, Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, said on Monday that they had all been detained and jailed for 30 days under a warrant that accused them of being a threat to public order.Leaders from Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) condemned the “illegal harassment” of his sisters. Since Khanwas arrestedand held in prison on corruption charges in 2023, his sisters have been vocal advocates for his release.His family and party allege that Khan is being kept in solitary confinement and has been denied visits and calls from his family for six months, as well as being allegedly prevented from accessing vital medical treatment foran eye condition.The arrest of Khan’s sisters marked a dramatic escalation of a crackdown on PTI members and supporters in the run up to a nationwide demonstration due to be held on Sunday – described as a “long march” – to demand the release of Khan and to protest an alleged erosion of democracy and the constitution under the ruling coalition government.None of Khan’s sisters hold a political position in PTI. Since protesting against their brother’s detention – including by camping outside the prison where he is held, demanding to see him – they have been named in various court cases. This is the first time they have all been held in prison.Imran Khan’s sons accuse Pakistani army chief of vendetta against imprisoned fatherRead moreAleema was arrested in Lahore on Sunday as she was travelling to a private club; her driver was also picked up by police. Uzma and Noreen were then arrested at around 3am on Monday morning, after they held a press conference to condemn Aleema’s detention at her house in Lahore.According to their lawyer, Rana Mudassir Umar, hundreds of police officers later surrounded the family home as more than 100 entered to arrest Uzma and Noreen, as well as their children, grandchildren – who are four and six years old – and the household staff. The house was raided and all their phones were taken.By 7am on Monday morning, the children and grandchildren had been released but the three sisters were held and charged under the country’s Maintenance of Public Order law, according to Umar.He said: “They have not been allowed any family access, no legal counsellor access and they were not even allowed to bring clothes or basic things.“We have challenged their arrests in the high court in Lahore and [are] hoping we will get a hearing soon.”While Pakistan is ostensibly ruled by a civilian coalition government, the army is widely regarded as the country’s most powerful establishment, led by Pakistan’s army chief,Field Marshall Asim Munir, who fell out with Khan while Khan was prime minister. The current government was brought to power in an election in 2024 which waswidely documented as rigged, allegedly by military intervention, to prevent Khan’s party returning to power.Speakingto the Guardianlast week, Khan’s two sons, who are based in London and fighting for his release, accused Munir of a “personal vendetta” against their father and alleged the Pakistani authorities were “slowly killing” Khan in prison.Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi said on Monday that the government would “find a permanent solution” to prevent to march going ahead and shutting down swathes of the country “once and for all”.Despite Khan’s lengthy incarceration, he is still regarded as Pakistan’smost popular politicianand there are fears among officials that large numbers could turn out to support PTI’s march on Sunday. It is being held as discontentment is rife on the streets amid an economic crisis and crippling petrol shortages due to the turmoil in the Middle East and the Gulf. Disgust at the alleged mistreatment of Khan is also widespread.Prisoner number 804: the plot to erase Imran KhanRead moreKhan’s party has faced constant harassmentover the past three years, with most senior PTI figures either in jail or pressed to leave politics.Sheikh Waqas Akram, a senior PTI leader, said the government feared that hundreds of thousands of people may turn out to the long march and “topple the government”, as protest movements have done recently in neighbouring countries such as Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka.Over the weekend, the capital ofPakistan, Islamabad, was transformed into a fortress of heavy security, with barriers and heavy armed security lining the roads and shipping containers placed to block the entrances into the city.“Punjab police are raiding houses, harassing families, bulldozing houses and arresting workers and families,” Akram said. “They are going to insane levels to crush the long march and stop it with violence and arrests. This illegitimate government know they can’t survive if people are allowed to protest and march on Islamabad in huge numbers.”Explore more on these topicsPakistanImran KhanSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Lindsay Clancy’s defense lawyer asks judge to investigate lone juror | US crime | The Guardian
description: Holdout juror in Clancy’s case, Michael Desronvil, sided with the prosecutors, arguing that Clancy knew what she was doing when she killed her three young children
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Holdout juror in Clancy’s case, Michael Desronvil, sided with the prosecutors, arguing that Clancy knew what she was doing when she killed her three young children
Content: Kevin Reddington and Lindsay Clancy look on as Judge William Sullivan (out of frame) instructs the jury to continue deliberating during Lindsay Clancy's murder trial at the Plymouth county superior court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on 4 September.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKevin Reddington and Lindsay Clancy look on as Judge William Sullivan (out of frame) instructs the jury to continue deliberating during Lindsay Clancy's murder trial at the Plymouth county superior court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on 4 September.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesUS crimeLindsay Clancy’s defense lawyer asks judge to investigate lone jurorHoldout juror in Clancy’s case, Michael Desronvil, sided with the prosecutors, arguing that Clancy knew what she was doing when she killed her three young childrenAssociated PressMon 21 Sep 2026 17.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 18.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLawyers for Lindsay Clancy have asked a judge to investigate the conduct of the lone juror who wanted to convict the mother fromMassachusettsof murder in the deaths of her three children.In a motion filed Friday but made public Monday, Clancy’s lawyers asked the court to question the juror about his alleged use of a cellphone during deliberations, his truthfulness on a questionnaire that prospective jurors filled out before the trial began and his truthfulness when jurors were questioned by the judge a day before the trial ended.The judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after the jury insisted it couldn’t reach a unanimous verdict, despite days of trying. Eleven of 12 jurors were ready to clear Clancy of criminal responsibility, with the majority feeling that she was in the grip of a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she strangled her kids. But one juror, Michael Desronvil, sided with the prosecutors, who had argued that Clancy knew what she was doing.Patrick Clancy, ex-husband of Lindsay Clancy, opens up on children’s killings in first televised interviewRead moreAmong other things, Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, asked the court to obtain a record of any calls or texts Desronvil made between 8am and 4.30pm on each day the jury deliberated. Phone use during deliberations is prohibited in the state.Prosecutors have yet to say whether they plan on putting Clancy on trial again. She remains charged with murder and is in a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved.In another motion on Monday, Clancy’s lawyers asked the judge to take the unusual step of dismissing the criminal case, rather than putting on a new trial, on the grounds that a mistrial shouldn’t have been declared in the first place.They argued that the judge should have replaced the holdout juror with an alternate during the deliberations after a jury foreperson complained to the judge that one juror was refusing to listen to the law on reasonable doubt.A spokesperson for Plymouth county district attorney Timothy Cruz would not comment on the motions.Desronvil hasn’t been accused of any wrongdoing in connection with his service on the jury, though other jurors complained that he was inflexible in his opinion that Clancy was guilty.In a statement released by his lawyer last week, Edward Paltzik, Desronvil said he “didn’t have any doubts” that Clancy knew what she was doing when she killed her three children.Explore more on these topicsUS crimeMassachusettsMental healthHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Paramount settles lawsuits with 12 US states, clearing way for Warner merger | Business | The Guardian
description: States including California and New York sued over concerns of ‘extinguishing competition’ with $81bn merger
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: States including California and New York sued over concerns of ‘extinguishing competition’ with $81bn merger
Content: Though the merger was approved by the justice department in June, a coalition of 12 states led by California filed a lawsuit to block it in July.Composite: AP, Bauer Griffin/GC ImagesView image in fullscreenThough the merger was approved by the justice department in June, a coalition of 12 states led by California filed a lawsuit to block it in July.Composite: AP, Bauer Griffin/GC ImagesBusinessParamount settles lawsuits with 12 US states, clearing way for Warner mergerStates including California and New York sued over concerns of ‘extinguishing competition’ with $81bn mergerGaya GuptaandUwa Ede-OsifoMon 21 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 14.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleParamounthas reached a settlement withCaliforniaand several other states that sued over a proposed $81bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery (WBD), the California attorney general announced Monday, clearing the way to consolidate some of Hollywood’s most recognizable TV networks and studios under one owner.Though the merger wasapprovedby the justice department in June, a coalition of 12 states, led by California, hadsuedoverconcernsthat combining two of the five last legacy studios in Hollywood would “extinguish competition” andlead tofewer movies in theaters and on streaming platforms.Rob Bonta, theCaliforniaattorney general who spearheaded the antitrust litigation, said in a news conference on Monday that Paramount had made an “enforceable commitment to significantly increase” production in the US and specifically in Los Angeles, which he said would mean “more jobs, more economic activity”.“This settlement is not a vote of support for this merger; it’s not a blessing of the broader merger,” he said. “Broadly speaking, we believe further consolidation in markets that are essential to American economic life doesn’t serve the American economy, consumers or competition well.”Four holdout states – Massachusetts, New York, Connecticut and Minnesota – held out on a deal until this weekend, according toBloomberg.‘Laws were broken’: multistate effort to stop Paramount’s $111bn merger heads to courtRead moreParamount, as part of the settlement, agreed that CBS and CNN would maintain independent editorial boards under the merger. Paramount also agreed to spend at least $300m in domestic production, and would be forced to pay a financial penalty ifthe newly merged company fails to distribute 30 films for the first two years of the deal and 32 movies in the three years after. In return, Paramount will not have to sell its cable channels, which include CBS, MTV, Nickelodeon and Showtime, as was discussed in negotiations, the Wall Street Journalreported.Bonta also added that together, the parties would select a trustee to monitor Paramount’s compliance with the terms of the settlement, and would be prepared to go to court if the company ever fails to comply.David Ellison, the CEO and owner of Paramount and son of billionaire tech mogul Larry Ellison, said on Monday that he was grateful to Bonta, other state attorney generals and California governor Gavin Newsom for “engaging in good faith to find a path forward to a resolution”, and reiterated his message that the merger would be “pro-competitive, pro-consumer and pro-worker”.“Our goal has always been to build a stronger Hollywood — one with more stories told, greater choice for consumers and stronger competition,” he said in a statement. “Bringing Paramount andWarner Bros. Discovery together will build that stronger Hollywood, creating expanded opportunity for our people and even more great entertainment for audiences around the world.”The legal battle has been a headache for Paramount executives, considering that a closing date past 30 September would havereportedly add millions of dollarsto the purchase price.Reportsemerged last week that, after months of speculation, WBD and Paramount were in the process of selling their studio lots in California and leaving the state amid the antitrust lawsuit, which would have been an enormous hit toLos Angeles’salreadystrugglingfilm and entertainmentindustry.Whispers of Paramount Skydance plotting a California exit had circulated for months, though there was speculation the reports amounted to strategically leaked leverage as the media company sought a bargaining chip in the lawsuit.In an August news release, Ellisoncalledthe lawsuit the “final obstacle” to the merger, describing the deal as “pro-competitive, pro-consumer and pro-worker”.Twelve stateswarnedthat a merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros Discovery would result in fewer entertainment options and higher prices for consumers.Bonta also has voiced concern about how a merger could affect CNN’s journalism. (CNN is owned by WBD.)David Ellison claims opposition to his mega-merger stems from potential CNN controlRead moreLast summer, Skydance Media bought Paramount in an $8.4bn merger, a deal led by Ellison. After US regulatorsapprovedthe deal, Paramount reached a$16m settlementwithDonald Trumpover a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. It also announced thecancellationof the Late Night with Stephen Colbert show, which aired itslast episodein May.After the merger, Ellison appointedBari Weissas editor-in-chief of CBS News. The network has since been roiled by allegations ofbiasfavoring the Trump administration.In aguest essaypublished in the New York Times last month, Ellison wrote that the anti-trust lawsuit stemmed from concerns over “whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN”.“I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views. I believe that news should be based on facts and truth,” Ellison wrote. “Great news organizations like CNN andCBSNews are here to tell it straight down the middle. That requires newsrooms that reflect the whole world, not one side of it. And it requires independence. Our journalists will continue to answer to the facts and to all the people they serve – not to any party or cause.”Explore more on these topicsBusinessParamount+Warner BrosCaliforniaLaw (US)MassachusettsNew YorknewsShareReuse this content

title: Google fined more than €400m by Irish regulator over its use of location data | Google | The Guardian
description: Watchdog says users may have been unaware their information was used to target adverts or infer their interests
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Watchdog says users may have been unaware their information was used to target adverts or infer their interests
Content: The DPC found that Google users could have been unaware of how their data was being used.Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe DPC found that Google users could have been unaware of how their data was being used.Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesGoogleGoogle fined more than €400m by Irish regulator over its use of location dataWatchdog says users may have been unaware their information was used to target adverts or infer their interestsLisa O’CarrollMon 21 Sep 2026 06.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle has been fined more than €400m (£345m) over the way it processed users’ location data, following claims that the tech giant had manipulated users into agreeing to be constantly tracked on their mobile phones.The fine, imposed by Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC), comes after complaints from multiple European consumer organisations that Google was following every step users took.Location-related adverts are familiar to holidaymakers, but seven European consumer organisations hadcomplained that undue use of location data can also lead to a breach of privacy.The DPC inquiry was prompted byresearch by the Norwegian consumer agency in 2018which suggested location data could reveal details such as religious beliefs (by tracking places of worship), political leanings (for example knowing a user has gone to demonstrations), health conditions (if a user has gone to hospital) and sexual orientation (if they have gone to certain bars).The DPC launched its inquiry six years ago and set out to find out whether Google had a valid legal basis for its use of location data.It found that Google users could have been unaware that their location was being used to influence them with adverts or to gather details about their health and interests.“Location data is a type of personal data which is processed by way of location tracking, and includes data collected or processed by Google, which by itself or in conjunction with other information an individual’s location can be inferred,” said Graham Doyle, a deputy commissioner at the DPC.“Location data can bring both benefits and harms to individuals.“It can greatly enhance the utility of online services, but it can also reveal a significant amount of information about an individual, including information that is inherently private,” Doyle added.Responding to the DPC’s ruling, a Google spokeperson said: “This case centres around historical policies that have since been updated. From 2019 onwards, we’ve significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple.”The European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) based its complaint on research by the Forbrukerrådet, the Norwegian consumer agency, whichclaimed Google used “various tricks”to ensure location history and web and app activity were enabled.“Today marks an important milestone in the effort to protect our rights online. People must be able to understand what they are agreeing to without being deceived or manipulated into making choices they otherwise would never have made,” says Finn Myrstad, director of digital policy at the Norwegian Consumer Council.BEUC said that geolocation data was “one of the most invasive forms of consumer surveillance”.Agustín Reyna, director general of BEUC, welcomed the ruling but said “the time needed to come to this conclusion is disproportionate with the seriousness of the infringement” arguing “late enforcement can be as harmful as no enforcement at all”.The DPC inquiry looked at “web and app activity”, “location history” and “location accuracy” between 25 May 2018 and 4 February 2020.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionImposing a fine of €403m, the DPC ordered Google to bring its processing into compliance with the EU’s general data protection regulation (GDPR) within six months.It is the fourth-largest fine imposed by the Irish regulator, which has EU-wide responsibility for all the US tech giants with EU headquarters in Ireland.It has previously fined Meta €1.2bn, TikTok €530m and Instagram (also Meta owned) €405m.Doyle said: “The GDPR provides a high level of protection of personal data throughout the EEA, and requires that the processing of personal data must be carried out in a lawful, fair and transparent manner.AI slowdown calls justified but collapse of bubble may be more immediate threat | Heather StewartRead more“As a result of Google’s failures in this regard, individuals could have been unaware that their location was being used to, for example, influence them with ads or to infer their interests, and could lose control over their personal data.“The retention of users’ location data for longer than necessary aggravated this loss of control,” added Doyle.There are three other ongoing statutory large-scale inquiries open that concern Google, all of which are at an advanced stage.Explore more on these topicsGoogleEuropean UnionSmartphonesAlphabetMobile phonesEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta bans ads for Virginia Woolf play in Spain because they relate to feminism | Meta | The Guardian
description: Theatre told that Facebook and Instagram filter out ads mentioning ‘social topics’ such as civil rights or feminism
Author: Stephen Burgen
Headline: Theatre told that Facebook and Instagram filter out ads mentioning ‘social topics’ such as civil rights or feminism
Content: Clara Sanchis in the one-woman performance of A Room of One’s Own.Photograph: Teatre RavalView image in fullscreenClara Sanchis in the one-woman performance of A Room of One’s Own.Photograph: Teatre RavalMetaMeta bans ads for Virginia Woolf play in Spain because they relate to feminismTheatre told that Facebook and Instagram filter out ads mentioning ‘social topics’ such as civil rights or feminismStephen Burgenin BarcelonaMon 21 Sep 2026 10.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA theatre in Barcelona has been banned from promoting a stage adaptation of Virginia Woolf’s A Room of One’s Own on Instagram and Facebook because the work includes “social topics”.When the newly reopened Teatre Raval, which seats 193 spectators, askedMeta, the parent company of the two social media sites, why its publicity had been blocked, it was told “any mention of civil rights, feminism or social reform [topics that are central to Woolf’s work] are usually classified as ‘social topics’ by our automatic system” and are filtered out.To resolve the situation, Meta recommended removing “key words” so that the text doesn’t appear to encourage activism.View image in fullscreenA promotion for A Room of One’s Own at Teatre Raval.Photograph: suppliedThe theatre published a statement saying: “We feel obliged to speak up about the injustice and violation of our rights by not being allowed to promote a feminist work, specifically a work by Virginia Woolf who was born in 1882.“What can we do? As a theatre we have to publicise our activities … and we have to make use of social media so that people are aware of cultural activities.”The stage production, a one-woman show starring Clara Sanchis, is an adaptation of a series of talks Woolf gave in 1928 at Newnham and Girton, which were then the only two colleges at Cambridge University that admitted women.The talks were published as an essay the following year on the situation of women in society and their access to education. Women had been admitted to study at Cambridge since 1869 but weren’t allowed to graduate with a degree until 1948.Woolf said that in order to produce high-quality fiction, “a woman must have money and a room of her own”. She wrote in her diary that she expected to be attacked as a feminist for what she had written.“We don’t know if the publicity has been rejected because of the name of Virginia Woolf or because of the word feminism, or both,” Sanchis told La Vanguardia newspaper.“In any case, it’s a way of erasing from the map advances that have taken centuries to achieve. We have given social media unlimited power and every day we can see how dangerous this is. It’s bias and manipulation.”Explore more on these topicsMetaFacebookInstagramSocial mediaVirginia WoolfBarcelonaSpainnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fears over interest rate rise and jobs send UK consumer confidence to three-year low | Economics | The Guardian
description: Blow to John Healey before budget as UK households face ‘notable strain’ on their finances
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Blow to John Healey before budget as UK households face ‘notable strain’ on their finances
Content: Consumers are concerned about the likelihood of an increase in interest rates by the Bank of England, S&P Global said.Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenConsumers are concerned about the likelihood of an increase in interest rates by the Bank of England, S&P Global said.Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty ImagesEconomicsFears over interest rate rise and jobs send UK consumer confidence to three-year lowBlow to John Healey before budget as UK households face ‘notable strain’ on their financesPhillip InmanMon 21 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFears of a steep rise in mortgage payments and increasing job insecurity have sent UK consumer confidence tumbling to a three-month low, according to a leading survey.In a blow to John Healey before next month’s budget, the S&P Global consumer sentiment index dropped to 42.7 in September from 42.9 in August, indicating “a notable strain on financial confidence across UK households”.The chancellor could announce tax risesin his first budget to offset the rising cost of government borrowing, which has soared in response to the conflict in the Middle East.Burnham’s talk of ‘breathing space’ at odds with reality of future Bank rate risesRead moreS&P Global said consumers were concerned about the likelihood of an increase in interest rates by the Bank of England. More than 50% of 1,500 respondents said they expected a rise in the cost of borrowing over the next year.Fixed-rate mortgage costs have already jumped to multi-year highs in the UK, while the threat of artificial intelligence and caution among employers about hiring new staff sent consumer confidence in the jobs market plunging to its lowest level in three-and-a-half years.The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate rose to 5.88% on Monday, its highest since 16 April and up from 5.84% last Friday, while the average five-year is at its highest since October 2023, at 5.92%, up from 5.88%, data from Moneyfacts showed.The rise in mortgage costs is expected to add about £150 to monthly mortgage payments, based on a typical loan of £250,000 over 25 years, since the start of March 2026.Official figures have shown that the average direct debit to cover monthly mortgage costs has risen over the past four years from about £600 to £900.Maryam Baluch, an economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said a downbeat mood was spreading across UK households “as improved sentiment surrounding the new government is eroded by renewed worries over energy prices, the cost of living and job prospects”.She said: “Against a backdrop of rising volatility in energy markets linked to tensions in the Middle East, households increasingly reported difficulties accessing credit, suggesting that expectations of tighter monetary conditions are beginning to feed through to borrowing conditions. Together, these factors point to cautiousness about both financial prospects and pose some downside risks to the broader economic outlook.”Analysts believe the jobs market has proved resilient since the US attack on Iran and a steep rise in the cost of fuel and energy, but a steady decline in the number of payrolled employees over the past six months and a drop in vacancies to a five-year low have shown employers are worried about their profitability over the next year.The British Chamber of Commerce has called for the government to give businesses extra support after a series of tax rises over the past two years, including an increase in employers national insurance payments.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA survey by the business organisation of 5,000 companies in the second quarter of 2026 found that only 17% were planning to increase investment in the coming months, a post-pandemic low.Last week, Andy Burnham said he will need to take “difficult decisions” on the economy to ensure that it “remains on track”.In response to the growing clamour for tax cuts to support businesses and households hit by the cost of living crisis, the Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, said at his party conference that the UK should cut fuel duty to offset some of the rise in petrol and diesel prices at the pumps.The German government on Monday announced plans for a cut in tax on fuel of about 15p to take effect on 1 October.Healey could limit his tax rises to wealthier groups, including a rise in capital gains tax. However, analysts say he is unlikely to raise sufficient funds from discreet tax rises to pay for higher defence spending and the rise in debt costs while preserving a reserve buffer, often referred to as headroom, of at least £20bn.Explore more on these topicsEconomicsInterest ratesRetail industryMortgage ratesMortgagesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Our culture is rich and we need our own space’: the fight to build a permanent centre for Deaf people | Architecture | The Guardian
description: In the UK, 18 million people are hard of hearing – yet there is no dedicated centre for the Deaf community. Now urban planner and activist Amanprit Arnold has made it her mission
Author: Alice Fisher
Headline: In the UK, 18 million people are hard of hearing – yet there is no dedicated centre for the Deaf community. Now urban planner and activist Amanprit Arnold has made it her mission
Content: ‘Being in an environment that’s built for you is so important’ … Amanprit Arnold speaks at an urban planning eventView image in fullscreen‘Being in an environment that’s built for you is so important’ … Amanprit Arnold speaks at an urban planning eventArchitecture‘Our culture is rich and we need our own space’: the fight to build a permanent centre for Deaf peopleIn the UK, 18 million people are hard of hearing – yet there is no dedicated centre for the Deaf community. Now urban planner and activist Amanprit Arnold has made it her missionAlice FisherMon 21 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMeeting outdoors became second nature for most of us over this long, hot summer, but Amanprit Arnold doesn’t get the luxury of choice. She’s sitting at a terrace table when we meet at a cafe because she’s a member of the Deaf community (Deaf with a capital D denotes membership of a unique cultural and linguistic minority).“Nowhere inLondonis specifically designed for me,” says Arnold, who was born deaf and used hearing aids before getting cochlear implants at 21. “Inside a cafe, the acoustics can be so bad. It’s much easier for me to hear out here.”Despite there being18 million people with hearing issues in the UK, deaf people can often be made to feel like outsiders (even when they’re not sitting outside). Mainstream representation has grown thanks to actorRose Ayling-Ellislifting the glitterball trophy on Strictly Come Dancing in 2021 and Fury on the Gladiators reboot. Critically acclaimed films such asSound of MetalandCoda– which won the best picture Oscar in 2022 – showcased the talents of deaf actors and writers, and the mesmerising skills of sign language interpreters at rap performances regularly go viral. But this has not led to a dedicated centre for the Deaf arts anywhere in the UK.View image in fullscreenSign of the times … an image by the Deaf Architecture Front.Photograph: Deaf Architecture FrontArnold wants to change that. She has started the DeafCity Hub campaign to create or adapt a building using deaf-friendly architectural guidelines calledDeafSpace principlesto provide, at last, a co-working and cultural space for her community.double quotation markWe have a really strong cultural identity element and we need somewhere to celebrate thatWhile there are cafes and clubs that bring deaf people together socially around the UK, Arnold sees the DeafCity Hub as a national centre as well as a meeting place. This month, the project has landed a year-long “meanwhile” space (a building awaiting redevelopment) through a partnership with Westminster city council and the Oxford Street Development Corporation, which gives her the chance to prove a place like this is needed.“There is greater visibility of deaf people in the media,” says Arnold, “but when it comes to property and place-making for them, there’s nothing. We have a really strong cultural identity element and we need somewhere to celebrate that, somewhere made for us.”Arnold’s career is in urban planning and strategy, but there’s activism in her background, too. (“In my family, that’s what we do,” she says with a smile.) Her father was race relations director for Birmingham city council in the 1990s andher grandfather was a trade unionist and antiracism campaigner. Arnold’s design agency,Disability Urbanism, specialises in accessibility, helping city planners and real estate developers create welcoming environments for people with disabilities.View image in fullscreenFizzled out … a poster from the 1980s promoting the IDCCShe sees DeafCity Hub as a revival of a 1986 plan for an International Deaf Cultural Centre in London that fizzled out. The 1980s were a heady time for activists, especially in the US, where there were Deaf civil rights protests, the first Oscar for a deaf actor (Marlee Matlinfor 1986’s Children of a Lesser God) and the establishment ofGallaudet University, specifically for deaf people, and the appointment of the university’s first deaf president.In the UK, the BBC launched See Hear, a current affairs programme for deaf people, and TV subtitle provision improved. The British Sign Language Act only received royal assent in 2022, legally recognising BSL as a British language of England, Scotland and Wales, and you still can’t take a GCSE in it (the expected launch date for this qualification is 2028).“Most communities have their own spaces,” says Arnold. “I know that if I go to Soho I’ll be in an LGBTQ+ community space, for example. I think creating DeafCity Hub as a deaf-owned and deaf-led arts space would assert that our culture is also rich.”Being able to access spoken language culture would also be on the DeafCity Hub agenda, as signers often find this difficult. “Theatres and cinemas will have an accessibility page on their websites, but performances with interpreters are rare,” Arnold continues. “You have to go to one specific show – and that’s normally set for noon on a Tuesday when most of us are at work.”Arnold has the 1980s material for the International Deaf Cultural Centre, from plans and optimistic posters to the original architect’s blueprints – which feature a Deaf history archive, a theatre and exhibition space, a bar, a quiet room and even a hostel. Looking through them, she recalls a quote that’s connected to the formation of Gallaudet University and has become a mantra for many activists: “We travel the world to learn about cultures and people. We go into their country to visit them. We now have a country.”The International Deaf Cultural Centre plans are not designed to the DeafSpace guidelines – this is the goal for DeafCity Hub. “Sign language is not just spoken word translated into hands: it’s a rich, spatial language rooted in visual geography, 3D space and facial syntax,” says Arnold. It needs space.View image in fullscreenPleasant and spacious … The London College of Fashion’s East Bank campus, designed by Allies & Morrison, is one of the few public buildings that adhere to DeafSpace principlesPhotograph: Simon MengesDeafSpace principles include features such as wide corridors and staircases that allow people to walk abreast while talking in BSL; natural light and soft colours to guard against eye strain; strategic use of glass and mirrors to improve sightlines; and rooms that accommodate circular seating so large groups can easily see each other’s hands and faces as they sign. If you’ve ever been to the London College of Fashion’sEast Bankcampus, you’ll have experienced the pleasant, spacious feel of DeafSpace, as it’s one of the few public buildings designed to these ideals.Arnold would also like Deaf sector charities to have a home at DeafCity Hub, using boardrooms without rectangular tables, in part to demonstrate how simple changes can make a big difference to her community. “Being in an environment that’s built for you is so important. I went to deaf school as a teenager and that meant I had a wonderful secondary school experience. I was opened up to Deaf culture and I want to be able to share what that was like with other deaf people.”Arnold’s positive experience is harder for deaf kids to access today. There are only22 deaf schools in the UK, down from 75 in the early 1980s. This is partly due to funding cuts and local government policy, but it’s also due to the uptake of cochlear implants, electrical devices that relay sound to the brain, enabling speech development. Arnold feels that the possibility of medical eradication makes it even more important to preserve Deaf culture.Disability by David Turner review – a revelatory new historyRead more“Deaf Gain is a celebrated term in our community, where we frame ourselves as contributors to society. People think it’s important to protect endangered ecosystems and oral dialects, so why would we treat a thriving visual culture and spatial language as something to be eliminated?”Arnold is delighted to have her meanwhile space, but for DeafCity Hub to secure a permanent home, they’ll need funding and a developer partner. If all goes well, she’d like the London space to act as a pilot for an international network of hubs – and for that to work she needs investment. “We need to design and shape accessibility and inclusivity from the start. A meanwhile space won’t be perfect, but it will act as an incubator to develop this idea further.”She has a lot to prove in the next 12 months but she’s ready for it. She gathers her plans and her blueprints from the cafe table, plans for somewhere she can finally call her own.TheDeafCity Hubcampaign launches on 21 September, before theInternational Day of Sign Languageson 23 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsArchitectureDeafness and hearing lossDisabilityHealthActivismCommunitiesLondonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Love and respect’ or ‘a cash grab’? The furious battle over the final album by the Fall | Music | The Guardian
description: Creators of Post Script, made with vocals by the late Mark E Smith, defend it as ‘a great, positive record’, but fiancee describes it as ‘ethically wrong’
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: Creators of Post Script, made with vocals by the late Mark E Smith, defend it as ‘a great, positive record’, but fiancee describes it as ‘ethically wrong’
Content: ‘Is it the Fall? Well, Mark is the Fall, so yes, these are Fall songs’ … Mark E Smith in 2007.Photograph: Everynight Images/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Is it the Fall? Well, Mark is the Fall, so yes, these are Fall songs’ … Mark E Smith in 2007.Photograph: Everynight Images/AlamyMusic‘Love and respect’ or ‘a cash grab’? The furious battle over the final album by the FallCreators of Post Script, made with vocals by the late Mark E Smith, defend it as ‘a great, positive record’, but fiancee describes it as ‘ethically wrong’Dave SimpsonMon 21 Sep 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 08.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe fiancee and last manager of the lateMark E Smith, frontman of the Fall, has hit out against the release of an album being marketed as the band’s final official album, calling it “ethically wrong” and a “cash grab”.When Post Script was first announced in June, several media reports assumed the nine-track album contained recordings that the final Fall lineup were working on before the singer’s death, in January 2018. However, it subsequently emerged that it contains unused studio vocals recorded between 2001 and 2014, to which longtime Fall associates Ed Blaney and Simon “Ding” Archer have posthumously added music.Pamela Vander said: “They’re selling it as ‘the final album’ so people will think Mark made it on his deathbed, but none of it [vocally] was made after New Facts Emerge [2017]. I have Mark’s actual last recordings – he was working on a cover of Madonna’s Material Girl – but by the time of his death he had made the decision that New Facts Emerge was the final album, made by the longest-lasting lineup of the Fall, who were with Mark for 10 years. So I don’t think anyone else should override a decision he made when he was alive.”A digital single, 30 Degrees, was released in June. The album is set for release by Cog Sinister on 2 October on CD, black vinyl, limited edition white vinyl and digital formats, with the approval of Smith’s estate. However, Vander said: “Mark’s life was complicated and Mark was very disorganised when it came to any sort of protection for his legacy. I was the manager and I’m not even sure who owns the name ‘the Fall’. It’s a cash grab, just a collection of some shit from the cutting room floor. I wouldn’t have minded if it was being released as ‘the Mark E Smith archive’ or something, but there’s something ethically wrong with releasing it as the Fall.”The situation is further complicated by the various parties’ long relationships with Smith. Blaney played in the Fall in the early 2000s, going on to be tour manager, manager and friend and their collaborations included the 2008 album Smith and Blaney. Archer, the group’s bassist in 2003-4, subsequently produced or engineered eight of the last nine Fall albums.View image in fullscreen‘Mark loved fronting the Fall’ … the band on Mark E Smith’s 50th birthday in 2007.Photograph: John Bentley/AlamyBlaney responded: “Making this record was intended as a fitting tribute to Mark/the Fall because the vocals were there waiting to be put to good use. Mark also trusted Ding whenever he worked with him, so the foundation was there. [In the studio] we felt Mark’s presence: things happened that had Mark’s hallmark all over them.“Words like ‘cashing in’ make me laugh. It was about love and respect for Mark: he was the Fall, and Mark’s vocals were recorded as the Fall, hence it’s being released as the Fall. Mark sounds great and it’s a great, positive record.”When approached for comment by the Guardian, Rob Ayling, director of Cog Sinister, said “the album speaks for itself”, and Archer declined to answer questions. He previously posted on Facebook: “I recorded most of Mark’s vocal takes for 12 years. We would regularly throw down Mark’s freshest ideas to whatever backing he deemed fit at the time: a drone, a drum beat or a cappella, or down the corridor to test the acoustics. Some of these ideas went to the band for development and some were dropped. Others went into the vault with phrases like ‘put that in the safe’ or ‘you can do what you like with that one, cock’. I’d never had the time to check the safe but Post Script provided an opportunity for these loose ends to be tied up. Ed and I found some gems that just needed fleshing out and arranging.“Neither of us are attempting to be the last lineup. The word ‘final’ in the original statement was meant to indicate it will be the last LP of unheard studio recordings. Is it the Fall? Well, Mark is the Fall, so yes, these are Fall songs. If you’re not convinced, don’t buy it.”View image in fullscreenMark E Smith and Pamela Vander.Photograph: Pamela VanderVander was in a relationship with Smith for the last three years of his life, painted the cover of New Facts Emerge, is named in his will (along with his three sisters) and became his carer when he was dying from lung and kidney cancer.LA fans, Mark E Smith’s sisters and Frank Skinner doing the quiz: inside the totally wired festival on the FallRead moreShe said: “He was my soulmate and I’ve not had another boyfriend since he passed. Mark loved fronting the Fall and it was his decision to keep performing until the very end. That man would have died on stage and been happy doing that. He wasn’t embarrassed or scared to go on stage in a wheelchair. To see someone going under physically like that – not being able to use his legs and such – but remain so sharp mentally to the very end was quite a thing to witness. After Salford Royal [hospital] let him go home, in the end it was just me and Mark in the house. When he passed it was almost supernatural. Rain suddenly started crashing down, like a monsoon. It messed me up for ages.”Having initially kept her counsel because “I’d not been in that [Fall] world for years”, she said she decided to speak out against the new release because “it’s been eating me up. I feel it’s still my job to stand up for Mark.”Explore more on these topicsMusicMark E SmithThe FallIndiePop and rockMusic industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Seasons review – Portuguese pastoral offers poetic excavation of myth and mapping | Movies | The Guardian
description: The rugged roads and lush vegetation of southern Portugal are showcased in this weaving-together of disparate threads of history and landscape
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: The rugged roads and lush vegetation of southern Portugal are showcased in this weaving-together of disparate threads of history and landscape
Content: A form of a cinematic excavation … The Seasons.Photograph: PR ImageView image in fullscreenA form of a cinematic excavation … The Seasons.Photograph: PR ImageMoviesReviewThe Seasons review – Portuguese pastoral offers poetic excavation of myth and mappingThe rugged roads and lush vegetation of southern Portugal are showcased in this weaving-together of disparate threads of history and landscapePhuong LeMon 21 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a sea of doomsday ecological documentaries, Maureen Fazendeiro’s pastoral marvel is a sight for sore eyes. A solo debut feature for the Lisbon-based French director, this hybrid film studies the historical and geographical contours of Alentejo, a rural region in southernPortugal. The opening is set to a jaunty soundtrack of energetic percussion beats and twinkling organ notes, taking in the resplendent vistas of the landscape, with its rugged roads and lush vegetation. We see, too, a small archaeological tool hunt for ancient relics beneath layers of golden dust. Mirroring these acts of care and attention, Fazendeiro’s film takes the form of a cinematic excavation, fusing present-day tableaux with archival materials, folkloric legends with historical records.The abundant use of tracking shots not only takes in the wondrous biodiversity of Alentejo but also facilitates a fluid movement between separate epochs. Observational scenes of green hills, boundless blue skies and roaming livestock are overlaid with narrated excerpts from second world war-era letters written by German archaeologists Georg and Vera Leisner. Credited with producing the first inventory of megalithic monuments in Alentejo, the pair imbues their wartime correspondence with the joy of discovery and the sadness of exile.Elsewhere, history is preserved in oral tradition. One scene observes a circle of elders, in which a woman laments the rise of fascism and the fall of socialism in song, wistful melodies that reminds us of the years of António de Oliveira Salazar’s dictatorship. Another striking sequence takes a leap of imagination by re-staging a 17th-century myth. In weaving together these disparate threads of narrative, Fazendeiro’s sumptuous film offers an alternative form of geographical mapping, in which a landscape can be read like a text or a poem, to be preserved and passed on to future generations.The Seasons isat the ICA, London, from 25 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsPortugalEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Still feel a jolt of joy’: why Dirty Dancing is my feelgood movie | Dirty Dancing | The Guardian
description: The latest in our ongoing series of writers highlighting their most rewatched comfort films remembers a 1987 teenage girl classic
Author: Hannah Marriott
Headline: The latest in our ongoing series of writers highlighting their most rewatched comfort films remembers a 1987 teenage girl classic
Content: Jennifer Grey and Patrick Swayze in Dirty DancingPhotograph: /Lions Gate Entertainment Inc.View image in fullscreenJennifer Grey and Patrick Swayze in Dirty DancingPhotograph: /Lions Gate Entertainment Inc.My feelgood movieDirty Dancing‘Still feel a jolt of joy’: why Dirty Dancing is my feelgood movieThe latest in our ongoing series of writers highlighting their most rewatched comfort films remembers a 1987 teenage girl classicHannah MarriottMon 21 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is probably a Swedish word for the emotional state engendered in me byDirty Dancing. A kind of turbo-nostalgia which blends solace, joy and a sense of continuity with a yearning so acute I can feel it in my ribs.I must have been around 12 years old when I first watched Baby (Jennifer Grey) and Johnny (Patrick Swayze) fall in love while bumping pelvises as dance partners (before Strictly Come Dancing, this trajectory felt more surprising.)The movie must have seemed quite raunchy to me then. Light on actual sex, but heavy on petting during extended scenes of hot, fully-clothed couples grinding to a soundtrack of objectively incredible music. Catnip, then, for curious tweenage girls.‘I never pass up a rewatch’: why Valley Girl is my feelgood movieRead moreFor several years, Dirty Dancing was the wallpaper to every sleepover I went to. Its catchphrases were social currency at my girls’ school. Shouting “I carried a watermelon,” or “nobody puts Baby in the corner!” across a crowded classroom signaled a nuanced understanding of the Year 7 zeitgeist. And, of course, we all tried to do the lift. So many memories of uniformed girls landing on top of other uniformed girls at break time; so many scraped knees and elbows.Its soundtrack was omnipresent at school discos. There were so many bangers, like The Ronette’s Be My Baby, though there was also (I’ve Had) The Time of My Life, which still strikes Pavlovian terror into my heart. Those opening lines mean: it’s slow dance time, time to hide in the loo! Because the fear of not being picked by a boy – of being publicly stranded – was just too much to bear. We were that uncool. Which was why we loved Dirty Dancing, because its protagonist, named Baby – none-too subtly for a coming-of-age tale – was a dweeb at first too.When Baby arrives at Kellerman’s, a stale Catskills resort, in the summer of 1963, she is child-like and awkward, prone to saying embarrassing things. She yearns to be part of the world she discovers in the camp’s staff quarters. There, badass dance instructors gyrate to songs such as Do You Love Me by The Contours behind closed doors. Her dull vacation takes a turn when Johnny – the biggest badass of all, all biceps, dark glasses and oscillating pelvis – happens to urgently need a partner for an important performance. Montages, and romance, ensue.So much has changed since I learnt this movie by heart – for me and for the world – – that when I watch it I almost can’t believe it still exists, preserved exactly as it was, looking and sounding somewhat out of time, like a dream, with its 1980s-meets-1960s soundtrack, its pastel palette and its costume design, blending 1980s perms and leotards with cat’s eye glasses and A-line frocks.There is a mournful quality to the aesthetic as a whole, which is heavy on mist and rain, on chirping crickets and colored lanterns reflecting on the lake. Much of the soundtrack is mournful too, particularly to the song She’s Like the Wind, sung by Swayze – watching it now, knowing that he died at the age of just 57, is additionally tragic.The dancing style, which Johnny at one point calls “soul dancing”, is clearly inspired by Black culture, but there are few Black characters, and none in starring roles. Meanwhile, the age of the characters (if not the actors, who were 26 and 34) is awkward. Baby is 17, Johnny 24, and he feels a great deal more grown up than her as the movie opens. Meanwhile, Johnny is working class, Baby is upper middle class, which plays into certain class tropes when, at the end, he says that she has “taught me about the kind of person I wanna be”.I don’t remember noticing any of that as a child, but I do think something else struck me – even if it was subconsciously. That’s how unusual it was to see a movie in which the male character, Johnny, was the object of lust, moreso than the female lead. Though Johnny is Baby’s mentor on the dancefloor – and yes, that’s a metaphor – she notices him first, and she is the more active player when their relationship turns romantic. It still feels rare that this movie is about her wanting, not his. Having grown up watching 1980s and 1990s Disney films, my school mates and I had probably never seen that on screen before. I haven’t seen it that much since. No wonder we were so obsessed that, three decades on, I still know all the songs, dance moves and lines, and still feel a jolt of joy when Johnny kicks off that exuberant final scene by announcing that nobody puts Baby in the corner.Dirty Dancing is available to rent digitally in the US, on ITVX in the UK and Amazon Prime in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsDirty DancingMy feelgood moviePatrick SwayzeRomance filmsDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Michael Gove finally gets to play prime minister in The Wargame | Television | The Guardian
description: Gove and Nicola Sturgeon join a simulated cabinet facing an escalating crisis. Plus: Stacey Dooley investigates ‘heightmaxxing’. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Gove and Nicola Sturgeon join a simulated cabinet facing an escalating crisis. Plus: Stacey Dooley investigates ‘heightmaxxing’. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Battle hardened … Michael Gove and Nicola Sturgeon are among the contenders of The Wargame.Photograph: Justin Downing/SkyView image in fullscreenBattle hardened … Michael Gove and Nicola Sturgeon are among the contenders of The Wargame.Photograph: Justin Downing/SkyTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Michael Gove finally gets to play prime minister in The WargameGove and Nicola Sturgeon join a simulated cabinet facing an escalating crisis. Plus: Stacey Dooley investigates ‘heightmaxxing’. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hollie Richardson,Hannah VerdierandGraeme VirtueMon 21 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Wargame9pm, Sky OneUsing political figures from our recent past, this docudrama maps out a British response to an escalating pattern of Russian aggression. Alongside Michael Gove (who gets to cosplay being prime minister at last), politicos including Harriet Harman andNicola Sturgeontake their places round the cabinet table. Credible commitment to the concept is essential to make the drama elements work, and all manage it reasonably well – particularly the unnamed Potus with Russian sympathies …Phil HarrisonClickbait Clinic With Stacey Dooley8.30pm, BBC OneLeg-lengthening surgery. If you can stomach it, hardyStacey Dooleyinvites us to watch the process of a procedure (breaking both legs, inserting screws) to kick off this new series. She’s looking into various health and wellness trends going viral on social media – this one being “heightmaxxing”.Hollie RichardsonFinding Britain’s Slave Traders With David Olusoga9pm, BBC TwoIf anyone doubted the violence and moral corruption underpinning Britain’s imperial past, this two-part documentary will set them straight.David Olusogainvestigates the register of British slave traders, which illuminates the links between the history of modern institutions (including the royal family) and the trade in human misery. Bleak but important.PH999: What Happened Next9pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenBrutal … 999: What Happened Next on Channel 4.Photograph: Channel 4There are some brutal “it could happen to you” stories in tonight’s episode, which traces the aftermath of emergency calls. A woman getting ready for a Christmas night out is stabbed in her own home and a gang stages a series of burglaries in an affluent area.Hannah VerdierColin from Accounts10pm, BBC TwoGordon (Patrick Brammall) and Ashley (Harriet Dyer) have split up from their very attractive partners – but that doesn’t mean they’re ready to get back together. In fact, Ashley brings a date to a sex party, which Gordon ends up at too. It unravels into another hilarious night of excruciating events.HRLucy Letby: Scapegoat?10pm, Channel 5After being found guilty of killing babies in her care, the UK’s most notorious neonatal nurse was jailed for life in 2023. But in the three years since Letby’s sentencing, the prosecution’s clinical and statistical evidence has been repeatedly challenged. This one-off documentary re-examines key points in a highly emotive case.Graeme VirtueExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightStacey DooleyDavid OlusogafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rising Up at Night review – community spirit shines bright in Kinshasa’s shadows | Movies | The Guardian
description: Religion and collective resilience are beacons of hope in an electricity-deprived DRC in this otherworldly documentary debut
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Religion and collective resilience are beacons of hope in an electricity-deprived DRC in this otherworldly documentary debut
Content: Otherworldly … Rising Up at Night.Photograph: PR HANDOUTView image in fullscreenOtherworldly … Rising Up at Night.Photograph: PR HANDOUTMoviesReviewRising Up at Night review – community spirit shines bright in Kinshasa’s shadowsReligion and collective resilience are beacons of hope in an electricity-deprived DRC in this otherworldly documentary debutPhuong LeMon 21 Sep 2026 04.05 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 06.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Nelson Makengo’s feature documentary debut, night stretches on to infinity. The film opens on a black screen – a void of darkness – while a recording of a fervent sermon sounds like rolling thunder. In Kinshasa, the capital city of theDemocratic Republic of the Congo, an electricity shortage has long plagued the inhabitants, leaving them to cling on to religion as a beacon of hope. Their plight is worsened by climate disasters resulting in floods. Viewed through Makengo’s lens, nocturnal life acquires an otherworldly dimension, as basic human necessities become an elusive luxury.Shot mostly in Makengo’s neighbourhood of Kisenso, the film observes the ways in which struggling city dwellers adapt to a life lived in the shadows. Meals are eaten by candlelight, while churchgoers wear light-up medallions to illuminate their prayer books. Such survival tactics speak to a collective resilience, while also rendering these previously mundane activities eerily dystopian. The matriarchs of the community lament the rise of crime and sexual assaults that occur in the absence of public lighting, while younger members of the neighbourhood raise funds to retrieve stolen electric cables. In the absence of state support, this community spirit is the only energy that perseveres in times of extreme precarity.Makengo layers his intricate compositions with a dense soundscape that oscillates between urban noises, feverish religious chants and sombre news reports. Time and again we hear of plans for a hydroelectric plant backed by a major Chinese corporation, a multi-billion-dollar project that has undergone numerous delays. For the people of Kisenso, the future remains uncertain, but their moving camaraderie continues to shine bright in the face of hardship.Rising Up at Night is on True Story from 25 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsDemocratic Republic of the CongoAfricareviewsShareReuse this content
