title: Bluebeard’s Castle/Oedipus Rex review – gory, gruesome and gripping double bill  | Opera | The Guardian
description: Joe Hill-Gibbins’ claustrophobic staging of Bartók’s opera of dark symbolism is paired with his brand new production of Stravinsky’s psychological drama
Author: Rian Evans
Headline: Joe Hill-Gibbins’ claustrophobic staging of Bartók’s opera of dark symbolism is paired with his brand new production of Stravinsky’s psychological drama
Content: Powerful  … Christine Rice as Judith and Nathan Berg as Bluebeard in Welsh National Opera’s Bluebeard’s Castle.Photograph: Dafydd OwenView image in fullscreenPowerful  … Christine Rice as Judith and Nathan Berg as Bluebeard in Welsh National Opera’s Bluebeard’s Castle.Photograph: Dafydd OwenOperaReviewBluebeard’s Castle/Oedipus Rex review – gory, gruesome and gripping double billWales Millennium Centre, CardiffJoe Hill-Gibbins’ claustrophobic staging of Bartók’s opera of dark symbolism is paired with his brand new production of Stravinsky’s psychological drama, with Peter Hoare superb as the tragic heroRian EvansMon 21 Sep 2026 09.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 10.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWelsh National Operamight be marking its 80th year, but any feelgood factor is decidedly absent from their season-opener. Bartók’s only opera and Stravinsky’s opera-oratorio form a challenging double-bill: serial murders, patricide and incest, blood and more blood, but gripping performances made this a powerful experience.Béla Balázs’s libretto for Bluebeard’s Castle transformed the Perrault fairytale and its happy ending into an intense psychological drama: the castle with its weeping walls and seven locked doors a metaphor for the secret inner workings of the male psyche, and Judith, Bluebeard’s new wife, his fourth, the archetypal woman, too curious for her own good.View image in fullscreenIntimacy as palpable as the unfolding horror … Nathan Berg as Bluebeard.Photograph: Dafydd OwenIn this stagingfirst seen at English National Opera in 2024, director Joe Hill-Gibbins tightens the focus even more sharply so that the castle doors and its keys are also metaphorical, with LJ Parkinson’s Bard – the shamanicregös(narrator) of Hungarian tradition – offering the signature contents of the hidden rooms. Cutlery for weaponry, treasury gold thrown about in sweeping gestures, bouquets of flowers, all are tailored – both to the intricacies of the score and to the setting of the single long table – to mirror the emotional wrangling as, one by one, Judith demands that the doors be opened. The feat ofChristine Rice’s expressive Judith andNathan Berg’s implacable Bluebeard is to create an intimacy as palpable as the unfolding horror.By way of preface to Bartók’s dark symbolism, and in a departure from the ENO version, the women of the WNO chorus, ghostly presences in white, intoned the antiphon O Rubor Sanguinis and the responsory Rex Noster Promptus Est of Hildegard von Bingen, redolent of the blood of martyrdom and of innocents. Their emergence as the final door is opened identifies them as Bluebeard’s previous wives in their wedding finery, 14 all told. But here again, this production departs from the norm, since Judith does not join them – she is condemned instead to live an eternal hell with Bluebeard. His final utterance, “darkness”, with its tritone, the devil’s interval, spells the impossibility of redemption.View image in fullscreenIn total vocal command … Stephen Richardson (Creon & Messenger) and Peter Hoare (Oedipus) in Oedipus Rex.Photograph: Dafydd OwenHill-Gibbins’s Oedipus Rex is new and, using the full width of the Millennium Centre stage and a formidable 35-strong male chorus embodying the force of the Theban populace, lends a scale that fulfils Stravinsky’s aim of a classical monumentality, reinforced by the Latin translation of Jean Cocteau’s original text. The crushing weight of fate is always present, everything stark black, save for a huge half-globe of light – its dazzle sometimes rendering the surtitles invisible – the bright glamour of Rice’s impassioned Jocasta and the blood-red suit ofPeter Hoare’s Oedipus. Hoare, in total vocal command, conveyed convincingly the gradual disintegration of kingly mien, slow to realise the awful truth that he did indeed kill his father and marry his mother, finally inflicting on himself the ultimate dark of blindness.For all the ritualistic element, nothing was static, with arguably too much running around and crawling, and some of Parkinson’s narration was under-projected. But, bound by the authoritative conducting ofLidiya Yankovskaya, who brought Bartók’s eloquence to the fore, and found playful moments as well as grave solemnity in the Stravinsky, this was strong stuff.At the Wales Millennium Centre, Cardiff, 25 September, then touring to Llandudno, Oxford and Plymouth.Explore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicWelsh National OperareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Celebrity, sex and motherhood misery: the 10 best books by Rachel Cusk … ranked! | Books | The Guardian
description: From an abstract portrait of an actor who might be Natalie Portman to a groundbreaking work of autofiction, we rate the best from the coolly controversial author
Author: John Self
Headline: From an abstract portrait of an actor who might be Natalie Portman to a groundbreaking work of autofiction, we rate the best from the coolly controversial author
Content: Breaking free of conventional fiction … Rachel Cusk.Photograph: Enric Fontcuberta/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBreaking free of conventional fiction … Rachel Cusk.Photograph: Enric Fontcuberta/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockRankedBooksCelebrity, sex and motherhood misery: the 10 best books by Rachel Cusk … ranked!From an abstract portrait of an actor who might be Natalie Portman to a groundbreaking work of autofiction, we rate the best from the coolly controversial authorJohn SelfMon 21 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreen10Life of M(2026)In Cusk’s headline-grabbing latest, a writer invents the biography of a film star who sounds very like Natalie Portman. Set in the now standard late-Cusk sans serif typeface (no frivolous flourishes!), Life of M serves up observations on fame in a light fictional coating. “To always be playing a part is to have no home.” Having made her name as a devilishly good creator of brainy social comedies, Cusk’s pivot to wintry autofiction since the Outline trilogy appears to have reached its logical conclusion in this flat, abstracted portrait of empty celebrity. The New York Times called it “rarefied, cosmopolitan, self-serious”.Sample line:“Everything I did or said in her company was false. It was as if I was acting, while M came across as authentic and real.”View image in fullscreen9The Lucky Ones(2003)A collection of stories about diverse characters who are linked by the influence of a newspaper columnist. They start weakly – Cusk struggles to embody a working-class female prisoner – but improve once she turns her caustic eye to ski trips and lawyers. The short form enables Cusk to show a narrative strength we don’t always see.Sample line:“Jane and Thomas were ironing out their lives in preparation for parenthood, starching and folding and putting away their youth, their excitement, their spontaneity.”View image in fullscreen8Saving Agnes(1993)After a cracking first line (“The house, like the party, was subsiding”), Cusk’s cheerfully comic debut tickles the reader throughout, as Agnes Day looks for love in contemporary London. Published to acclaim (and a Whitbread award) when Cusk was 26, it has a young writer’s weakness for using elaborate locutions as a shortcut to comedy, but there’s energy on every page, and her phrasing is always perfect: Agnes’s friend Merlin has “a salary for which Elizabeth Bennet would have left Darcy’s dinner burning in the oven”.Sample line:“Like a mirror he gave back nothing but what was already there; smash it and he would be gone, leaving her with nothing but a rearranged face and a few years of bad luck.”View image in fullscreen7The Temporary(1995)Cusk’s sparky second novel is a romantic dramedy. Two Londoners – publishing temp Francine and posh Ralph – bond over a dried-out risotto “like a dish of planetary matter brought back by an alien”. Francine’s house moves frustrate her mother (“You’ve quite ruined my new address book, what with all the crossings-out”); then Ralph wants to move on too. “I thought she understood it was just a temporary thing.” The story builds to an impressively messy climax, with Cusk switching between viewpoints and building tension.Sample line: “‘I’m something of an intellectual myself,’ Neil had said, straightening a tie across which autonomous golf clubs roamed.”View image in fullscreen6Second Place(2021)A writer, M, invites the devilish painter L to live in her home, and some chewy stranger-in-our-midst stuff ensues, upending family life and giving the opportunity for some classic Cuskian observations. “I need to get at the truth of a thing and dig and dig until it is dragged painfully to light.” There’s drama – as L humiliates M and her husband – and comedy, as M’s daughter’s boyfriend reads everyone his terrible novel-in-progress. Inspired by DH Lawrence’s stay in New Mexico in the 1920s, Second Place is a curious novel, and it’s the weirdness that makes it interesting.Sample line:“I’ve been criticised all my life – it’s how I’ve come to know that I’m there.”View image in fullscreen5A Life’s Work(2001)Cusk’s memoir of “all that love and terror and strangeness” of becoming a mother. It’s a book of scorched-earth candour: Cusk acknowledges her own misery at the drudgery of early motherhood and curses the asininity of childcare books. It was of course controversial, not for its writing – few could fault that – but for daring to challenge a Pollyanna-ish portrayal of parenthood. Cusk was unabashed: “This is not a childcare manual, ladies. In these pages you have to think for yourselves.”Sample line: “When I found myself pregnant again when Albertine was six months old I greeted my old cell with the cheerless acceptance of the convict intercepted at large.”View image in fullscreen4Arlington Park(2006)This novel’s Joycean opening settles down to an exquisitely written social comedy. The story of five young mothers, it feels at times like a fictional extension of A Life’s Work: each resents the confinements of motherhood. Perhaps this is what gives the novel its jaundiced eye; not just snobbish (“Mandy Clapp – it was the name on the badge of someone working at a supermarket checkout”) but misanthropic: everyone gets it. “She’d get pretty damned jumpy if her husband’s salary didn’t come rolling in like a Pacific breaker every month, or if people stopped thinking she looked like Felicity Kendal.” But it’s brilliantly funny.Sample line: “It was funny that she had ended up as a teacher, back at school. It made it seem that she wasn’t bright or gifted or exceptional at all. She was merely good at going to school.”View image in fullscreen3In the Fold(2005)This novel is a perfect amalgam of the qualities of early Cusk: funny, cynical, rigorous and linguistically precise. Its narrative of characters who are socially and materially conformist but terrified of appearing conventional centres on a man who falls in with a wealthy family. But the upheavals of the plot – things collapse and break – are less important than the sinuous sentences and streams of dialogue. Hidden here, though, we can perhaps see early evidence of Cusk’s desire to break free of conventional fiction. As one character has it: “Better to be broken than to be a slave of method!”Sample line:“[The schoolboys] make a list of the mothers they’d most like to sleep with. This is the first time she hasn’t made it. It’s soembarrassingfor her.”2The Country Life(1997)longest novel is the blackest of all her early comedies, the humour as often situational as verbal. Stella Benson abandons her job and boyfriend to become an au pair for a rural family’s disabled son. She’s not there long before strange, sinister things start to happen. She defaces the gardens by vomiting pink luncheon meat over them. She discovers a book titled The Runaway Bride by Stella Benson. This is a novel of broad and deep character insight, of social awareness – and of unexpected sexual awakening.Sample line: “I am normally a slow and careful eater, having been schooled by my mother in the many social atrocities it is possible unwittingly to commit during the ingestion of food.”View image in fullscreen1The Outline trilogy(2014-18)“I had no desire to prove that one book was better than another,” says Faye, the narrator. Well, we do! Outline’s revolution took Cusk’s art to a new place, wholly rejecting traditional character and description, and defining writer Faye – who bears similarities to Cusk – in relation to the people she meets on a trip to Athens. “I was beginning to see my own fears and desires manifested outside myself.” There are stories aplenty, but the overall tone is spare and cool, making something entirely original from the wreckage of Cusk’s need to dispose of her old ways. Two sequels followed – Transit and Kudos – but it was the first book that really shook things up. Critics argued that while it offered “few of the standard expected rewards of fiction”, it was nonetheless “a triumph of attitude and daring”.Sample line: “But what other people thought was no longer of any help to me. Those thoughts only existed within certain structures, and I had definitively left those structures.”Explore more on these topicsBooksRankedRachel CuskFictionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From the ridicule of Trump to the rise of Jack Welch: how the 1980s shaped and changed America | Books | The Guardian
description: In When America Roared, Pulitzer-winning reporter Jonathan Kaufman looks back to a decade of greed and excess, and uses it to explore where we are today
Author: Martin Pengelly
Headline: In When America Roared, Pulitzer-winning reporter Jonathan Kaufman looks back to a decade of greed and excess, and uses it to explore where we are today
Content: ‘You can just see the way he looks at the world: the glitz, the cheapness, the gold brocade everywhere. That screams 1980s’ … Donald Trump in 1987.Photograph: Joe McNally/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘You can just see the way he looks at the world: the glitz, the cheapness, the gold brocade everywhere. That screams 1980s’ … Donald Trump in 1987.Photograph: Joe McNally/Getty ImagesBooksFrom the ridicule of Trump to the rise of Jack Welch: how the 1980s shaped and changed AmericaIn When America Roared, Pulitzer-winning reporter Jonathan Kaufman looks back to a decade of greed and excess, and uses it to explore where we are todayMartin PengellyMon 21 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump is “so much a creature of the 80s but even in the 80s, everyone made fun of him,” Jonathan Kaufman said. General Electric CEO Jack Welch, “the most prominent business figure in the country, maybe in the world, mocked him. No one took him seriously.“Even today, if you look at the [White House] ballroom, you look at all the things he’s doing, it’s this 1980s aesthetic, right? You can just see the way he looks at the world: the glitz, the cheapness, the gold brocade everywhere. That screams 1980s. All he needs is big hair and leg warmers and listening to, I don’t know, synthetic pop, and he’d be right back in 1985.”Kaufman’s new book,When America Roared, tells the story of “How the 1980s Saved, then Broke, the Coun­try – and Led Us to Today”, a time when Trump has to be taken seriously as he breaks us all over again.A Pulitzer-winning reporter,Kaufmanworked in the 80s for the Boston Globe and the Wall Street Journal. Now director of the School of Journalism at Northeastern University and the author of three books on Jewish culture and history, he has written a page-turning account of the decade, its activists and reactionaries, its failures and successes. Trump included.“All my books have been in a sense biographies, trying to understand through people,” Kaufman said. “I think there’s this tendency to talk about the 1980s or the 1960s as if they’re this concept that sort of landed and changed everything but in fact it was people making decisions, so some of the choices [of subjects] were prominent. Jack Welch: that’s an easy call if you’re writing about business.”View image in fullscreenTrump and Jack Welch in 2017.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesWelchdied in 2020, aged 84. Kaufman shows how at GE he broke the American corporate model, energizing profits but brutalizing workers, his blast-like impact earning him the nickname “Neutron Jack”. A complex character, his portrait in When America Roared is rigorously journalistic, sympathetic but unsparing. It arrives with the fruits of his labor present for all to see, in figures showing US workers are less rewardedthan at any time on record.Also “intrigued by some of the things that were going on that maybe didn’t get as much attention”, Kaufman “was drawn to Karen Nussbaum”, the feminist labor leader and activist,still campaigning at 76, decades after providing the name and “the inspiration forthe film 9 to 5, which Dolly Parton wrote the famous song for and which was a huge movie that came out in December 1980. Ronald Reagan loved it. If you watch it today, it’s still a great film. It’s a comedy with Jane Fonda, but the real story wasn’t known as well, and I wanted to understand that.“John Rogerswas someone I’d met in the 80s who is now the most prominent Black person on Wall Street. When I met him, he had just opened this little firm in Chicago, and he had voted for Reagan. I was working for the Journal, so he was a great source for me. But then over time, when I went back to him, he had become very close to Barack Obama, and his views had changed.“In a way, the most intriguing person I wrote about was someone I’d lost touch with: my old college roommate,Evan Wolfson. We were at a reunion, and people were coming up to him almost as if he was kind of this mythical figure. He led the gay marriage movement. It succeeded in 2015 but he came up with the idea in the 1980s. He was at Harvard Law School and wrote this 100-plus-page paper about gay marriage, and everyone laughed at him. It seemed such an absurd idea. Aids was everywhere. I reconnected with him, then discovered that he had really put together this extraordinary strategy ofhow to win gay marriage, which I think today is relevant because once again we’re in very conservative times.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Penguin Random HouseJournalism and history have their cliches: journalism is the first draft of history, history teaches us to avoid past mistakes. A journalist at the time he now writes about, Kaufman aimed to write “the second draft of history”, a highly readable story with lessons to teach.Considering “people who were maybe below the radar who had more of an impact than we thought”, Kaufman said “probably the most important of those is this fellow Mark Fowler, who was sort of an obscure bureaucrat”, Federal Communications Commission chair under Ronald Reagan.“My wife [Barbara Howard] is also a journalist. And when we started going out in the 80s, she was working in radio journalism for commercial stations, and she used rail about the FCC. I was like, ‘Who ever heard of the FCC? Who cares?’ But she was talking about deregulation and what was going on, and was she right … I connected with Fowler [now 84], and he turns out to have been pivotal in all the media changes. He paved the way for Rupert Murdoch to move into television, paved the way for the polarization of media.”Reading Kaufman’s account of how Fowler – “a very charming guy, I have to say, very affable” – made possible Fox News and all that came with it, Rush Limbaugh and talk radio too, it’s impossible not to think ofBrendan Carr, Trump’s FCC hatchet manattacking critics, clearing the way for rightwing voices, mocking first amendment rights. Speaking to Kaufman, Fowler disapproved of Trump’s methods and character but approved of his results. It’s a pointer to why so many Americans have tolerated Trump’s brutal assault on norms and structures beyond the media sphere. For free marketeers as well as anti-woke warriors, Trump has delivered.“The Democrats could not figure out for 12 years how to beat Reagan,” Kaufman said. “That’s something very important to think about because I think the Democrats are going through some of the same disputes now: liberal versus conservative, ‘Are we out of touch?’“But it also struck me that Republicans always talk about the ‘deep state’ and this belief that it runs everything. Frankly, if you look at deregulation of the media, or how the Federalist Society started rebuilding the judiciary , it’s the Republicans who created the deep state, in many ways – and incredibly effectively, too. I think they systematically changed the way people think about business. They changed the media. They clearly changed the courts, and now that thinking continues in their war against universities and so forth.”Trump may have been formed bythe mob lawyer Roy Cohn, who he met in the 70s, but he came to fame in the 80s. His rise to the White House in 2016 would not have been predicted in that day-glo decade, but here we are. Republicans “did get everything they wanted”, Kaufman said, “and I think Democrats and liberals are still flailing around, trying to figure out how did they do it, and how do we fight back.”When America Roared isout nowExplore more on these topicsBooksHistory booksDonald TrumpfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The American Way of Killing by Malcolm Gladwell review – wide of the mark | Malcolm Gladwell | The Guardian
description: Gladwell’s highly readable investigation into US gun culture fails to engage with the bigger questions
Author: Gary Younge
Headline: Gladwell’s highly readable investigation into US gun culture fails to engage with the bigger questions
Content: A shop selling guns in Orem, Utah.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA shop selling guns in Orem, Utah.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesBook of the dayMalcolm GladwellReviewThe American Way of Killing by Malcolm Gladwell review – wide of the markGladwell’s highly readable investigation into US gun culture fails to engage with the bigger questionsGary YoungeMon 21 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnce, while having a steak dinner with Republicans in a small town in Indiana, the man sitting opposite me asked: “How do you cope in London, when Muslims elected that mayor and you have all that gun control?” I’d been in enough such situations to know that there was no “winning” a conversation that starts like this and so did my best to playfully bat the question away.“Well, the Muslims didn’t elect a mayor – Londoners elected a Muslim mayor,” I said. “And we don’t talk much about gun control for the same reason we don’t talk about polar bear control: we don’t have many polar bears and we don’t have many guns.”The quip didn’t land. The table looked at me somewhat bemused. The local party leader leaned over to help dig me out. “They don’t have freedom,” he explained. “They don’t understand freedom.”In the two decades I spent reporting from America – 12 years as a correspondent for this paper – gun culture was one of two major issues that was difficult to translate (the other was health care). After every high-profile mass shooting, editors in London would ask whether this would finally prompt gun control, while in the US the sale of guns would go up as people “sought protection” from the next shooter.Malcolm Gladwell’s The American Way of Killing will not help the translation much. Gladwell, who grew up in Canada, sets out to ask why: “a young boy like me can grow up [in one place] without any first-hand experience of lethal violence at all, [while] in another a young man can bury more than a dozen of his closest friends by his 30th birthday … What is so different about the United States?” It’s a big question. And if there’s one thing Gladwell loves, it is big questions.He is the bestselling author of several popular books including The Tipping Point, which seeks to pinpoint the process by which individual choices turn into social epidemics; Blink, which investigates how we make informed decisions through our unconscious; and Outliers, which seeks to explain success and talent through graft. His method is to blend a breezy, readable writing style with a kind of Socratic, analytical approach that revels in its lack of ideological commitment; exquisite writing and pitch perfect story underpinned by moral ambivalence, which presents its findings as both mould-breaking and iconoclastic.As social commentary his books are witty, vivid and accessible, providing the kind of nuggets that do well at dinner parties so long as nobody there is remotely impacted by the topic at hand. As meaningful guides to social policy and political intervention they are occasionally insightful but, for the most part, thin and, at their worst, counterproductive. Gladwell’s approach may appear to work when addressing a subject readers have never really thought about, but it breaks down with one – like guns in the US – that has been covered extensively.Unlike in his previous books, he doesn’t aspire to construct a single argument and then write it through from beginning to end. Instead, he offers a series of discrete, and at times related, observations around America’s relationship to gun violence. His curiosity sprawls across disciplines and themes. He interviews doctors, sociologists, former police chiefs, criminologists, public health specialists, historians, psychologists, legal scholars, and surgeons, while his research takes in supreme court cases, slave history, 17th-century law, physiology, 18th-century grammar and firearms technology.double quotation markBy avoiding analysis of structural inequalities he fails to engage with who gets murdered by guns and whyEvoking the parable of the blind men and the elephant he promises: “chapters on the trunk and the leg and the tusk, and at the end my hope is that by seeing all the parts in one place you will finally get a sense of the whole elephant – and understand that what seems from the outside like an intractable problem need not be intractable at all”.Many of the chapters make useful corrections to the dominant narrative that are well known but bear repeating. He shows how the drop in gun deaths is due to improvements in surgery and other medical interventions rather than a drop in the number of shootings – showing how America can simultaneously be just as violent but less deadly. He explains how the “militia” mentioned in the second amendment were more about suppressing slave rebellions than defending themselves from state tyranny. He shows that most gun murders are the result of “expressive violence”–impulsive eruptions of anger – rather than “instrumental violence”–conscious, pre-meditated decisions to break the law.Some are of marginal interest but little real consequence. Following a fairly involved introduction to gun technology he explains why the narrow focus on assault rifles is misguided. He devotes considerable space to litigating case law from 17th-century England which has come up in supreme court trials, as though settling it would in some way settle the legal case around gun control.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA key theme running through the first part of the book is that America’s gun debate (if one can call it that) is undermined by a series of dishonest conversations that disable any substantive conversation. That is true. When Americans think of gun violence they imagine school massacres, gang members and cop shootings. The reality is you are more likely to be shot dead by someone you know than someone you don’t; most people who are killed by guns kill themselves; you are more likely to be shot dead if you have a gun in the house than if you don’t; mass shootings comprise a minority of gun murders; almost twice as many white people are killed by guns than black people; most Americans favour gun control and believe an increase in the number of guns will be bad for the country.But much of the conversation that Gladwell initiates in the book is not honest either. By avoiding any serious analysis of systemic and structural inequalities – particularly in terms of race and class – he fails to engage with who gets murdered by guns and why. (He alludes to it, obliquely, in a section about how trauma centres are routinely located a significant distance from where black, brown and poor people tend to live, which costs lives.) He talks to doctors on the southside of Chicago, in Baltimore and sociologists in Alabama’s black belt – areas where many black and poor people are shot – without comment as to why that should be.He advocates for more police, pointing out that the US has fewer police per capita than most European countries (which I certainly would never have guessed), without reflecting on who they tend to shoot and for what reasons. In a nation where non-racial democracy is a relatively new and fragile practice, that could lead to an escalation of violence rather than suppressing it. He derides the slogan to Defund the Police without acknowledging that a central plank of that demand was to shift resources from policing to mental health care, youth work and other social programmes that would address root causes. He deconstructs the confused syntax of the second amendment and concludes that the problem is not that a well-funded lobby, embedded in the far-right, wields disproportionate influence on America’s polity and judiciary, but that “it was written according to a set of rules and grammatical norms that no longer exist”.As a result the reader is left with a sense that, when it comes to the US and guns, there are various things amiss, but with little idea of how substantial a difference they make to the problem, why they have not been addressed and who suffers as a result. Gladwell manages to skilfully depict the odd trunk, tusk and leg but somehow misses several elephants in the room.Gary Younge is a professor of sociology at the University of Manchester and author of Another Day in the Death of America. The American Way of Killing: The Invention of an Epidemic by Malcolm Gladwell is published by Little, Brown (£25). To support the Guardian, buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: The Recovery House by Derek Owusu review – a uniquely honest view of mental health | Books | The Guardian
description: Writing from firsthand experience, the author offers an affecting meditation on art, mental fragility and faith
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Writing from firsthand experience, the author offers an affecting meditation on art, mental fragility and faith
Content: Preternatural tenderness … Derek Owusu.Photograph: Josima SeniorView image in fullscreenPreternatural tenderness … Derek Owusu.Photograph: Josima SeniorBooksReviewThe Recovery House by Derek Owusu review – a uniquely honest view of mental healthWriting from firsthand experience, the author offers an affecting meditation on art, mental fragility and faithEmma LoffhagenMon 21 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 04.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“What’s in your head?” Dolores O’Riordan’s raw, plaintive refrain loops through the Cranberries’ 1994 hit Zombie. A protest song about the Troubles could, on paper, hardly seem further removed from Derek Owusu’s third novel, about a young writer recovering from a mental health crisis. But in an author’s note before The Recovery House begins, Owusu instructs the reader to listen to the song “at least two to four times before going beyond this page”. Gradually it becomes clear that the song’s central question is one Owusu’s protagonist asks in various forms throughout the novel.Can we ever fully understand what is going on in our own heads? We meet Jamal, a young novelist who has woken up in a recovery house – a residential alternative to hospital admission – after a breakdown. It transpires that he has overdosed,is an alcoholic, and has been diagnosed with borderline personality disorder. He is in a frazzled, frantic state, initially less interested in getting better than in piecing together how he got there.The house itself is hardly a sanctuary in the conventional sense: Jamal finds a single bed with protruding springs, dead cockroaches in the nightstand and restless corridors in which people in various states of distress move around one another. Jamal’s nurses watch him; he watches them back. Owusu knows the world he is writing about – he spent a summer in a recovery house himself after a mental health crisis, and there is an intimacy to the way he renders this suspended, in-between place.Writing is both Jamal’s vocation and his illness. Like Owusu, he has published two books and won an award for his first; the expectations surrounding the third have become unbearable, and he eventually remembers that it was the attempt to write it that precipitated his breakdown. He comes to the frightening realisation that “the thing that inspired me is the thing that’s trying to kill me”. His frustration with the world of publishing is also evident: “why does everyone in this industry want something from you even though we’re all very aware that things usually take time.”double quotation markAt just 160 pages, The Recovery House is a very small book about some very large questionsA woman staying in the room below Jamal sings Zombie’s chorus in the night, over and over, until he finds himself singing it too, flooding his mind in interstitial moments. The singer, Joy, eventually slips a pen and paper beneath his door, something the nurses have refused him for fear of what writing will provoke. From there, they develop a tender, almost soulmate-like friendship, which becomes inflected with religion when the pair begin a weekly Bible study session together. Faith, as rendered by Owusu, is not cruel or exacting. There is something almost prelapsarian in Jamal and Joy’s relationship with God, as there is about their friendship – an innocent, platonic love. Between them, “What’s in your head?” transforms from a fear into an invitation: tell me.The recovery house gradually becomes a strange, fragile ecosystem for Jamal’s convalescence. He shares cigarettes with its motley crew of residents, observes their dramas and begins to emerge from himself. It offers something a hospital cannot: a temporary, disparate community of people who understand that we are perhaps all closer to the precipice of collapse than we like to imagine. “Who was well in the world anyway?” one of the patients asks, concluding: “there was only the sick and those who didn’t realise it yet”.At just 160 pages, The Recovery House is a very small book about some very large questions: what separates illness from inspiration? When does that inspiration become compulsion, when does self-examination slip into self-destruction? Owusu is interested in the porous boundaries between these states, and his prose mimics them. Written in long, free-flowing sentences, with sparse punctuation and no conventional chapter markings, the novel has the rhythm of a poem, one thought spilling into the next before it can be contained.Owusu’s novel is slight enough to cradle in your hands, and it feels as though it must be handled in this way: with care, liable to shatter if held too tightly. It is a uniquely honest and affecting meditation on art, religion and mental health, told with a preternatural tenderness. At times it is almost painfully raw, reading like an excavation of the soul of a writer wondering whether, in turning his life into art, he has also been exploiting it.The Recovery House by Derek Owusu is published by Merky Books (£16.99). title: Silent Hill: Townfall review – shame and suffering on the Scottish coast | Games | The Guardian
description: Tragedy, and an apocalyptic fog, befall a fishing community. It is up to outsider Simon to offer some kind of closure
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: Tragedy, and an apocalyptic fog, befall a fishing community. It is up to outsider Simon to offer some kind of closure
Content: Slow-burning … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Screen BurnView image in fullscreenSlow-burning … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Screen BurnGamesReviewSilent Hill: Townfall review – shame and suffering on the Scottish coastPlayStation 5 (version played), PC; Screen BurnTragedy, and an apocalyptic fog, befall a fishing community. It is up to outsider Simon to offer some kind of closureLewis GordonMon 21 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 12.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou spend a considerable portion of Silent Hill: Townfall in a kind of foetal position, cowering behind objects that will be eerily familiar to anyone who lived in the UK during the 1990s. Cars seem to be modelled on the era’s boxy Volkswagen Golfs; logos adorning phone boxes should narrowly escape the attention of copyright lawyers at BT Group. (For millennials, the deja vu will likely intensify the horror, as if stepping back into a childhood nightmare.) Simon, the nerdy, unassuming star of the game, pokes his head around corners to catch a glimpse of the demonic entities that wish to maim him, before shrinking back down again with a downwards motion of the analogue stick. In such moments, it’s easy to imagine him wrapping his arms around his knees, clasping his eyes shut and wishing himself away from this place.The game’s setting, St Amelia, is based on the fishing communities of the East Neuk of Fife. The terror lurking here is wonderfully specific: absent lairds, island poverty, an oil-drilling corporation. Anguished beasts lumber down quaint streets lined with sandstone houses and fluttering bunting. Thisvenerable horror seriesmay have shifted to Scotland, yet we remain firmly in classic Silent Hill territory – weather and all. St Amelia finds itself suffused in supernatural fog and the vast majority of its inhabitants have vanished following some kind of mass tragedy. The artful, evocative presentation is such that you can almost taste the in-game air, the briny seaside tang diluted by rainy mist.Visually, this scuzzy, grotty take on Silent Hill from Glasgow studio Screen Burn leans on bold juxtapositions of colour, shadow, and ominous silhouettes. Sometimes the stricken town is bathed in blood-red moonlight; often, pitch-black interiors are illuminated by harsh white torchlight. The arresting imagery brings to mind found-footage horror films such asRecand the spine-tingling camcorder sections of UK classic,The Descent. Simon soon finds a portable television with strange, arcane power: it receives odd, elliptical messages from a nurse called Zoe, and tracks nearby monsters whose outline appears in scratchy low resolution on its small screen.The action is slow-burning and absorbing: Simon lopes about town, hiding from depraved monsters and occasionally bludgeoning them to death with a pipe. To enter some buildings, he has to make an incision with a scalpel in a fleshy door opening as thick, fresh blood oozes out. Gradually, Simon’s reason for visiting St Amelia in the first place becomes clear: guilt. But he’s not the only one racked with it. Zoe, voiced with terrific glassy distance by Kezia Burrows, has her own hangups. The third playable character in this triple-threat portrait of shame and suffering is alpha male Richard, the CEO of an energy company that professed to bring prosperity to the island.There were times when I was so locked in that the hours seemed to pass by in the blink of an eye, as if time had gone wonky just like in St Amelia. One memorable stretch takes place in a municipal-style high-rise building. Armed with a shotgun, and attempting to avoid the game’s nippiest, nastiest enemies, I ascended and descended each floor, as if playing a brutal, Ballardian take onThe Raid. I have never felt such dread at the prospect of entering an open-plan office, knowing what lurked among mouldering office furniture and knackered desktop PCs.View image in fullscreenShrouded in fog … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Screen Burn InteractiveEvery element – scavenging for items, creeping between bins, running at full pelt when all else fails – pulls you deeper into Townfall. Its design broadly adheres todiegetic principles, in that most information is conveyed to you within the game: to view the map, for example, Simon physically pulls it out – the action never pauses. To save your progress, you must find a telephone in St Amelia, manually pick up the receiver, and then dial a number.Puzzles function similarly. You snoop through emails, install floppy disks, and pocket important bits of paper, usually in an effort to gain a key code. These puzzles, though relayed via grounded, dated real-world tech, follow a serendipitous dream logic; even getting stuck feels coherent within the game’s uncanny psychogeographic claustrophobia. (That is, until it doesn’t. Close to the game’s conclusion, one esoteric puzzle about deciphering industrial symbols killed my progress, and my bafflement, frustration and rage had less to do with Townfall’s hallucinatory horror and more to do with its obtuseness.)skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNot even a fiendishly illegible puzzle could derail Townfall. This is a taut, smart tale, less about psychosexual terror than psychosocial dread. What’s most surprising is where the game’s sympathies lie: not with Simon, nurse Zoe, or bullyboy Richard, but the people of St Amelia. Their memorial in the centre of town is one of the game’s clearest images, unobscured by fog, though we’re never privy to the exact events that lead to their deaths. Townfall seems to understand that some things should remain shrouded in fog. The fate of St Amelia naturally festers in our imagination. How very Silent Hill.Silent Hill: Townfall is released 24 September; £44.99Explore more on these topicsGamesSilent HillreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Roman Sands RE:Build review – marooned in a crumbling vaporwave dream | Games | The Guardian
description: The latest work from the team behind Paratopic is part compulsive time-loop management sim, part eerie subterranean adventure
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The latest work from the team behind Paratopic is part compulsive time-loop management sim, part eerie subterranean adventure
Content: Tantalising escape route … Roman Sands RE:Build.Photograph: Arbitrary MetricView image in fullscreenTantalising escape route … Roman Sands RE:Build.Photograph: Arbitrary MetricGamesReviewRoman Sands RE:Build review – marooned in a crumbling vaporwave dreamPC, Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox; Arbitrary MetricThe latest work from the team behind Paratopic is part compulsive time-loop management sim, part eerie subterranean adventureDiego Nicolás ArgüelloMon 21 Sep 2026 04.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 04.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFetch the chair from storage. Deliver a message that causes disgust. Clean vomit in the afternoon and pour another glass in the evening. In Roman Sands RE:Build, you provide concierge service to delirious, broken people who couldn’t care less about the sweat on your forehead and the bags under your eyes.In this reimagining of the 2019 visual novel Roman Sands, crafted by the team behind the Americana horror road trip Paratopic, you’re trapped in a beach resort and tethered in a time loop. The task is deceivingly simple: fulfil menial directives from four gluttonous individuals, unlock tools and items to open more rooms and then do it all over again.The loop is as monotonous as it sounds – and that’s the point. The visuals and sound work collide in flamboyantvaporwave-inspired story exposition. Reward animations are exaggerated to feed your lizard brain with dopamine, satirising the reward loops that make other games feel like a visit to a casino – somemore maliciouslythan others. There’s gig economy commentary to boot.Over time, I familiarised myself with everybody’s routine and needs. I was effective to the point of becoming uncomfortable about how entranced I was, squeezing every possible score multiplier out of every day so that I could spend fake money on stuff I didn’t need from agachaponmachine.View image in fullscreenChilling in the spa in Roman Sands RE:Build.Photograph: Arbitrary MetricBut this is only one half of Roman Sands RE:Build. Completing a series of (often obtuse) puzzles in the resort opens the cracks of the reality you’re trapped in, showing a tantalising escape route. In Act 2, the compulsive time-management is dimmed down in tone and rhythm.Here it’s just you, your dead cow and a familiar voice on the radio, in the bowels of a subterranean research station. A parasite threatens to dismantle an already decaying refuge. Stuck in yet another loop, you must locate spare parts to fix an increasingly demanding machine, all while managing your oxygen level and completing small puzzles with barely enough light to read your PDA. It’s a stark contrast to the luxury resort, yet both acts have you navigating spaces where the walls (and their captives) are barely holding together.Unfortunately this thematic cohesion is not matched by Roman Sands’ technical cohesion. The game froze multiple times, some button prompts didn’t appear until I restarted and occasionally a puzzle’s visual language was totally inscrutable, leaving me running in circles, unsure of how to progress. These problems frustrated me no end.I’m glad I got to see the story through, however, with its not-so-subtle homages to the likes of Danganronpa and Evangelion. It remains one step away from its mysteries and doesn’t take them to extreme lengths. There’s a profound and alluring melancholy etched into this work, a broken and messy world that’s strange enough to foster questions, but smart enough not to provide every answer.Roman Sands RE:Build is out now; £14.99Explore more on these topicsGamesSimulation gamesIndie gamesAdventure gamesPCPuzzle gamesGame playreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Nish Kumar: Angry Humour from a Really Nice Guy review – enraged and extremely funny | Comedy | The Guardian
description: There is real skill in making us laugh about things that are depressing. And the gags come thick and fast in the ex-Mash Report host’s touring show
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: There is real skill in making us laugh about things that are depressing. And the gags come thick and fast in the ex-Mash Report host’s touring show
Content: Deeply principled joke maker … Nish Kumar at Hackney Empire.Photograph: Paul GilbeyView image in fullscreenDeeply principled joke maker … Nish Kumar at Hackney Empire.Photograph: Paul GilbeyComedyReviewNish Kumar: Angry Humour from a Really Nice Guy review – enraged and extremely funnyHackney Empire, LondonThere is real skill in making us laugh about things that are depressing. And the gags come thick and fast in the ex-Mash Report host’s touring showAnya RyanMon 21 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNish Kumar is angry. And why shouldn’t he be? The world is one big, damning catastrophe. So here the ex-Mash Report host is, in his trademark linguistically dextrous, mile-a-minute style, to run us through the current affairs and colonial-history hellscape. Yes, we get Donald Trump jokes. And yes, there’s more than one mention of how the internet has corrupted us all. But, God, does it feel good to hear someone, clearly enraged, scream the things this Hackney audience is, more than likely, also thinking.He’s the UK’s leading lefty comedian – and for good reason. There is real skill in making us laugh about things that are, broadly, very depressing. Of course, Kumar knows he is preaching to the converted; he states plainly that his audience are a bunch of non-heckling, hand-raising “geeks” who are already on board with his views. Part of the show grapples with that discomfort; he believes passionately in standup as an art form – and it has made him big money – but for the first time, he’s wondered whether now is the right time for his usual political satire. Should we really be laughing when things are, well, this bad?‘I should not be allowed to do interviews’: Nish Kumar on courting controversy and clashing with comicsRead moreIt is a concern you feel could genuinely keep Kumar – and his mother – awake at night. Still, he serves up gags impressively thick and fast. At 41, his conversations with his peers centre largely around their workout routines. But even then, Kumar’s mind wanders to how the actions of the British empire have changed the genetic makeup of south Asian bodies – making it harder for him to lose weight. One by one, he goes through the generations from boomers to gen alphas and speaks of their individual virtues and failings. Some of his most vicious bile is reserved for Jimmy Carr and others who appeared at last autumn’sRiyadh comedy festival.We get a little insight into Kumar’s personal life, too – musings on his 14-year relationship with his partner and fellow comedian Amy Annette may not quite fit the tone of the rest of the show, but are a sweet, reflective addition. And a chat with one “weird little” 13-year-old fan in the crowd is enough to swell your heart and make you believe in the power of comedy to change things. This is Kumar at his very best: a deeply principled joke maker, ready to set society’s wrongs alight.Touring until 27 NovemberExplore more on these topicsComedyNish KumarreviewsShareReuse this content

title: How much is being close to your favorite artist worth? Superfans are reshaping the concert industry | Culture | The Guardian
description: Some admit to spending thousands of dollars for barricade spots and other VIP perks at concerts, which is slowly becoming common
Author: Rosalind Adams
Headline: Some admit to spending thousands of dollars for barricade spots and other VIP perks at concerts, which is slowly becoming common
Content: Fans wearing themed outfits sit and stand while waiting in line to be admitted to the Harry Styles Love On Tour 2022 concert at Madison Square Garden in New York City on 22 August 2022.Photograph: Alexi Rosenfeld/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFans wearing themed outfits sit and stand while waiting in line to be admitted to the Harry Styles Love On Tour 2022 concert at Madison Square Garden in New York City on 22 August 2022.Photograph: Alexi Rosenfeld/Getty ImagesCultureHow much is being close to your favorite artist worth? Superfans are reshaping the concert industrySome admit to spending thousands of dollars for barricade spots and other VIP perks at concerts, which is slowly becoming commonRosalind AdamsMon 21 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenHarry Stylesannounced a fall residency at Madison Square Garden, 43-year-old Tara Bess knew she had to be there. She didn’t want to spend hours camping for a prime spot in the general admission area, so Bess bought a VIP ticket for $1,400 from a resale ticket site, which allowed her to enter the arena early and secure a spot at the barricade.“When you’re up close, you can see him closing his eyes and almost meditating to the music,” Bess said. “You can hear the click of equipment on stage, you just feel very connected to the performance.”After seeing the show from the VIP area earlier this month, she took her sister to see it a second time for a more modest price. To afford the trip from her home in Florida, Bess worked a second job as an Uber driver and saved up for nine months. Bess is part of a growing number of fans who are shelling out for VIP tickets or other perks in order to secure prime concert seats and increase their chances of interacting with their favorite artists.Fans are paying thousands of dollars not just to see their favorite artists live, but to get closer to the performance and have a more exclusive experience.“It’s become more of a norm when you really want to get close to an artist,” said Eddie Meehan, the CEO of Please & Thank You, a VIP events company that’s worked with artists including Robyn and Audrey Hobert. “The growth of it, especially post-Covid, has been astronomical.”Even artists who have traditionally shied away from charging fans for extras have started offering premium tickets to meet demand, said Randy Nichols, a longtime artist manager. Ultimately, the experience is up to the artist and can include exclusive merchandise, meet-and-greets or access to the soundcheck.“Fans want to show their love and their loyalty and get to have that interaction and are more than happy to spend the money,” Nichols said. Typically, a higher percentage of a VIP ticket goes back to the artist than a standard ticket. Those earnings can be a welcome boost for artists as revenue from album sales have declined in the streaming era.The live music industry is noticing the opportunity. Superfans spend 80% more on music each month than casual fans, according toLuminate, a music data company. A 2025 Goldman Sachs report estimated that appealing to superfans could earn the industry an additional $4bn per year.View image in fullscreenFans watch Olivia Rodrigo perform on the Daytime Stage at the 2021 iHeartRadio music festival at Area15 in Las Vegas on 18 September 2021.Photograph: Denise Truscello/Getty Images for iHeartMediaFans who don’t purchase VIP tickets still have a chance to make it to the barricade of a general admission area by showing up early. Some venues discourage fans from camping overnight or may announce that lines won’t be honored until the morning of a show. Some venues have started offering fans the option to skip the entrance line for an additional fee, similar to theme parks. At some concerts, this means the first rows are filled with people who have paid more to be there.Despite the demand, the trend is more typical of larger, corporate-owned venues, said Stephen Parker, the executive director of the National Independent Venue Association. Many venues are wary of charging for these extras at a general admission show.“That egalitarian access for everyone is something that venues have worked really hard to preserve, and ultimately sometimes that’s not compatible with the VIP experience,” he said.The extras can rankle fanbases as competition for the best spots of a show has led to concertgoers who don’t pay for VIP tickets to show up earlier and earlier. Music subreddits are frequentlyfloodedwithpostsasking what time fans need to arrive to get a spot at the barricade. While the answer varies, a two-hour concert can easily extend into an all-day affair to secure a spot in the front.In a June interview with the UK radio station Kiss FM, Olivia Rodrigo described the extreme lengths some fans go to in order to hold their spots at the barricade. “I’ve been to certain concerts and certain festivals where people wear diapers so they can be front row of the show and that’s been an experience that I have smelled,” she said.Bess admitted that she avoided drinking water all day before the Harry Styles show, worried about losing her spot once the show got started. But the crowd ended up being easygoing. “I was definitely expecting a much more aggressive environment but it wasn’t that at all,” she said.Still, for longtime fans who have built a connection with an artist through following their career, paying for VIP is a way to continue supporting the artist.Kesha was on stage during her Freedom Tour last month when she spotted a fan at the front of the crowd holding up a sign saying she had a tooth to give the pop star.“I’m gonna have to get these teeth really fast,” Kesha said, pausing the show. She carefully descended down the steps of the stage in a pair of towering gold boots to grab the package. “I collect human teeth, it’s not weird!” she told the crowd.The tooth belonged to Holly Fisher, who lives in North Carolina and has been a fan of Kesha since high school. After her dentist scheduled an appointment to have a tooth pulled this summer, she knew immediately that she wanted to give it to Kesha. Fisher paid $475 for a VIP ticket, which included access to a soundcheck and early entry to the venue. When the doors opened, Fisher was first through the entrance and grabbed the spot at the center of the barricade with her friends directly in front of the stage.View image in fullscreenHolly Fisher (second from the left) with friends at barricade for Kesha’s concert.Photograph: Courtesy Holly FisherBeing in the front row was a way for Fisher to celebrate Kesha after following her from her early rise to her legal disputes with her former manager, Dr Luke, and now into her new chapter as an independent artist.“It really was this full circle moment for the people who had been there since the beginning,” said Fisher. “Like holy shit, she did it, she made it out alive. I’m just so happy for her.”As videos of concerts flood social media, a premium ticket is a way to have a more unique experience than just being in the building, said Amber Harms, who flew to Chicago to see two BTS shows on their summer tour. Harms became a fan of theK-popgroup while its members were serving their mandatory military service in South Korea.“A lot of that connection or that ability to connect with them in an actual real world environment, wasn’t something available to me at the time that I got into the fandom,” she said.On the second night, she shelled out $3,400 on a resale ticket site for two seats in the front row. While she called the resale prices “ridiculous”, the experience was worth it.“It’s wonderful to be at the concert, but if you can actually be five feet away from them, it’s even better,” said Harms. When one of the members splashed the crowd with a bottle of water and then tossed it into the crowd, Harms’s mother was close enough to snag it as a souvenir.“We were screaming like overexcited pterodactyls,” she said.Explore more on these topicsCultureHarry StylesTicket pricesMusic industryPop and rockBTSK-popfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Heart of the action: why organ couriers are cinema’s new heroes | Movies | The Guardian
description: Whether its a nod to frontline Covid heroes or a return to biology in a world of digital noise, there’s a rich vein of new films featuring organ deliveries, including Runner and the latest Resident Evil
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Whether its a nod to frontline Covid heroes or a return to biology in a world of digital noise, there’s a rich vein of new films featuring organ deliveries, including Runner and the latest Resident Evil
Content: A life or death mission … Owen Wilson and Alan Ritchson in Runner.Photograph: Runner Productions/PAView image in fullscreenA life or death mission … Owen Wilson and Alan Ritchson in Runner.Photograph: Runner Productions/PAMoviesHeart of the action: why organ couriers are cinema’s new heroesWhether its a nod to frontline Covid heroes or a return to biology in a world of digital noise, there’s a rich vein of new films featuring organ deliveries, including Runner and the latest Resident EvilJonathan WellsMon 21 Sep 2026 05.23 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHollywood loves a ticking clock – especially when there’s a delivery involved. For decades, dangerous cargo has been entrusted to certain types of action hero: spies, soldiers, hitmen, Jason Statham.Lately, however, Hollywood seems interested in a different kind of hero – not to mention a different kind of cargo. Forget your nuclear launch codes, stolen diamonds and mysterious briefcases, for human organs are the new MacGuffins du jour, and the medical professionals charged with getting them to the ICU have become unlikely action heroes.TakeRunner, directed by Scott Waugh, which stars Alan “Reacher” Ritchson as a delivery driver caught in a race against time, and Owen Wilson as an organ courier carrying a liver with a life-or-death deadline. “If she doesn’t get this today,” Wilson says of the girl awaiting the transplant, “she’s not going to make it.”It’s action movie gold. And using an organ as a plot device is smart because suspense is built into the biology: it’s a ticking clock in a cooler. It also unlocks a whole new melange of medical action scenarios: ambulance car chases, surgical scissor knife-fights, hospital shootouts. (Runner, naturally, has the full bloody bingo card.)Co-writer Miles Hubley says he and writing partner Tommy White wanted “a device that wasn’t just about money”, adding: “Neither of us had ever seen a movie where the precious cargo everyone wants was a fragile, life-saving piece of tissue.”View image in fullscreenHe stole my heart … Jason Statham in 2009’s Crank 2: High Voltage.Photograph: Lionsgate/Sportsphoto/AllstarWaugh agrees: an organ gives the film “emotional urgency”. “It’s the idea of a protagonist being driven not by revenge or saving the world, but simply by an obligation to deliver something on time,” he says. “You’ve got a deadline and someone whose life depends on you arriving.”Films such as bike-courier thrillerPremium Rushand the Safdie brothers’Uncut Gemshave set pulses racing using similar time-sensitive tactics, while Statham’s The Transporter built a whole franchise from the idea of a courier up against it. But the medical slant ups the ante even further: organs make the stakes more visceral, more personal.Crank 2: High Voltage understood this. Also starring Statham, it took the organ-chase motif one step further: his character was tasked with tracking down his own stolen heart. Repo Men flipped the script again, with Jude Law on the run to avoid having his artificial heart reclaimed. Organ drama is a rich vein, as it were.double quotation markThere’s something about how physical, vital and undeniably real an organ is ... It’s profoundly humanBut making the medical couriers the good guys is a new twist for 2026. Usually, characters in the organ game are on the shady side, whether in dramas such as Dirty Pretty Things or full-blown horror movies like The Harvest. A new horror, out a week after Runner, transplants this trope, giving theResident Evilfranchise a new protagonist: Austin Abrams’ medical courier.“This could be some eight-year-old boy’s heart or someone’s mom’s brain,” Abrams says in the film. But it’s also more than that. He’s carrying what everyone else is losing – their hope and humanity – in a medical bag. In fact, so important is this particular MacGuffin that US cinema chain Regal has turned it into anovelty popcorn bucket, fake bloodstains and all.View image in fullscreenIn the bag … Austin Abrams in Resident Evil.Photograph: CTMG/PABut why now? Why are medical couriers suddenly getting their action-hero moment? Perhaps it’s the pandemic, and we’re finally giving frontline workers their due. Of course you could go toe-to-toe with the cartel or endure an apocalyptic mutant zombie virus – you fought off Covid! Sure, it’s not much of a thank you, but getting the baddie-busting big-screen treatment beats 50% off at Pret and the odd round of applause.Hubley, too, says he wanted “grounded heroes, who you could imagine bumping into at the grocery store”. And an organ courier brings another dimension to that everyman appeal. “In a world with so much abstract digital noise, there’s something about how physical, vital and undeniably real an organ is. It’s a living thing that can’t be copied, faked or altered. It decays. It can’t be sent over email, or stored on a hard drive. It’s profoundly human.”Resident Evil review – Zach Cregger’s rebooted action horror is a wild rollercoaster rideRead moreNext year, Heartless will put another organ in the delivery bag. Jason Isaacs stars, while The Transporter Refuelled’s Camille Delamarre directs. Delamarre, too, sees a post-pandemic connection. “We’re more conscious of how fragile and irreplaceable the human body is,” says the director. “For me, an organ is the ultimate cargo because it’s not really cargo at all: it’s someone’s life. With a heart, you don’t need to explain the danger. Everyone in the cinema has one beating inside them.”And then there’s the symbolism. “A heart works on two levels. It’s literally keeping someone alive, but it’s also the universal symbol of life, love and mortality. You immediately understand why it matters,” he adds.That’s not to say Runner’s liver doesn’t land. Nor does the spoiler lurking in Resident Evil’s medical bag. The human body, after all, has plenty of organs left for Hollywood to parcel out. And who wouldn’t want to watch Tom Cruise fly a couple of kidneys through a tornado, or Statham hotfoot it across London with a bag full of gallbladders? Heartless may tell us whether this is a passing fad or a new action-movie staple, but if Hollywood’s latest organ harvest is anything to go by, the most compelling clock doesn’t tick any more – it beats.Explore more on these topicsFilmAction and adventure filmsDrama filmsThrillersResident EvilOrgan donationHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content
