title: The pet I’ll never forget: Bud, the parrot with a crisp addiction who was too fat to fly | Birds | The Guardian
description: When my husband and I adopted her, Bud had to go on a strict diet. Thankfully, she got healthy and became the diva everyone loves today
Author: Jayni Makwana
Headline: When my husband and I adopted her, Bud had to go on a strict diet. Thankfully, she got healthy and became the diva everyone loves today
Content: The most endearing creature in the world … Bud.Photograph: Courtesy of Chloe ShortenView image in fullscreenThe most endearing creature in the world … Bud.Photograph: Courtesy of Chloe ShortenThe pet I'll never forgetBirdsThe pet I’ll never forget: Bud, the parrot with a crisp addiction who was too fat to flyWhen my husband and I adopted her, Bud had to go on a strict diet. Thankfully, she got healthy and became the diva everyone loves todayChloe Shorten, as told toJayni MakwanaMon 21 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBud came into my life at the start of the Covid pandemic in 2020. I work at RSPCA Norwich as head of animal welfare and, when we all had to work from home, I offered to foster Bud, ablue-fronted amazon parrot. My husband and I thought it would be a short-term thing, but by the time the pandemic had settled down we had really bonded with her, so she never left.Back then, Bud had a crisp addiction and was too overweight to fly. She was about 200g heavier than a parrot should be. We had to put her on a strict diet because she had some health concerns – we found a lipoma, a fatty lump, on her keel bone (which runs down from the breast); it doesn’t bother her, but we still have to monitor it. Thankfully, she has lost weight; her feathers are all better quality and she loves her life.Some parrots like constant human interaction, but Bud enjoys her own space. She has just turned 28 (parrots can live for 50 to 60 years) and is a bit of a diva. Bud knows what she wants and when she wants it. She can be the most endearing creature in the world, and then suddenly have a tantrum like a toddler. She can be quite challenging, but she is really lovely.View image in fullscreenOur naughty little green chicken … Chloe and her husband, Jason, with Bud.Photograph: Courtesy of Chloe ShortenShe has a great sense of comedic timing. When I’m speaking to my neighbours, she will sometimes shout “Bye!” in the middle of a conversation and they think someone is asking them to leave. There are also hilarious but embarrassing moments, such as when she starts whistling at builders. She just has a way of making you laugh, and she always brightens up my life in some way.Bud also surprises me with what she knows from her youth. Earlier this summer, we were watching the World Cup and she started tweeting along to the German national anthem. And she loves rock music, especially the piano part of Welcome to the Black Parade byMy Chemical Romance.Bud has definitely made me more patient. It took my husband, Jason, and I two years to find a cage that she liked; before that, she kept having meltdowns. Parrots don’t like change, but she has been very resilient. It has been brilliant to see her transformation.Bud is a big part of our life now. I am more tolerant, because I don’t give up when she is having a tantrum – I know she’s worth the effort in the end. We are constantly looking for new ways to make her happy. She’s our naughty little green chicken, and we wouldn’t change her for the world.Explore more on these topicsBirdsThe pet I'll never forgetPetsAnimalsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The agony of life with chronic body odour: ‘I swear I’ve tried every deodorant’ | Health | The Guardian
description: Modern lifestyles seem to be exacerbating the problem of bromhidrosis – an underresearched condition that is widely misunderstood and devastating for sufferers
Author: Elle Hunt
Headline: Modern lifestyles seem to be exacerbating the problem of bromhidrosis – an underresearched condition that is widely misunderstood and devastating for sufferers
Content: Illustration: Zosia Bońkowska/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Zosia Bońkowska/The GuardianHealthThe agony of life with chronic body odour: ‘I swear I’ve tried every deodorant’Modern lifestyles seem to be exacerbating the problem of bromhidrosis – an underresearched condition that is widely misunderstood and devastating for sufferersElle HuntMon 21 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf Hayat goes out to eat, she’ll choose a table far away from other diners, ideally by a door or open window. She likewise tries to avoid people at the cinema or on planes, even if it means paying extra – whatever it takes to avoid being too close to others.She chalks it up to a persistent past insecurity. “I still have that paranoia … It’s just in my head, because of everything I went through.”For more than a decade, 66-year-old Hayat lived with bromhidrosis: chronic body odour. Though the term applies to BO from any cause, including poor hygiene, it is more typically driven by a bacterial imbalance or other health issue.View image in fullscreenResearch shows that ‘15 minutes after a shower, you will already have started smelling’.Photograph: Catherine Falls Commercial/Getty Images (Posed by a model)For those individuals, it’s not a question of bathing more often, or switching to a higher-strength deodorant: their body is working against them, and the impact can be ruinous. “Fifteen minutes after a shower, they’ve already started smelling,” says Chris Callewaert, a senior research fellow at Ghent University, Belgium, and one of the few scientists in the world specialising in body odour.Callewaert describes bromhidrosis as a natural bodily process gone awry, most typically involving the apocrine glands. These are concentrated around the armpits, breasts and groin, and secrete lipids, steroids and proteins. This sweat itself is odourless; BO is produced by the natural bacteria on the skin and inside the hair follicles as they digest the fatty secretion.In people with apocrine bromhidrosis – that is to say, abnormal or abnormally offensive body odour – some aspect of that process is out of balance, says Callewaert. They may have overactive apocrine glands, perhaps, or an overabundance of specific “smelly bacteria”.Body odour can come on abruptly: with puberty, a change to the microbiome, a disease affecting the metabolism, or even as a side-effect of medication. But once established, it can prove difficult to shift, Callewaert says. “It’s often multifactorial, and not easy to perceive the deeper origin or to fix it. Sometimes people have been stuck with this for many, many years.”View image in fullscreenBody odour can come on abruptly with puberty, a change to the microbiome, or even as a side-effect of medicationPhotograph: bymuratdeniz/Getty Images (Posed by a model)In Hayat’s case, she developed bromhidrosis along with hyperhidrosis – excessive and uncontrollable sweating, a distinct but often coexistent condition – during menopause. In 2007, when she was 48, she had an ovary removed, which disrupted her oestrogen production. “After that, life started to change. It was absolutely disruptive,” she says.She was constantly overheated, “burning inside” even during New York’s freezing winters. On the subway, she would be wearing a sleeveless top and sandals, her hair dripping wet from sweat, while other commuters were in heavy coats, boots and scarves. “People were looking at me like I was crazy,” she says.That was only half of it. She also smelled – from her armpits, under her breasts, her groin. Her fellow New Yorkers did not hold back from letting her know. Some covered their noses as she passed, or moved away from her. “Those were the polite ones,” Hayat says. Others verbally abused her; more than once, she was harassed off the train. “It was awful, a total nightmare.”Hayat understood the strong reactions: “It’s normal – you don’t want to be next to anybody who smells bad.” But over-the-counter and prescription remedies made no difference. Hayat estimates that she spent thousands of dollars searching fruitlessly for relief. “At one point I was seeing endocrinologists, gynaecologists, general cardiologists … I had a whole team, trying to find out what was going on in my body.”There is no set diagnostic threshold at which bad BO becomes bromhidrosis, which makes it difficult to estimate how common it is.A 2024 reviewdescribed it as prevalent, at least in the west, and taking a “significant” toll on patients’ social and psychological wellbeing. Yet there is very little focused attention on the condition or specialised support.“It is underserved,” says Angela Ballard, a registered nurse and communications director for the International Hyperhidrosis Society (IHS). The US-based organisation was founded in 2003 to advocate for the estimated 4.8% of people who live with uncontrollable sweating, but has expanded its focus to include bromhidrosis and body odour, given the frequent overlap and lack of other resources.“There is not a lot of information, and I think that’s sort of indicative. People are ashamed,” Ballard says. “They don’t talk about it with their healthcare providers, even their friends.”The stigma over BO persists despite it being a natural part of life, from puberty to pregnancy and beyond. According to the IHS, an estimated 50% of the 1.6m women entering menopause annually in the US alone experience increased underarm sweat and odour.Ballard says a diagnosis of bromhidrosis is tied to “the level of distress it’s causing a person”, and its effect on their wellbeing and day-to-day function: “How much is this impacting your self-esteem, your confidence, your social life?”View image in fullscreenBotox injections can reduce sweat production.Photograph: Steklo_KRD/Alamy (Posed by a model)There are strategies that can help with alleviating the odour, she says – from the straightforward (using antibacterial soap, avoiding certain fabrics, improving laundry practices) to the unexpected (laser hair removal or waxing, which limit sites for bacteria, and Botox, which reduces sweat production) and, increasingly, hi-tech.The miraDry, for instance, is an FDA-approved handheld microwave device that destroys the sweat glands, odour glands and hair follicles in the armpits, and has proved to be effective at managing hyperhidrosis, and sometimes bromhidrosis too.But, often, even a combination of strategies can only do so much to improve the smell. Meanwhile, managing the social anxiety, second-guessing and paranoia is a separate concern. “You feel like people are judging you, that they think it’s your fault, when you’ve perhaps tried everything,” Ballard says. “It can really spiral.”The toll can be far-reaching. “People will choose jobs where they can work from home, or skip certain social occasions where their odour could be more apparent … You may hesitate to hug someone or get too close to other people.”Having been diagnosed with hyperhidrosis as a child, Ellie, 30, began struggling with body odour as she got older. She had wanted to pursue teaching, “but I just couldn’t imagine standing in front of a room full of students all sweaty, fearing smelling bad,” she says.She now works as an accounting assistant. “There were several career paths I wanted to pursue but didn’t.” She considers herself fortunate to not have been so affected in her intimate relationships.Many people with bromhidrosis report it negatively affecting their confidence and success in dating, but Ellie says her husband, who has known her since she was a teenager, has always been “completely unfazed”. She was, however, very nearly dissuaded from having children, for fear of passing on her conditions.But Ellie now has a young daughter: “While excessive sweating and body odour is extremely unfortunate, it is not a reason to not want to live. Even if I do end up passing this down, I will be the best advocate possible for my daughter.”With doctors having been, generally, “pretty dismissive”, Ellie has developed her own coping strategies, such as wearing only cotton socks and never leaving the house without a full change of clothes on hand. “I swear I’ve tried every deodorant on the market.”Added to the frustrations and challenges of managing her bromhidrosis are other people’s assumptions – that she is either oblivious to how she smells, or wilfully not doing anything about it. “Don’t think we don’t realise. Odds are, we’re trying everything we can to mask it, and get rid of it, but sometimes there is no way.”Callewaert’s research has found that people who know or fear that they have BO are actually more attentive to personal hygiene than others. But, he says, the anxious striving to get on top of bromhidrosis can worsen the problem by further imbalancing the microbiome and stoking the production of sweat. “They have stress and, as such, they have odour, and because they have odour, they have more stress: it’s self-enforcing.”View image in fullscreen‘People might develop anxiety or depression – on average, their quality of life is lower.’Photograph: Tara Moore/Getty Images (Posed by a model)Over time, bromhidrosis can become as much a psychological issue as a physiological one. People with the condition often self-isolate, exacerbating the negative effect on wellbeing, and they might develop anxiety or depression, says Callewaert: “On average, their quality of life is lower.”Faced with “embarrassing situations and mistreatment”, Hayat organised her life around managing others’ discomfort. Aged 50, she learned to drive and got a car so that she might bypass public transport – no mean feat in New York – and began flying business class for the extra space. “Economically, it was a sacrifice, but for my wellbeing, it was perfect to be as far away as I could from people,” Hayat says.Her family thought she was behaving irrationally and told her she didn’t even smell: “They used to say: ‘It’s all in your head.” But Hayat didn’t feel that she could trust them over the feedback she was getting in public, “because they love me”.The experience went so far as to test Hayat’s faith: she says she often turned to the Bible in search of solace and answers. “It was really frustrating: ‘Why me? Why do I have to go through this? What did I do?’”Her world shrank. “Before menopause, I used to go to the theatre, the movies, to clubs to dance, to restaurants … I stopped all of that.” For more than a decade, she did not go anywhere other than work.The office was difficult enough. Hayat’s colleagues knew she had a medical condition, but were far from sympathetic, she says. A younger co-worker made a show of using a room spray in Hayat’s presence; she overheard another pair of colleagues talking about her, waving their hands in front of their noses.Hayat says that her working environment became so hostile that she considered suicide. But eventually, she sought help from her employer’s human resources department, which moved swiftly to find her a spot far from those colleagues and gave her the option of taking action against them for bullying. She declined, but “they made me feel really supported”.View image in fullscreen‘Maybe someone is going through menopause …’Photograph: Highwaystarz-Photography/Getty Images (Posed by a model)Later in her career, Hayat took advantage of advances in remote working, such as telephone meetings and Zoom calls. She also became more adept at managing her sweating and stress, and with it the smell: “I found ways to survive.”The strict social penalty against having body odour is worsened by the casualness and flippancy with which the topic is often treated. Even doctors can be dismissive, instructing patients to simply apply more deodorant. “People are being brushed off very easily [because] ‘it’s not life-threatening’,” says Callewaert.That doesn’t just discount the real suffering of living with bromhidrosis: a subtle change in body odour has been associated with diabetes, Parkinson’s disease and cancer, he says. “Knowing that body odour can be a symptom for underlying diseases, it’s a real sign that needs to be picked up.”In most cases, however, strong BO stems from the microbiome and poor gut health. A stronger and more offensive body odour is linked to diets high in meat and fast food, and low in vegetables. “Leading a healthy lifestyle will help in smelling better,” Callewaert says. High stress is also a factor.With the microbiome makeup often stubborn to shift, progress can be slow. Even using antiperspirants and deodorant can exacerbate odour, he says, killing beneficial bacteria while encouraging the more stress-resistant, “smelly” kind to bounce back stronger and more numerous.At best, these “underarm cosmetics” – widespread only since the mid-20th century – are a short-term solution, Callewaert says. He argues that their use has led to worse BO at the population level, together with the trends, at least in the west, for poor nutrition, high stress and unhealthy guts. So Callewaert – who publicly styles himself as “Dr Armpit” – has been developing what he hopes might prove a silver bullet to BO: his own range of patented probiotic deodorants.In the meantime, Ballard calls for greater understanding of body odour as a natural product of bacteria on our skin, and compassion for people who might be struggling to keep it in check. Instead of leaping to the assumption that someone who smells must be skipping showers, we might consider their experience, she says.“Maybe they have bromhidrosis, and it took a lot for them to get out the door to go to work and live their lives. Maybe they have another medical condition, and they have to take medication that has changed their body odour. Or maybe they’re going through menopause … You can notice that you smell something, and stop before the judgment.”For Hayat, recently retired, the bullying she experienced over her bromhidrosis affected her wellbeing as much as the condition itself. After a decade of the menopause wreaking havoc, her symptoms began to ease. “It got better, thank God,” she says fervently. “It’s still not 100% managed – it’s just that I learned to get by.”She, too, urges compassion – after all, no one is above body odour. “You can be smelling like roses now, but eventually, for whatever reason, your body’s gonna change.”All case studies’ names have been changedIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Vintage Gucci, a £5 rug and a salt duck: your best secondhand finds | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Readers and the Filter team share the best buys they still treasure, from charity-shop gems to Vinted bargains. Plus, the fashion experts’ guide to women’s basics
Author: Hannah Booth
Headline: Readers and the Filter team share the best buys they still treasure, from charity-shop gems to Vinted bargains. Plus, the fashion experts’ guide to women’s basics
Content: One person’s cast-off … many love the thrill of finding something preloved that’s worth keeping.Photograph: Matej Kastelic/Alamy/AlamyView image in fullscreenOne person’s cast-off … many love the thrill of finding something preloved that’s worth keeping.Photograph: Matej Kastelic/Alamy/AlamyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The Filter UK newsletterLife and styleVintage Gucci, a £5 rug and a salt duck: your best secondhand findsReaders and the Filter team share the best buys they still treasure, from charity-shop gems to Vinted bargains. Plus, the fashion experts’ guide to women’s basicsHannah BoothMon 21 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe love secondhand shopping here on the Filter – whether it’sSecond Hand Septemberor not. You can unearth one-off, affordable pieces, and feel good about not adding overconsumption to your list of things to worry about. So to inspire us, we asked you for your best-ever preloved finds, whether that’s furniture or fashion or more (and added a few of our own, too).“An Ercol daybed I bought on eBay for £50, in need of some TLC,” readerFionatold us. “Stripped, re-webbed and with a new cushion, it is now a thing of beauty and very comfortable.”“The best thing I ever bought secondhand is a mahogany dining table 30 years ago: I can’t remember how much I paid, but it was a fraction of the cost of a new one. It’s Edwardian and very solid. Soon after, we found four Victorian balloon-back chairs that nearly matched two we already had. The chairs were professionally re-covered so cost more than the table in the end. They’re all now heirlooms,”Antheatold us.View image in fullscreenWorth its salt: Filter deputy editor Monica Horridge’s £2 charity-shop duck.Photograph: Monica Horridge/The GuardianRugs are often extremely good value secondhand. “I got a gorgeous rug for £5 from a charity shop in Newcastle,”Eileen de Quadratold us. “Stunning.”“I found a beautiful rug atAntiques at Wendover,” said Filter production editorEmily Goddard. “It looks like an oushak rug, but the lack of a label means I can’t be sure it is made of wool. Either way, the quality is incredible, the colours rich, and it cost about £30. It’s starting to get a bit thin in places, but it’s still vibrant and luxuriously soft.”Filter contributorLucy Paviafound a 19th-century French dairy bowl at theYorkshire Fleafor £40. “Terracotta with a lovely buttery yellow glaze. It sits in the middle of my kitchen, and I grow bulbs in it in winter when everything outside is a bit dreary.”Secondhand styleClothes are, of course, a secondhand staple. Filter fashion writerPeter Bevandiscovered “a Gucci oversized navy pinstripe shirt in a tiny thrift store in San Francisco for about $60. Whenever I’m getting dressed in a rush, I throw it on with navy trousers. It looks polished without a second thought.”View image in fullscreenSuede success: Millie Fender in her £20 Vinted find.Photograph: Millie Fender/The GuardianFilter commissioning editorMillie Fenderusually buys leather or suede secondhand. “I found the perfect 90s Liz Claiborne brown suede jacket on Vinted recently. It fits like a glove and cleaned up beautifully after a trip to the dry cleaners. I paid £20, but because I already had that sitting in my Vinted balance, I’m telling myself it was free.”Guardian lifestyle trends writerLeah Harperrecently found the perfect cropped white T-shirt in a pop-up vintage market above a local pub. “I paid £2.50 entry and the T-shirt cost a fiver. It’s from American sportswear brand Champion and, this summer, I have paired it with everything from a suede midi skirt (also vintage) to preppy Adidas shorts. A good white T-shirt can be surprisingly difficult to find.”“I found an old red men’s lumberjack shirt from a bargain bin at a shop in Paris in 2009 – it cost €5,” saysLucy. “It’s a lovely thick cotton that’s softened over time and is so comfortable. It’s a little frayed on the sleeves now but lovely for knocking about in at home – particularly gardening, as the deep front pocket fits packets of seeds and secateurs.”View image in fullscreenTrainer triumph: barely worn Nike trainers for £7.20 from Vinted.Photograph: Hannah Booth/The GuardianFor me, secondhand shops online are great for children’s clothes: they’re often in good condition, as kids often outgrow them before they’ve been worn much. And it saves me from having to buy new coats and shoes every six months as my daughter grows. I found the Nike trainers pictured above on Vinted last week – barely worn – for £7.20.Sometimes, though, it’s the unexpected knick-knacks you stumble on that make secondhand shopping such a delight. “I found a ceramic duck for about £2, and it’s turned out to be my best-ever charity shop find,” says Filter deputy editor,Monica Horridge. “Affectionately called Salt Duck by all my housemates and now my husband, it’s held my Maldon salt next to the hob for almost 20 years.”This week’s picksFrom the perfect jeans to wedgie-free knickers: fashion experts’ guide to the best women’s basicsAre you washing your sportswear wrong? An expert guide to making it last longerThe best iPhones: which Apple smartphone is right for you, according to our expertThe definitive guide to men’s shirts: 19 of the best for every occasionThe best ice-cream makers for gelato, soft serve and sorbets – tested‘An intense caramelised toffee flavour’: the best supermarket maple syrup, tasted and ratedThe best mattress toppers for a more comfortable night’s sleep, testedEditor’s pickView image in fullscreenCheaper than a pricey gym membership and less clutter than a set of dumbbells, resistance bands are one of the easiest ways to up your workout game from home. Ultra-marathoner and fitness expert Kieran Alger tested 18 of thebest resistance band setsover a month, using them in workouts, pre-run warm-ups and even yoga.Monica HorridgeDeputy editor, the FilterIn case you missed it …View image in fullscreenGamers: as the nights draw in, the allure of an evening’s gaming starts to grow. Make sure you’re looking after your back and posture, though. Guardian gaming writer (and sometime sufferer of lower-back pain) Keith Stuart put 10 of thebest gaming chairsthrough their paces over five days each, spending up to four hours a day sitting in them. His gaming-mad sons helped him with his testing, and his wife rated the chairs on their suitability as office chairs, too. And hisbest budget buywas reduced at the time of writing.Get involvedView image in fullscreenPour show or poor show? Tell us about the things you treasure because they just work.Photograph: Stefania Pelfini, La Waziya Photography/GettyStylish sandals that don’t rub; teapots that don’t drip; a scent that doesn’t wear off by lunchtime: do you own or use an item that does what it’s supposed to do – and does it really well? If so, we’d love to hear from you. Let us know by emailing us atthefilter@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Filter UK newsletterHomesInteriorsVintage fashionShops and shoppingSustainable fashionMen's fashionnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Tattie scones and scrambled eggs, toasted bannocks with honey butter and roast plums – Anna Higham’s big breakfast recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Scottish breakfasts are worth getting up for: think eggs and potato cakes in a freshly baked roll, or toasted barley bread laced with sticky plums and honey butter
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Scottish breakfasts are worth getting up for: think eggs and potato cakes in a freshly baked roll, or toasted barley bread laced with sticky plums and honey butter
Content: Anna Higham’s morning rolls filled with tattie scones and scrambled eggs.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.View image in fullscreenAnna Higham’s morning rolls filled with tattie scones and scrambled eggs.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.FoodTattie scones and scrambled eggs, toasted bannocks with honey butter and roast plums – Anna Higham’s big breakfast recipesScottish breakfasts are worth getting up for: think eggs and potato cakes in a freshly baked roll, or toasted barley bread laced with sticky plums and honey butterAnna HighamMon 21 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 06.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve long wanted a space to cook the food that really excites me, andClementine, which opens its doors in north London next month, is exactly that. These two recipes capture what the cafe is all about. This is food that feels both considered and completely unfussy: crisp morning rolls stuffed with folded scrambled eggs and tattie scones, and griddled barley bannocks served warm with salted honey butter and roast plums. Breakfasts worth getting out of bed for.Morning rolls with tattie scone and scrambled eggsPrep10 minProve9 hr+Cook1 hr 45 minMakes4For the morning rolls375g strong white stone-ground bread flour, plus extra for dusting4g sugar4g salt5g dried active yeast40g lard, or vegetable shortening210g cold waterFor the tattie scones1kg maris piper potatoes165g strong stone-ground flour,plus extra for dusting1½ tsp fine salt1 tsp baking powder60g melted unsalted butterFor the eggs2 tbsp salted butter6 eggs1 tbsp creme fraicheSalt and black pepperRed or brown sauce,to serveFirst, make the morning rolls. Combine the dry ingredients in a bowl, then rub in the lard. Add the water, mix to form a rough dough, then cover with a damp tea towel and leave to rest for 10 minutes.Knead the dough until it feels smooth, springy and has good stretch – about 10 minutes in a mixer on medium speed, 25 minutes by hand. Transfer the dough to a lightly oiled container, cover with a damp tea towel and leave for about an hour to double in size.Turn out the dough on to a well-floured surface, roll it into a rectangle, then divide into 12 equal pieces of about 120g each. Pinch the four corners of one piece of dough into the centre, then flip over. Allow the dough to stick slightly to the worktop and, with a cupped hand, work it into a tight ball. Now use a dough scraper to release it from the bench, then transfer to a lined, high-sided baking tray. Repeat with the remaining pieces of dough, spacing them evenly apart. Sprinkle each with a little flour, cover with a damp cloth and refrigerate overnight.Heat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/475F/gas 9, then bake the rolls for 25-30 minutes, until dark and “well fired” on top; remove and leave to cool slightly.Meanwhile, peel and cut the potatoes into chunks, boil in well-salted water until tender, then drain and mash (or use a potato ricer). Mix in the remaining tattie scone ingredients to make a dough, then divide in two.Put a frying pan on a medium heat. Cut out a 10cm circle of baking paper, flour it well and put one block of the potato dough on top. Roll this into an even 10cm round, score it into quarters, then flip into the hot pan. Cook for three to five minutes, until it puffs up and colours on the bottom, then flip and cook for a minute or two, until coloured on the other side. Transfer to a rack while you roll and cook the remaining dough.Melt a tablespoon of butter in the same frying pan on a medium heat. Whisk the eggs, creme fraiche, salt and pepper, then pour into the hot pan and leave the bottom to set, much as you would an omelette. Use a spatula to push the set egg into the centre, cook until the mix is 75% set, then fold over and take off the heat.Put the remaining tablespoon of butter in a hot pan and, once foaming, fry the tattie scones until golden brown with crisp edges, flipping once halfway. Divide the tattie scones along the score lines, then split the buns and fill with two tattie scones and the eggs. The choice of red or brown sauce is entirely your own.Barley bannocks with honey butter and roast plumsView image in fullscreenAnna Higham’s barley bannocks with honey butter and roast plums.Prep10 minCook1 hrServes6For the bannocks200g barley flour100g plain flour2 tsp bicarbonate of soda1 tsp baking powder1 generous pinch salt60g cold butter300ml buttermilkFor the honey butter100g salted cultured butter, at room temperature30g local runny honeyFor the roast plums6 red or purple plums1 tbsp light brown sugar1 tsp red-wine vinegarMix all the dry ingredients for the bannocks in a large bowl. Grate in the butter, toss it through to coat, then add the buttermilk, holding back 50ml or so in case your flour doesn’t need all of it. Mix gently to a soft dough, then divide into three portions.Roll each portion into a roughly 2½cm-thick disc, then cut each disc into quarters. Put a heavy skillet or griddle pan on a medium heat, then, working in batches, cook the bannocks for about five minutes on each side. Wrap in a tea towel and keep in a warm oven while you cook the rest. (Bannocks freeze very well, so, if need be, freeze any leftovers, ready to warm up whenever you need a wholesome treat.)In a small bowl, whisk all the honey butter ingredients until smooth and light.Wash, halve and stone the plums, keeping the stones. Mix the light brown sugar, vinegar and two tablespoons of water. Crack open the plum stones by wrapping them in a tea towel and smashing with a rolling pin, then remove the kernels and add to the sugar mix. Toss the plums in this mixture, then transfer to a roasting tin and bake at 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7 for 10-15 minutes, until slightly caramelised and starting to collapse.Split open the warm bannocks, add a generous amount of the honey butter and spoon the roast plums on top.Anna Higham is the owner ofQuincebakery andClementine, both in north London.Explore more on these topicsFoodBreakfastBreadBritish food and drinkEggsBakingFruitrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Jamie Oliver’s recipes for fish pie pasta bake and tomato and feta lentils | Jamie Oliver | The Guardian
description: Sometimes cooking is about celebration or indulgence, but there are other times when you just need a speedy but delicious midweek meal
Author: Jamie Oliver
Headline: Sometimes cooking is about celebration or indulgence, but there are other times when you just need a speedy but delicious midweek meal
Content: Jamie Oliver’s fIsh pie pasta bake.Photograph: David Loftus/Jamie Oliver Enterprises LtdView image in fullscreenJamie Oliver’s fIsh pie pasta bake.Photograph: David Loftus/Jamie Oliver Enterprises LtdQuick and easyJamie OliverJamie Oliver’s recipes for fish pie pasta bake and tomato and feta lentilsSometimes cooking is about celebration or indulgence, but there are other times when you just need a speedy but delicious midweek mealJamie OliverMon 21 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 09.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOf course, the act of cooking can be many things – joy, ritual, nourishment, comfort, celebration, indulgence – but this fish pie pasta bake and tomato and feta lentils are strictly about speed. Because, in reality, these are exactly the kind of recipes we all need in our repertoire, ready to whip out on a Wednesday night.Fish pie pasta bake (pictured top)Prep5 minCook20 minServes4320g frozen spinach1 onion(160g)Olive oil300g dried macaroni50g plain flour2 heapedtsp English mustard500ml semi-skimmed milkSalt and black pepper400g frozen fish pie mix, from sustainable sources100gcheddar2 red chicory60g rocketRed-wine vinegarExtra-virgin olive oilTurn on the grill to high. Boil the kettle. Defrost the spinach in a bowl in the microwave. Peel and finely chop the onion, and place in a large ovenproof frying pan on a high heat with one tablespoon of olive oil. Cook, stirring regularly, for five minutes, or until soft. Cook the pasta in a pan of boiling salted water for eight minutes, until al dente, then drain, reserving a mugful of the starchy cooking water.Stir the flour and mustard into the onions, then gradually stir in the milk. Add the spinach to the pan, water and all, then season. Stir in the fish chunks and simmer for five minutes on a medium heat, then stir in the drained pasta, along with a splash of the reserved water, if needed. Coarsely grate and mix in half the cheese, grating the rest over the top. Carefully transfer to the highest shelf of the grill for a few minutes, until golden and bubbling.Meanwhile, finely slice the chicory bases and separate the leaves, toss with the rocket and a tablespoon each of red-wine vinegar and extra-virgin olive oil, then season. Serve with the fish pie pasta bake.Tomato and feta lentilsView image in fullscreenJamie Oliver’s tomato and feta lentils.Photograph: David Loftus/Jamie Oliver Enterprises LtdPrep5 minCook20 minServes44garlic cloves1 fresh redchilliOlive oil500g ripe tomatoes1460g jarroastred peppers½pomegranate30g shelled unsalted pistachios1 bunchdill(20g)4 flatbreads2400g tinslentilsRed-wine vinegarSalt and black pepper100g fetaPeel the garlic and finely slice with the chilli, then put in a shallow casserole pan on a medium-high heat with two tablespoons of olive oil. Cook, stirring regularly, until soft but not coloured. Chop and add the tomatoes. Tip the peppers, juice and all, into a blender, blitz smooth, then pour into the pan. Cook, stirring occasionally, for eight minutes, or until thickened.Meanwhile, hold the pomegranate half cut side down in your palm and bash the back of it so the seeds tumble out into a bowl. Finely chop the pistachios. Pick and chop the dill. Warm the flatbreads.Drain the lentils and add to the pan with a half-tablespoon of red-wine vinegar. Simmer for a final five minutes, then stir through half the pomegranate seeds and half the chopped dill, and season.Scatter over the pistachios and the remaining pomegranate seeds, crumble over the feta, and sprinkle over the remaining dill. Serve with warm flatbreads.These recipes are edited extracts from 20-Minute Meals by Jamie Oliver, published by Penguin Michael Joseph © Jamie Oliver Enterprises Limited (2026, 20MM) at £30.
