title: ‘RAMageddon’: tech crunch hikes the price of your next iPhone by £100 | Mobile phones | The Guardian
description: Shortage of memory chips and other critical components reverses trend of electronics becoming cheaper
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Shortage of memory chips and other critical components reverses trend of electronics becoming cheaper
Content: Sales of smartphones are predicted to fall steeply this year.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSales of smartphones are predicted to fall steeply this year.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianMobile phones‘RAMageddon’: tech crunch hikes the price of your next iPhone by £100Shortage of memory chips and other critical components reverses trend of electronics becoming cheaperSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorMon 21 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple’s recent product launch caused headlines around the world as it unveiled its first folding phone. But hidden in the slick technology showcase was a nasty surprise: a £100 increase in the price of all iPhones, including older models.It is blamed on “RAMageddon”, which has reversed a decades-long trend of electronics becoming cheaper. It is the fallout from the AI gold rushhoovering up every memory chipavailable for vast datacentres. This has led to a severe shortage of the chips, and other critical components, for electronics, including phones.The situation has dramatically driven up costs, with some chips five times dearer than previously listed. Therefore the everyday electronics products people rely on are suddenly significantly more expensive to make, and that is being passed on to consumers.“Two things are happening at once,” says Francisco Jeronimo, the vice-president of client devices at research company IDC. “Component costs have risen sharply, with memory alone up more than 300% year on year.”Because older iPhones use the same expensive memory as the new ones,Appleis pricing them as current products, he adds.View image in fullscreenApple presented its foldable iPhone Duo earlier this month.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersThe iPhone is not the first product to have a “RAMageddon” price increase, but it is the single biggest-selling electrical product in the world. For many, this means the real cost of the AI splurge will be £100 without getting anything more for your money.Other manufacturers of smartphones have also increased the price of new models, with Samsung andGoogle adding up to £80to their flagship phones.Apple has also increased the price of its refurbished stock by £60 to £70, including the older iPhone 15 that is no longer sold new in the shops. However, according to data from Uswitch, the increase in cost has yet to reach the third-party refurbished iPhone market.“A refurbished iPhone 16 has held at about £503 all summer, roughly where it was before the 18 Pro launch,” says Ernest Doku, a Uswitch mobiles expert. “A refurbished 14 is about £10 cheaper than it was in June, while the 16 has simply stopped falling in price.”double quotation markComputer manufacturers have had to raise prices several times over the past 18 monthsMost smartphone makers, other than Apple, have discontinued older models that were no longer economically viable, and likely wouldn’t sell at higher prices. The impact has been particularly acute at the lower end of the market.In its latest forecast, IDC predicts there will be the steepest annual contraction in worldwide smartphone sales on record this year, falling almost 17% to just over 1bn handsets. “People are buying fewer phones and paying considerably more for those they do buy,” Jeronimo says.View image in fullscreenMicrosoft added as much as £220 to the cost of some of its Surface computers.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThere have been bigger price rises for other electronics. Computer makers, which are much more exposed to rapidly jumping memory and chip costs, have had to raise prices several times over the past 18 months.Microsoft added up to £220 to some of its Surface computers but also released versions with half as much memory as a way to attempt to keep prices down.The move has forced the company to try to redesign Windows torun more comfortably with only 8GB of RAM, which it hasn’t for several years.Many of PC maker Dell’s high-end laptops havejumped by as much as 25%, while the repairable laptop maker Framework has had tocontinually adjust pricesas costs fluctuate.Even Apple added £100 to itslower-cost MacBook Neo, as well as rises to most models in itsMac and iPad lines in June. “We have never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly,” the company says in a statement.Games consolesaren’t immune, either. In a rare state of affairs, Microsoft recently increased the price of its near six-year-old console to £670, up from its original launch price of £449.“Console storage and memory prices have increased by more than 2.5 times, and we expect another doubling by the autumn of 2027,”the company says.View image in fullscreenOlder iPhones use the same expensive memory as the new ones, so Apple prices them as current products.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianUnfortunately, £100 added to the cost of a phone may only be the start of the price pain, with key memory producers, including SK Hynix, suggesting the shortages could last beyond 2030.Jeronimo says memory prices are going to continue rising well into 2027, even if the pace has slowed from the “extraordinary spikes” seen earlier this year. “Even once memory costs ease, I do not expect smartphone prices to fall back to the same levels as last year.“Increases in this industry tend to be sticky. Once customers have absorbed a higher price and manufacturers have rebuilt their margins, companies hold the line and add value through storage or features, rather than cutting the ticket price.”The bad news for consumers is that “the era of cheap smartphones – or any device to be honest – is over,” Jeronimo says.Explore more on these topicsMobile phonesSmartphonesConsumer affairsAppleiPhoneMicrosoftDellnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I have to keep reliving it’: infected blood claimants being asked to prove eligibility | Contaminated blood scandal | The Guardian
description: Claimants having to find decades-old medical records to prove they qualify for compensation despite inquiry’s recommendations
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Claimants having to find decades-old medical records to prove they qualify for compensation despite inquiry’s recommendations
Content: Suzanne Morgan, whose mother, Marie Jupe, contracted hepatitis C after receiving a routine blood transfusion.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSuzanne Morgan, whose mother, Marie Jupe, contracted hepatitis C after receiving a routine blood transfusion.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianContaminated blood scandal‘I have to keep reliving it’: infected blood claimants being asked to prove eligibilityClaimants having to find decades-old medical records to prove they qualify for compensation despite inquiry’s recommendationsRachel HallMon 21 Sep 2026 07.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSuzanne Morgan will never forget the day her mother died. It was nine months after she had gone into hospital with gallstones, where she received a routine blood transfusion.“She went downhill rapidly,” Morgan recalled. Her mother haemorrhaged in her liver, and the next day she was dead.The family were astonished to be told that she had hepatitis C, and doubly shocked to learn that they couldn’t see her because her body was sealed due to contagion risk, leading them to suspect she was HIV positive.Morgan, who was pregnant at the time, said: “I went into full-blown miscarriage. I was in total shock. I was hysterical.”That was 35 years ago, and the family now know Morgan’s mother died because she was given infected blood. Yet Morgan has found herself forced to “keep reliving” the horror through the infected blood compensation scheme.Like many other victims of the scandal and their families, she has been asked to dig out decades-old medical records to prove she qualifies, despite the public inquiry’s recommendations that eligibility be determined “on the balance of probability”.Suzanne Morgan with her mother, Marie Jupe, who died after being given infected blood.Photograph: Family handout“I have been everywhere to try and get medical notes of any sort. I cannot get them,” said Morgan.Infected blood campaigners who spoke to the Guardian shared their fury that thousands like Morgan face being locked out of the Infected Blood Compensation Authority (IBCA) payment scheme due to its stringent approach.Rachel Halford, the chief executive of theHepatitis CTrust, said this was “placing an intolerable burden on people who have already endured decades of injustice”.Victims and bereaved families had been asked to prove “even the most basic of things”, such as whether they lived with their deceased spouses or siblings, she added. Some have had to show old school records, tenancy agreements, utility bills or family photos.“People feel they are being treated as potential fraudsters rather than victims of one of the greatest scandals in our history,” said Halford, adding that there have been complaints of unfairness after different compensation awards for people with similar experiences.Halford said the community hoped that Andy Burnham, who has long campaigned for victims of the infected blood scandal to receive justice, would offer his support. “As prime minister, we need him to live up to that reputation and the promises he has made,” she Halford.Yet Rosie McKearney, a policy specialist at the Hepatitis C Trust, said the community was “shocked” that Burnham had moved responsibility for the scandal from a cabinet-level secretary of state to a junior minister.Research from the Haemophilia Society suggests that two years since the IBCA’s inception just 15% of projected compensation claims have been dealt with. In a letter sent to the IBCA’s chief executive, David Foley, the campaigners said they were “concerned and angry at the lack of progress”, especially its “unreasonable and sometimes impossible bureaucratic demands”.The Haemophilia Society is calling for regulatory change to shift the burden of evidence from applicants to the state, meaning that all applicants with a bleeding disorder would be entitled to compensation unless proved otherwise.Kate Burt, its chief executive, said that the current system was “putting haemophilia treatment centres under intolerable pressure”, with staff “asked to sift through patients’ medical notes to find evidence”, knowing that errors could cost the applicant thousands of pounds.“This is highly technical work, relying on expert knowledge to find fragments of crucial information, yet centres are expected to fund this themselves,” she said, adding that one consultant told her they work unpaid on Saturdays to answer the IBCA’s inquiries.View image in fullscreenSuzanne’s mother, Mari, as a young woman.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianCharlotte Evans, a lawyer at Leigh Day who is representing several victims and their families in their IBCA applications, said “the balance of probabilities” was the standard of proof for medical negligence claims.She said it represented a comparatively lower threshold, which considers a risky procedure that took place at the same time as infected blood was used as indicative that a blood product had been administered.Instead of assessing all the available evidence to build up a picture of what most likely happened, applicants are being asked to prove beyond reasonable doubt that they received a specific blood product.“The scheme is supposed to provide a simpler process,” she said, adding that although the government and the IBCA had an obligation to ensure taxpayers’ money was properly spent, “the question is whether those obligations, and IBCA’s understanding of the same, go beyond what the regulations actually require”.The reasons for this disconnect remained unclear, she said. “It may be that certain individuals [assessing claims] haven’t been given the appropriate guidance or training.”Lynne Kelly, the chair of Haemophilia Wales, observed a “tick box” approach from the claims managers she had met. “The Cabinet Office is completely controlling the Infected Blood Compensation Authority scheme. It’s meant to be an independent, arm’s length body,” she said, adding that she believed the eligibility criteria was intended to “minimise the amount of compensation paid out”.For Zena Whittaker, that extra compensation would both give closure and a comfortable retirement, enabling her to stop worrying about putting the heating on.She is still haunted by the memory of asking a doctor how much longer her son Andrew had to live. He replied: “We don’t know, because it depends whether the hep C takes him first, or the Aids.”As a haemophiliac, Andrew received multiple blood transfusions, making it more likely than not that he also had hepatitis C. Yet medical records were destroyed when his hospital merged with another.“It’s just coming up to the anniversary [of his death], which makes everything raw,” Whittaker said. “It’s 31 years since he died and it brought it all back again.”Luke O’Shea Phillips is also struggling with a bureaucratic nightmare. He was given an infected clotting product as a three-year-old, but because he was not given a liver biopsy due to the risk of bleeding for haemophiliacs, he is unable to prove how bad his liver damage was, resulting in a shortfall in compensation he estimates at up to £1m.“I wasn’t told I had hepatitis C until I was 15. So just as life was beginning to open up, I was suddenly told what had already been done to it,” he said. “My infection is my life, and it’s unrecognised in every way.”A spokesperson for the IBCA said: “Missing or destroyed records will not prevent someone from making a claim. We will determine what is most likely from all available evidence.“Our claim managers work with the person claiming to help them gather information from a range of sources to support their claim. We consider all evidence: medical records, witness testimony, and other family records can all be used to support a claim.“Every compensation claim is unique, with individual circumstances, so they cannot be compared.”A government spokesperson said: “The government has listened and learned through constant engagement with the community to make changes to the compensation scheme to ensure the community receive the compensation they deserve.“The government will continue to be held accountable for its work in the usual ways across both Houses of Parliament.”Explore more on these topicsContaminated blood scandalHepatitis CHealth policyHealthPublic services policynewsShareReuse this content

title: McQueen comes home to happy, dark place at London fashion week | Alexander McQueen | The Guardian
description: Brand returns to its physical and unconventional roots as it battles undergoes stark restructuring
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Brand returns to its physical and unconventional roots as it battles undergoes stark restructuring
Content: Highlights from the Alexander McQueen spring summer 2027 collection at London fashion week.Composite: Indigital.tvView image in fullscreenHighlights from the Alexander McQueen spring summer 2027 collection at London fashion week.Composite: Indigital.tvAlexander McQueenMcQueen comes home to happy, dark place at London fashion weekBrand returns to its physical and unconventional roots as it battles undergoes stark restructuringJess Cartner-MorleyMon 21 Sep 2026 05.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBack when a young Lee McQueen was showing atLondon fashion week, there was Dante, the show in a Hawksmoor church with a skeleton in the front row and a blaring soundtrack of organ music and gunfire. And there was Voss, where models were trapped inside a giant mirrored box set up as a psychiatric ward.Twenty-five years later, theAlexander McQueenbrand returned from the Paris schedule to a creepily beautiful subterranean 17th century London chapel, with steel harnesses, bulky ankle strapped heels that looked like electronic monitoring tags, and a chain mail dress of tiny silver skulls.View image in fullscreenThe skull chain mail dress.Photograph: Indigital TVDarkness is a McQueen happy place. Which is fortunate, because dark times have come for the legendary brand. In the 2000s Lee McQueen was the toast of Paris, growing in sophistication and ambition, until tragedy struck in 2010.After his death, the talent and emotional intelligence of his successor, Sarah Burton, who designed Kate Middleton’s wedding dress in 2011, kept the name riding high when many thought it would fall apart. But the McQueen name is now losing its heat and the brand is in trouble, undergoing a stark restructuring plan of shuttered stores and job losses.Bringing McQueen home to the city where the name is still revered was the first decision made by Gianfranco d’Attis, who became the new chief executive in June, and the energy of this show proved it was the right call. McQueen hits different in London.View image in fullscreen‘Jackets paid homage to the radical tailoring of Tommy Nutter.’Photograph: Indigital TVThe new business strategy is to streamline and refocus McQueen: fewer trainers and sweatshirts, more evening gowns (red carpet remains a strength) and British tailoring. For the homecoming, the creative director, Seán McGirr, now in his third year at the brand, went deep into British references. He picked the vaulted undercroft venue because it felt like being inside his favourite painting in the National Gallery,Piero della Francesca’s The Baptism of Christ. Jackets paid homage to the radical tailoring of Tommy Nutter, Keith Flint hair horns to rave culture. “London is a constant stimulation,” he said backstage. “Style on the street is not conventional. I love the wrongness of it.”View image in fullscreenMcQueen’s creative director, Seán McGirr, and the actor Emilia Clarke backstage at the show.Photograph: Dave Benett/Sam Simpson/Getty Images for McQueenMcGirr is 38, with a dimpled smile and a soft Dublin accent. His instincts track lighter and sweeter than this house ever did in its reckless youth. Organza was whipped into meringue-like peaks at the shoulders of a corsetted ivory lace dress – he said he wanted the famous McQueen exaggerated shoulders “to look like angel wings. I wanted the message to feel ethereal, and light in a sense.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenOrganza extravaganza.Photograph: Indigital TVThe Roksanda show, at a rooftop garden next to the National Theatre, was a sunny contrast to McQueen, swathes of cherry- and lavender-coloured silk glinting under a blue sky. Thickly plaited rope belts in contrast colours were a tribute to the monumental fabric sculptures of Françoise Grossen, and a celebration of “the feminine energy of braiding, which is connected to hair, to craft, to housework”, the designer Roksanda Ilinčić said.View image in fullscreenA model walks the runway at the Roksanda show.Photograph: Hoda Davaine/Getty ImagesExplore more on these topicsAlexander McQueenLondon fashion weekFashion weeksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Harry Styles walked eight miles in loafers. Is he ruining his feet? There’s only one way to find out | Men's shoes | The Guardian
description: For his trek across New York City, the singer wore a pair of Prada slip-ons. I tried to do the same in my penny loafers – and soon found out why experts advise against it
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: For his trek across New York City, the singer wore a pair of Prada slip-ons. I tried to do the same in my penny loafers – and soon found out why experts advise against it
Content: ‘I was pretty footsore by suppertime’ … day one for Tim Dowling.Photograph: Ethan Parker/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I was pretty footsore by suppertime’ … day one for Tim Dowling.Photograph: Ethan Parker/The GuardianMen's shoesHarry Styles walked eight miles in loafers. Is he ruining his feet? There’s only one way to find outFor his trek across New York City, the singer wore a pair of Prada slip-ons. I tried to do the same in my penny loafers – and soon found out why experts advise against itTim DowlingMon 21 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast month, just before his 30-night residency at Madison Square Garden,Harry Styleswas spotted walking the streets of New York. According to the paparazzi who trailed him throughout his journey, he walked eight miles – all the way from Brooklyn into Manhattan – in loafers.If, like me, you own a pair of loafers, your first thought is probably: that doesn’t sound like a good idea. On Instagram, Grazia called Styles’ shoes “perhaps the least sensible footwear for such an undertaking”.You might imagine that single outing would have taught Styles a lesson, but he was photographed a few days later in the same pair of loafers, which all the evidence suggests are dark brown, pre-distressedPrada“Shuffle” shoes that cost £910. At that price I wouldn’t even wear them outside – they look soft and flimsy, like a cross between a moccasin and a ballet slipper.View image in fullscreenHarry, what were you thinking?Photograph: XNY/Star Max/GC ImagesHowever, following Styles’ example, I’m suddenly determined to get more mileage out of my own, underused slip-ons. I mean to wear them every day, all day, for a week – and to walk at least eight miles in them, if not in one day, then at least cumulatively.But first I have a question: could it be bad for my feet? What are the actual risks of such an undertaking?“A loafer by construction has a smaller volume in the forefoot than a shoe that has a substantial fastening,” says Dr Helen Branthwaite, chief clinical advisor at the Royal College of Podiatry. In other words, a slip-on shoe is narrow at the front because, without laces or straps, it’s the only way it can hold on to your foot. “This may cause some compression to the toes if the shape and volume of the front of the shoe is not the same as the wearer’s foot.”I send a link to a Styles/loafer pap shot to Christophe Champs, an orthotics specialist and the founder of the Podo clinic in London. “The main problem I see in that picture is a summer look,” he says. “Summer is the worst season for us.” Pounding hard city pavements in insubstantial shoes with no heel contour or arch support – slippers, loafers, flip-flops – can cause real problems. During this past hot summer, Champs says his clinic saw a fivefold increase in patients presenting withplantar fasciitis– a painful inflammation of the tissue connecting your heel to your toes.For a couple of years the fashion world has remarked upon a gradual decline in the number of trainers appearing at runway shows, and the corresponding trend for loafers. “The younger customer is asking for styles that were particularly hot in the 1970s,” shoemaker Tim Little, owner of footwear brand Grenson, told Esquire in January. “Thin, slim-soled, often tasselled, and, above all easy on the feet.” GQ also recently declared that loafers were the “most crucial shoes of 2026”.View image in fullscreenDowling brings NYC style to suburban London.Photograph: Ethan Parker/The GuardianIt’s raining the first time I decide to wear my loafers all day, and I’m pretty footsore by suppertime, having covered no more than three miles. Along the way I’ve experienced both toe compression and heel slippage. But the shoes also hurt because I’ve never worn them long enough to break them in properly, even though I bought them years ago. Mine are sturdy, thick-soled penny loafers, quite unlike Styles’ pair.Styles’ shoes, I’ve come to understand, are a fashionable slip-on subset sometimes known as a “scrunch loafer”. They’re so completely without structure that they look as if they’ve been run over by a steamroller. Perversely, Styles’ loafers have laces.But, according to Champs, there is a bigger and more common problem than walking eight miles in scrunch loafers: the widespread habit of wearing running shoes on one’s daily commute. He says the soles of most cheap modern trainers are too high, too light and too cushioned to provide proper support. “You look at people from behind and it’s painful,” he says. “They’re on big fat sponges. So at least Harry doesn’t have this.”His compromise recommendation for men’s walk-to-work footwear is a well-made dress shoe. “It’s time now to bring patients back into dress shoes,” he says. “But when my patients see my shoes they tell me, ‘Christophe, that for me is wedding and funeral.’” When he holds up his shoe to the Zoom camera for me, I’m surprised to see they’re not unlike my loafers, albeit with a pair of his own orthotic inserts tucked inside (Champs got into the orthotics game because of foot injuries he suffered as an athlete).View image in fullscreenLooking good on the pit stop.Photograph: Ethan Parker/The GuardianOn my second day in loafers, I manage five miles in total, but by the evening I can feel my crowded fourth toes beginning to climb up over their larger neighbours. I’m beginning to see the appeal of Styles’ £910 slippers – at least your foot isn’t boxed in all day. And while it would probably be wise to alert fans to the dangers of emulating his choice of long-distance travelling shoe, it doesn’t mean it’s necessarily a problem for Styles himself.“IfHarry Stylesis comfortable in loafers, and he can dance and walk in them, then he must have a strong foot, with a complementary shape to the shoe in question,” says Branthwaite, pointing out that Styles is a trained performer. “If someone else wishes to walk eight miles in his shoes, then they would also need to do the same training and practice.”In Champs’ opinion, Styles’ footwear, while wholly inappropriate for an eight-mile hike, is by no means the worst option. “Those shoes are not so bad for a short walk,” he says. “It’s actually more dangerous to wear decent shoes that are out of shape because they’ve been used for too long. Shoes need three things: to be recent, decent and laced up.”That’s enough advice to persuade me to give up my loafer marathon halfway through day three, and long before I’ve walked eight miles in them. Then again, looking at all the other shoes in my cupboard, it’s possible they’re still my best bet.Later I was made aware of even more recent paparazzi shots that showed Styles wearing flat-soled light blue trainers. Maybe he’s learned his lesson after all.Explore more on these topicsMen's shoesHarry StylesMen's fashionPradafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Three countries, one hike: an Alpine adventure in Austria, Slovenia and Italy | Austria holidays | The Guardian
description: The Alpe Adria loop is an eight-day walking trail that crisscrosses borders, taking in dramatic peaks, glorious meadows and charming places to stay
Author: Sarah Baxter
Headline: The Alpe Adria loop is an eight-day walking trail that crisscrosses borders, taking in dramatic peaks, glorious meadows and charming places to stay
Content: The Italian mountain village of Valbruna has a view of Jôf Fuart, one of the Julian Alps’ most imposing peaks.Photograph: Nicola Simeoni/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Italian mountain village of Valbruna has a view of Jôf Fuart, one of the Julian Alps’ most imposing peaks.Photograph: Nicola Simeoni/AlamyAustria holidaysThree countries, one hike: an Alpine adventure in Austria, Slovenia and ItalyThe Alpe Adria loop is an eight-day walking trail that crisscrosses borders, taking in dramatic peaks, glorious meadows and charming places to staySarah BaxterMon 21 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 02.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Achtung! Staatsgrenze!” OK, the signpost marking the “state border” didn’t have exclamation marks but, with its no-nonsense Prussian font, it did feel quite shouty. The only thing was, no one on the Feistritzer Alm – a peaceful sweep of Alpine pasture at the meeting of Austria and Italy – was paying any attention to it at all.Hikers hiked straight past. Mountain bikers used it to prop up their cycles. Cows grazed willy-nilly. And the patrons of the Schutzhütte Oisternig enjoyed their cold beers regardless of which country they were in. While official boundaries may have changed in these parts over the centuries, the magnificence of the mountains has not.View image in fullscreenMy husband and I had woken that morning in Austria, in the Carinthian village of Feistritz. After breakfast at the oldGasthof Alte Post, we’d bought a loaf from thebäckerei, climbed past the 15th-century church as its bells called worshippers for prayers and continued up through pine forest to these high Alpine meadows – and into Italy.We were hiking theAlpe Adria, a long-distance trail jointly developed by Austria, Slovenia and Italy that runs from the foot of Grossglockner (Austria’s highest mountain at 3,798 metres) to the Adriatic coast. At 750km (466 miles), the full trail is too long for most people’s summer holidays. But a 135km (84 mile) loop – moderate-graded, doable in a week, with walking days of 15-24km (9-15 miles) – has been created where the three nations meet, to offer a multicultural taster. It’s an appealing idea; hikers love circuiting multiple countries – just look at the numbers crowding the Tour du Mont Blanc these days. While the Alpe Adria loop isn’t quite as dramatic as that, it does offer a much quieter alternative.View image in fullscreenThe writer near the Vratca Pass.We started our journey by catching an early Eurostar to Amsterdam, where there was time for canals, beer and crispybitterballenbefore boarding the Nightjet sleeper to Salzburg. In our adjoining capsule-like cabins, we watched the Netherlands segue into Germany, and woke at dawn to pasture, pines and peaks. On the final train from Salzburg to Villach, where we were beginning the loop, the Alps pressed closer, drawing us in.Now, on the Feistritzer Alm, a day and a half into the walk, Austria was behind us (for the time being) and Italy beckoned, beautifully. Just around the hill from the Schutzhütte Oisternig sat the chapel of Our Lady of the Snows (or the Chiesa Madonna della Neve/Almkapelle Maria Schnee, depending on your linguistic preferences); beyond spread deep-green foothills and the jagged Julian Alps, sawing into a hot-blue sky.double quotation markAfter a magical ascent, I sat on the terrace and stared at the peaks, transfixedFrom here, the rest of the day was all downhill, a drop through blessed shade and butterflies, on paths weaving through the pines and peeping out to the peaks, to end in the village of Valbruna, at theValbruna Inn. We had a wonderful room, and spent time on our balcony, gazing past the geraniums to the sheer Jôf Fuart range, which reaches up to 2,666 metres.We also spent time in the hotel’s Julius Kugy Library, a cosy den of books on alpinism, named after a writer-mountaineer legend. Born in 1858 to a Slovenian family in Gorizia – then part of the Austrian empire, now in Italy – Kugy is credited with opening up the Julian Alps. He never lost his reverence for nature, always encouraging others to explore with respect, curiosity and awe. I picked up one of his books and read from his introduction: “[This] tries to describe the mountains as a source of happiness, because such they were in my life.”I couldn’t have agreed more and, with great happiness, we continued the next morning, following the Alpe Adria from Valbruna, across the Saisera River and up through fir and spruce to theSanctuary of Monte Lussari, a ridge-top pilgrim church and hamlet, where the Virgin Mary is said to have appeared in 1360. I was less moved by the miracle, or the shops selling branded tote bags, liqueurs and slippers, than by the mountains scattered far and wide. We lingered to enjoy the view, then descended via alpenrose and ambling goats to Tarvisio, finding a different kind of happiness in the town’s gelaterias. Then, later that evening, we sat with cold beers on our balcony at theHotel Nevada, watching as a storm crashed through, briefly erasing every mountain.View image in fullscreenThe village of Monte Lussari.Photograph: Marco Lissoni/AlamyThe next day brought more joy as the trail took us along the woodland-weavingSentiero del Orsoand then via a busy cycle path to the Fusine lakes. These twin glacial bowls are so arrestingly blue-green you’d think they’d been AI-ed if you weren’t standing right there. We found a quiet spot to picnic, listening to the whinnying of little grebes and staring beyond the dazzling water to the afternoon’s challenge via the rocks ahead: the haul up toRifugio Zacchi.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Alpe Adria loop usually ends each day in a valley bottom, where there are plenty of inns. But not tonight. Zacchi sits at 1,380 metres, tight-hugged by the intimidating peaks that mark the Slovenian border. After a muggy, magical ascent through forest to the refuge, I sat on the terrace, drinking a superb Aperol spritz, and stared at them, transfixed; a few booms of thunder rippled, just in case the power of nature had been in doubt.View image in fullscreenThe blue-green Fusine lakes.Photograph: Liubomir Paut-Fluerasu/AlamyThe food at Zacchi was excellent – venison ragù, chargrilled peppers, potato-pancake-likefrico, made with local montasio cheese. Also excellent was the fact that, in a stroke of luck, we had a dorm to ourselves. We woke, refreshed and ready for the next border hop.The most striking route would have been over the forbidding-looking Vratca Pass. The Alpe Adria took us there, for views east into Triglav national park, but didn’t cross. Instead, the trail backtracked down on the Italian side to follow a path through the verdant Sava Valley to the outdoorsy town of Kranjska Gora.It was a pleasant entrance into Slovenia; however, our exit was spectacular. To get back to Austria the next day, we had to cross the Karavanke Alps and conquer the highest point of our route, the 1,842-metre Schwarzkogel. It was an unrelenting climb, at first amid pasture and shingle roofs, with sublime views to the Julian peaks, then deep in forest serenaded by thrushes, streams trickling to our side.As we neared the top, we could see south across Slovenia’s surging summits, north across Carinthia’s electric-blue lakes and low hills. Squat white marker-stones began to appear too, strung along the ridge’s spine – an international border marked more casually than most front gardens. We slalomed between the posts, enjoying both the freedom of movement and the majesty of nature. For millennia the Alps have been physical and cultural barriers. The Alpe Adria is a bringing together; a source of mountain happiness.The trip was provided by Walks Worldwide; the eight-day, self-guidedAlpe Adria Tri-Country Trekis from£895 B&B.Accommodation in London was provided byGenerator(rooms from £75, dormbeds from £11)Explore more on these topicsAustria holidaysSlovenia holidaysItaly holidaysWalking holidaysEurope holidaysWalkingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A job that changed me: I cried nearly every day working in aged care, then realised I could bring joy instead | Life and style | The Guardian
description: I once asked a resident what she would do if she could do anything. She replied: ‘I’d run in a field’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I once asked a resident what she would do if she could do anything. She replied: ‘I’d run in a field’
Content: Carolyn Mullen: ‘I became so grateful for the chance to share the residents’ lives with them, as well as being more grateful for my own life and abilities.’Composite: Guardian design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCarolyn Mullen: ‘I became so grateful for the chance to share the residents’ lives with them, as well as being more grateful for my own life and abilities.’Composite: Guardian design/Getty ImagesA job that changed meLife and styleA job that changed me: I cried nearly every day working in aged care, then realised I could bring joy insteadI once asked a resident what she would do if she could do anything. She replied: ‘I’d run in a field’Carolyn MullenMon 21 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 19.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn my 40s, I was beginning to wonder where I fit in the employment world. I had a variety of jobs including an improv instructor, actor and corporate facilitator, then Covid arrived and all those people-facing roles disappeared.Living in Sydney, with my kids at school and a mortgage to pay, I took on some temp work through an agency.I was placed in anaged careresidential home, working on reception. Within the first hour I was in tears. I was really confronted by the residents as I hadn’t been around older people much before, especially people with dementia. I worked there for a month and cried every day.A few months later the temp agency called again. The same aged care company had some full-time reception work at another residence, and had requested “the lady who cried all the time”. I took the job.On my first day I was nervous. I didn’t want people’s first impressions of me to be someone who was too sensitive to work there. At one point, after I found myself in the bathroom letting go of a couple of tears, I gave myself a good pep talk.A job that changed me: Working the pool kiosk in the summer of ’82, I was excited when older boys came by – but I learned that respect is better than attentionRead moreThe desk itself was at the front entrance, between the residents’ rooms and the lounge and dining area. All residents would walk past me to and from meals and activities.Most of them had dementia, so every day was different. Some mornings it was calm and smiles; other mornings it’d be residents refusing showers, or asking me to call their mum to take them home.They were from all walks of life: different backgrounds and parts of Australia, and their ages ranged from their mid-60s to late-90s. No one really felt the age they were, and for those who didn’t have dementia, their bodies simply weren’t allowing them to do what they wanted to do.There were many memorable moments. One non-verbal resident had worked in a similar job in her working life; she would sit with me and I would share my files and pens so she could complete her tasks, as she used to do.Another resident would sit with me, waiting for her parents to pick her up from the movies, and ask me to call them and find out how long it would be until they arrived.One other resident would mention we’d been robbed, which alarmed me the first time I heard it – before I realised that we hadn’t, and this was part of her behaviour that she would repeat day after day. As an actor I could draw upon my skills of repeating a scene many times, so when we were “robbed”, I would say I was aware and had already called the police, who were on their way to investigate.I met a beautiful artist who used to paint but due to tremors had turned her eye to photography. At lunch I would go out for a walk and take photographs of flowers and trees for her, then we would chat about her art, our views of the world and how we lived as creatives.I once asked another resident what she would do if she could do anything. She replied: “I’d run in a field.” I think of that often, especially when I’m passing an open space.There were some tough times during Covid lockdowns. I can only imagine how frightful the staff must have looked to the residents in our personal protective equipment. We couldn’t accept visitors, so families would call each other on the phone and wave through the windows.Early on during my time there, I told a colleague that in my previous role at the other residence, I’d cried a lot, because I’d been confronted by being with older people. She suggested it was a matter of perspective. I thought about what I saw when I looked in residents’ eyes and realised it was my own fears of ageing, my own mortality and what my path ahead would be.That colleague’s comment changed how I showed up. I decided that I could bring joy and love to the job each day. I became so grateful for the chance to share the residents’ lives with them, as well as being more grateful for my own life and abilities, and for my parents and the time we spend together.I worked at the residence for three years. My time there underlined how much we all matter, at all ages, and how we should take the time to share stories and acknowledge and appreciate each other. And even with dementia, some residents remembered me, trusted in me and wanted to sit with me for comfort. It was an honour.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleA job that changed meAgeingOlder peopleAged careAustralian lifestyleDementiafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A new start after 60: I’m 92 and cycling is my life – despite the crash that left me unconscious | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Arthur Plummer got a bike when he retired at 65 and joined a cycling club as one of its youngest members. Now he is its oldest but still racking up 5,000km every year
Author: Paula Cocozza
Headline: Arthur Plummer got a bike when he retired at 65 and joined a cycling club as one of its youngest members. Now he is its oldest but still racking up 5,000km every year
Content: ‘My bike is my best friend’ … Arthur Plummer, photographed in Waterloo, Ontario, in September 2026.Photograph: Ema Suvajac/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘My bike is my best friend’ … Arthur Plummer, photographed in Waterloo, Ontario, in September 2026.Photograph: Ema Suvajac/The GuardianA new start after 60Life and styleA new start after 60: I’m 92 and cycling is my life – despite the crash that left me unconsciousArthur Plummer got a bike when he retired at 65 and joined a cycling club as one of its youngest members. Now he is its oldest but still racking up 5,000km every yearPaula CocozzaMon 21 Sep 2026 01.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Arthur Plummer retired at 65, he bought a secondhand bicycle. His sister was a member of a cycling club for seniors in the Canadian city of Waterloo, Ontario, where they lived, and Plummer joined, too, becoming one of the club’s youngest members. Now he is 92 and its oldest member – but he still cycles thousands of kilometres every year. His odometer for this year so far reads 4,270km (2,650 miles). After our conversation, he intends to cycle another 40km.“I love cycling,” he says. “Wherever I go, even if I ride on the same roads, there’s something new happening. When I get on my bike, I feel great. I come home at about 3pm and I feel exhausted. However, it’s the nicest feeling. It’s exhilarating, and it’s resulted in me being extremely healthy.”Even when, in his late 80s, Plummer developed polymyalgia rheumatica (an inflammatory condition that causes pain, stiffness and inflammation in the shoulders, neck and hips) and was unable to walk, cycling helped him to move again. “I was in a wheelchair and I would sit outside in my driveway and people would go by and I felt trapped,” he says. “I can’t walk,” he thought, “but if I can get on my bike, I bet I could ride.” So that’s what he did.Although his legs are strong, walking is still uncomfortable; he has a shortened stride and sometimes struggles to keep up with his wife and friends on holiday.Cycling, on the other hand, brings freedom. Plummer has cycled “on every street you can go on” within 100 sq miles (260 sq km) of where he lives. He often takes his bike on the bus so that he can explore farther afield. “I’m looking for new vistas,” he says.View image in fullscreen‘Looking for new vistas’ … Arthur Plummer.Photograph: Ema Suvajac/The GuardianPlummer wasn’t into sports when he was growing up. His parents, he says, “were not well off”. His father worked in a rubber factory, his mother looked after the home and worked as a waiter, and as a sales assistant in a clothes shop. “There were few luxuries. It was a tough life, but it was a good life.“In 1934, when I was born, it was the norm to not have money.” His classmates were either rich or poor. “And we stayed apart. It was an advantage to be poor, because you had more friends.”There wasn’t time to cycle in younger adulthood. After college, Plummer worked as an estimator or quantity surveyor, initially on hydro projects in northern Quebec, before returning to Ontario. Along the way, he became a single parent to three daughters, then aged nine, 11 and 13 – “a wonderful experience”, he says.Later, he partnered with four others in a company that oversaw construction and renovation projects in schools. But he found the job very stressful and when a colleague had a heart attack, he decided he needed to change jobs. At 50, he became a municipal building inspector, a job he did until retirement. Sometimes, he would drive past a colleague who commuted by bike, even pedalling through a winter snow squall. “You know how you remember some things for ever in your life? I thought: ‘Wow, he’s an avid cyclist.’”When he took up cycling himself, Plummer rode at a maximum sustained speed of 25kph. Now that’s dropped to between 15 and 20kph, and he has reduced his distance target to 5,000km a year. He is mindful of risks – he stopped skiing at 90 for fear of breaking a limb – but he has gone over his handlebars six times, and a few years ago he collided with a car that ran a red light. Mercifully, he escaped with cuts and bruises.“I apparently went head first on to the road, broke my helmet and passed out. People tell me that when I woke, I ran straight to my bike,” he says. “There is a kind of a connection between the rider and the bike.”A new start after 60: stuck in a hospital bed, I decided to retire. Now I’m a tap dancerRead moreA couple of years ago, Plummer moved into a high-rise apartment, “living the urban lifestyle downtown”, and now keeps his carbon-fibre Cannondale bike on a rack next to his bed. “My bike is my best friend,” he says. “We are a team.” If Plummer wakes in the night, he acknowledges his bike “with a greeting: ‘Hey there, buddy’”.Cycling brings its own momentum. “I am so full of energy, I can’t believe it myself sometimes. I want to get out and use that energy to cycle,” Plummer says. “I hope my last day is on my bike. I have a saying: I’m cycling to eternity and it’s further than I thought.”Tell us: has your life taken a new direction after the age of 60?Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsLife and styleA new start after 60CyclingOlder peopleFitnessfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pixel 11 Pro XL: Google’s big-screen superphone with top-class camera | Pixel | The Guardian
description: Fantastic display and two-day battery life plus everything that’s great about Google’s more pocketable Pixel Pros
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Fantastic display and two-day battery life plus everything that’s great about Google’s more pocketable Pixel Pros
Content: The Pixel 11 Pro XL is for those who want the big-screen Google experience.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Pixel 11 Pro XL is for those who want the big-screen Google experience.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.PixelReviewPixel 11 Pro XL: Google’s big-screen superphone with top-class cameraFantastic display and two-day battery life plus everything that’s great about Google’s more pocketable Pixel ProsSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorMon 21 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle’s latest super-sized Pixel takes everything that’s great about the relatively pocket-friendly 11 Pro and adds a huge, high-quality screen and a big battery.That makes the Pixel 11 Pro XL one of the largest smartphones available in Europe and the US, competing directly withSamsung’s giant Galaxy S26 Ultraand Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro Max, with an equally sizeable £1,279 (€1,399/$1,299/A$2,099) price tag – £80 (€100/$100/A$100) more than last year with less memory because of thecost of RAMageddon.The XL sticks with the tried-and-tested formula from the previous few years of super-sized Pixels: a fantastic 6.8in OLED on the front, polished aluminium sides and a glass back with a large camera bar poking through it. The new model is 6g lighter and 0.1mm smaller in every dimension thanlast year’s Pixel 10 Pro XL, but you would be hard-pressed to notice.View image in fullscreenThe new XL has the same gimmicky HiLight LED on the backas the smaller 11 Pro, which glows when you talk to Gemini or a favourite contact rings, but is of little real use.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe phone has the same Tensor G6 chip, 12 or 16GB of RAM (depending on variant) and at least 256GB of storage as the rest of thePixelline for 2026. The XL feels super snappy in day-to-day use and the chip can handle mid-level gaming but comes up short in raw performance compared with top chips in rivals. Those looking for the best frame-rate or graphics in games best look elsewhere.The battery life is the longest of the current Pixels, lasting just about two days between charges, including more than six hours actively using the screen across a mix of 5G and wifi for browsing, messaging, apps and photos. That’s a few hours longer than the regular 11 Pro but slightly short of last year’s XL model. Most will only need to charge it every other night and it should outlast even the heaviest of use days.View image in fullscreenA full charge took about 90 minutes using a 45W or greater USB-C power adaptor (not included) or longer using a Qi 25W wireless charger.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 11 Pro XL runs the same Android 17 as its smaller sibling, with support until August 2033 and an overall very polished experience. It also comes with a six-month subscription toGoogle AI Pro subscriptionwith access to the video generatorGemini Omni, higher AI usage limits, 5TB of cloud storage and Google Health Premium.Many of the new cutting-edge local AI tools are best-in-class, including the proactive Gemini information suggestions and the turbocharged Rambler voice dictation tool built into the keyboard.View image in fullscreenModels sold in the US lack the sim card slot present in the top of phones sold the UK, EU and Australia, relying entirely on eSims.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSpecificationsScreen:6.8in 120Hz QHD+ OLED (486ppi)Processor:Google Tensor G6RAM:12 or 16GBStorage:256, 512GB or 1TBOperating system:Android17Camera:50MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 5x tele; 42MP selfieConnectivity:5G, eSIM, wifi 7, UWB, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread and GNSSWater resistance:IP68 (1.5m for 30 minutes)Dimensions:162.7 x 76.5 x 8.5 mmWeight:226gCameraView image in fullscreenThe camera app is fairly simple to use but has plenty of tools, quick options and modes to make the best of your photography.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe XL has the same excellent cameras as theregular 11 Pro, including a very good 42-megapixel selfie camera on the front.The triple rear camera is one of the very best on a smartphone, including a 50MP wide, 48MP ultra wide and 48MP 5x telephoto. New for this year is a significantly faster Night Sight low-light mode, which captures photos about three to four times faster with better detail and sharpness. The new Magic Capture mode shoots video and photos automatically with one press, which works great at parties. The Creator Suite has extensive tools to help produce social videos, too.The telephoto camera can perform an excellent 10x magnification crop zoom, with very good digital zoom stretching up to 30x before being processed by generative AI for up to 120x magnification.The new Camera Looks feature allows you to modify how the Pixel captures and processes your photos for the first time, even if that means making your pictures look technically worse, opening up lots of creative potential.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe glass back hides Qi2 25W wireless charging and magnetic accessory support.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe batteryis rated to lastin excess of 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google, third-party shops or self-repair,with manualsandparts available.The Pixel 11 Pro XL contains 33% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down thephone’s environmental impactin its report and willrecycle old devicesfor free.PriceThe Google Pixel 11 Pro XL costs from£1,279(€1,399/$1,299/A$2,099) in a choice of four colours.For comparison, thePixel 11costs£879,Pixel 11 Procosts£1,079,Pixel 11 Pro Foldcosts from£1,799, thePixel 10acosts£499, theSamsung Galaxy S26 Ultracosts£1,279and the iPhone 18 Pro Max costs£1,299.VerdictGoogle’s super-phone takes everything that’s good about its pocket-friendlyPixel 11 Proand adds a huge, fantastic screen and a bigger battery.It is wide and quite heavy, making it a two-hand phone most of the time, but its large display offers a similar screen area when watching widescreen video asGoogle’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold.The camera system is one of the very best, and can be customised extensively for great creative licence. The phone feels responsive, lasts up to two days between charges and is packed with cutting-edge AI, much of which is actually useful.The Pixel 11 Pro XL is a great, massive phone. But it isn’t a dramatic upgrade on those that came before it and falls short in performance and power-user features compared withSamsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra.Pros:excellent and huge screen, two-day battery life, great camera with 5x and 10x optical magnification and extensive customisation, seven years of software updates, impressive local and proactive AI, Qi2.2 wireless charging and magnetic accessory support, fast fingerprint and face recognition, six months of Google AI Pro included.Cons:very expensive, less memory than before, huge and heavy, face unlock option not as secure as Face ID, raw performance and battery life short of best-in-class, no physical sim card slot in the US, not a massive upgrade.View image in fullscreenThe in-screen fingerprint scanner is one of the best in the business: fast, forgiving and accurate.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsPixelGoogleAndroidSmartphonesAlphabetMobile phonesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Starwatch: Autumnal equinox in northern hemisphere, spring in the south | Astronomy | The Guardian
description: Precise moment of equinox in UK is 1.05am on Wednesday – but day and night will not be equal until Friday
Author: Stuart Clark
Headline: Precise moment of equinox in UK is 1.05am on Wednesday – but day and night will not be equal until Friday
Content: People watch the sun setting in Northolt, London, on the evening before the 2025 autumnal equinox.Photograph: Stephen Chung/AlamyView image in fullscreenPeople watch the sun setting in Northolt, London, on the evening before the 2025 autumnal equinox.Photograph: Stephen Chung/AlamyStarwatchAstronomyStarwatch: Autumnal equinox in northern hemisphere, spring in the southPrecise moment of equinox in UK is 1.05am on Wednesday – but day and night will not be equal until FridayStuart ClarkMon 21 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe September or autumnal equinox takes place this week. It marks the astronomical beginning of autumn in the northern hemisphere and spring in the southern hemisphere. This year, the precise moment of the equinox falls at 01.05 BST on 23 September.It is commonly said the equinox is when day and night are equal, because the name derives from the Latin for “equal night”, but in practice that is not quite true. An equinox occurs when the sun crosses the celestial equator, the imaginary projection of Earth’s equator into the sky.As Earth moves around its orbit, the sun’s apparent position shifts north and south of the celestial equator. At the equinox it crosses from one side to the other. But even then, day and night are not precisely equal.This is because the sun appears as a disc rather than a point of light, and the bending of its rays by our atmosphere means we can still see it even when it is just below the horizon. Together, these effects make the measured daytime several minutes longer than 12 hours at the equinox.In the UK, the date on which day and night come closest to being equal will be a couple of days later, around 25 September. This is called the equilux, for “equal light”.Explore more on these topicsAstronomyStarwatchThe sunAutumnfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I lost my children, and I’m afraid of losing my baby again’: a day in the life of a pregnant woman in Gaza | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Alaa lives in a tent pitched on the ruins of her house, which was destroyed by an Israeli airstrike that killed all three of her children. In one month, she will give birth again.
Author: Tess McClure
Headline: Alaa lives in a tent pitched on the ruins of her house, which was destroyed by an Israeli airstrike that killed all three of her children. In one month, she will give birth again.
Content: Alaa. Art direction by Guardian DesignGaza: a week in the lifeGaza‘I lost my children, and I’m afraid of losing my baby again’: a day in the life of a pregnant woman in GazaAlaa lives in a tent pitched on the ruins of her house, which was destroyed by an Israeli airstrike that killed all three of her children. In one month, she will give birth again.Supported byAbout this contentSeham Tanteshin Gaza andTess McClureMon 21 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.15 EDTShareAs the war inGazaapproaches its fourth year, this week, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each will tell the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the ongoing conflict.Alaa Hessi takes each step deliberately: raises her foot to land heavily on the stair above, takes a breath, slides her hand up the railing. Resting atop an uneven mess of rubble, the wooden staircase judders with each motion. Her movements are slowed by the heavy melon of her pregnant belly.At the top of the stairs, she pauses for breath, then walks on to the platform that once formed the upper storey of her family’s home. A tent is pitched where the house stood. Beneath her feet are the ruins of the house where she raised her three children, Waseem, 10, Mohannad, 7, and Khawla, 5. And where they died, all three killed by an Israeli airstrike that levelled the home.In about one month*, Alaa will give birth again.Daybreakdouble quotation markThe sound that wakes me in the morning is the buzzing of flies inside the tent, and the noise of our neighbours.Privacy in the tents is nonexistent,as is safety. Everyone here hears each other’s secrets. We hear people when they go to the bathroom. We can even hear them breathing. The window of my tent faces the yellow line directly. You can see the Israeli army positions from here, and sometimes they fire at us.Alaa makes tea over an open flame as cooking gas is scarce in GazaMy husband and I love drinking tea in the morning, but making tea has become a challenge, because Israel has prevented cooking gas from entering Gaza and gas is extremely scarce.We still rely on firewood and open flames for cooking and preparing hot drinks. Gathering wood and making a fire is enough to exhaust me.After I drink my tea, I tidy the tent and try to cook as early as possible before the sun becomes too intense. I also hand-wash my husband’s clothes and my own, which is physically exhausting now that I ameight months pregnant*.MorningAlaa opens the window – a tarpaulin flap at the side of the tent. A hole out into open air. As her eyes adjust to the brightness, it is clear that everything, as far as can be seen, is destroyed. The landscape is a mass of shattered concrete and twisted steel.Above: the view from Alaa’s tent. Below: Alaa walks to her prenatal appointmentdouble quotation markToday, I have a prenatal appointment, to check on the baby’s progress.The place is far away, and I walk there – usually there is no vehicle thatcan give me a ride. It’s 34C, and walking through bombed streets filled with rubble and insectsin the heat of the day is extremely hard.The place where I get prenatal care isa tent, not a proper healthcare facility.The doctorshave prescribed me nutritional supplements for my pregnancy. I have been pregnant before, and I can tell this pregnancy is different: no matter how much I try to make up for the nutritional deficiencies and food deprivation I lived through in the war, my body remains exhausted. Food is scarce. My husband buys me fruits and vegetables and refuses to eat them himself, because he can only afford small amounts.When I learned that I was pregnant, I felt two completely opposite emotions. I was happy that I would have a child, but I also cried constantly because I missed my children – Waseem,Mohannadand Khawla. Everything reminds me of them. When I crave certain foods, I remember Waseem, because I loved those foods when I was pregnant with him.I do not tell nurses at the clinic about my circumstances and my children who died, because even the healthcare workers are emotionally exhausted. They are unable to offer comfort or psychological support. My story is not unusual in Gaza. Many women here have lost their children.After the appointment with the nutritionist, I also have an appointment with the maternity psychologist. They tell me to focus on my breathing: take a deep breath, hold itand let it out slowly.Then I walk home.satellite imageAfternoonTackling the stairs again, Alaa heaves a blue backpack up to the tent. It contains some of her dead children’s clothes, which she hopes the new baby might someday wear. Many of them were damaged by the bomb blast – ripped, their edges burned, but still wearable. She carefully unfolds a Snoopy T-shirt and a hat with two fluffy pompoms, pulls out a scarf for Castleview AFC – a small football club in Cork – that her son Waseem treasured. “He wore it all the time, even in summer. I would say, ‘Waseem it’s too hot, take it off!’ And he would say, “No, I love it.’”double quotation markI spend the afternoon with my brother, trying to decide how to store the clothes for the new baby.He suggests a sturdy cardboard or wooden box. The thing that we are worried about is the rats: the rats are everywhere. We hear them every night, and they always find their way into the tent. I sewed up the place where they entered, and they chewed a new way in– today we found another hole in the side of the tent.Alaa looks through the clothing that belonged to her three children, who were killed in an Israeli strikeI wonder if we could use rat poison, but my brother fears that then the rats will die here in the tentand spread disease.For the baby who’s coming, all I want is a safe place where the rats can’t reach. The baby will be so small, and I am terrified for him. I would like to have a proper crib for him, but cribs are hard to find in Gaza now, and the tent is already overcrowded.What I wish the world outside Gaza understood is how humiliating life in a tent really is. It is difficult, degrading and profoundly inhumane. Death still surrounds usin every direction.EveningAs late afternoon approaches, Alaa scrolls through her photos of her children. The smartphone that holds them, like so many in Gaza, is old, and its screen is cracked – after a long blockade, new smartphones are now being shipped in, but they are expensive, and many families cannot afford them. The children’s voices chime thinly from the speaker. Khawla and her older brother teasing each other. “Mama, I’m the sweet one!” Khawla shouts. Mohannad laughs, calls back: “No – I’m the sweet one!”Alaa watches videos of her three children, who were killed in an air strikedouble quotation markI only really speak about my children with my husband. He is the only person who carries the same pain and truly understands what is in my heart.When I become weak, he gives me strength. When he struggles, I try to comfort him and support him emotionally. We spend hours talking about our children – their personalities, the things they loved and the way they behaved. We even visit their graves together.This place still holds the memories of my children. It reminds me of our beautiful life together before. When I look at this rubble, I remember my children – the life I shared with them, raising them, preparing food for themand teaching them. Everything beautiful disappeared after they were gone.Sometimes, fear controls me because I lost my children, and I’m afraid of losing my baby again. I hope my new baby will live a better life than the one his siblings experienced, and that he will be safe.* Shortly after this story was reported, Alaa gave birth to a healthy baby boy. She named him Waseem, after his older brother.CreditsVideo: Tantesh Media ServicesArt direction: Harry Fischer, Anaïs Mims, Barry Ainslie and Alessia AmitrianoVideo editor/producer: Joshua JacobVideo executive producers: Temujin Doran and Augusta AnthonyAdditional reporting and research: Aseel Mousa and Harriet Barber

title: ‘It’s unrecognisable’: How being a tax haven has changed Jersey | Jersey | The Guardian
description: While global billionaires and multinational companies have been lured to its shores, many islanders feel left behind and priced out, with food bank use increasing
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: While global billionaires and multinational companies have been lured to its shores, many islanders feel left behind and priced out, with food bank use increasing
Content: Jersey in the Channel Islands hosts global accountancy firms and and international banks.Photograph: imagegallery2/AlamyView image in fullscreenJersey in the Channel Islands hosts global accountancy firms and and international banks.Photograph: imagegallery2/AlamyJersey‘It’s unrecognisable’: How being a tax haven has changed JerseyWhile global billionaires and multinational companies have been lured to its shores, many islanders feel left behind and priced out, with food bank use increasingKalyeena Makortoffin JerseyMon 21 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a late Friday afternoon on the Channel Island ofJersey, tourists and locals are flocking to St Helier’s waterfront where the town’s sprawling beach has emerged at low tide.In one direction, they face the calm waters of St Aubin’s Bay, ringed by a seaside promenade and punctuated with a tidal island hosting the 16th century Elizabeth Castle.Back on shore, however, it is all business. Gleaming glass buildings hosting global accountancy firms and and international banks hint at the £4bn offshore finance industry dominating this nine-by-five-mile island’s economy.For decades, low taxes and corporate secrecy have lured the wealth of global billionaires and multinational companies to Jersey’s shores, requiring a high-paid cadre of bankers, accountants and lawyers who now make up more than half of the island’s economic output, and two in every five jobs.It has also made Jersey one of the world’s richest economies, giving its 104,500 population a GDP per head that is nearly 60% higher than the UK.But those tactics have come at a cost, not least to Jersey’s international reputation, with the island consistently securinga top-10 slotin the Tax Justice Network’s international tax haven rankings. It also came under fire after thePanamaandParadise papers data leaks, which shone a light on how elites were hiding wealth in offshore hubs such as Jersey.But Jersey isn’t the only place chasing global wealth, and foreign governments that have built on and replicated the island’s model are now threatening to eat its lunch.“Without urgent intervention, Jersey’s future success as a financial centre is at risk, with inevitable repercussions for the Jersey way of life,”a government-backed review, led by NatWest Group’s former chair Howard Davies, warned in March.View image in fullscreenJersey cows waiting to be shipped to Denmark from St Helier harbour around 1880.Photograph: Philip Godfray/Societe Jersiaise Photographic ArchiveIn response, Jersey’s government is charging ahead with a £31m four-year plan aimed at slashing red tape, boosting the British crown dependency’s global profile and diversifying into popular crypto assets, all to keep it relevant in a rapidly changing world. “The risk of complacency is real,” the report warns. “Standing still means falling behind.”This is not the first time Jersey has faced an economic crossroads.Its boom and bust history stretches back to the 1700s, when it was home to a lucrative fine knitting industry. Once knitting was killed off by machines, oyster catching and shipbuilding took over, until overfishing and steam power closed shipyards.Entrepreneurial farmers then discovered and bred new exports: the docile and milk-rich Jersey cow, followed by a blight-resistant potato that still bears the island’s name, requiring a swathe of migrant workers to support farmers. “The cycle of Jersey’s industries has tended to see everyone getting involved where there’s a lot of money to be made,” says Lucy Layton, outreach curator at Jersey Heritage.View image in fullscreenLucy Layton, outreach curator at Jersey Heritage.Photograph: Gary Grimshaw/The GuardianA century later, as postwar Jersey tried to recover from Nazi occupation, tourism boomed, aided by thepopularity of the Bergerac detective series. That industry was eventually ruined by discount airlines offering cheap holidays to sunnier European destinations, ushering in a new economic era focused on billionaires and corporations looking for a low-tax home for their wealth.Jersey has crafted an alluring package to draw in global wealth, involving zero inheritance or capital gains tax, and no corporation tax – outside of financial services firms, which are charged just 10% on their earnings. Meanwhile, an army of high-earning bankers, lawyers and accountants face a maximum of 20% income tax on the island, compared with 45% in London.But wealthy Britons have been choosing the glass towers of Dubai over Jersey’s low-rise seaside towns, while rich families overseas are hedging their bets and spreading cash across a number of offshore hubs.The Panama and Paradise papers data leaks have also influenced money flows. “People now are much more selective about the jurisdictions that they deal with,” says Joe Moynihan, chief executive of the sector’s promotional body, Jersey Finance. “They don’t want their organisation, or indeed their family, to be associated with a jurisdiction that could potentially damage their reputation.”However, Moynihan says Jersey’s reputation is strong: “We’re well regulated, with plenty of expertise, good legislation and an independent judiciary, which is becoming increasingly important in the crazy world that we live in.”View image in fullscreenJoe Moynihan, the chief executive of Jersey Finance.Photograph: Gary Grimshaw/The GuardianBut Jersey is still losing ground. Authorities say they need to regain a competitive edge, including by diversifying into crypto assets – such as stablecoins and tokens – to draw a younger wealthy client. Ian Gorst, the island’s finance minister, says it is also looking to cut back on “regulatory friction”.To some, that may sound like an opportunity to cut corners, but Gorst insists this is not about watering down rules meant to stop financial crime, corruption or sanctions evasion. Jersey’songoing battlewith the Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich over his frozen assets is a case in point, he says. “What I think it shows is that Jersey can stand alongside the UK in fighting these issues.”Cooperation with the UK, though, only goes so far. Gorst has so far resistedpressure from Westminster’s anti-corruption champion Margaret Hodgeto publicly release its beneficial ownership register, showing who ultimately owns Jersey-based companies. “I don’t intend to make our register public, and I’ve been clear to the UK about that,” he says.But not everyone is on board with the government’s finance-first agenda.Laura Craig, the owner of the Little Wren gift shop in St Helier, has lived in Jersey for 45 years. “For me personally, I would like to see Jersey have more of a balance in industry,” she says, including a return to more tourism.View image in fullscreenLaura Craig, the owner of Little Wren gift shop.Photograph: Gary Grimshaw/The GuardianSt Helier itself has changed over Craig’s lifetime, with the old granite-frontage that once dominated the town’s waterfront having been reclaimed and built up for the finance industry. “It’s unrecognisable to when I was a little girl,” Craig adds. “All the big buildings on there now are banks and finance houses.”Many say the influx of wealthy bankers has pushed up house prices across the tiny island, just 14 miles off the coast of France. “They just increase the cost of living for everybody,” says Antonio De’Lemos, co-owner of the La Topaze D’or antiques shop in St Helier market.View image in fullscreenAntonio De’Lemos, co-owner of the La Topaze D’or antiques shop in St Helier market.Photograph: Gary GrimshawHe fears Jersey’s reputation has also taken a blow. “I don’t like to be in Jersey, knowing this is a tax paradise. And let’s be honest, it is,” he says. However, he acknowledges that it has become taboo to criticise the sector. “The establishment don’t like when you speak up.”While Jersey’s authorities are panicked about losing billionaires to Singapore and Dubai, many islanders are struggling to make ends meet. Thenumber of food bank users tripledin the three years to 2024, and demand has continued.Just streets away from St Helier’s financial district, Vini Jones, the general manager of the Grace Trust charity, is helping prepare a free weekly meal at St Paul’s Church for dozens of locals. “You can move here, you can get a job, you could send your kids to school, you can go to your office at the weekends, you go to the beach, and you can have absolutely no idea or concept of what it’s actually like for a lot of people who live in Jersey,” he says.View image in fullscreenVini Jones, the general manager of the Grace Trust charity, which works with struggling islanders.Photograph: Gary Grimshaw/The GuardianJones, who moved to Jersey from London in 2000, doesn’t blame the finance industry, which he says helps fund the charity’s work. If the finance sector took a blow “it would be a bit of an earthquake but I think that people can get pretty resourceful”, he says. “We may see a little bit less coming our way in donations if that was the case, but I think there’s still a good community spirit in Jersey that people will rise to.”That community spirit is palpable across the island, including in Gorey, a 15-minute drive up the coast from St Helier. There, 76-year-old Liz Viney is manning a ticket table at the Saturday car boot sale. She says that while some islanders would like to see the bankers go, it would be more painful than they expect.“There’s a large part of the community here who would be quite pleased to revert back to being agricultural and fisheries and everything. But I don’t think we can go back there … who would support [the economy]? Who would pay the taxes? I think we have to live the life that, well, God gives us. And at the moment we are paid by the finance community. That’s what keeps us going.”Explore more on these topicsJerseyTax havensThe super-richChannel IslandsEuropenewsShareReuse this content
