title: Healthcare in Africa ‘under growing strain’ after US withdrawal from aid programs, report warns | USAID | The Guardian
description: Accra Reset’s report states countries in the region and global south should take greater control of their health development after USAID debacle
Author: Tobi Thomas
Headline: Accra Reset’s report states countries in the region and global south should take greater control of their health development after USAID debacle
Content: Protesters gather outside USAID headquarters on 3 February 2025 in Washington DC.Photograph: Kayla Bartkowski/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters gather outside USAID headquarters on 3 February 2025 in Washington DC.Photograph: Kayla Bartkowski/Getty ImagesUSAIDHealthcare in Africa ‘under growing strain’ after US withdrawal from aid programs, report warnsAccra Reset’s report states countries in the region and global south should take greater control of their health development after USAID debacleTobi Thomashealth and inequalities correspondentMon 21 Sep 2026 18.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe United States’ withdrawal from key aid programs has put has put healthcare inAfricaand the Global South “under growing strain” a new report warns.The report says the Trump administration’s cuts to programs such as US Agency for International Development (USAID), as well as the Covid-19 pandemic and rising costs of living globally have brought “new urgency” for the need to reform healthcare in the region.The report, titled A Sovereign Future ForHealth, was created by the Accra Reset, a global health initiative led by John Dramani Mahama, Ghana’s president, that believes countries in Africa and the wider global south should have greater control over their health development rather than being dependent on aid from western countries and international institutions.A key statistic cited by Mahama and Accra Reset is that Africa produces less than 1% of its vaccines while carrying about 25% of the global disease burden.The report cites how abrupt changes to global health financing, such as the US withdrawal from several global health initiatives, forced countries within the global south to urgently restructure their finances. The report points to the Trump administration’s decision to dissolveUSAID, which pushed Nigeria to absorb the 28,000 health workers who were previously employed by the agency at a cost of $200m.External financing for health in Africa contracted by close to 70% between 2021 and 2025, the report notes, meaning that African countries historically dependent on aid were forced to adapt quickly.The withdrawal of the US Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) funding for South Africa, which provided over$400m a year annuallyand is credited with saving 26m lives globally since 2003, led to HIV clinics closing across the country. That left 1.4 million people living with HIV to face uncertainty about their treatment.Such funding cuts caused “severe and devastating” disruption globally, according to research presented at the 26th International Aids Conference in Brazil earlier this year.At the World Health Assembly in May, Mahama saidGhanalost $78m following the closure of USAID programs which affected maternal healthcare, the treatment of malaria, nutrition and HIV/Aids interventions.The initiative’s latest report, published on Monday, comes amid these major cuts to international aid and growing pressure on countries to take greater ownership of their health systems. Mahama refers to these aid cuts as a clear example that donor dependency is not sustainable.“The Accra Reset is not an argument for traditional donors to do less on global health. It is an argument for doing it differently and doing it better. As countries take greater ownership of their health futures, donor countries should step up to support that transition – following the lead of countries that set their own priorities, and work alongside them to determine where outside support is most valuable,” said Naveen Rao, senior vice-president of the health initiative at the Rockefeller Foundation. “The Accra Reset shows how we can evolve to back country-led solutions while advancing our shared health and economic interests.”Mahama notes in the report that the “past few years have shaken global health cooperation to its foundations”.“The Covid-19 pandemic exposed the risks created by concentrated production and unequal access to essential health products; rising debt and fiscal pressures have constrained national health budgets; and declining development assistance is placing programs and services under growing strain,” he continued, adding: “These shocks have brought new urgency to reform debates that have continued for years with limited progress. It was in this context that we launched the Accra Reset and its Sovereign Health Agenda – to give renewed political force to the reform agenda and place the agency of countries of the Global South at its centre.”The report comes alongside a recent survey revealing the progressive attitudes many US citizens have towards foreign aid. Some 75% of Americans – including more than one in two (52%) who primarily support Donald Trump – agree that the US should restore disease prevention aid to contain the Ebola virus, according to polling of over 2,000 US adults commissioned by the Rockefeller Foundation.The polling also revealed that 65% of US adults support international cooperation even if it means compromising some national interests; 64% also believe Americans have a shared responsibility to others, including people in other countries whom they do not know.The Guardian has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for comment.Explore more on these topicsUSAIDHealthAfricaTrump administrationUS foreign policyGhanaAids and HIVnewsShareReuse this content

title: Banished to alien lands: Trump’s secret deportation deals | US immigration | The Guardian
description: After a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is one of thousands deported from the US on the back of shadowy deals made with dozens of countries. An in-depth investigation reveals the ‘show of force’ costing American taxpayers millions
Author: Louisa Loveluck
Headline: After a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is one of thousands deported from the US on the back of shadowy deals made with dozens of countries. An in-depth investigation reveals the ‘show of force’ costing American taxpayers millions
Content: Human rights lawyers say so-called third country national arrangements are part of a ‘show of force’ to discourage asylum seekers.Composite: Guardian Design/ReutersView image in fullscreenHuman rights lawyers say so-called third country national arrangements are part of a ‘show of force’ to discourage asylum seekers.Composite: Guardian Design/ReutersUS immigrationBanished to alien lands: Trump’s secret deportation dealsAfter a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is one of thousands deported from the US on the back of shadowy deals made with dozens of countries. An in-depth investigation reveals the ‘show of force’ costing American taxpayers millionsLouisa LoveluckMon 21 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 15.12 EDTShareNika’s storyView image in fullscreenNo one would tell the shackled detainees onboard theUS immigrationplane where they were going. The officers in charge would taunt them when they asked, they said. It was only when the seat-back video screens finally showed a map that the 18 migrants worked it out.Their destination wasCentral African Republic(CAR), a country few of them had even heard of.Nika, a 32-year-old Iranian woman, recalled how the handcuffs dug into her wrists. She begged the officers to loosen them, but they did not. Other passengers had it worse, she said. Some of the men were restrained in black and yellow body wraps, as if mummified, after resisting orders to get on the plane.Nika, who had fled Iran 18 months earlier after protesting against its regime, had imagined the US as a place of sanctuary. Iran was already one of the most repressive countries in the world when she left, and its horrors had only deepened since then: security forces gunned down thousands of other demonstrators this year, then Donald Trump’s administration launched the war there.After more than a year locked up in a US immigration detention centre, Nika, whose name the Guardian has changed to protect her family in Iran, was granted legal protections and freed on a judge’s orders. Within two weeks, the Department of Homeland Security had rearrested her, and days later she was on the plane heading 7,000 miles east.“They never told me they were going to deport me [to] this country,” she told the Guardian. “I don’t know anything aboutAfrica.”The Department of State warns US citizens not to travel to CAR because it says it is too dangerous. Nika spends most of her days there under a form of self-imprisonment, too scared to venture out from her small bedroom as she waits for an answer to the question on which her life depends: will she be sent back to Iran, and to a regime that could kill her?Nika is one of more than 25,000 peopledeported by the Trump administration to countries that are not their own. About 20,000 people have been bussed to Mexico, according to a count by Refugees International and Human Rights First. And more than 5,000 others have been put on flights to countries in Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean and central Asia to which they have no connection, and then, often, returned to the countries where US immigration judges had ruled their lives or liberty were at risk.Human rights lawyers describe these so-called third-country national arrangements as part of a “show of force” by the US intended to discourage migrants and asylum seekers from entering. People from Peru and Colombia have been sent to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). On 20 August, four Cubans, a Brazilian and a Cameroonianrefused to disembark in Liberia, and were sent to Equatorial Guinea instead.What is Trump’s third-country deportation policy and who does it target?Read moreIn order to compile the most comprehensive account of a policy that has mostly operated behind closed doors, the Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Paris-based Forbidden Stories. The consortium interviewed more than 100 people affected by, or involved in, the US drive to extinguish unauthorised immigration, and reviewed documents outlining details of the agreements made by US officials with governments around the world.It has tracked more than 100 flights that have carried migrants and asylum seekers to 28 different countries. This is likely to be an undercount as the consortium’s dataset only includes flights it was able to independently verify.The pace of flights is increasing. After an initial wave during the opening months of the second Trump administration, the number of deportations spiked in August again when, according to a count by Human Rights First, a record 16 flights carried people to 13 different countries that were not their own.A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that third-country removals were unlawful, arguing that they violated due process because people are not notified with enough time to mount a legal challenge to the decision to send them to another country. Human rights lawyers suggested this should immediately ground third-country deportation flights. The government is expected to appeal against the judgment, and to press ahead with its policy.A state department spokesperson said implementing the Trump administration’s immigration policies was a “top priority” and “we are unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America’s border security”. They added: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”The Trump administration has said the people it deports are criminals. Yet documents obtained by the Washington Post as part of this project show that a majority of the 35 countries that have signed deals with the US have said they will not accept migrants with violent criminal records.Map of the countries that have agreements with the US to accept people deported from the US as of 31 August 2026The people forced on to planes include those who spent most of their lives in the US, parents detained on the school run, the adult children of elderly relatives who depend on them for care.Many are people whose fear of returning home was deemed so credible that immigration judges barred their removal from the US. Nika had been granted “withholding of removal”, a protection for individuals who may face severe harm in their country of origin but are ineligible for asylum. On 28 May, not only was she released from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s custody, but she was eligible to find a job, to work, and to stay.Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/ReutersThe rug pullView image in fullscreenTrump’s deportation drive is being led by Stephen Miller (left)Nika’s lawyer, Sahar Jalili, is Iranian and, like her client, studied in Tehran. She took the case when she was pregnant, and often worked past the point of exhaustion. “That could be me,” she said of Nika.Combing through the case file, Jalili was shocked to learn ICE had officially decided to send Nika to CAR’s capital, Bangui, just eight days before a judge ordered her release from the detention centre. Her uncle’s family had prepared a room for her in Los Angeles. It took her two days to get there, and she spent a week with them, unfurling, after 18 months of hell.Her re-arrest on 8 June, during what ICE officers had presented as a routine check-in, felt like cruelty for cruelty’s sake, Jalili said.Nika said she had finished her appointment and left when an officer called her uncle and asked him to drive her back to pick up some papers.This time there were new questions. A man took Nika’s fingerprints, then her photograph, Jalili said. “Then he came back accompanied by a female ICE officer, and they said put your hands above your head.” She said she was arrested, handcuffed and led to the basement.Nika felt numb, she said, as she was transferred out of the detention facility that evening. Anti-ICE demonstrators smacked their palms on the side of the van as she passed through protests that had become a regular feature in LA.For Jalili, the previous two days had already been a blur, as she and her colleagues battled to save two other Iranian women from being put on the same plane for Bangui. The lawyers managed to get the other two women off the plane, but not Nika. The only difference between them was that Nika was detained last, so by the time a network of immigration lawyers had learned of her case, there was not enough time before the flight departed.Jalili said she begged every ICE officer: “Give me two days. Just two days.” She recalled: “They told me that they had respected the judge’s order to release her. But they’d never promised not to send her to a third country.”Image credit: Guardian Design/AP/ReutersAfrican dealsView image in fullscreenWhen Rabbiatu Kuyateh, 58, learned that the country she had been sent to, Ghana, was deporting her to her childhood homeland, she was so scared it took a scrum of people to force her into the waiting van.A video captured the moment last November when she was dragged, shoeless and distraught, by her hair. She still remembers the crack of her head on the stone steps as she begged not to be returned to Sierra Leone, screaming: “I’m not going.”Rabbiatu Kuyateh being forcibly removed from her temporary accommodation in GhanaKuyateh was a nurse and had spent most of her life in the US with her parents, after fleeing Sierra Leone. She cared for American coronavirus patients during the pandemic and had looked after disabled adults and children in the years since.She had scrapped hard for the life she built, she said. She had raised her son, Mohamed, alone and they had bought a house together. By the time Trump was re-elected in 2024, her parents were so frail she began each day by checking on them before her shift, and then returning to make sure they were ready for bed.In order to accelerate its expulsion of people such as Kuyateh, the Trump administration has remade the very institutions that were once intended to protect migrants who fled persecution.“I would describe [this] as the Trump administration’s way of trying to undermine the concept of asylum and refugee protection,” said Alma David, one of the leading immigration lawyers tracking the policy. “While the US understands that they can’t deport them to their home country legally, what they can do is basically send them through this third country that perceives itself as a transit hub.”Chart of monthly total number of people deported from the US by airThe drive is being led by Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, who has been open about his desire toend mostmigration to the US. In interviews with the Washington Post as part of the Deportation Project, current and former US officials said Miller had rolled out the third-country removals policy by pushing key appointments inside the state department that have allowed him to overrule other foreign policy objectives in service of his agenda.Among them is Christian Ehrhardt, a career state department official who heads the newly formed Office of Remigration – its nameincorporating a term adopted by the far rightto describe the forcible expulsion of minority ethnic immigrants. Ehrhardt has helped secure at least 13 third-country deportation agreements in Africa, after diplomatic tours through the continent.Internal records reviewed by the Washington Post show the Trump administration has pledged at least $410m (£307m) to secure such agreements with 35 different countries, almost a third of them in Africa.They indicate that $30m was earmarked for Cameroon, in order to support UN operations in the country, in return for accepting 1,000 migrants. The US has so far sent only 44. The DRC was promised $75m towards UN operations there, in return for accepting 2,000 migrants. It has only received 15, and flights to Kinshasa are on hold due to the country’s Ebola outbreak.The arrangements differ from country to country. A handful, including Eswatini, have agreed to accept people with violent criminal histories. But many have said they will not take anyone with a record of violence or other types of serious crimes. The state department did not respond to questions about details of these agreements.Ghana will only take people from west Africa; CAR did not specify nationalities, and the passengers on Nika’s plane were from places including Afghanistan, Iraq and Kyrgyzstan. Most of them had no ties to Africa at all, she said.On 1 July 2025, Kuyateh’s son, Mohamed, had accompanied her to a routine ICE check-in, as her immigration status required. He remembered his mother feeling anxious that the cuffs on an officer’s belt were for her. “I doubt it,” Mohamed told her. But when they called Kuyateh into an interrogation room, he was told to wait outside.“That’s the last time I saw her,” he said.During Kuyateh’s four months in ICE custody, Mohamed spoke to her often. He had not heard from her on the day in November when he said he was called by another detainee who told him she had been sent to Texas. “And I was just like, why is she going to Texas?”Two days later Kuyateh called him in tears. She was in Ghana, about to be sent to Sierra Leone.The footage of her being dragged into a bus, beginning the onward deportation, appeared to anger the Ghanaian authorities when it spread across social media, according to Malick, the Senegalese man, also deported from the US, who filmed it. The Guardian has given him a pseudonym out of concern for his safety. “They got angry,” Malick said. “They came in the evening, at night, with two trucks full of soldiers.”He said the troops drove his group to a remote military camp with faltering electricity and little contact with the outside world. The Ghanaian government did not respond to questions from the Guardian.One woman sent to the camp said she grew so scared of what might happen if she was returned to her native Senegal that she attempted suicide by drinking bleach. She was treated in hospital, then sent back to Senegal anyway. “I drank the bleach because I wanted to die,” she said. “Because they wanted to force me to go back to my country.”Image credit: Guardian Design/Rabbiatu KuyatehMalariaView image in fullscreenOnboard Nika’s flight on 11 June this year, the inflight video showed Ghana as its initial destination, so the passengers assumed that was where they were going. But their stop in the capital, Accra, was brief. The 18 passengers then landed in Bangui at 9.45pm, flight monitors said. The officers onboard removed their cuffs, but did not get off the plane.Deportation plane arriving in Bangui on 11 JuneFor several hours, the group did not meet anyone who spoke English. “They were communicating with hand gestures, like, get on a bus, and then they put us on a bus. And then they took us to give us some vaccinations, and I didn’t know what they were going to inject me with,” Nika said. It turned out to be for yellow fever.Her room was in an apartment block. She was told she could stay for three months. But the idea of returning to Iran was unfathomable.US-based Iranian rights groups say they have been unable to determine the fates of hundreds of other Iranian nationals deported back home during the course of the US-Israeli war on Iran. A recent lawsuit filed against ICE alleges the administration has shared the records of Iranian asylum-seekers with the very regime they had fled, further elevating the risk for those sent back.When a headache started clouding her brain, Nika thought it was a migraine. She felt sick, her body hurt. She had been bitten by so many mosquitoes that her skin looked bruised, she said. A medical report, seen by the Guardian, confirmed she had malaria. Speaking by phone, Nika said: “I didn’t even know what that was.”Map of nationalities of people deported to Central African RepublicBack in Los Angeles, Jalili waited anxiously on updates about Nika’s situation. There were injections every 12 hours to clear her bloodstream of parasites. The bad news did not stop when she was well enough to return to her accommodation. Jalili was horrified to learn Nika had been deported from the US without her passport, meaning she had neither identification documents, nor a visa, and on trips to the hospital and vegetable market, police officers used her lack of papers to make threats.The CAR government did not respond to a request for comment.The second time she was stopped, Nika said, the police officer mimed the action of putting cuffs on her. The message, she said, was: “I can take you in, unless you pay us.”Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/ReutersOld tools to grease the wheelsView image in fullscreenAs the Trump administration accelerates its third-country deportations, CAR is one of 13 host countries where the deported are being supported by the International Organization forMigration(IOM), a UN agency, which provides them with food, lodgings and psychological counsel upon their arrival.Although the Trump administration has announced sweeping cuts to its funding for UN agencies, there seem to be exceptions where the funds enable this deportation programme.In March last year, the state department spelled out the logic. From now on, it said, humanitarian funding would be used to “reduce mass and illegal immigration, such as funding voluntary returns of illegal aliens, incentivising governments to implement safe third-country agreements, and building the migration management capacity of other countries”.According to a federal government database that tracks spending, more than 60% of US grants to the IOM during the second Trump administration have gone to programmes in countries that accept deported migrants. In CAR, that meant an allocation of $85m. The highest US contribution to IOM in CAR under the Biden administration, according to the database, was $14m.Chart which shows US commitments made to Central African   Republic via the International Organization for MigrationNika said she had been treated well by the agency. “The people here are doing their best,” she said. The accommodation was secure and transport was provided when needed. “But at the same time, it’s not living. I’m breathing here, I’m not dying. But I can’t leave the house without a driver they provide here. I can’t find jobs. I don’t speak their language.”The potential for a negative perception of its involvement in the programme is something the IOM has grappled with. An internal risk assessment for a programme supporting third-country nationals sent from the US to one African country, seen by the Guardian, warns it could lead the agency to be “perceived as complicit”.An IOM spokesperson said in a statement that such assessments were conducted in order to ascertain whether host nations were able to commit to safeguards for the migrants, but added: “We are fully cognisant that states use financial assistance to advance their national priorities. However, IOM’s decisions to accept funding, provide post-arrival assistance, or support assisted voluntary return are guided by our own mandate and principles, and rest on a single question: whether our engagement will improve the lives of the migrants affected. In these instances, we believe strongly it does.”Many in the human rights field are uncomfortable the UN is easing the process for governments that agree to cooperate with the Trump administration.“It just feels very incongruous for IOM to be the organisation in charge of these men and women,” said Alma David. “These aren’t migrants in your typical sense. These aren’t people who chose to migrate,” she said. “These are people who were kidnapped, essentially.”Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AlamyLife in the shadowsView image in fullscreenPeople who had been returned from third countries to the places they were born describe a life now lived in the shadows. Kuyateh left Sierra Leone within days of being sent back there. The Guardian is not naming her location. “I don’t sleep at night,” she said. “Sometimes I just wake up. I’ll be sitting down like, what am I doing here? Why am I here?”She called her family every day. Sometimes, she said, she felt too sad to turn on the video and see their faces. She could get through the conversation with her mother without tears, she said, “but whenever I talk to my daddy, I’ll be crying. And when I sit here, I think about them. It hurts so much.”She was not sure what scared her more: the thought of dying alone in a foreign country, or knowing that her parents might die without her at their bedside.Freedom oppressed: the journalists caught up in Trump’s ICE crackdownRead moreAnnan, a gay man who fled Ghana after he was outed, and then hunted, by members of his family, said he was terrified when he touched back down in Accra. He had refused to disembark during his initial deportation from the US to Sierra Leone, and had to be forcibly removed from the plane, he said. He later begged authorities not to return him, he said, but they did not listen.In a statement, the Sierra Leonean government said it took its “international obligations seriously” but that questions relating to immigration protections afforded by an American court were for the US government to address.It added: “So far, no individual returned to Sierra Leone under the TCNA [third-country national arrangement] has requested to remain in Sierra Leone or not to be returned to his or her country of choice either in west Africa or beyond.”Annan’s mother had used her savings to pay for his escape to the US. She was distraught when he called to say he was back. “She knew she couldn’t protect me,” he said.He shared footage of where he lived now: an abandoned building with no electricity or running water in a neighbouring country, he said. He spent his daylight hours hiding, and walked almost an hour to find food when darkness fell. His bed was a blanket on the floor, although he barely slept, he said, too scared of being infected by one of the insects that crawled or buzzed around him. He said the loneliness felt crippling.In recent weeks, someone had texted him anonymously, saying that his survival, as a gay man, would not be tolerated. The message made him feel hopeless: he could run, it said, but he could not hide for ever.Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Rabbiatu KuyatehExhaustionView image in fullscreenIn Los Angeles, Jalili is getting more calls about clients bound for deportation flights. In June, a 30-year-old Iranian woman with a blood disorder that made her so weak she needed a walker was told she would be sent to the landlocked south African nation of Eswatini.Another client was “going crazy”, Jalili said. “They’re coming up with a new country for her every week.”Immigration lawyers said that while their jobs had always been hard, the scale of the efforts to obstruct those opposing the Trump administration’s drive to quash all types of irregular migration was unprecedented.When a client is detained, avenues of accountability have largely been shut, including the office of an independent ombudsman for immigration detention, which was responsible for investigating abuses and misconduct.In court, immigration lawyers can face hostile judges after the Trump administration purged some of those deemed insufficiently loyal to the deportation agenda. Meanwhile, the cost of even filing a case has risen steeply, under the terms of a bill passed through Congress in July last year.Jalili, like many others, spent much of the first Trump administration mounting legal challenges against a policy ofseparating children from their parents at the US-Mexico border. Knowing that what would follow might be worse, she decided on the eve of Trump’s re-election to start her own firm to fight the coming stormIt was not uncommon for calls from the desperate families of new ICE detainees to wake her in the night.One of the biggest challenges, said Erica Reilly, an immigration attorney based in Washington DC, was basic communication with ICE officers.“You send all these emails to deportation officers, and you’re like: ‘Hi, just following up again on the email I sent you last week, and the week before that, and the week before that, and the week before that, that you haven’t responded to,’” she said. “And they know they don’t have to because there’s no accountability.”Get in touchContact our investigations teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailinvestigations.contact@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreThe worst thing, she said, was the powerlessness. But the cruelty and the lack of access, she had come to believe, “that’s all the point”.“I think that the administration is doing what they can to get enough people to say, well, the alternative is too scary or too uncertain or too bad. I’ll just leave on my own.”Getting through the day meant reformulating the wins, Reilly said. “Getting a call back from a deportation officer shouldn’t be a win, but in this environment it is.”Jalili said she did her best to focus on the battles she could win. When she heard Nika’s flight had left for Bangui, she sank to the floor, called her mother, and began to cry. “It’s not a situation where you can just say: ‘Oh, I did my best.’”Nika had lost the life she knew in Iran. The US offered little better. Jalili listed the cost.“Being detained for 17 months. Being released from the federal judge’s order for 10 days. Being stripped away from her uncle’s hands. Being put in a car and then on a flight in shackles, and for 24 hours, sitting on that flight. She must have felt so lonely.”Image credit: Guardian Design/Alamy/AP/EPAAdditional reporting by Alice Speri

title: Colombia declares public calamity as wildfire threatens popular tourist area | Colombia | The Guardian
description: Wildfire forces evacuations and burns through mountains surrounding Villa de Leyva in the north-east
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Wildfire forces evacuations and burns through mountains surrounding Villa de Leyva in the north-east
Content: A volunteer looks on as a forest fire burns on San Marcos Hill in the municipality of Villa de Leyva, Colombia, on 20 September 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA volunteer looks on as a forest fire burns on San Marcos Hill in the municipality of Villa de Leyva, Colombia, on 20 September 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesColombiaColombia declares public calamity as wildfire threatens popular tourist areaWildfire forces evacuations and burns through mountains surrounding Villa de Leyva in the north-eastAssociated Press in BogotáMon 21 Sep 2026 13.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleColombian authorities declared a public calamity as a wildfire burned through mountains surrounding one of the country’s best-known colonial towns in the north-east, scorching large swaths of vegetation and forcing evacuations.Nearly 20 active fires are burning across the South American country. Dry conditions have increased fire danger in Colombia as it braces for the effects of El Niño, which can help wildfires spread.The fire in Villa de Leyva, a popular tourist destination about 160km (100 miles) north-east of the capital, Bogotá, began Saturday on a mountain overlooking the town. By Sunday evening, authorities said about 290 hectares (717 acres) had been affected – an area roughly equivalent to 400 soccer fields – and the blaze was about 50% under control.Strong winds have complicated efforts to contain the flames, which at times advanced toward populated areas. Local authorities declared an emergency, suspended in-person classes Monday and carried out preventive evacuations, including at hotels near the fire.View image in fullscreenFlames and smoke rise from a wildfire in Villa de Leyva, Colombia, on 20 September 2026.Photograph: Sebastian Arguello/ReutersMore than 400 firefighters, emergency workers, residents and volunteers took part in the response, while four helicopters dropped water on the flames. Carlos Amaya, the governor of Boyaca, where Villa de Leyva is located, said aircraft carried out about 170 water drops Sunday, releasing 240,000 liters (63,400 gallons).Fabio Arjona, Colombia’s environment minister, said preliminary information from the disaster management agency suggested it may have been deliberately started, but authorities were still investigating.Abelardo de la Espriella, the Colombian president, said Sunday on X the Villa de Leyva fire was about 50% controlled and contained on the ground.Colombia’s national disaster management agency said in its latest nationwide update that authorities were monitoring 27 forest fires, with 19 still active and eight under control. Nine of the active fires were in Tolima, a mountainous region south-west of Bogotá, while others were burning across several parts of the country’s Andean region.The weather agency said last week that 279 municipalities were under some level of wildfire warning, including 36 under its highest, red-alert level, with much of the risk concentrated in the Andean and Caribbean regions.Between 16 June 16 and 6 August, Colombia recorded 438 forest fires in 191 municipalities, affecting about 7,153 hectares of vegetation, according to government figures.NeighboringEcuadoris also battling a wave of wildfires. Ecuador’s national risk management agency said Sunday that 12 fires remained active across the country, while more than 21,800 hectares of vegetation have burned so far this year.High temperatures and strong winds have helped flames spread rapidly in some areas. A fire on the slopes of Ecuador’s Imbabura volcano burned about 300 hectares before being brought under control Sunday after three days of firefighting.El Niño is a periodic warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean that can reduce rainfall and raise temperatures in parts of the country, creating conditions that allow wildfires to spread more easily.Disaster officials have said the period of greatest risk across the region from the developing El Niño is expected between October and April, with wildfires and water shortages among the main concerns.Explore more on these topicsColombiaWildfiresAmericasEl Niño southern oscillationEcuadornewsShareReuse this content

title: US strikes on alleged drug boats may constitute ‘crimes against humanity’, UN expert says | United Nations | The Guardian
description: Dozens of US attacks on boats in the Pacific and Caribbean have killed more than 230 people since September 2025
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Dozens of US attacks on boats in the Pacific and Caribbean have killed more than 230 people since September 2025
Content: Messiah Burnley, nephew of Chad Joseph, who family members believe was killed in a US military strike on a boat in the Caribbean, carries a girl in front of an altar for Joseph in the family home in Las Cuevas, Trinidad and Tobago, on 22 October 2025.Photograph: Andrea de Silva/ReutersView image in fullscreenMessiah Burnley, nephew of Chad Joseph, who family members believe was killed in a US military strike on a boat in the Caribbean, carries a girl in front of an altar for Joseph in the family home in Las Cuevas, Trinidad and Tobago, on 22 October 2025.Photograph: Andrea de Silva/ReutersUnited NationsUS strikes on alleged drug boats may constitute ‘crimes against humanity’, UN expert saysDozens of US attacks on boats in the Pacific and Caribbean have killed more than 230 people since September 2025Tiago Rogero, South America correspondentMon 21 Sep 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that the United States attacks on boats allegedly carrying drugs in the Pacific andCaribbean“constituted crimes against humanity”.The boat strikes, carried out since September 2025 on the stated grounds of stopping drugs being trafficked by sea to the US, have killed more than 230 people. The latest, on Saturday, killed four people in the Caribbean.The UN itself, along with several human rights organisations, lawyers and international law experts, had already described the bombings as “extrajudicial killings”, but special rapporteur Ben Saul went further.In a briefing note posted by Saul on social media on Sunday night and first reportedby the BBC, Saul wrote that, in addition to “serial extrajudicial killings”, the attacks were “in violation of the right to life, being unjustified in national or personal self-defence or under international humanitarian law, the international law of the sea, narcotics suppression conventions, or international counter-terrorism law”.He added: “There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law.”The report cites 68 US attacks that killed 223 people. It is unclear how recently the figures were updated – tallies by organisations such as the Washington Office on Latin America put thedeath tollat 234 people in 66 attacks.US Southern Command, which has coordinated the attacks, posted on Saturday, alongside a grainy video, that it had “executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean. Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists”.As has become standard in announcements of such attacks, the US did not identify the victims or provide any details about the alleged intelligence that supposedly confirmed their involvement in drug trafficking.Saul’s report rejects the claim made by Donald Trump before Congress that the strikes amounted to “self-defence” against “designated terrorist organizations”.The special rapporteur wrote that the crews were not “militarily armed and possessed the intent and capacity to launch military attacks” against the US.“Even assuming that the vessels and crew attacked were members of the criminal groups listed as terrorist, such organizations have not mounted any ‘armed attack’ on the United States so as to trigger a right of self-defence,” he added.The US Department of State has not yet responded to a request for comment.Although Trump recently claimed the bombings had stopped 97% of all illegal drugs entering the US by sea, according toavailable data, the attacks have hadno impacton the volume of cocaine entering the US.Journalists and human rights groups have managed toidentify some of the victims, who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, were at best low-ranked participants in trafficking networks.Explore more on these topicsUnited NationsTrump administrationUS politicsCaribbeanDrugsUS militaryAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man and police officer wounded in exchange of gunfire near Ontario synagogue | Canada | The Guardian
description: Officials say man was critically injured and officer was wounded in Yom Kippur incident near Belleville synagogue
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Officials say man was critically injured and officer was wounded in Yom Kippur incident near Belleville synagogue
Content: The Sons of Jacob synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, CanadaPhotograph: Google MapsView image in fullscreenThe Sons of Jacob synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, CanadaPhotograph: Google MapsCanadaMan and police officer wounded in exchange of gunfire near Ontario synagogueOfficials say man was critically injured and officer was wounded in Yom Kippur incident near Belleville synagogueAssociated PressMon 21 Sep 2026 10.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire on Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition.The Canadian province’s special investigations unit said the exchange of gunfire happened near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, about 110 miles (160km) east of Toronto. Belleville police said the officer encountered the man at about 7.10pm and that both were taken to a hospital.Police have not said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue or Jewish community was targeted. They said there was no risk to public safety and asked people to avoid the area while officers investigated.The special investigations unit, the civilian agency that investigates serious incidents involving police, said it sent investigators to the scene.Belleville police said they would not provide further information while the investigation was under way.Doug Ford, Ontario’s premier, said the shooting took place outside the synagogue as people gathered for Yom Kippur.“I’m disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur,” Ford said in a post on social media.Ford said Jewish people “have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear” and called for those responsible to be arrested and prosecuted.“My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones,” Ford said.York regional police said there was no known threat in the region but residents should expect increased patrols at places of worship.Sunday’s shooting comes months after Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, warned that the country was failing its Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism.Carney cited shootings at Jewish schools, firebombings of synagogues, and attacks on community centers and Jewish-owned businesses. His government announced millions in additional funding to help faith-based institutions pay for security infrastructure, training and personnel.Synagogues in the Toronto area have also previously been targeted by gunfire. In March, shots damaged the entrances of synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto. No one was injured. Police later arrested three suspects in connection with those shootings.Explore more on these topicsCanadaJudaismGun crimeAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Macron and Carney announce closer France-Canada ties amid Trump tensions | Canada | The Guardian
description: Two leaders meet in French territory off Canada as Ottawa seeks stronger relations with EU while fighting trade war with US
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Two leaders meet in French territory off Canada as Ottawa seeks stronger relations with EU while fighting trade war with US
Content: Canadian prime minister Mark Carney (left) and French president Emmanuel Macron in France’s territory of Saint-Pierre ​and Miquelon off Newfoundland, Canada, on Sunday. The two pledged stronger relations between their countries.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCanadian prime minister Mark Carney (left) and French president Emmanuel Macron in France’s territory of Saint-Pierre ​and Miquelon off Newfoundland, Canada, on Sunday. The two pledged stronger relations between their countries.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockCanadaMacron and Carney announce closer France-Canada ties amid Trump tensionsTwo leaders meet in French territory off Canada as Ottawa seeks stronger relations with EU while fighting trade war with USReutersSun 20 Sep 2026 21.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe leaders ofFranceand Canada have pledged closer ties to grapple with rising geopolitical tensions, climate change and the erosion of democratic values, after ⁠they met in a ⁠French territory off Canada’s Atlantic coast.The two leaders’ visit to Saint-Pierre ​and Miquelon – the first by a French president since 2014 and the first by a Canadian prime minister – came just weeks ⁠after Donald Trump posted an image showing the islands, as well as all ofCanadaand other countries in North America, covered by the US flag.Ottawa has been seeking closer ties with the ⁠EU amid an increasingly acrimonioustrade warwith the US.All smiles in Strasbourg but uncertainty clouds Canada’s EU membership planRead more“Our societies are being shaken by new storms: the upheavals, caused by climate ​change, the erosion of democratic norms, and new threats to ‌our sovereignty,” Canada’s Mark Carney said in a statement ‌alongside France’sEmmanuel Macronon Sunday. “The time has come to strengthen our ties.”Macron added that the two allies agreed to forge closer ties in sectors ranging ‌from space and climate to energy.“We both believe in democracy, the rule of law, respect for international law, respect for free and fair trade, science as the basis for our decisions, and the strategic autonomy that we defend,” the French president said.Diplomats said the visit by Macron, who was en route to the annual UN general assembly of world leaders, had a symbolic weight following Trump’s social media post.The image Trump shared showed the US flag draped over a map of the US, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, and was labelled “United States of America”. It included Saint-Pierre and Miquelon and French Caribbean territories.Responding to questions on Trump’s post, Macron dismissed any notion that the territories ​could not be French and said he did not need to reaffirm that point every day just because “people have strange ideas or say strange things”.For France, Saint-Pierre and Miquelon is strategically important due to its location on the doorstep of the US and the Arctic.The territory also occupies a key place in France’s cooperation with Canada, including over energy.Macron, whose government is facing increased pressure at home over rising fuel ⁠prices, said the talks had opened the door for bilateral discussions aimed at sealing concrete deals. ​Paris hopes Canada will broaden its exports of ​liquefied natural gas toEuroperather than primarily ​to Asia.“Canadian liquefied natural gas projects can help. They are important for Europe,” Macron said.The two leaders ​also discussed Canada’s relationship with the ‌EU after the bloc ​proposed ​that Ottawa become itsfirst associate member, something Macron said France supported.Trumpthreatened the EUwith “serious tariffs” and a halt to trade after the proposal – an idea he derided as “laughable”.Any move towards deeper integration is likely to face hurdles. More than a decade after the EU and Canada agreed to the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, and nine years after its provisional application began, several EU member states have yet to ratify the accord, including France.Explore more on these topicsCanadaFranceTrump administrationTrump tariffsMark CarneyEmmanuel MacronEuropean UnionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Japanese islands brace for Dujuan to become a typhoon again | Japan | The Guardian
description: Storm system expected to hit Izu Islands as it strengthens. Meanwhile, Atlantic hurricane season is unusually quiet
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Storm system expected to hit Izu Islands as it strengthens. Meanwhile, Atlantic hurricane season is unusually quiet
Content: Dujuan approaching Japan.Photograph: CSU/Cira and KMA/NMSC/ReutersView image in fullscreenDujuan approaching Japan.Photograph: CSU/Cira and KMA/NMSC/ReutersWeather trackerJapanAnalysisJapanese islands brace for Dujuan to become a typhoon againJodie Woodcock for MetDeskStorm system expected to hit Izu Islands as it strengthens. Meanwhile, Atlantic hurricane season is unusually quietMon 21 Sep 2026 05.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTShareTropical Storm Dujuan is skirting the coast ofJapanand despite avoiding a direct landfall, is still expected to leave its mark. Dujuan briefly reached typhoon status on Friday before weakening to a tropical storm again on Sunday morning. But it is expected to restrengthen back to a typhoon by Tuesday morning. Sustained winds could reach 80mph (129km/h), with gusts approaching 100mph.Although mainland Japan has avoided a direct hit, Dujuan’s track takes it across the Izu Islands, where evacuation warnings are in place. Heavy rain, flooding and landslide alerts are widespread, with high waves adding another threat to exposed coastal areas and islands.Some exceptional rainfall totals are expected, with about 200mm (7.9in) possible along the southern coasts of the Chubu and Kanto regions in just 24 hours – roughly equivalent to the average rainfall for the entire month of September. The Tokyo metropolitan area is among the areas facing the heaviest rain, with some models suggesting nearly 90mm could fall within six hours on Monday evening. Further south, the Izu peninsula could receive more than 80mm in just three hours – 38% of the month’s usual rainfall in a single evening. Dujuan is expected to continue north-eastwards before dissipating in the north-west Pacific later this week.The Atlantic hurricane season remains unusually quiet, despite Tropical Storm Fay developing south-west of the Azores over the weekend. Fay is not expected to strengthen further, extending the record for the latest first hurricane to form in a hurricane season during the satellite era. The previous date record was 11 September, set in 2002 with Hurricane Gustav and equalled in 2013 with Hurricane Humberto.South-westEuropemay get one last taste of summer with a blast of heat this week. Temperatures across Spain and Portugal will rise significantly above the monthly norm, to the low to mid 30s celsius. Even in north-west Spain, in Santiago de Compostela highs could reach about 35C (95F) on Tuesday, about 12C above the typical daytime high. Heading into the weekend, warmth will spread into central Europe, but most likely with less intensity than earlier in the week across the Iberian peninsula.Explore more on these topicsJapanWeather trackerExtreme weatherHurricanesAsia PacificEurope weatherSpainEuropeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: World leaders address climate crisis before UN meet amid record-breaking El Niño | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Prime ministers of Australia and Iceland discuss effects on their countries even as some shy away in face of war and inflation
Author: Sara Sneath
Headline: Prime ministers of Australia and Iceland discuss effects on their countries even as some shy away in face of war and inflation
Content: Anthony Albanese speaks at the opening of Climate Week in New York, on 21 September 2026.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese speaks at the opening of Climate Week in New York, on 21 September 2026.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesClimate crisisWorld leaders address climate crisis before UN meet amid record-breaking El NiñoPrime ministers of Australia and Iceland discuss effects on their countries even as some shy away in face of war and inflationSara Sneathin New York andOliver MilmanMon 21 Sep 2026 17.26 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 19.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWorld political leaders are descending onNew Yorkfor the UN general assembly and some of them are putting the climate crisis on the agenda as they spoke on Monday at the start of the city’s annual Climate Week.This year’s Climate Week – which runs alongside UNGA – comes after months of extreme heat in large parts of the world including Europe and the US, wildfires in Africa, flash flooding in Asia and arecord-breaking El Niño.The prime minister of Australia, Anthony Albanese, gave the opening keynote address Monday while Iceland’s prime minister, Kristrún Frostadóttir, gave the closing remarks. Both spoke about the effects of the climate crisis on their countries, the measures they are taking to transition away from fossil fuels, and their support for other countries to do the same.View image in fullscreenKristrún Frostadóttir holds a press conference after Iceland rejected EU accession talks in a close-fought referendum, in Reykjavik, Iceland, 30 August 2026.Photograph: Leonhard Föger/Reuters“Global weather has always been treacherous. But the science told us unmistakably that as the world warms these events will become more frequent and intense. And those scientific forecasts have come to be,” Albanese said,highlighting the country’s effortsto support other Pacific nations in fighting the climate crisis.Frostadóttir said the Nordic country’s move to geothermal energy was catalysed by the global oil crisis. In the early-1970s, most Icelandic homes were burning imported oil for heat.“Household budgets were hit and a small island nation, far from every market, every supplier, learned the hard way to depend on something you cannot control,” she said. “So we made a choice. Instead of riding out the volatility, we turned to what was right under our feet.”California braces for record El Niño storms as governor declares emergencyRead moreIn a matter of years, Reykjavík built a large-scale geothermal district heating system. Other towns in Iceland followed, many switching within a decade. “This took unwavering political support. Financial support mechanisms that helped ordinary households make the switch without ruinous upfront costs,” Frostadóttir said. “And, perhaps rarest of all in today’s world, across party consensus that outlasted several governments.”Now, nearly every home in Iceland is heated with renewable energy, and more than 90% of it is geothermal.Yet little was said on the opening day of Climate Week about the US government’s recentefforts to block climate action, such as the Trump administration’s move to pay nearly $4bn in taxpayer dollars to stop offshore wind projects and measures to weaken emissions standards for vehicles and coal-fired power plants. Instead of talking about political stalling and backsliding on climate action, speakers focused on the security and economic reasons that are making the need to transition impossible to ignore.Selwin Hart, assistant secretary general for climate action at the UN, said the Iran war had further proven this point. “This crisis, as horrible as it is, is really serving as a wake-up call for countries, businesses and people really to break the fossil fuel addiction and accelerate the transition as fast and as quickly as possible,” he told the Guardian.View image in fullscreenSelwin Hart speaks during the international conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia, on 28 April 2026.Photograph: Raúl Arboleda/AFP/Getty ImagesLt Gen Richard Nugee, aretired senior British army officer, said that militaries need to be able to operate in the environment in which they find themselves, and those environments are changing. “A really good example of that is the sea in the gulf is getting so hot and is predicted to get so hot that the water won’t cool the engines of our ships,” he said. Nugee said that militaries should be paying attention to climate adaption technologies, not only for their lower emissions but their potential for strategic advantages.“I don’t believe there is renewable energy that will drive a 70-ton tank. It’s not that,” he said. “But our small armed vehicles, why not make them hybrid? Which is better for our stealth, better for the crews because there’s less noise and less vibration.”The UK’s foreign minister Ed Miliband also spoke about the risks of continued reliance on fossil fuels given the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the US’s war in Iran, describing the inherent instability as the “fossil fuel roller coaster”.View image in fullscreenEd Miliband at the opening ceremony of the Climate Week.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP“Climate and nature must be embedded in national security systems, in threat assessments, and contingency planning,” Miliband said. “Countries need to pool information because a shock beginning in one country can rapidly travel through supply chains, financial markets and migration patterns to other countries.”Meanwhile, the private sector is using the transition to renewable energy to protect its bottom line. Karen Pflug, the chief sustainability officer at Ingka Group, the largest Ikea retailer, said that energy efficiency in their stores has allowed the company to save millions of dollars every year.Pflug said the company just announced a new solar park in South Carolina, which will have 178,000 solar panels. “So regardless of what’s happening from a political point of view I think it’s in fact making good business sense,” she said. “The economic imperative is there.”Leaders also stressed the need to transition sooner than later. Iceland’s Frostadóttir said: “The only real question left for leaders, for all of us in this room, is what it takes to keep moving forward faster than the disruptions that have yet to hit us. Our answer, from a small island in the North Atlantic is this: start before you must. Build the resilience before the crisis tests it.”‘Jaw-dropping’ El Niño bursts through temperature record months before peakRead moreClimate Week has been held annually in New York since 2009 and organizers said this year’s iteration will be the largest yet, with more than 100,000 attendees drawn from politics, business and activism. But they also admitted an uptick in “climate hushing” whereby business leaders and politicians have shied away from talking about the climate crisis amid a relentless focus on wars, inflation and economic strife that has swept the world.“There has been this disconnect this summer where we have felt climate change like no other year with some massive disasters and the degree to which leaders want to speak about this issue,” said Helen Clarkson, chief executive of the Climate Group, organizer of Climate Week.“Undoubtedly people care about the cost of living but we see in the polling people care about the climate too, they aren’t oblivious to what is going on. A word we heard a lot today in speeches is that we need courage to make that connection to people and join the dots.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisUnited NationsNew YorkIcelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man charged and boy, 11, in serious condition after being shot in face in Sydney  | Sydney | The Guardian
description: A man, 18, has been charged with concealing a serious indictable offence after the boy was found with injuries in Norwest
Author: Achol Arok
Headline: A man, 18, has been charged with concealing a serious indictable offence after the boy was found with injuries in Norwest
Content: Emergency services responded to reports of a shooting at a home in Norwest, in Sydney’s north-west, on Monday night.Photograph: Ronnie Amini/AAPView image in fullscreenEmergency services responded to reports of a shooting at a home in Norwest, in Sydney’s north-west, on Monday night.Photograph: Ronnie Amini/AAPSydneyMan charged and boy, 11, in serious condition after being shot in face in SydneyA man, 18, has been charged with concealing a serious indictable offence after the boy was found with injuries in NorwestFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAchol ArokandCatie McLeodMon 21 Sep 2026 16.24 EDTFirst published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 04.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn 11-year-old boy has been taken to hospital in a serious condition after being shot in a home in Sydney’s north-west.The child was receiving life-saving treatment in hospital on Monday night after suffering gunshot wounds to his face and neck, police said.Three men, all aged 18, were arrested – on Tuesday morning, police advised two were later released pending further inquiries.The third man has been charged with concealing a serious indictable offence.The boy was found injured at about 5pm at a unit on Fairway Drive, Norwest, after emergency services arrived in response to reports of a shooting at the property.Paramedics treated the boy at the scene before taking him to hospital.Initial reports indicated the shots were fired from within the home.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailSpeaking a few hours after the incident, Supt Naomi Moore said four 18-year-old men and a 44-year-old woman had been inside the unit at the time, all of whom were unharmed and were assisting with the investigation.Moore said while the investigation was just starting, police had no information to suggest the incident was related to organised crime.There have been at least six suspected mistaken-identity shootingsin Sydney since the start of last year.Last week, two teenage boys were charged with murder after the recent shooting death of a university student in Sydney, which police say was a case of mistaken identity.Moore assured people in the community who were “fearful on the streets at the moment” that police did not believe Monday’s shooting in Norwood was related to organised crime.Police were investigating how the gun came to be in the house, as there were no firearms registered to that address, she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMoore said she was not sure what type of gun had been used, or where the weapon was located.“In terms of what happened in that apartment, it is far too early for me to say right now,” she said.“[But] we have all sorts of resources down there … to ensure that we do get to the bottom of what happened in that unit tonight.”Police had established an “expansive” crime scene as investigations into the incident continued.“It’s a tragic situation with an 11-year-old child suffering this injury,” Moore said.“The mother is with the child at the moment – she is as distressed as any parent would be about what she is dealing with at the moment.”The man will appear in Blacktown court on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsSydneyNew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Datacentres in Victoria to be banned in residential areas | Datacentres - Australia | The Guardian
description: New rules also include a ban near schools and childcare centres and require them to source their own renewable energy
Author: Benita Kolovos
Headline: New rules also include a ban near schools and childcare centres and require them to source their own renewable energy
Content: NextDC's Artarmon datacentre in Sydney. The company has bought 169ha of land just outside  Geelong, which had been earmarked for future residential development.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNextDC's Artarmon datacentre in Sydney. The company has bought 169ha of land just outside  Geelong, which had been earmarked for future residential development.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesDatacentres - AustraliaDatacentres in Victoria to be banned in residential areasNew rules also include a ban near schools and childcare centres and require them to source their own renewable energyFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastBenita KolovosVictorian state correspondentMon 21 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 17.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDatacentres inVictoriawill be banned in residential areas and required to use renewable energy and contribute to the community under new state government rules.On Tuesday, the premier, Ben Carroll, will release the government’s sustainable datacentre action plan after it was approved by cabinet on Monday.The government claims the rules are the “strongest” and “clearest” governing datacentres in the country.“In Victoria, we set the rules – datacentres must power themselves, protect homes and pay their way,” Carroll said before Tuesday’s announcement.“If we get that right, we can all share in their economic benefits, especially the local community.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe new rules include a ban on datacentres near schools and childcare centres and in rural areas that cannot support them, along with a 150-metre buffer zone between new developments and homes.Datacentres will be required to source their own renewable energy and will have to pay for connection costs and network upgrades.They will also need to use recycled or non-drinking water for cooling or offset their usage.The government said new datacentres will also have to give back to community via a “local investment guarantee”, which could include jobs, Tafes and parks. They will also be required to employ Victorians during construction and train people for long-term jobs when up and running.The plan also includes mandating “fair community consultation”, as well as existing noise limits fire and safety rules.Anthony Albanese says he wants to do AI ‘the Australian way’ – videoThe federal government had previously flagged plans to require all new datacentres to be powered by renewable energy rather than coal and gas butwas forced to back downon the mandate after opposition from the Queensland and Northern Territory leaders.Last year, the then Victorian premier, Jacinta Allan, vowed to make Victoria the datacentre capital of the country.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut there has been growing community opposition in the lead-up to the November election, particularly in Labor-held seats.They include Footscray, held by Labor’s Katie Hall on 4.2% margin against the Greens, who ran a “stop AI data centres day of action” in the electorate on Saturday.NextDC has lodged an application with the state government for fast-tracked approval to expand itsFootscray datacentre, known as M3, to cover 10ha, drawing 225MW of power and running 24/7. Some residential homes are within15 metres of the datacentre’s boundary, which is zoned in an industrial area.Hall is a long-term opponent of the datacentre’s expansion.NextDC has also bought 169ha of land just outside Geelong, which had been earmarked for future residential development. The Labor MP for Lara, Ella George,expressed concern about the acquisitionto the Age in July.There are also Syncline Energy’s plans to develop a 350ha, 2.4GW datacentre in Plumpton, in Melbourne’s outer north-west, which is opposed by federal Labor MPs Alice Jordan-Baird and Sam Rae.The proposed centre islarger than any currently operating in Australiaand would consume more electricity than is generated by Victoria’s largest power station, Loy Yang A.Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - AustraliaVictoriaVictorian politicsEnergy (Australia news)Urban planningEnergy (Environment)Renewable energynewsShareReuse this content

title: Chancellor vows to stay on for Germany’s ‘democratic future’ after latest loss to far-right AfD | Germany | The Guardian
description: Merz seeks to shore up support after CDU loses two state elections and is ejected from Mecklenburg parliament
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Merz seeks to shore up support after CDU loses two state elections and is ejected from Mecklenburg parliament
Content: Merz described the results as a ‘disaster’.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersView image in fullscreenMerz described the results as a ‘disaster’.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersGermanyChancellor vows to stay on for Germany’s ‘democratic future’ after latest loss to far-right AfDMerz seeks to shore up support after CDU loses two state elections and is ejected from Mecklenburg parliamentLatest German election humiliation puts Merz on borrowed time as CDU unrest growsKate Connollyin BerlinMon 21 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTFirst published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 08.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGermany’s beleaguered leader,Friedrich Merz, has vowed to keep his fractious coalition government together for the good of the country’s “democratic future” after his conservative party suffered a drubbing at the polls in two state elections.Merz, who has vowed to plough ahead with an unpopular reform agenda, dismissed speculation over his position, saying it was vital that he and his coalition government remained in place.10:54Rise of the far right in Germany: how worried should we be? – The LatestLatest German election humiliation puts Merz on borrowed time as CDU unrest growsRead more“We are determined to live up to the historic responsibilities our country is facing,” Merz said on Monday. “It is about nothing less, and nothing more, than the democratic future of our country.”Germany faces political uncertainty in the aftermath of three hefty defeats for Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) this month, which saw it ousted from a state parliament for the first time, and the far right and far left making strong gains at its expense.Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state election 2026 resultsOn Sunday the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) emerged victorious in the coastal northern state ofMecklenburg-Western Pomerania for the third time in a German state, securing 38%. The anti-immigration, pro-Russia AfD party’s leaders predicted Merz would be out of office in months, as they set their sights on securing victory at the next federal election in 2029.“The chancellor certainly won’t make it to the end of the year,” Leif-Erik Holm, the AfD’s top candidate in Mecklenburg, said. “I think the twilight of the chancellor’s era has begun.”View image in fullscreenThe AfD’s Leif-Erik Holm, Kristin Brinker, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla after the state election results.Photograph: snapshot/Future Image/B Elmenthaler/ShutterstockMerz described the results as a “disaster”, in particular the CDU’s ejection from Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s state parliament, where it failed to reach the 5% barrier needed after losing more than half of its voters to the far-right AfD and centre-left Social Democrats. The result was all the more shocking as Mecklenburg was once a CDU stronghold.In Berlin on Sunday, the CDU fell to second place behind the far-left Linke party, which is on track to lead the next government in the city-state and could give Berlin its first Turkish-born mayor in its lead candidate, Elif Eralp.Berlin results chartIn Mecklenburg, the SPD under its existing state leader, Manuela Schwesig, is expected to lead a three-party coalition government. Her campaign had focused almost wholly on presenting herself as a buttress against the AfD, as well as distancing herself from the federal government’s reform agenda. The SPD is Merz’s coalition partner in the federal government.Although the CDU’s poor performance had been predicted, Sunday’s outcomes only added to the extreme pressure on Merz already afterthe CDU’s crushing defeat to the AfD in the state of Saxony-Anhalttwo weeks ago, which triggered the first serious speculation over his future as leader.Last week, the CDU’s powerful regional leaders governing in eight states gave their backing to Merz, but questions remain as to how sustained their support will be. At the same time there appear to be few candidates willing to step up to the post, which is increasingly being viewed as a poisoned chalice.On Monday, Merz dismissed the idea that the outcome was a personal rebuke. “The reasons for these election results go far beyond my own person,” he said. “We are witnessing a profound transformation of the political party system in Germany as well as in many other countries around the world.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKarin Prien, the CDU’s deputy leader, listening to Friedrich Merz in Berlin a week before the latest state elections.Photograph: Nadja Wohlleben/ReutersKarin Prien, the education minister and deputy CDU leader, accepted accusations that the government was failing to take voters’ fears seriously enough. But she said the government had no choice other than to continue trying to reform Germany from within, at a time of chronic economic weakness and global instability.“Without support and steadfastness we will not be able to achieve the necessary reforms, which are by no means a given. Nevertheless, not everything can remain as it is,” she told the broadcaster Deutschlandfunk.“The chancellor knows he will have to change, at least in how he addresses the people … We are a strong country, we have every chance of mastering this challenge together, but I believe that cooperating with each other will be crucial for this, and for the party it means we must broaden our appeal.”Doubts over the efficacy and fairness of the government’s agenda – which includes an overhaul of the pension system, a reduction in overbearing bureaucracy and cuts to income tax for the less well-off – played heavily into both election campaigns.On Monday, SPD leaders said they remained confident in their coalition with the CDU, but said that changes to the agenda were necessary.View image in fullscreenThe SPD’s Lars Klingbeil flanked by his party co-leader Baerbel Bas (left), and Manuela Schwesig, the state leader in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.Photograph: Christoph Rutenkolk/EPALars Klingbeil, the deputy chancellor and finance minister, said: “Saying we will ignore what the voters said to us in three state polls won’t work.”While the country needed reforms, he said, they “must be fair and they need support in the population”. The labour minister, Bärbel Bas, also of the SPD, said the plans needed a “reality check”, but said “nothing would be more lethal than letting this coalition break apart over some technicality”.Rubbing salt into Merz’s wounds, the Kremlin on Monday waded into the election analysis, calling the AfD’s win in Mecklenburg a response to Berlin’s refusal to buy cheap Russian gas, which has jolted the economy and caused prices to soar, contributing to voter dissatisfaction.The Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said: “Naturally, Germans, ​or at ​least some of them, are looking for an alternative to the current authorities in order to improve their situation. That is a natural process.”Explore more on these topicsGermanyFriedrich MerzEuropeAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)The far rightnewsShareReuse this content

Author: Frances Mao
Headline: CDU suffered heavy losses in two regional elections, including in home state of former leader Angela Merkel, where it polled just 4.9%
Content: 08.13 EDTGermany's Merz 'grateful' centre-left SPD wants to remain in coalitionGerman chancellor ⁠Friedrich Merz has said that he ⁠is grateful ⁠the ​centre-left Social Democrats wanted to remain ⁠in a coalition with his conservatives after a ⁠dramatic setback for ​his ‌CDU party ‌in state elections.“I am ‌grateful that we have heard from the Social Democrats this morning that they intend ‌to remain part of the coalition in Berlin,” ​Merz said at a press conference.“That applies to us ⁠too, and it applies ​to ​me as well. title: Putin consolidates grip on Russia as 49 Ukraine war veterans elected to parliament | Russia | The Guardian
description: United Russia party’s record victory in tightly controlled vote likely to be used as evidence of support for war against Ukraine
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: United Russia party’s record victory in tightly controlled vote likely to be used as evidence of support for war against Ukraine
