Content: United Russia, the party led by Vladimir Putin before his presidency, won 355 of 450 Duma seats.Photograph: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/APView image in fullscreenUnited Russia, the party led by Vladimir Putin before his presidency, won 355 of 450 Duma seats.Photograph: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/APRussiaPutin consolidates grip on Russia as 49 Ukraine war veterans elected to parliamentUnited Russia party’s record victory in tightly controlled vote likely to be used as evidence of support for war against UkraineLuke Hardingand agenciesMon 21 Sep 2026 09.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia’s new parliament will include 49 deputies who have taken part in the war againstUkraine, officials have said after a landslide victory by the ruling United Russia party in widely criticised elections.The pro-Kremlin party won a record 355 seats in the country’s 450-seat Duma lower house of parliament, according to preliminary figures. The result further consolidates Vladimir Putin’s grip on power and gives United Russia a super-majority bigger thanits previous 2016 recordof 343 seats.The polls arethe first to be held since Putin’s 2022 full-scale invasion. United Russia’s general secretary, Vladimir Yakushev, said 86 veterans from Moscow’s “special military operation” were likely to have been elected. “This is quite a substantial contribution,” he said. He later revised the number to 49.View image in fullscreenAs Russia counted the votes from its widely criticised election, Kremlin forces attacked targets in Ukraine, damaging the historic Zaporizhzhia National University.Photograph: Ukrinform/ShutterstockPutin’s press spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said the vote showed that Russians supported their longtime leader,who has ruled as prime minister or president since 2000. “These indicators, of course, point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state,” Peskov said.Western governments denounced the polls held in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine as a “sham”. Russia’s supreme court last month banned the only party that opposes the war, Yabloko, from participating, leaving liberal voters with no option to express discontent.Kaja Kallas, the EU’s top diplomat, called the election “another major setback for Russian democracy”. “The Kremlin silenced dissent and shut out international election monitors,” Kallas wrote on X, adding: “The veneer of democracy is all that remains.”The elections come amidspeculation that Putin may announce a large mobilisationcampaign this autumn, in an attempt to inject fresh momentum to Russia’s bogged down military campaign. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has suggested the Kremlin wants to recruit another 300,000 troops.View image in fullscreenAftermath of a Russian drone attack in Zaporizhzhia.Photograph: ReutersIn recent months, Russia has escalated its bombardment, pummelling Kyiv andother Ukrainian citieswith jet-powered attack drones. Ukraine has launched its own deep strikes,hitting Moscow’s oil refinery on Sunday, as part of what Zelenskyy has dubbed “long-range sanctions”.Russia’s has also intensified its campaign to seize a string of cities in Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, including Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. So far, it has been unable to break through, with Ukrainian commanders reporting their own counteroffensive near the city of Lyman.Inside Russia, criticism of the conflict is banned. Anti-war bloggershave been arrested and jailed. A local politician, Boris Nadezhdin, who previously tried to stand in presidential elections on a peace ticket, wasbarred from September’s electionsand accused of being a “foreign agent”.The other parties that won seats in this month’s poll all support the “special military operation”. They include the communists, who came second with 40 seats, the ultra-nationalist LDPR party, with 25, and the New People party, with 20. Chechnya’s leader, Ramzan Kadyrov, a Putin ally, was re-elected and said to have won more than 99% of the votes.View image in fullscreenA shopping centre, struck during Russia’s drone attack on in Zaporizhzhia.Photograph: Reuters/StringerRussia’s elections chief, Ella Pamfilova, said United Russia had won a resounding victory with 57.83%, with 95% of ballots counted, up from the 49.8% it won in the last parliamentary election, in 2021. She praised voters for resisting “psychological pressure”.Overnight, Russia carried out what Zelenskyy called a “brutal, targeted attack” on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia. He said a nine-storey residential building, a university building, a shopping centre, and a boiler house were all damaged, with five people injured. A woman in Kharkiv region was killed in a drone strike.Zelenskyy said: “Russia is not scaling back its escalatory actions and is signalling a readiness to expand the war. All this is happening against the backdrop of global stability already having been shattered by this war. We must continue to pressure the aggressor to bring this war to an end.”Explore more on these topicsRussiaVladimir PutinEuropeUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyynewsShareReuse this content

title: Google fined more than €400m by Irish regulator over its use of location data | Google | The Guardian
description: Watchdog says users may have been unaware their information was used to target adverts or infer their interests
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Watchdog says users may have been unaware their information was used to target adverts or infer their interests
Content: The DPC found that Google users could have been unaware of how their data was being used.Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe DPC found that Google users could have been unaware of how their data was being used.Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesGoogleGoogle fined more than €400m by Irish regulator over its use of location dataWatchdog says users may have been unaware their information was used to target adverts or infer their interestsLisa O’CarrollMon 21 Sep 2026 06.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle has been fined more than €400m (£345m) over the way it processed users’ location data, following claims that the tech giant had manipulated users into agreeing to be constantly tracked on their mobile phones.The fine, imposed by Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC), comes after complaints from multiple European consumer organisations that Google was following every step users took.Location-related adverts are familiar to holidaymakers, but seven European consumer organisations hadcomplained that undue use of location data can also lead to a breach of privacy.The DPC inquiry was prompted byresearch by the Norwegian consumer agency in 2018which suggested location data could reveal details such as religious beliefs (by tracking places of worship), political leanings (for example knowing a user has gone to demonstrations), health conditions (if a user has gone to hospital) and sexual orientation (if they have gone to certain bars).The DPC launched its inquiry six years ago and set out to find out whether Google had a valid legal basis for its use of location data.It found that Google users could have been unaware that their location was being used to influence them with adverts or to gather details about their health and interests.“Location data is a type of personal data which is processed by way of location tracking, and includes data collected or processed by Google, which by itself or in conjunction with other information an individual’s location can be inferred,” said Graham Doyle, a deputy commissioner at the DPC.“Location data can bring both benefits and harms to individuals.“It can greatly enhance the utility of online services, but it can also reveal a significant amount of information about an individual, including information that is inherently private,” Doyle added.Responding to the DPC’s ruling, a Google spokeperson said: “This case centres around historical policies that have since been updated. From 2019 onwards, we’ve significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple.”The European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) based its complaint on research by the Forbrukerrådet, the Norwegian consumer agency, whichclaimed Google used “various tricks”to ensure location history and web and app activity were enabled.“Today marks an important milestone in the effort to protect our rights online. People must be able to understand what they are agreeing to without being deceived or manipulated into making choices they otherwise would never have made,” says Finn Myrstad, director of digital policy at the Norwegian Consumer Council.BEUC said that geolocation data was “one of the most invasive forms of consumer surveillance”.Agustín Reyna, director general of BEUC, welcomed the ruling but said “the time needed to come to this conclusion is disproportionate with the seriousness of the infringement” arguing “late enforcement can be as harmful as no enforcement at all”.The DPC inquiry looked at “web and app activity”, “location history” and “location accuracy” between 25 May 2018 and 4 February 2020.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionImposing a fine of €403m, the DPC ordered Google to bring its processing into compliance with the EU’s general data protection regulation (GDPR) within six months.It is the fourth-largest fine imposed by the Irish regulator, which has EU-wide responsibility for all the US tech giants with EU headquarters in Ireland.It has previously fined Meta €1.2bn, TikTok €530m and Instagram (also Meta owned) €405m.Doyle said: “The GDPR provides a high level of protection of personal data throughout the EEA, and requires that the processing of personal data must be carried out in a lawful, fair and transparent manner.AI slowdown calls justified but collapse of bubble may be more immediate threat | Heather StewartRead more“As a result of Google’s failures in this regard, individuals could have been unaware that their location was being used to, for example, influence them with ads or to infer their interests, and could lose control over their personal data.“The retention of users’ location data for longer than necessary aggravated this loss of control,” added Doyle.There are three other ongoing statutory large-scale inquiries open that concern Google, all of which are at an advanced stage.Explore more on these topicsGoogleEuropean UnionSmartphonesAlphabetMobile phonesEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Latest German election humiliation puts Merz on borrowed time as CDU unrest grows | Germany | The Guardian
description: Chancellor acknowledges disastrous state election results but vow to push on is likely to further alienate voters, and his own party
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Chancellor acknowledges disastrous state election results but vow to push on is likely to further alienate voters, and his own party
Content: The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, arriving for a CDU board meeting in Berlin after the state elections.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe chancellor, Friedrich Merz, arriving for a CDU board meeting in Berlin after the state elections.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersGermanyAnalysisLatest German election humiliation puts Merz on borrowed time as CDU unrest growsDeborah Colein BerlinChancellor acknowledges disastrous state election results but vow to push on is likely to further alienate voters, and his own partyGerman chancellor clinging to power after another loss to far-right AfDMon 21 Sep 2026 06.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareFriedrich Merz called it a “disaster”, and that was even before the full scale of the catastrophe for himself and his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) came into view afterSunday’s state elections.In what one outlet called a“power move”, the German chancellor made a highly unusual televised speech just minutes after polls closed in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, attempting to get ahead of the narrative with apledge to stay on and fight for his economic recovery programme.10:54Rise of the far right in Germany: how worried should we be? – The LatestBut as the results trickled in, it became apparent that the CDU had not only scored its worst-ever result in a state election, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, it had crashed out of a regional parliament altogether for the first time in postwar history with just 4.9% of the vote in the region on the Baltic coast.The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) came out on top for the third time in a German state, drawing 38% against 35.5% for the centre-left Social Democrats, Merz’s federal coalition partner.Bar graph of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state election resultsAlthough the AfD has little chance of taking power because of a “firewall” of non-cooperation agreed by the other main parties, the anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendly party could celebrate a further success in destabilising the German political establishment.In Berlin, the CDU will almost certainly have to vacate city hall once the coalition negotiations wrap up after a stinging defeat to the leftwing Linke party, which is calling for the expropriation of corporate landlords to address a housing crisis.Bar graph of Berlin state election resultsPolls had been predicting the humiliating result for Merz’s conservatives, which came after ahistoric rout two weeks ago in the former communist state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the CDU scored just 17% to the AfD’s nearly 44%.But the cumulative effect of these losses, coupled with Merz’s dire approval ratings and a far right with clear momentum, can hardly be exaggerated. Despite his vow to stay the course, many regard the German leader to be on borrowed time.“Friedrich Merz is fighting for his political survival,” said the Berenberg bank’s chief economist, Holger Schmieding. “Although Merz has vowed to stay on as chancellor to spearhead the much needed pro-growth reforms, it will not be easy for him to contain the unrest within his party.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSpeculation was already rifeafter the Saxony-Anhalt race about aKanzlertausch, or chancellor swap. But as long asnone of the potential successorsappears ready to wield the dagger, and Merz remains unwilling to step aside, a volatile deadlock will reign.Merz, 70, gathered the CDU leadership at the party headquarters in Berlin to watch the exit polls together late on Sunday.Local media reported thatsome of those assembled loudly objectedto the defiant, full-steam-ahead speech he planned to deliver regarding his programme, saying that it amounted to ignoring what voters were shouting from the rooftops with their choices.Merzcancelled a planned trip to New York this weekto speak before the UN general assembly, already anticipating he would need to be in Berlin to grapple with the state elections’ aftermath.Now, more than ever, he will have his work cut out for him after just 16 months in office.Explore more on these topicsGermanyFriedrich MerzThe far rightEuropeAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)analysisShareReuse this content

title: UK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fighters | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham seeks stability in Middle East to bring down prices at home as first meeting with Trump looms
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Andy Burnham seeks stability in Middle East to bring down prices at home as first meeting with Trump looms
Content: Inside the cockpit of an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft of the type that will help to refuel Saudi jets.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenInside the cockpit of an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft of the type that will help to refuel Saudi jets.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAAndy BurnhamUK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fightersAndy Burnham seeks stability in Middle East to bring down prices at home as first meeting with Trump loomsPippa CrerarPolitical editorMon 21 Sep 2026 17.33 EDTFirst published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK has agreed to provide defensive air support toSaudi Arabiato help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump.The prime minister said he had agreed to a request for air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets to defend energy infrastructure against the Iran-backed rebels and help keep oil flowing from the Gulf to ease global economic turmoil.Burnham also revealed he will use his first meeting with Trump on Tuesday to urge the US president to de-escalate the conflict in Iran, warning that “dark clouds of global instability” are directly affecting people’s lives all over the world.The turmoil in the Middle East has pushed up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and increasing government borrowing costs to multi-year highs just weeks before a crucial first budget for the new government.On the flight to theUnited Nationsin New York, Burnham told reporters that an RAF Voyager would help refuel Saudi jets for several weeks, in his first military deployment since taking power, after the Houthis advanced to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait.The key Gulf ally has used the waterway as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz. The RAF operational support is in addition to the UK Sky Sabre air defence system already operating.“We have received a request from Saudi Arabia for military support and … I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling. On cost of living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain, the wider region … we need to keep those pathways open,” Burnham said.The prime minister also plans to press Trump to wind down US action in Iran, which has destabilised the region, blocked key supply chains and unleashed global economic volatility, including in the UK, where the government will struggle to drive down the cost of living as a result.“Of course the message is that we want to see an end to the conflict as quickly as possible and we stand ready to play our part,” Burnham said when asked if he would raise the issue in talks with Trump.As well as the focus on the Middle East, other major international challenges, including the war in Ukraine and artificial intelligence, are expected to dominate Burnham’s meetings at the UN general assembly.The global security backdrop to the summit is bleak: European leaders have warned that Russia couldlaunch a drone or missile attack on Nato territory within monthsto test the strength of the alliance.Burnham’s speech to the UN is expected to focus on harnessing the power of AI, amid concerns at home over the safety of the rapidly advancing technology. He will be accompanied on the trip by his AI minister, Kanishka Narayan.The prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump is a significant moment, with the US president still said to be angry over the UK’s refusal to support his military action in Iran, and ongoing tensions over levels of defence spending.Burnham will attempt to highlight the importance of the security partnership after the UK and US launched a heavyweight torpedo, designed to sink ships and deep-diving submarines, in British waters last week from a Plymouth-made drone named Excalibur.Government insiders, however, are taking some solace from Trump’s low-key response to UKsanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, after weeks of diplomacy with the White House over the summer.They are also hoping to avoid a clash over energy policy. The prime minister is expected to signal to Trump that he is in favour of more drilling in the North Sea, including the Jackdaw gasfield that is likely to get the green light within weeks.Analysts believe the balance of risk for the bilateral relationship has shifted since Keir Starmer was in office, given the Republicans face a difficult set of midterm elections and the US president’s personal ratings are plummeting.Trump is also likely to be more focused on his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and his address to the UN, which comes shortly before the talks on Tuesday.Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would try to pursue a “third way” in his relationship with the US president, neither as adversarial as the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, nor as publicly fawning as Starmer’s early approach, and relying on the strength of his personality.Asked whether he felt he could trust Trump, Burnham said: “Yes, of course, we trust our allies. Of course, we do.” Pressed whether this applied to the US president personally, he repeated: “Yes.”Downing Street said the prime minister wanted to use his UN meetings – which will also include the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen – to “drive opportunity and deliver hope”, making progress on areas with the potential to deliver for people at home.Burnham has focused on domestic issues since his arrival in No 10, despite Starmer warning that it would be impossible to separate them from global affairs, given how the Ukraine war is weighing heavily on UK security and the Iran conflict on the economy.On the flight Burnham acknowledged they were inseparable. “[Starmer] was right to say it’s about how we deliver back at home and the situation in the Middle East is a very clear example of that. It is a very big driver of the cost of living pressures that we’re currently facing,” he said.Before the trip, Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “The British people at home are at the forefront of the prime minister’s mission in New York this week. Because to deliver at home, we must ensure we are leading international efforts to brighten a darkening global picture …“To give people the breathing space they need, he is clear we must work with our international partners to face up to the biggest challenges of our generation. So this week at [the UN general assembly] he will be leading the charge on the global issues that impact people’s lives at home.”Burnham will tell world leaders the UK will focus on AI and climate change when it hosts the G20 in Manchester next year, potentially causing ripples with Trump, who has previously criticised the UK’s stance on global warming.The meeting gives Burnham an opportunity, however, to host international allies on his home turf, although the location of the summit was chosen under the Starmer administration.Burnham has been accompanied on the trip by his wife, Marie-France van Heel, who No 10 said would be meeting her international counterparts and supporting the prime minister, whose father, Roy, died last week.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamDonald TrumpDefence policyMilitaryUnited NationsMiddle East and north AfricaHouthisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Charges dropped against Stanford students over pro-Palestine protest | US universities | The Guardian
description: Students faced prison terms and thousands of dollars in restitution over campus protest against Israel’s war on Gaza
Author: Alice Speri
Headline: Students faced prison terms and thousands of dollars in restitution over campus protest against Israel’s war on Gaza
Content: The pro-Palestinian encampment at Stanford in April 2024.Photograph: Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe pro-Palestinian encampment at Stanford in April 2024.Photograph: Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty ImagesUS universitiesCharges dropped against Stanford students over pro-Palestine protestStudents faced prison terms and thousands of dollars in restitution over campus protest against Israel’s war on GazaAlice SperiMon 21 Sep 2026 13.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 15.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive Stanford University studentswho facedprison sentences and thousands of dollars in restitution in connection to a campus protest againstIsrael’s war on Gazahad all charges dropped on Monday.The students also had their restitution severely reduced, ending a two-year legal saga that also saw the lead prosecutor in the case removed by the court.Part of a group of 12, the students had been charged with felony conspiracy to trespass and felony vandalism in connection to an hour-long, June 2024 occupation during which the group barricaded themselves inside the university president’s office to demand Stanford consider a student resolution to divest fromIsrael, among other requests.Some accepted plea deals or other diversion offers but five of the studentswent to trialearlier this year. The month-long trial ended with a hung jury but Jeff Rosen, the Santa Clara county district attorney, immediately announced his intention to retry the case before a judge ordered his recusal in May over a conflict of interest that, the judge said during court proceedings, would “render it unlikely that the defendants will receive fair treatment”.The case has since been taken over by theCaliforniaattorney general’s office, which reached a resolution with the students. That resolution meant dropping all charges in exchange for 100 hours of community service at a nonprofit of their choosing and a total restitution of about $50,000, far less than the $1m prosecutors initially threatened them with and the $ 329,000 they each risked being found liable for at trial. The charges were the most severe handed out against students in connection to pro-Palestine protests on campus.A spokesperson for Rosen referred questions about the case to theCaliforniaattorney general’s office. A spokesperson for the attorney general said that the office handled the case “with the same level of attention to detail, impartiality, and thoroughness that we bring to every criminal case entrusted to us”.“We believe this outcome serves the best interests of the community and all parties involved,” the spokesperson added.Stanford University did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.Three of the students who had previously accepted misdemeanor pleas will also have their convictions withdrawn as part of Monday’s agreement once they complete the required community service.Two of the defendants who went to trial earlier this year, German Gonzalez and Amy Zhai, spoke of their relief in exclusive interviews with the Guardian. The ordeal severely upended their lives and they shared their deep frustration at what they saw as Stanford and Rosen’s effort to criminalize and silence speech in support of Palestinians. They said that they hoped their win would encourage other students to continue to speak out.“The most significant part of this is that I can continue to be involved in thePalestinemovement in ways that were kind of curtailed by also being actively a defendant in a criminal case,” said Zhai, who graduated from Stanford as the trial got under way and is now in law school at a different university. “[The prosecution] was intended to silence speech about Palestine, and for everything that they threw at this case, they have failed.”Zhai added: “People still very much care about Palestine but I think they are afraid, and reasonably so, because of everything that’s happened with the escalation of repression over the past two years. It takes victories like this one to encourage people to turn their beliefs into action.”Thousands of students were arrested over their involvement in pro-Palestiniancampus protestsin the spring of 2024. Dozens were suspended or expelled from their universities, but most of those who also faced criminal charges have seen thosecharges dropped.Abbee Cox, a member of the Stanford students’ legal team, told the Guardian that Monday’s resolution was in line with those reached in other cases relating to campus protests, which have mostly ended in diversion deals rather than severe sentences.“The attorney general’s office has addressed this in a manner consistent with the way other peaceful student protesters at Stanford have been treated over the years – protesters against apartheid, against the Vietnam War,” she said. “But it took almost two and a half years of this painful and protracted and incredibly stressful battle to get there. And it took a fair prosecutor to get us there in the end.”As protests flared up on campuses across the country in the first year of the Gaza war, the Stanford students briefly occupied the president’s office, renaming the building after Adnan al-Bursh, a Palestinian surgeon who was reportedlytortured to deathwhile in Israeli detention.They were immediatelyarrested, suspended, and banned from campus for two terms, but it was not until a year later, in April 2025, that Rosen announced criminal charges against the group, declaring at a press conference that “dissent is American, vandalism is criminal”.Rosen was ultimately removed from the case in May, after the students’ legal team submitted evidence to the court that he had used the pending case to fundraise for his re-election, citing it in a webpage dedicated to showcasing his work to fight against “antisemitism”. The page was also emailed to a listserv of more than 600 people, soliciting donations. Rosen responded to the recusal effort by accusing the student’s defense attorney of engaging in a “f—— antisemitic trope”in an interviewwith a local publication.In pre-trial motions, Rosen had sought to ban the students from discussing “genocide”, as well as the political motivations behind the protest and free speech issues – a request the court denied. But he had successfully blocked the defendants’ efforts to have an international human rights expert testify, and from invoking the first amendment as a defense, on the grounds that the alleged conduct does not constitute protected speech.Gonzalez, a sophomore student at the time of the protest, is set to graduate this year but said he feels under scrutiny by university administrators.“It’s difficult to go to classes and try to walk from your library to your classroom and get followed by campus security,” he said. “It feels demeaning, being surveilled to that degree … All I have done is stand up for what I believe in.”Explore more on these topicsUS universitiesUS campus protestsPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaIsraelUS foreign policyProtest (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Houthis move to seize strategic terrain after Trump calls off airstrikes at last minute | Houthis | The Guardian
description: US president reportedly changed his mind over Saudi Arabia’s pleas for assistance as bombs were being loaded
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: US president reportedly changed his mind over Saudi Arabia’s pleas for assistance as bombs were being loaded
Content: Houthi troops stand guard during a protest against Saudi Arabia in Sana'a, Yemen last week.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAView image in fullscreenHouthi troops stand guard during a protest against Saudi Arabia in Sana'a, Yemen last week.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAHouthisHouthis move to seize strategic terrain after Trump calls off airstrikes at last minuteUS president reportedly changed his mind over Saudi Arabia’s pleas for assistance as bombs were being loadedPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentMon 21 Sep 2026 12.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHouthi fighters are moving to seize strategic heights in Yemen that would cut the Red Sea coast off from areas held ​by Saudi-backed forces afterDonald Trumpcalled off US strikes on the group at the last minute, reportedly as bombs were being loaded on to aircraft.Amidincreasingly heavy fighting in Yemen, which has displaced tens of thousands of people in recent weeks, the New York Times reported on Monday that the US president had flip-flopped wildly in recent days after a call from Saudi Arabia for US strikes on the Houthis.It comes amid the Houthis’ rapid advance on the ground with the group gaining control over much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and advancing to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait, whichSaudi Arabiahas used as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz.In the call reported by the New York Times, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, implored Trump to step in to help halt the Houthi advance after weeks of such appeals. Trump, who had been resisting joining the Saudi war in Yemen, after the call then told the Pentagon to prepare for airstrikes against theHouthisbefore reversing course once again, the report said.View image in fullscreenA camp for people displaced by the fighting in Yemen, near the city of Aden.Photograph: ReutersTrump has frequently given mixed signals to Riyadh, telling reporters during a visit to Ireland earlier this month that the Houthis “called us, and they don’t want to fight us”, adding that the group was “allowing ships to pass” the Bab al-Mandab strait and that the situation would “work out very well”.He added that the Houthi problem was limited to “one country” an apparent reference to Saudi Arabia promising to “take care of fixing that”.The UN says hostilities inYemenhave displaced at least 125,000 people since the start of September. Taiz city has received the largest number of displaced persons, taking in up to 86,000 Yemenis since the recent escalation began.The rapid advance by the Iran-aligned group this ‌month has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theatre and further threatened global energy supplies.Washington has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Prince Mohammed to join the fight in Yemen with the Houthis claiming on Saturday they had fired on Riyadh, where columns of smoke were visible near the main airport.Flames and large plume of black smoke seen rising near Riyadh airportThe Yemeni president, ⁠Rashad al-Alimi, ⁠spoke to Trump on Sunday, requesting ‌support for his ‌UN-recognised government in its fight against the Houthis. Trump ⁠made no direct pledge ​of military ​support during ​the call, sources said.Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on Houthi positions in the strategic Kahboub mountains, according to the group, but making little impact on the ​advance of its fighters.Fighting has centred on the outskirts of the remote Al-Wazi’iyah district in Taiz province and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast, which separate the Red Sea coast from the city of Aden, where the government is based. The Houthis aim to secure the rear of their forces around the Bab al-Mandab strait by taking control of the mountains, which would also allow them to open new ‌fronts, according to ⁠sources who spoke to Reuters.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMark Carney is making an eloquent case for an alliance sidelining the US | Ted WidmerRead moreThe surge in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has created a new dilemma for Trump, under pressure to help defend Washington’s close Saudi allies but anxious not to further expand thedeeply unpopularwar he launched in February against Iran.The US bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire with the group and has kept out of the conflict since.Amid thebroad failure of the US-Israeli war against Iran, and with the US midterm elections looming, the Trump administration’s priorities appear to be to secure at least some oil supplies through the strait of Hormuz, while avoiding a wider entanglement in Yemen.That, however, invites longer-term risks, not least the growing alienation of key US allies in the Gulf, including Saudi Arabia, where Washington is increasingly seen as an unreliable ally, that could also undermine the so-called “security for oil” understanding where the US provides a defence umbrella for Gulf states in exchange for energy supplies.Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsHouthisDonald TrumpYemenUS-Israel war on IranUS foreign policyTrump administrationSaudi ArabianewsShareReuse this content

title: Pakistan jails sisters of Imran Khan before protest seeking his release | Pakistan | The Guardian
description: Police crack down on family and political supporters of former PM who say authorities are ‘slowly killing’ him in prison
Author: Shah Meer Baloch
Headline: Police crack down on family and political supporters of former PM who say authorities are ‘slowly killing’ him in prison
Content: Khan’s sisters Aleema Khanum, Uzma Khanum and Noreen Niazi among supporters of the former Pakistan PM in Rawalpindi last December.Photograph: Salahuddin/ReutersView image in fullscreenKhan’s sisters Aleema Khanum, Uzma Khanum and Noreen Niazi among supporters of the former Pakistan PM in Rawalpindi last December.Photograph: Salahuddin/ReutersPakistanPakistan jails sisters of Imran Khan before protest seeking his releasePolice crack down on family and political supporters of former PM who say authorities are ‘slowly killing’ him in prisonShah Meer Balochin Islamabad andHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiMon 21 Sep 2026 10.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree sisters of Pakistan’s incarcerated former prime ministerImran Khanhave been arrested amid a heavy-handed government crackdown on plans for a nationwide protest to demand Khan’s release.The lawyer for the three sisters, Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, said on Monday that they had all been detained and jailed for 30 days under a warrant that accused them of being a threat to public order.Leaders from Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) condemned the “illegal harassment” of his sisters. Since Khanwas arrestedand held in prison on corruption charges in 2023, his sisters have been vocal advocates for his release.His family and party allege that Khan is being kept in solitary confinement and has been denied visits and calls from his family for six months, as well as being allegedly prevented from accessing vital medical treatment foran eye condition.The arrest of Khan’s sisters marked a dramatic escalation of a crackdown on PTI members and supporters in the run up to a nationwide demonstration due to be held on Sunday – described as a “long march” – to demand the release of Khan and to protest an alleged erosion of democracy and the constitution under the ruling coalition government.None of Khan’s sisters hold a political position in PTI. Since protesting against their brother’s detention – including by camping outside the prison where he is held, demanding to see him – they have been named in various court cases. This is the first time they have all been held in prison.Imran Khan’s sons accuse Pakistani army chief of vendetta against imprisoned fatherRead moreAleema was arrested in Lahore on Sunday as she was travelling to a private club; her driver was also picked up by police. Uzma and Noreen were then arrested at around 3am on Monday morning, after they held a press conference to condemn Aleema’s detention at her house in Lahore.According to their lawyer, Rana Mudassir Umar, hundreds of police officers later surrounded the family home as more than 100 entered to arrest Uzma and Noreen, as well as their children, grandchildren – who are four and six years old – and the household staff. The house was raided and all their phones were taken.By 7am on Monday morning, the children and grandchildren had been released but the three sisters were held and charged under the country’s Maintenance of Public Order law, according to Umar.He said: “They have not been allowed any family access, no legal counsellor access and they were not even allowed to bring clothes or basic things.“We have challenged their arrests in the high court in Lahore and [are] hoping we will get a hearing soon.”While Pakistan is ostensibly ruled by a civilian coalition government, the army is widely regarded as the country’s most powerful establishment, led by Pakistan’s army chief,Field Marshall Asim Munir, who fell out with Khan while Khan was prime minister. The current government was brought to power in an election in 2024 which waswidely documented as rigged, allegedly by military intervention, to prevent Khan’s party returning to power.Speakingto the Guardianlast week, Khan’s two sons, who are based in London and fighting for his release, accused Munir of a “personal vendetta” against their father and alleged the Pakistani authorities were “slowly killing” Khan in prison.Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi said on Monday that the government would “find a permanent solution” to prevent to march going ahead and shutting down swathes of the country “once and for all”.Despite Khan’s lengthy incarceration, he is still regarded as Pakistan’smost popular politicianand there are fears among officials that large numbers could turn out to support PTI’s march on Sunday. It is being held as discontentment is rife on the streets amid an economic crisis and crippling petrol shortages due to the turmoil in the Middle East and the Gulf. Disgust at the alleged mistreatment of Khan is also widespread.Prisoner number 804: the plot to erase Imran KhanRead moreKhan’s party has faced constant harassmentover the past three years, with most senior PTI figures either in jail or pressed to leave politics.Sheikh Waqas Akram, a senior PTI leader, said the government feared that hundreds of thousands of people may turn out to the long march and “topple the government”, as protest movements have done recently in neighbouring countries such as Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka.Over the weekend, the capital ofPakistan, Islamabad, was transformed into a fortress of heavy security, with barriers and heavy armed security lining the roads and shipping containers placed to block the entrances into the city.“Punjab police are raiding houses, harassing families, bulldozing houses and arresting workers and families,” Akram said. “They are going to insane levels to crush the long march and stop it with violence and arrests. This illegitimate government know they can’t survive if people are allowed to protest and march on Islamabad in huge numbers.”Explore more on these topicsPakistanImran KhanSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Young people’s Pip claims for ADHD and autism ‘rising fastest in affluent areas’ | Society | The Guardian
description: Experts say trend across England probably reflects swifter access to diagnoses as wealthier families go private
Author: Will Parman
Headline: Experts say trend across England probably reflects swifter access to diagnoses as wealthier families go private
Content: Obtaining a clinical diagnosis is likely to increase the chances of a successful Pip claim.Photograph: Johner RF/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenObtaining a clinical diagnosis is likely to increase the chances of a successful Pip claim.Photograph: Johner RF/Getty ImagesSocietyYoung people’s Pip claims for ADHD and autism ‘rising fastest in affluent areas’Experts say trend across England probably reflects swifter access to diagnoses as wealthier families go privatePatrick ButlerandWill ParmanMon 21 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome of the most affluent areas ofEnglandhave had the sharpest rises in the proportion of young people claiming disability benefits for ADHD and autism since the pandemic, according to new research.Claims for the personal independence payment (Pip) benefit for these health conditions were typically proportionally far higher in deprived areas with higher rates of poverty, low educational outcomes and insecure employment.However, the fastest growth in ADHD and autism-related Pip claims has been in some of the country’s most prosperous areas such as Wokingham, Warwick, and parts of Hampshire and Surrey.This trend probably reflects swifter access to ADHD and autism diagnoses in more affluent areas, say the researchers, in part highlighting the ability of wealthier families to skip longNHSwaiting lists and pay privately for clinical diagnoses.They say the relative gap in Pip claims between rich and poor areas is shrinking, with growth rates in wealthy places such as Runnymede in Surrey outstripping the likes of Blackpool and Stoke-on-Trent.The research also found that Pip claim rates for ADHD and autism were higher among white people than other ethnic groups. This was reflected in lower than expected claims in ethnically diverse areas such as Newham and Brent, in London, and Leicester.One of the sharpest rises was seen in leafy Surrey Heath (a 630% increase in Pip clams for autism and ADHD since 2019), while in contrast, the relatively deprived towns of Mansfield and Great Yarmouth saw 30% and 50% increases respectively.The researchers say this shift is counterintuitive and unique to ADHD and autism. There is no evidence of similar trends in learning disability, depression, anxiety or physical conditions. Records from GPs show higher rates of new ADHD diagnosis in relatively affluent areas.Sally Gainsbury, a senior policy analyst at the Nuffield Trust, which carried out the research, said the findings probably reflected “substantial inequality in access” to private and NHS diagnostic services, meaning “people with better resources and more support are often able to get to the front of the queue quicker”.It may also reflect the ability of more privileged individuals to navigate a notoriously difficult and unpredictable Pip claims process, Gainsbury said. Obtaining a clinical diagnosis is likely to increase the chances of a successful Pip claim.Pip is designed to help claimants with the extra costs of disability, such as energy, transport and food. It is not means-tested or linked to employment status and is paid to individuals whose condition impairs their ability to carry out everyday tasks.About 205,000 16- to 24-year-olds received Pip for disabilities linked to ADHD or autism in April this year, a more than threefold increase since 2019, at a cost in 2025-26 of £1.36bn. The average Pip claim for this cohort was £8,800 a year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPlan to limit NHS diagnoses of ADHD attacked as ‘rationing’ healthcareRead moreThe sharp rise in numbers of young people claiming Pip and other disability benefits, particularly since the pandemic, has been at the centre of a political debate about the sustainability of working-age disability benefits spending, which is forecast to rise from £14bn in 2019 to £34bn in 2030.The issue has become aculture war topic. Rightwing media and politicians have questioned the validity of Pip claims they say are the result of exaggerated mental health symptoms, and alleged overdiagnosis of neurodivergent conditions.The Nuffield Trust research comes in advance of a government-commissioned report on mental health, autism and ADHD diagnoses. It isexpected to recommenda “needs-based” system whereby overstretched NHS services target patients most acutely affected by ADHD, such as those who are at risk of self-harm or unable to work.Led by Prof Peter Fonagy, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst at University College London, the interim review published earlier this year concluded that the system forces children and adults to obtain a formal diagnosis in order to get support.Explore more on these topicsSocietyNeurodiversityAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderNHSAutismWelfareHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cut NHS red tape and boost productivity to prevent 20,000 early deaths a year in England, report urges | Health policy | The Guardian
description: Boosting productivity could result in four extra years of good health for people on average, report says
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Boosting productivity could result in four extra years of good health for people on average, report says
Content: There is ‘substantial scope to improve outcomes within the funding already available to the NHS’, the report found.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenThere is ‘substantial scope to improve outcomes within the funding already available to the NHS’, the report found.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAHealth policyCut NHS red tape and boost productivity to prevent 20,000 early deaths a year in England, report urgesChanges could save £33bn and result in average of four extra years of good health for people, report saysAndrew GregoryHealth editorMon 21 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe NHS inEnglandcould prevent 20,000 deaths and save £33bn a year by cutting red tape and boosting productivity, a report says.Research by theHealthFoundation found the health service has been held back for decades by excessive regulation, short-term planning and insufficient capability to deliver major change.But rewiring theNHS, the world’s largest single healthcare system, by harnessing new technology, empowering staff and increasing capital investment could save both lives and money, it found.There is “substantial scope to improve outcomes within the funding already available to the NHS”, which could result in up to four extra years of good health for people on average, the report said.In terms of where deaths could be prevented, focusing on diagnosing cancer earlier and finding people with high blood pressure or conditions such as diabetes quicker would be key, it added.The report called for a series of changes, such as releasing the NHS from unnecessary regulation, reporting and compliance tasks, as well as launching a “test-and-learn” approach to scaling up things that could improve productivity, such as use of artificial intelligence.“Our analysis suggests that if the NHS in England achieved outcomes closer to the best-performing comparable health systems, without spending more each year, it could potentially result in 18,500–20,600 fewer deaths each year from treatable causes and 2.5 to 4.5 additional years that people spend in good health on average,” the report said.Increasing NHS productivity is “sometimes … seen as exhorting hard-working staff to work even harder, in a system already under considerable strain” but this view must be challenged, it added. “At its heart, productivity means achieving better health outcomes from the resources available.”The biggest issues affecting productivity included the “constant churn”, too many targets, and not enough focus on health outcomes.Researchers also heard from staff how poor IT wasted clinical time, how limited estate and equipment constrained healthcare and how gaps in administrative support shifted additional work to clinicians.While AI offered opportunities, the “NHS has repeatedly struggled to take advantage of the potential”, the report said.Anita Charlesworth, report author and senior economic adviser at the Health Foundation, said: “This is mission critical for the NHS, which cannot simply keep doing more of the same.“The problem is not a lack of committed and talented people or an absence of ideas; it is that the NHS is not set up to deliver sustained productivity growth.“Our research points to a fundamental redesign of the operating conditions – not another disruptive reorganisation, but a reset to make improving productivity a defining focus for the NHS over the next decade and beyond.”Sir Ciarán Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents and supports the health and care system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said he agreed more could be done to deliver further productivity gains but there were “big barriers” that would need to be addressed.“Lack of capital investment has been a long-running drag on NHS productivity. More must be done to turn the tide on years of neglect … We also agree that a more streamlined, supportive regulatory system which encourages local autonomy and innovation will be vital for future progress.”Explore more on these topicsHealth policyNHSHealthPublic services policyHospitalsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Halt super-intelligent AI with non-proliferation treaty, Ed Davey to say | Liberal Democrat conference | The Guardian
description: At Lib Dems’ conference in Brighton, leader will accuse Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and ‘tech bros’ to solve problem
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: At Lib Dems’ conference in Brighton, leader will accuse Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and ‘tech bros’ to solve problem
Content: Ed Davey on the beach at Brighton during the Lib Dems’ party conference, where he is expected to lay out plans for a new international AI safety agency.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEd Davey on the beach at Brighton during the Lib Dems’ party conference, where he is expected to lay out plans for a new international AI safety agency.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockLiberal Democrat conferenceHalt super-intelligent AI with non-proliferation treaty, Ed Davey to sayAt Lib Dems’ conference in Brighton, leader will accuse Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and ‘tech bros’ to solve problemAlexandra ToppingandPeter WalkerMon 21 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEd Davey is to call for a global nuclear-style non-proliferation treaty to halt the development of super-intelligent AI when he makes his keynote speech at theLiberal Democrat conference, accusing Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and “tech bros” to solve the problem.When he addresses the faithful on the final day of the gathering in Brighton, the party leader will call for a global pause on super-intelligent AI, comparing it to a nuclear arms race that could result in technology that could “destroy us all”.Davey is expected to lay out plans in his speech on Tuesday for a new international AI safety agency – modelled on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and headquartered in the UK, after numerous warnings from AI researchersthat artificial intelligence could wipe out humanitywithin the decade. “We didn’t leave the atom bomb to a few billionaires to police themselves,” he will say.Davey is expected to call for a new global movement to work together to protect humanity from the risks of super-intelligent AI, saying that the IAEA was built by nations “working together to control a technology that could destroy us all”, but warning that the future of AI is being decided by “a tiny number of the richest and most powerful in California and in Beijing” with no guardrails to slow down development.“As liberals – we know that something as existential as nuclear weapons or climate change cannot be left in the hands of a powerful few. And so it must be with AI. We can’t leave it to Mark Zuckerberg, to Sam Altman, or to Elon Musk to save us,” Davey will say.On Monday, the prime minister announced a new AI partnership with the US ahead of Trump’s address to the UN general assembly on Tuesday.But Davey will say the plan “doesn’t come close to meeting the scale of this threat” and “only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros”.It comes after the Lib Dems’ home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, on Monday announced thatthe party proposed a big tech levyand promised to create a new online crime agency focused on offences including child sexual abuse material, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and deepfake AI-generated pornographic images.Wilkinson said the Lib Dems would properly regulate use ofMeta’s smart glasses, which he called “perv goggles”, telling the conference that the glasses “are more than a benign piece of tech that provides a bit of fun” and that people – especially women – were being recorded without consent or warning. “This is becoming the new norm, because this government won’t stand up to big tech to protect our civil liberties,” he said.On Sunday Davey set out a proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period, as well as reducing the bus fare cap from £3 to £1 and other transport-related cost of living policies.View image in fullscreenEd Davey views the stands as he tours the exhibition hall during the conference in Brighton.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PADavey defended himself in a series of interviews on Monday about complaints his party lacks vision, saying it was pointless to try to compete with the attention-grabbing ideas of the likes of Reform UK and the Greens.“It’s a very noisy environment at the moment,” he told the BBC. “But let me tell you, some of the noise generated by the populists are things that divide our country, that are nasty, or that are just completely crazy. I don’t want to do that. I want to tell people that we have really well thought through policies that will cut their taxes.”Asked if he would propose further tax cuts in the wake of the pledge to slash 10p from fuel duty for three months, Davey replied: “Absolutely.” These would, he said, be financed by higher economic growth due to the Lib Dem proposal to seek entry to the EU’s single market.The Lib Dem leader did praise Burnham for wanting to reform adult social care, but told Sky News the “jury is out” on whether Burnham will deliver as prime minister. But Davey was positive about some of what Burnham has done.“I think it’s good when other parties start talking about Liberal Democrat priorities,” he said. “We have led the debate on social care and carers because it’s so important for our health service. We’ve led the debate on political change because we need to change our political system, and Mr Burnham seems to be up for that.”Explore more on these topicsLiberal Democrat conferenceLiberal DemocratsAI (artificial intelligence)Ed DaveyComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Celia Birtwell ‘humanises’ Burberry in London fashion week closing show | London fashion week | The Guardian
description: Textile designer brings florals, vines and smiley doodles to brand’s luxury checks for one-off paired collection
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Textile designer brings florals, vines and smiley doodles to brand’s luxury checks for one-off paired collection
Content: Models showing leafy prints in the Burberry meets Birtwell spring-summer 2027 collection.Photograph: Katie Collins/ReutersView image in fullscreenModels showing leafy prints in the Burberry meets Birtwell spring-summer 2027 collection.Photograph: Katie Collins/ReutersLondon fashion weekCelia Birtwell ‘humanises’ Burberry in London fashion week closing showTextile designer brings florals, vines and smiley doodles to brand’s luxury checks for one-off paired collectionJess Cartner-MorleyMon 21 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 18.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBurberry and Celia Birtwell are both national treasures of sorts. One is Britain’s grandest luxury name, the other the textile designer who dressed bohemian 1960s London in her prints and has a place in art history as David Hockney’s favourite muse.Burberry’s designer, Daniel Lee, has always loved Birtwell’s prints. When the two met this spring, he fell for “her energy, and her zest for life”, and a one-off Burberry meets Birtwell collection that closedLondon fashion weekwas born.Burberry’s calling card is a graphic check; Birtwell is all blowsy doodled florals and psychedelic snaking vines. “The check is so dominant and so brilliant that at first I thought: what can I do here?” Birtwell said before the show. She hand-painted a less regimented version, which Lee loved. “She made the check more human. If you are buying a luxury product it’s not a necessity, it’s an emotional purchase, so it needs to feel human.” A doodle of round, Smartie-bright faces from her archive, drawn 20 years ago but never produced, became another print of the season.View image in fullscreenCelia Birtwell’s doodled smiley faces on Burberry’s spring-summer 2027 collection.Photograph: Katie Collins/ReutersThe mood of the show, held around the corner from Burberry HQ at Chelsea School of Art, was buoyant: charming prints, soft silhouettes, and the eclectic guest list that is as much a Burberry signature as the check itself: actor Fiona Shaw and footballer Djed Spence on the front row, with rapper Central Cee making a cameo on the catwalk.Burberry isbouncing backfromits crisis years, steered by its chief executive,Joshua Schulman, and designer Lee. This summer, the brand reported its first revenue growth in three years, as retail sales rose 5% year-on-year in the second quarter. Schulman’s strategy is offering “value for money in a luxury context”, which translates as pivoting from an ill-fated attempt to sell Burberry handbags at Hermès prices to more realistic price tags. Lee has brought a youthful, gen Z inflection to the Britishness that is Burberry’s calling card.View image in fullscreenCoats and more at the Burberry show.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAA successful element of its turnaround has been Burberry zeroing in on the outerwear market, where Burberry has bona fides to best every other name. British heritage is a trump card when it comes to coats, and the appeal of the Burberry name reaches from arctic explorers to football fans. For this summer collection, trenches came in slinky silk taffeta, with puffball hems and ruched collars; one model carried an embroidered umbrella, against summer showers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo amplify itsLondonfashion week message, Burberry is staging a small display in an upstairs gallery of the V&A museum in South Kensington, which will be open to the public until 3 January. The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon includes a military overcoat worn by a lieutenant colonel in the British army in 1939, designer Hardy Amies’ own Burberry trench, as well as metallic leather and gold snakeskin runway trenches from recent catwalk shows.Explore more on these topicsLondon fashion weekBurberryFashion weeksFashion industryWomen's coats and jacketsLondonLuxury goods sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Airlines urge action after UK flights delayed and cancelled again | Transport | The Guardian
description: Nats says fault at Prestwick has been ‘fixed’ after airports in Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland are hit
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Nats says fault at Prestwick has been ‘fixed’ after airports in Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland are hit
Content: An affected passenger at George Best Belfast City airport.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAView image in fullscreenAn affected passenger at George Best Belfast City airport.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PATransportAirlines urge action after UK flights delayed and cancelled againNats says fault at Prestwick has been ‘fixed’ after airports in Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland are hitGwyn TophamTransport correspondentMon 21 Sep 2026 16.45 EDTFirst published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 05.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAirlines have called for “action and accountability” over the UK’s air traffic control services after a technical issue led to flights being disrupted for the second time in a fortnight.Dozens were cancelled and others severely delayed after a fault on Monday morning at National Air Traffic Services (Nats), this time at its second control centre at Prestwick in South Ayrshire.The fault, predominantly affecting Scotland,Northern Irelandand northern England, was fixed by about 10.30am, but only after airlines including British Airways and easyJet were forced to make cancellations.Flight chaos for hundreds of thousands was caused in ‘millisecond’ by software errorRead moreA Nats spokesperson said it had been “working with airports and airlines to safely lift air traffic regulations as quickly as we can to minimise any further disruption”, and apologised for the disruption. They said the problem was “unrelated to the issue two weeks ago”.Despite the relatively quick fix, at least 200 flights in and out of UK airports were expected to be cancelled by the end of Monday, according to the analysts Cirium.The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, posted on X just after 10.30am, notifying that the latest technical issue had been resolved.She wrote: “I know this will be deeply frustrating for passengers after the previous issue. There may be some delays as things reset.”The incident came less than two weeks after a serious problem at the Nats control centre in Englanddisrupted travel for hundreds of thousandsof passengers, and only three days after the companyreleased an initial reportthat promised to “continually improve the critical service we provide”.Nats said Monday’s incident had been caused by a connectivity issue at its Prestwick centre.Among the stranded passengers at Glasgow were a bride and groom who had expected to fly to their Las Vegas wedding with family and friends. Their BA flight to Heathrow was cancelled, meaning they would miss their connection to the US on Monday, and they rebooked for Tuesday.The bride-to-be, Barbara Ann Stoddart, said: “I’m completely stressed out. I have still to go to the county court in Vegas to go and get the marriage licence, and I’ve got to be there three days in advance … If there’s any hiccups I might not be getting married on Saturday now.”View image in fullscreenBarbara Ann Stoddart and her fiance, Andrew Lithgow.Photograph: Lucinda Cameron/PAThe Civil Aviation Authority said it had reminded airlines of their responsibilities to look after passengers whose flights were delayed or cancelled, but that passengers were unlikely to receive compensation for delayed or cancelled flights.“We consider that disruption caused by the technical issue at Nats Prestwick centre inScotlandon 21 September is likely to be considered the result of ‘extraordinary circumstances’ under passenger rights rules.“This means that although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident,” a CAA spokesperson said.Airlines called for action to address repeated failures, with Ryanair reiterating its calls for the Nats chief executive, Martin Rolfe, to resign.EasyJet, one of the most-affected airlines on Monday, said the latest flight disruption “once again calls into question the resilience of Nats’s systems and demonstrates the need for firm actions to prevent these repeated failures”.BA described it as “yet another technical fault with Nats” and said it was disappointing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJet2’s chief executive, Steve Heapy, said it was “simply not good enough for this critical national infrastructure to keep letting customers down”.“What customers and airlines need now is action, accountability and proper resilience, and we need it urgently,” he said.Ryanair’s chief operations officer, Neal McMahon, said: “Just three days after Nats assured airlines and passengers that it had introduced robust ‘mitigation plans’, its flight data processing system has failed again.“More than 25,000 Ryanair passengers have already suffered disruption, with more than 140 Ryanair flights delayed.“Enough is enough. Martin Rolfe should resign today.”Rolfe, who was paid £1.4m last year including bonuses, has come under increasing pressure since the major outage on 8 September, the third high-profile incident in just over three years. Rolfe apologised and said he took full responsibility, but Nats has denied that the incidents are related.A “radar-related issue” in July 2025 a caused an air traffic control failure that disrupted the journeys of thousands of passengers and forced the cancellation of more than 160 flights.The biggest incident, in August 2023, affected more than 700,000 passengers when flights were grounded across the UK after a “rogue flight plan” sparked a system failure.Alexander has commissioned the CAA to conduct an independent review of Nats and check the findings of its initial report into the 8 September breakdown. She said the government still needed “to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos”.Andy Burnham, asked whether the head of Nats should be sacked, said Alexander would have to “get to the bottom” of the problems.“These are clearly serious issues and they need to be fully investigated, and I know the transport secretary is taking these issues extremely seriously,” said the prime minister.“Further issues today do cause even greater concern, but initially this is a matter for the transport secretary to get to the bottom of what is behind this and why there has been a recurrence.”Explore more on these topicsTransportAir transportAirline industryScotlandNorth of EnglandNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flights resume across US north-east after FAA communications failure  | US news | The Guardian
description: Thousands of flights were delayed or canceled after a primary line failed and a backup fiber-optic cable was severed
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Thousands of flights were delayed or canceled after a primary line failed and a backup fiber-optic cable was severed
Content: The FAA ordered a ground stop at Newark Liberty (above), Philadelphia and Teterboro airports.Photograph: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe FAA ordered a ground stop at Newark Liberty (above), Philadelphia and Teterboro airports.Photograph: Smith Collection/Gado/Getty ImagesUS newsFlights resume across US north-east after FAA communications failureThousands of flights were delayed or canceled after a primary line failed and a backup fiber-optic cable was severedJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonMon 21 Sep 2026 19.56 EDTFirst published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 14.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAirport operations across the US north-east resumed Monday evening after a communications line failure snarled flights at some of the country’s busiest airports, leading to thousands of flight cancellations and delays.Flights were halted at several airports after a primary communications line failed at a key Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) facility in Philadelphia. The backup fiber optic line, which delivers internet service, was inadvertently severed by a railroad construction crew, resulting in a telecommunications crash and hundreds of canceled flights at Newark, LaGuardia, JFK, Philadelphia and Boston airports.Transportation secretary Sean Duffy said in a Monday eveningsocial media postthat the backup lines had been fixed and all affected airports were again operating.“It will take some time to clear all existing delays, so please check with your airline for the latest information,” Duffy wrote.The technical problems stem from the same FAA facility in Philadelphia that caused numerous disruptions at Newark Liberty international airport in the spring of 2025.Regional control centers like these have two lines that carry radar and communications data in and out: the primary and the backup. The FAA said a circuit on the primary failed Monday morning, and when the system tried to switch to the backup, workers discovered that the fiber optic line had been cut.Earlier in the day, Duffy said an Amtrak construction crew was to blame. Amtrak, however, pointed to a New Jersey Transit construction crew that was working in the area between Newark and New Brunswick, New Jersey.The disruption coincided with the publication of agovernment accountability office (GAO) report, which found that the FAA has yet to finish risk assessments or update security documentation covering threats from spoofing, jamming and other attacks on the radio spectrum – prompting a prominent senator to warn of a “major threat” to national security.The FAA also lacks a real-time system to detect all such threats, the report said, meaning it can generally only investigate incidents after they are reported.Investigators warned that a hacker could send fraudulent messages, such as false cancellations of flight clearances, to aircraft, with the potential to cause delays, disrupt airspace or create safety risks. Two systems used to send text messages to aircraft predate modern cybersecurity standards and lack common protections such as encryption, according to the report.The watchdog’s findings prompted calls for swift action. “The FAA’s failure to require the aviation industry to use secure communications is a major threat to US national security, to our economy and the safety of the flying public,” said Ron Wyden, the US senator for Oregon, who has long campaigned on privacy, surveillance and cybersecurity issues.“The FAA needs to issue new standards, as soon as possible, to protect the security of airline communications.”The GAO made nine recommendations, including a formal risk assessment of seven of eight reviewed systems, continuous monitoring for interference, spoofing and jamming, and formal guidance on information sharing. The Department of Transportation, replying for the FAA, agreed with all nine.Monday’s disruption is the latest in a run of problems around Newark. In April 2025, anoutage blanked controllers’ screensfor roughly 60 to 90 seconds and cut their contact with aircraft, prompting the FAA to halt departures. The FAAlater movedthe Philadelphia Tracon to a new fiber-optic link with New York on two separate paths, as part of measures to improve reliability.The FAA handles more than 44,000 flights a day and about 3 million passengers, the GAO noted.Wyden, who sits on the Senate intelligence committee, added: “This sobering report from [the] GAO reveals that the technology used by air traffic controllers to communicate with aircraft is incredibly insecure, can be intercepted, impersonated, and jammed, and that hackers and foreign governments can exploit these vulnerabilities to disrupt air travel and even put passengers at risk.”The GAO also pointed to jamming and spoofing abroad. Estonia and Finland have accused Russia of interfering with satellite navigation in their airspace, which Moscow denies.One incidentlast Septemberinvolved a Spanish military jet carrying the country’s defense minister.The Associated Press contributedExplore more on these topicsUS newsUS politicsAir transportnewsShareReuse this content

title: US judge declines to block transfer of wildlife refuge land to Musk’s SpaceX | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Environmental groups vow to continue opposition to deal that would expand site for Elon Musk rocket company
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Environmental groups vow to continue opposition to deal that would expand site for Elon Musk rocket company
Content: SpaceX's mega rocket Starship makes a test flight from Starbase in Texas in May.Photograph: Eric Gay/APView image in fullscreenSpaceX's mega rocket Starship makes a test flight from Starbase in Texas in May.Photograph: Eric Gay/APTrump administrationUS judge declines to block transfer of wildlife refuge land to Musk’s SpaceXEnvironmental groups vow to continue opposition to deal that would expand site for Elon Musk rocket companyAssociated PressMon 21 Sep 2026 19.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA federal judge on Monday refused to block theTrump administrationfrom giving SpaceX more than 700 acres of wildlife refuge as part of a land swap in Texas, while environmental groups vowed to continue their legal challenge.US district judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr declined the plaintiffs’ request for a preliminary injunction to prevent the parcel exchange, saying they failed to prove it would worsen ecological risks to a Gulf coast region already transformed by billionaire Elon Musk’s rocket operations.In June, the US Fish and Wildlife Service approved moving forward with the deal withSpaceX, which would surrender 683 acres the company owns in exchange for the federal land in the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge. The 103,000-acre refuge spans four counties along the Texas border and is home to animal habitats and historical landmarks.Maps show the land SpaceX would acquire would be closer to the company’s launchpad near the US-Mexico border.The swap amounts to a gift of public lands to SpaceX, “clearing the way for bulldozers to tear into this wildlife refuge as soon as next week and turn a public treasure into a private payday”, said Laiken Jordahl, a spokesperson with the Center for Biological Diversity, which filed the lawsuit alongside other opponents including tribal groups. Jordahl said Monday that the litigation will continue even as the exchange goes forward.“This court order is not the final word. These lands hold incredible spiritual, historical and conservation value for the people and wildlife of SouthTexas. We won’t stop fighting to keep this irreplaceable public wildlife refuge safe from SpaceX bulldozers,” Jordahl said in a statement.The lawsuit asks the federal court to halt the exchange, which has worried SpaceX opponents in the area who have long criticized the company’s expanding footprint over lost access to beaches and concerns over exploding rockets.The Fish and Wildlife Service did not respond to a request for comment on Monday’s decision. Previously, a spokesperson had said the agency does not comment on ongoing litigation.The agency issued a final environmental assessment report in June that determined the exchange would cause no significant impact to the area.
