After Iran shut down the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s energy supplies transited before the recent war, Saudi Arabia was forced to move much of its oil shipments via itseast-west pipelineto Saudi ports along the Red Sea. That exposed Saudi dependence on both the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab waterways.After announcing their blockade in July, the Houthis fired on several Saudi vessels in the Red Sea, forcing the kingdom to reroute a significant portion of its oil exports to Asia through a far longer and more expensive journey. Thatalternative routecan take ships more than 30 days, and it involves transiting through the Suez Canal, the Mediterranean Sea, and around the southern tip of Africa, before finally reaching customers in Asia, who buy the bulk of Saudi oil.To make matters worse for the Saudis – and global oil prices – the east-west pipeline was struck recently by a drone attack blamed on Iranian-backed Shia militias in Iraq. Saudi officials were forced to shut down the nearly 750-mile-long pipeline on 11 September, and it’s unclear how long repairs will take. If the network is offline for a month, it couldreduce global oil supplyby 120m barrels and raise crude prices as high as $120 a barrel.As the Houthis carried out their lightning offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince and de facto ruler, Mohammed bin Salman,reportedly called Trumptwice on 10 September, urging him to order US airstrikes against the Yemeni rebels. For now, Trump has ruled out direct US attacks against the Houthis, despite the appeals from his ally and benefactor Prince Mohammed. (After a mob of Trump supporters stormed the US Capitol in January 2021, several US banks and large companiesdistanced themselvesfrom the president’s family business, the Trump Organization. But Saudi Arabia and its crown prince becamea crucial sourceof new real estate and other deals for the family firm while Trump was out of power.)Trump’s decision to keep the US out of the Houthi-Saudi conflict is one of the best foreign policy choices of his second term so far, although it’s dwarfed by his catastrophic decision to launch a war against Iran. Trump seems to realize that neither the US,Saudi Arabianor other Arab states have been able to bomb the Houthis into submission – despite trying for more than a decade.Yemen’s civil war has been a complex conflict for decades, with Saudi Arabia, Iran and the US supporting different factions at various times. TheHouthis, who are officially known as Ansar Allah (the Partisans of God), emerged in the 1990s as a Shia tribal movement based in northern Yemen that fought multiple battles against the central Yemeni government and other tribes aligned with Saudi Arabia. The conflict escalated significantly in September 2014, when the Houthis overran Sana’a, and within a few months forced the internationally recognized government to flee to the kingdom, which shares a long border with Yemen.The Guardian view on the Houthi advance in Yemen: another vital Middle East artery becomes a battlefield | EditorialRead moreIn early 2015, Saudi Arabia led a coalition of Sunni Arab states to intervene in the war, trying to push the Houthis out of the capital and restore Yemen’s Saudi-backed government into power. Barack Obama and his administrationsupported the Saudisand their allies, especially the United Arab Emirates, with US weapons and extensive intelligence sharing.Despite thousands of airstrikes and a Saudi-led blockade, the Houthis survived the onslaught.Yemenwas effectively divided into two states, with the Houthis in control of Sana’a and large parts of the north, while the Yemeni government controlled much of the south and a competing capital in the port city of Aden. After seven years of stalemate, Saudi Arabia decided to cut its losses and agreed to a ceasefire with the Houthis in 2022, after which the group stopped its attacks on Saudi territory until resuming them this summer.Negotiations over a permanent peace agreement in Yemen stalled for several years, mainly over economic incentives for the Houthis and recognizing the militia’s rule over parts of Yemen. In recent weeks, the Houthis sensed an advantage in the regional chaos and global economic turmoil unleashed by Trump’s war onIran.The Houthis are trying to gain new leverage by taking control of their own regional energy chokepoint and capturing more territory from their enemies in Yemen. For now, no one seems to be able to stop them.Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York UniversityExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranOpinionIranYemenHouthisSaudi ArabiaUS foreign policyMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Europe is under attack from three sides – but the EU and Nato are unfit to defend us | Nathalie Tocci | The Guardian
description: Ursula von der Leyen’s outreach to Canada and new security proposals are wise – but she may not be the right messenger, says Guardian Europe columnist Nathalie Tocci
Author: Nathalie Tocci
Headline: Ursula von der Leyen’s outreach to Canada and new security proposals are wise – but she may not be the right messenger, says Guardian Europe columnist Nathalie Tocci
Content: ‘The EU is slow and cumbersome, built for peacetime. Its membership, while large, is not wide enough, excluding key players in the wider European space.’Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The EU is slow and cumbersome, built for peacetime. Its membership, while large, is not wide enough, excluding key players in the wider European space.’Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersOpinionEuropeEurope is under attack from three sides – but the EU and Nato are unfit to defend usNathalie TocciUrsula von der Leyen’s outreach to Canada and new security proposals are wise – but she may not be the right messengerMon 21 Sep 2026 11.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 16.25 EDTShareEurope’s strategic predicament is ever clearer, and ever darker. The continent is at war, which is being fought militarily in Ukraine, but is escalating rapidly across Europe through hybrid attacks.Germany’s disclosurethat it blames Russia for the drone attack at Leipzig airport; a Russian drone strikeon a trainnear the Ukraine-Poland border; an Italian jet shooting down aRussian drone over Lithuania; flares fired from a Russian warshipat a Danish helicopter– all within the space of a couple of weeks – tell a coherent story. Whether because Russia is bogged down and unable to advance in Ukraine, or because it believes the US will not come to Europe’s rescue, Vladimir Putin’s regime is ever more bent on escalating its aggression in Europe.Canada is seeking new global neighbours – no wonder, as Trump rolls out stupidities at scale | David MoscropRead morePutin’s calculus is not irrational. Trump never misses a chance to lash out at Europe – the latest example being histhreats of further tariffson the EU if Brussels proceeds to offer Canada “associate membership”. Europeans have grown numb to Trump’s insults and threats, but these threats do underline his deep antipathy, suggesting that if a Russian attack warranted a response, Trump might look the other way. The US certainly can’t be relied on to have Europe’s back.This is the context in which Ursula von der Leyen caused surprise last week byproposing associate membershipof the EU for Canada. To bolster Europe’s defences, the European Commission president also wants a “European security council”, and a mutual solidarity mechanism to respond to hybrid attacks.While they have distinct rationales, these ideas fit into the same strategic logic: in a world of predatory powers, the “rest of the west” must huddle together.The threats are not only external. Along with Putin’s Russia and Maga America, the rise of the far right in Europe completes a triangle of threats. The far right is a threat to liberal democracy. But by instigating internal division and pushing for disintegration, it also supports the divide-and-rule designs of predatory external powers, representing a challenge to Europe’s independence and sovereignty.It has taken the earthquake of theAfD’s successesin German regional elections for von der Leyen toacknowledge openlythat Europe’s threats are also homegrown. Better late than never.European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against NatoRead moreFaced with this unprecedented convergence of threats from three sides, leaders are scrambling for a response. Nato has what it takes to defend Europe againstRussia. But if its majority shareholder – the US – is unwilling to step in, the question of its plans, structures and capacities is moot. If a hybrid attack on a European country caused civilian casualties, would Nato be bypassed if Washington signalled its unwillingness to act? Collective defence would not even be invoked if the anticipated result were the US’s betrayal of its European allies.This is where von der Leyen’s emergency protocol comes in, filling the gap between the high-water mark of mutual assistance – article 42.7 of the EU’s founding treaty, which covers armed aggression – and nothing at all. The attacked state would activate the protocol, an emergency European Council would convene, and the commission and EU high representative would propose responses, including evacuation and medical support, stockpiling and energy security, economic coercion, military mobility and more. The mechanism could extend to like-minded non-EU partners, starting with Canada, Norway, the UK and Ukraine. The proposal to offer Canada associate membership, while still undefined, can be read in this light as well.On paper, it all makes sense. In practice, it is hard to see such a mechanism operating seamlessly, let alone rapidly, given the EU’s organisational complexities, its slowness to act and its internal divisions.Hence the proposal for a European security council, consisting of those countries willing and able to contribute to the defence of Europe, without the US if need be. Some of these countries would be EU members, but not all – again, Canada, the UK, Ukraine and possibly Turkey.Both the problem and the solution are clear. To protect itself against predatory powers, what remains of the west must cooperate ever more closely. But the existing multilateral organisations –Natoand the EU – are unfit for purpose. Nato will remain anchored to the US, while the EU is slow and cumbersome, built for peacetime. Its membership, while large, is not wide enough, excluding key players in the wider European space.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDeveloping alternative forms of EU membership could be of interest not just to Canada, but to the UK, too. The ideawas first raisedby Berlin for Ukraine, in fact, but Kyiv turned down the offer, seeing it as second-class. Ukraine deserves full EU membership, but if a substantial associate membership is on the table in the short term, it should take that, while continuing to press for more.The rise of far-right nationalism means that reaching consensus within the EU will become harder, not easier – which is precisely where the proposal for a smaller, more agile European security council comes in, provided far-right governments do not simultaneously come to power across major European countries.Von der Leyen’s security proposals are sensible and urgently needed. The potential pitfall lies not in the message, but in the messenger.In her years at the helm of the commission she has grown a reputation for centralising power and overstepping boundaries, irking other EU officials in Brussels as well as European capitals. When it comes to security and defence especially, sovereignty is jealously guarded by the EU’s nation state governments. It would be tragic if European governments ended up killing off a set of good ideas because of Europe’s institutional turf wars. Rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic is the last thing Europe and its partners need right now.Nathalie Tocci is a Guardian Europe columnistExplore more on these topicsEuropeOpinionRussiaEuropean UnionVladimir PutinUrsula von der LeyenNatocommentShareReuse this content

title: Complaining about healthcare can feel like an act of betrayal. But there is a real cost to silence | Ranjana Srivastava | The Guardian
description: The demands on doctors are only intensifying. From dissatisfied patients, I would ask for a measure of grace, understanding and, where possible, forgiveness
Author: Ranjana Srivastava
Headline: The demands on doctors are only intensifying. From dissatisfied patients, I would ask for a measure of grace, understanding and, where possible, forgiveness
Content: Serious failures in healthcare can arise from poor communication and the feeling of not being taken seriously, writes Ranjana Srivastava.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSerious failures in healthcare can arise from poor communication and the feeling of not being taken seriously, writes Ranjana Srivastava.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianOpinionHealthComplaining about healthcare can feel like an act of betrayal. But there is a real cost to silenceRanjana SrivastavaThe demands on doctors are only intensifying. From dissatisfied patients, I would ask for a measure of grace, understanding and, where possible, forgivenessGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMon 21 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 19.17 EDTShareSome years ago, an old friend needed surgery. I couldn’t move her up the waitlist, but I did introduce her to a surgeon. Unfortunately, a year later she told me that the surgery had left her in excruciating pain. I urged her to return to the surgeon. After all, which doctor would not be sympathetic?But over dinner, her halting account of the appointment was devastating to hear. She had felt dismissed and ridiculed, made to feel as if it were her fault. I asked if she would allow me to approach him. In my experience, most doctors want to know when they have caused distress or harm and welcome the opportunity to make amends.The easy bit was convincing my friend. The hard bit was calling the surgeon. I rehearsed what to say and wondered if I was out of line. But having been the subject of a few complaints myself, I felt sure that he would want to know.We terminated a pregnancy so our daughter never had to suffer. It was agony. It cannot be the right of One Nation – or any anti-abortion activist – to choose for us | AnonymousRead moreI told him that our long association gave me the confidence to say that his patient felt ill-served. I trusted him to reassess her kindly, even if he couldn’t fix her. To my surprise he had no memory of being rude, and I didn’t pursue the matter. My friend was seen again, this time with more sympathy, although her problem wasn’t easily remediable. She later told me she had learnt the value of persistence.Only weeks later, I receive a frantic late-night text from another, normally very calm, friend.He has been in hospital for several days, being treated for pneumonia, with unstable vital signs and severe pain. Yet he feels no better. From the images he sends me, I can’t see an obvious explanation for his symptoms. One specialist has referred him to another; everyone is ordering tests but no one is talking to him.Then came the incident that prompted his text. After hours of pain, two nurses arrived with analgesia. As they were about to inject, he pointed to the red wristband documenting his morphine allergy. Horrified, they discarded the drug, but the near-miss terrified him.I don’t know his doctors or his medical history and certainly don’t want to become an armchair specialist. But I know that he deserves better. I ask whether he has approached his doctors. He says they ignore him. And the nurses? They defer to the doctors. I put myself in his shoes and imagine how unsettling it would be to feel seriously unwell, surrounded by knowledgable professionals, yet trapped in a vacuum of information.So I suggest the solution of last resort: ask to see the most senior person available and calmly convey that, in the morning, he intends to make a formal complaint about the failures in his care and communication.It is something of a self-indictment that the threat of a complaint becomes the turning point in his care.The next morning, the same doctors are “like different people”: sitting at his bedside, explaining his scans and bloods, acknowledging the prescribing error and ensuring more diligent care.The result is a revised diagnosis, appropriate treatment and respectful care. He goes home glad to be alive. He never files the complaint.Complainingabout healthcare can feel like an act of betrayal. We see doctors at our most vulnerable, and most of us would rather believe we did something wrong than that someone failed us.Patients are often told they have rights. The difficulty is knowing when to complain, how far to go and whom to approach. But there is a cost to silence: to the patient, to other patients and to the healthcare system.Not every difficult healthcare encounter requires aformal complaint. Vexatious complaints waste precious time and resources and, where minor clinical friction or misunderstanding can be resolved through direct communication, it should be.Like many doctors, I spend hours responding to complaints wishing the patient had simply told me. Time spent drafting and re-drafting explanations that meet bureaucratic guidelines would be far better spent caring for patients. But there is a lesson in humility in asking what it was about my own demeanour that inhibited a patient from “simply telling me”.To be honest, I am surprised more people don’t complain, given the serious failures in healthcare that can arise frompoor communicationand the feeling of not being taken seriously. This is especially concerning when additional barriers to speaking up exist for disadvantaged people, older people and those from culturally diverse backgrounds. I have been on the receiving end,through my elderly Indian mother, and – I hate to say it – on the giving end, when I have been less attentive than I ought to.Health officials in turmoil over 11th-hour backflip on aged care algorithm override powers, emails revealRead moreComplaining is onerous. And while doctors might think of themselves as “regular people”, they can underestimate the power imbalance between themselves and the patients who depend on them.I like to think my practice is motivated by commitment to my patients. But I also want to avoid unnecessary complaints that fracture my peace and render me less effective.The demands on doctors are only intensifying. From dissatisfied patients, I would ask for a measure of grace, understanding and, where possible, forgiveness. Complaints are not a weapon; they are just one way of seeking resolution.In return, patients should have high expectations of their doctors. To err may be human, but to acknowledge and repair is equally so.Every health organisation has a mechanism for raising concerns. A liaison officer or patient advocate can listen, help formulate the concern and direct it to the right person. Many complaints are resolved right there and, if not, patients can seek advice from the relevant regulatory bodies.But formal process is only ever part of the story. My friend still sees her surgeon. My other friend remembers less about his diagnosis than the days he went unheard.Given the myriad human needs doctors are pressed up against, there will never be a world without complaints. Nor should there be. The goal is not to make patients complain less or doctors less defensive. It is to ensure that no patient who should be heard goes unheard.Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. Her latest book is Every Word Matters: Writing to Engage the PublicExplore more on these topicsHealthOpinionHospitalsDoctorscommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: Private karaoke is the death of socialism – only a pub singalong is good enough for the people | Kelli Blanchett | The Guardian
description: Community, camaraderie, connection: I learned about all these things while hosting pub karaoke nights. Sticky private booths are their absolute antithesis, says freelance writer Kelli Blanchett
Author: Kelli Blanchett
Headline: Community, camaraderie, connection: I learned about all these things while hosting pub karaoke nights. Sticky private booths are their absolute antithesis, says freelance writer Kelli Blanchett
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onClass issuesThe hill I will die on: Private karaoke is the death of socialism – only a pub singalong is good enough for the peopleKelli BlanchettCommunity, camaraderie, connection: I learned about all these things while hosting pub karaoke nights. Sticky private booths are their absolute antithesisMon 21 Sep 2026 09.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTShareOn a gloomy Wednesday evening, my best friend and I decided we wanted to scratch our singing itch. We searched for a pub that was hosting karaoke but couldn’t find anything in our area. So we headed to the local branch of a well-known private-booth karaoke bar instead. But it wasn’t just the astounding £18 per hour (per person!) charge or the poor sound quality that made the whole experience so profoundly sad.Private karaoke booths are sticky little cubicles for people who like singing but don’t want to be seen. They’re places where you pay a premium to avoid rubbing shoulders with strangers or making new connections. The whole point is to avoid exposure to the real world, which fundamentally misunderstands the power of karaoke.I grew up in a former steel town. Twice a week, my mum hosted karaoke at a local pub, and because we couldn’t afford a babysitter, my sister and I went with her. When Mum’s caring responsibilities for my dad increased, she passed on the mantle to me, aged 17, to earn a bit of cash and keep the family business alive. Sitting with strangers across generations, hearing the stories behind their song choices, sharing rounds of drinks and political opinions, I felt like a sponge, soaking up different walks of life.This is why when I talk about karaoke I’m not picturing these private, pay-by-the-hour cells. I’m thinking about the working-class pubs and clubs of Britain, where coming face to face with your community was more than half the point.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: Games are the opposite of fun, and I’d ban them for anyone over 12 | Emily WatkinsRead morePub karaoke is social cohesion in action. The root of socialism is to be supportive of your fellow man, to uphold them and work collectively. Whiletraditional performance art is often expensive, formal and ringfenced by wealth, private education and elite tastes, karaoke was always for the people.The death of these spaces alongside the rise in private-hire karaoke booths is denying us this cohesion. Unionism was born in the pub – collective thinking comes from being with people, exchanging ideas and belting out the classics. When you hear a plumber from Kettering sing Careless Whisper by George Michael, an angel gains its wings. When an audience comes together to support a person they don’t know, the seeds of collectivism are sown.We all crave connection, and this can’t be achieved in the cramped confinement of a beer-drenched booth in front of a tiny, curated audience of people we already know. Don’t succumb to the isolationism these corporations are foisting on us – instead, let’s get back to the pub, hand in hand, singing Sweet Caroline and hyping up our fellow strangers.Kelli Blanchett is a freelance writer, disabled activist and musicianExplore more on these topicsClass issuesThe hill I will die onSocialismcommentShareReuse this content

title: All the signs say another financial crisis is coming. Here’s why we need to prepare for it now | Larry Elliott | The Guardian
description: War, AI disruption and markets in turmoil: the warnings are all there. But lessons from the 2008 crash could help us, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Author: Larry Elliott
Headline: War, AI disruption and markets in turmoil: the warnings are all there. But lessons from the 2008 crash could help us, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Content: A broker at the Frankfurt stock exchange, Germany, on 16 September 2008.Photograph: Daniel Roland/APView image in fullscreenA broker at the Frankfurt stock exchange, Germany, on 16 September 2008.Photograph: Daniel Roland/APOpinionMarket turmoilAll the signs say another financial crisis is coming. Here’s why we need to prepare for it nowLarry ElliottWar, AI disruption and markets in turmoil: the warnings are all there. But lessons from the 2008 crash could help usMon 21 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.14 EDTShareBad stuff happens in September. For some reason, it is a month that has had more than its fair share of financial crises, perhaps because problems that have been bubbling away come into sharper focus once the summer holidays are over. Britaincame off the Gold Standardin September 1931. The pound was turfed out of Europe’s Exchange Rate Mechanism in September 1992. And 18 years ago this week, the collapse of Lehman Brothers plunged the global economy into deep recession.This September, there are again reasons to be nervous. There are soaring oil prices, which are feeding through intohigher petrol and diesel prices, adding to cost of living pressures. There is asell-off in government bondsaround the world. There is thewarning from AI bossesthat it would be wise to slow the pace of development in their industry. Mixed together, they are the ingredients for another troubled September.Of course, it may all be a false alarm. It is now more than six months since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran and so far the impact of closing the strait of Hormuz has been far less severe than was expected back in the spring. It is possible the fear currently gripping bond markets will quickly pass, especially if the wars in Ukraine and Iran end soon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAre global stock markets heading for a crash?Read moreThe constant refrain from Donald Trump that oil tankers will soon be passing unhindered once again through the strait of Hormuz has limited the rise in crude prices. Growth has not been hit that much, and in both the US and the UK,AI has been part of that story.There are, though, signs that the war in Iran is having an effect, albeit with a longer lag than originally expected. Markets no longer believe Trump when he says a deal with Iran is about to be clinched. As a result, the rise in oil prices to more than $100 a barrel in recent weeks has heightened fears of persistent inflation and of higher interest rates from central banks. And despite crude prices not escalating,the cost of petrol and dieselremains high, thanks to a shortage of refining capacity.For months, share prices have been underpinned by the belief that there is no ceiling on the growth of technology stocks, particularly those involved in AI. That theory is now being tested and as far as Wall Street is concerned, the recent intervention by the AI bosses was spectacularly ill-timed.Trump’s rejection of the need for tighter regulation on the AI industry speaks volumes. This is only partly to do with the US-China battle to win the technology war. Financial markets now look as fragile as they have been at any time since September 2008, and with US midterm elections looming, the president needs to prevent the AI-led stock market bubble from popping.History never repeats itself exactly. There are similarities between September 2026 and September 2008, but there are differences too. The crash of 2008 was the result of banks over-reaching themselves to finance US real estate. The banks seem to be far less exposed this time, and while some of the investment in technology stocks may have been predicated on unrealistic assumptions about future profits, AI is clearly going to have a positive long-term economic impact in a way that the investment in housing pre-2008 did not. It is wrong to think all bubbles are the same.That said, there are lessons to be learned from the events of 2008. One is that if a financial crisis morphs into an economic slump – as it did 18 years ago – then orthodoxy goes out of the window. There will be no more talk of interest-rate increases from central banks or of the need for finance ministries to slash budget deficits.Indeed, therecent bond buybacksby the US treasury, which were designed to reduce the upward pressure on mortgage interest rates, car loans and credit card debt, were both an indication of how nervous the Trump administration is about the current state of financial markets and a taste of the more vigorous intervention that a full-blown financial crisis would prompt.An even bigger lesson is the need to control what happens after a crash. Last time, the left was caught unawares and allowed the right to seize the initiative. Already there are signs in Britain of the same dynamic, with the chancellor, John Healey, coming under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending in next month’s budget.This would be self-defeating, not least because it would run counter to Andy Burnham’s (to my mind, entirely correct) argument that 40 years of neoliberalism was a mistake that needs rectifying. It would also come at a time when – as this week’s TUC conference in Brighton showed – there is genuine support on the left for a comprehensive strategy to re-industrialise Britain.A range of trade unions – Unite, RMT, CWU, GMB and Equity – made it clear at the conference that they wanted a much more interventionist approach, and acollection of essays, to which I contributed, has just been published, fleshing out what Burnham would need to do to make good on his re-industrialisation pledge.If not now, then sooner or later there will be another financial crisis. People forget. They become complacent. They overlook the strains in financial markets that have been allowed to become too big and too powerful. So while recent events may blow over, it would also be sensible to plan for another September meltdown. Just in case.Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsMarket turmoilOpinionGlobal economyEconomicsFinancial crisisStock marketsBondscommentShareReuse this content

title: Exhausted by optimisation, I’m seeking solace in the past. As Sibelius’s swans soar skywards, so do my spirits | Joseph Earp | The Guardian
description: Humans have always been capable of transcending the lock box of daily life with little more technology at their side than wood, string, a baton and their voices
Author: Joseph Earp
Headline: Humans have always been capable of transcending the lock box of daily life with little more technology at their side than wood, string, a baton and their voices
Content: ‘Above a bed of swirling strings, a sudden peal of brass sounds out: wings uplifted, moving heavenward. It regularly brings me to tears.’Photograph: FLPA/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Above a bed of swirling strings, a sudden peal of brass sounds out: wings uplifted, moving heavenward. It regularly brings me to tears.’Photograph: FLPA/AlamyOpinionClassical musicExhausted by optimisation, I’m seeking solace in the past. As Sibelius’s swans soar skywards, so do my spiritsJoseph EarpHumans have always been capable of transcending the lock box of daily life with little more technology at their side than wood, string, a baton and their voicesMon 21 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 02.47 EDTShareAt this fundamentally exhausting moment in human history, we find ourselves slap bang in the middle of a progress arms race, where everything – literally everything – is posed as perfectable.That’s not just thanks to the AI industry, though its acolytes shout the loudest when they tell us that their plagiarism robots can help us blast through life more efficiently. Somehow, the myth of endlessly optimisable production has infiltrated every part of our lives.Now, you can listen to your podcasts on double speed for ultimate uptake, max out your sleep for ultimate restoration, biohack your mind for ultimate clarity, and relax more intensely than your peers.In such a landscape, where nothing is ever good enough or fine as it is, the past only appears more distant. We used to marvel at how people lived their lives a hundred years ago; now we’re being told even life before AI should be viewed as a kind of rudimentary stone age, filled with cavemen who submitted to the barbaric indignity of writing their own emails.double quotation markMy love of classical composition has been with me always but in the last year or so, this love has become an obsessionCall me a luddite but this endless pursuit of progress for progress’s sake has, if anything, pushed me the opposite way. Exhausted by art that promises to explain how we live right now, marketed with buzzwords and posed as the diagnosis to problems I have become too fatigued to even care about, I find myself instead retreating further and further backwards into the annals of art – and, in particular, into the world of classical music.My love of classical composition has been with me always but in the last year or so, this love has become an obsession. To my partner’s mild alarm, I now cook dinner while listening to the abstract atonal textures of Morton Feldman. I’ll go for a run while blasting Steve Reich’s Radio Rewrite (the repetitive rhythms really do something special to your pacing, believe me). When asked to plug into a shared aux chord, I experience a blast of mild panic, knowing that a quick play of Schoenberg is likely to clear the room.Should a tech tycoon be able to pay his way into conducting a world-class orchestra? And should they really sell tickets?Read moreIf this makes me sound insufferable, then it’s because I probably am becoming so. But what it also makes me feel is immensely, profoundly uplifted. It’s not just that listening to Gustav Mahler’s Fifth Symphony, a dizzyingly agonised exploration of mortality, reminds me that humans have always been capable of transcending the lock box of daily life with little more technology at their side than wood, string, a baton and their voices. It’s that I am reminded, with stunning clarity, that Mahler wasn’t so different to us after all.Just a few weeks ago, my partner and I watched the Australian Chamber Orchestra perform a selection of Alfred Schnittke’s works. Schnittke, ailed by poor health, targeted by Soviet bureaucracy, lived in a world fundamentally unfamiliar to mine, at least on the surface. When the orchestra began squeaking out his ugly yet uplifted chords, I knew almost nothing about the man. By the time they were done, I felt as though I knew everything. His anxiety about the frailty of his own body and his age permeated every note.The performance did what all art should do – it reached out, wordlessly, and insisted on the ugliness and the beauty of human experience, and the transcendence we reach when we aim to capture them both. I recognised it. And that recognition, spanning time, reminded me how little things actually change.There’s one piece of music in particular that I can’t stop listening to these days, from the Finnish composer Jean Sibelius’ Fifth Symphony. Sibelius’ life wasn’t happy – an alcoholic and a chain smoker, he enjoyed significant popularity but critical drubbing. Though often emphatic, his Fifth also broils with moments of confusion and melancholy, chords souring almost as soon as they have erupted.But there’s also a moment in its third movement when Sibelius mimics the sounds of birds taking flight near his country home. Above a bed of swirling strings, a sudden peal of brass sounds out: wings uplifted, moving heavenward. It regularly brings me to tears. Not just thanks to the music itself, but the image of Sibelius, watching the skies, wowed by the birds, seeking to turn them into song. And because it reminds me that, while we might have complicated and entangled our lives, we haven’t fundamentally altered them.Sure, technologymight one day kill us allbut it won’t be able to erode or change some deep bedrock inside us. Something intangible, untouchable, that happens when we step outside and watch birds take flight. Something we might call our humanity itself.Joseph Earp is a critic, painter and novelist. His latest book isPainting Portraits of Everyone I’ve Ever DatedExplore more on these topicsClassical musicOpinionJean SibeliusGustav MahlercommentShareReuse this content

title: What do you think of the MPs’ inquiry into UK Eurovision song contest failure? I give it nul points | Laura Snapes | The Guardian
description: There are obvious reasons why the UK flops and flops again, but that isn’t the point. This annual debacle is now part of our national identity, says deputy music editor Laura Snapes
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: There are obvious reasons why the UK flops and flops again, but that isn’t the point. This annual debacle is now part of our national identity, says deputy music editor Laura Snapes
Content: The UK's Eurovision 2026 entry, Look Mum No Computer, on stage in Vienna, Austria, 8 May 2026.Photograph: BBC/EBU/PAView image in fullscreenThe UK's Eurovision 2026 entry, Look Mum No Computer, on stage in Vienna, Austria, 8 May 2026.Photograph: BBC/EBU/PAOpinionEurovisionWhat do you think of the MPs’ inquiry into UK Eurovision song contest failure? I give it nul pointsLaura SnapesThere are obvious reasons why the UK flops and flops again, but that isn’t the point. This annual debacle is now part of our national identityMon 21 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 07.39 EDTShareGiven that Britain’s politics are quite a sizeable reason that we do so badly in Eurovision: here’s something that will definitely, absolutely, categorically help us do better in the competition … interference from MPs.Digital, culture, media and sport committee chair Caroline Dinenage has announced thatMPs will scrutinise the UK’s reliable failure in the competitionto see where we’re going wrong, with a hearing to be held over the coming months. The answers surely don’t take that long to work out.“We want to get to the bottom of who chooses our entrant,” Dinenage said. Currently that’s the BBC, with the assistance of a label or management company. Is our embarrassing misfortune down to “bad song choice, weak performance or something else”, she asked. Can you hear three red cherries dinging? Our songs are embarrassing, the humdrum performances indicative of a nation who think we’re too good for Eurovision high camp, and the “something else” is the lingering whiff of Brexit.View image in fullscreenBonnie Tyler at the 2013 Eurovision in Malmo Arena, Sweden.Photograph: Scanpix Scanpix/ReutersDinenage’s statement concluded by fretting about why we continually come last, or as good as, when as a nation we have “world-class songwriters and musicians”? Let me help there: that’s because no world-class British songwriter or musician would enter Eurovision at this point. No matter how good the song, our reputation as the dunce of the competition is fixed in perpetuity. We’ve tried wacky. We’ve tried the electro-swing beloved of the continent. We’ve tried oldies, besmirching Bonnie and Engelbert’s good names.Nada. At this point, I doubt that even Paul McCartney could pluck victory from the pyro-belching jaws of defeat. No self-respecting artist is going to sacrifice their beautiful creation to those cruel, gnashing European heathens.But!they wail.What about pluckySam Ryder, whofinished secondin2022?Space Man is quite a good song, I’ll grant you that. In summer 2022, at a very trying time in my life, it caught me unawares and made me cry. Improbably, later that day, I actually saw Ryder himself at a service station en route to the south-west and thanked him, very earnestly, for writing it, and got a warm fist bump in return. But Space Man also came second that year because of the UK’s staunch support for Ukraine after Russia invaded months earlier. Fair play, said Europe. You can have that one.(Just a thought: if it turns out that supporting nations experiencing destruction of human life and habitat by aggressive neighbours is one route to Eurovision success, maybe that is something that our politicians could consider doing a great deal more of.)View image in fullscreenSam Ryder at Eurovision 2022 in Turin, Italy.Photograph: Jussi Nukari/REX/ShutterstockRyder was appointed our saviour by Tap management, who look after artists includingLana Del Rey. Apparently capable of delivering victory for our beleaguered nation, they held on to the mantle for 2023 and sentMae Mullerto the competition. She finished second from bottom. In 2024, we pivoted and tried An Actual Popstar People Like,Olly Alexanderformerly of Years & Years, with a song co-written and produced by cutting-edge Charli xcx collaborators. What could possibly go wrong? He finished 18th out of 25.There is no reliable pipeline to Eurovision success available to the UK. The public can’t be trusted: in 2019, the last time the UK voted on our entrant, we sent a winsome young lad called Michael Rice,who had a mere 11 pointsto declareat customs on the way back from the contest in Tel Aviv. Perversely, I would quite like to see what musician British MPs – a group exactly not renowned for their music taste – would send to the competition on our behalf, but I’m not sure it would set back the rot.If anything, they should have some dignity and extract us from the competition: as one of its major funders, the UK gets a pass to the final every year without having to compete for a spot. If a football club finished bottom of the Premier League every year but was artificially kept in because of money, we would burn their ground down. Only relegated to the qualifiers may we rebuild.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenOlly Alexander at Eurovision 2024 in Malmo Arena in Sweden.Photograph: Corinne Cumming/EBU/PAMPs’ concern, while endearing, is also misplaced. Being crap at Eurovision is part of our national identity. (If indeed you’re still watching it:thousands have boycottedthe broadcast owing to Israel’s continued inclusion, including our principled Irish neighbours, another reason Britain may struggle to find credible competitors.) Sure, yes, we are very good at pop music – only fellow competitors Sweden have us licked in that regard – but complaining that those talents don’t work properly in this context comes across as sour grapes, like a medal-winning sprinter moaning that they lost the dads’ race at their kid’s sports day.As a competition, Eurovision is less Champions League – statistically proving who’s the best – than it is a kind of musical Crufts, upping the gaiety of nations with competitive displays of ridiculousness. It’s not about naming who’s Best At Pop. Britain’s failure doesn’t matter. If we must try to remedy this, I have two solutions. Pop music is soft power, and this battered country has no softer power than Mr Blobby. Let’s return an old cricketer to the crease for his first musical release in 23 years. If our rotund hero loses – UNLIKELY – he can just destroy the studio.Or, if the government insist on getting involved, here’s a thought. You may have heard that our new PM doesn’t just like the Smiths,he freaking loves the Smiths. He’s got a gold disc of The Queen Is Dead on the wall at the new No 10 North office. He recently jammed to Rusholme Ruffians on the frontline in Kyiv. He saw them live back in the day. Only he can call for the one referendum that will get hearts and minds back on Britain’s side: to forcibly reunite the band and send them to the competition. Morrissey performing live to 130 million viewers worldwide – what could possibly go wrong?Laura Snapes is the Guardian’s deputy music editorExplore more on these topicsEurovisionOpinionBritish identity and societycommentShareReuse this content

title: If you really hate it when music and film stars do politics, here’s the answer: give us politics that works | Nesrine Malik | The Guardian
description: The problem is not famous people speaking out, as they always have. It is the feeling that leaders have failed, obliging celebrities to fill the vacuum, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: The problem is not famous people speaking out, as they always have. It is the feeling that leaders have failed, obliging celebrities to fill the vacuum, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Content: Ed Sheeran performing at the O2 Arena in London on 6 December 2025.Photograph: Matt Crossick/Shutterstock for GlobalView image in fullscreenEd Sheeran performing at the O2 Arena in London on 6 December 2025.Photograph: Matt Crossick/Shutterstock for GlobalOpinionActivismIf you really hate it when music and film stars do politics, here’s the answer: give us politics that worksNesrine MalikThe problem is not famous people speaking out, as they always have. It is the feeling that leaders have failed, obliging celebrities to fill the vacuumMon 21 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 06.29 EDTShareEvery time a public figure in entertainment speaks up about politics in a way deemed “controversial”, it is as if it’s the first time that has ever happened. The outrage is fresh; critics rediscover and announce, as if they have just captured an elusive, profound notion, that art should be separate from politics. A form of disciplining is dispensed. Please, Mr or Miss Moneybags, with your preening notions that you have anything intelligent or informed to say aboutimmigration policyor Palestine. Stick to football. Stick to pop music. Stick to acting. Stick to children’s shows.Even at a time when a political moment has engulfed everything, this response continues to be born again, without regard for history or ability to confront rupture. The horror of Gaza hasbroken the art world, roiledHollywood,fractured literary institutions. And still, as Ed Sheeran stands alone on stage following the withdrawal of all his support acts (in solidarity with Macklemore, who was removed from the tour due to a pro-Palestinian speech), he told his audience that he wants his music to be “about unity, not division”. The speed at which his tour unravelled is not evidence of the incompatibility of music and politics, necessitating that they remain separate to avoid that “division”. It is a study in how it is becoming increasingly unnatural to separate them.View image in fullscreenEd Sheeran delivers a speech to his fans after support acts pulled out of his tour.Photograph: Ed Sheeran InstagramAgain, this is not new. The enmeshment of entertainment and politics is organic and part of many conflicts and political outrages in recent memory. Vietnam, South Africa, Darfur – all had a cohort of celebrities involved in objecting, lobbying and raising awareness. Figures such as Macklemore orGary LinekerorMark RuffaloorMs Rachelare not breaking with convention and plunging industries into turmoil and controversy, but partaking in a long legacy of activism that includes, to name a few, Nina Simone,Donald Sutherland,Kurt Vonnegut,Marlon Brando, Mia Farrow,George Michaeland George Clooney.You can disagree with the stances they have taken. But the belief that they are somehow not qualified to take and express them, and that art and entertainment are sacrosanct, is ignorant at best, disingenuous at worst. Public figures are people who have the same passions that everybody else has, and they have politics that they wish to advance with the tools at their disposal. Some people go on protests, give money, write to their representatives; others have a public forum and a profile they can leverage.They don’t have a responsibility to do so, but absolutely have the right to. And I suspect the reason they are met with such belittlement and outrage by their opponents is that there is an understanding that once politics spills over into entertainment, an uncontainable sort of trouble starts. This is where the separation of art and politics becomes a denial of the role the former plays in our psyches. Artists, writers, entertainers and sportspeople provide escapism, yes, if that’s what you want to get out of their work, but they also channel an expansiveness of the soul. They are fundamentally a collectivising force, one trained on a talent that stirs feeling. That is why you pick up a book or listen to a song or watch a movie or follow a team, to feel something. It is an exercise in being human, often in communion with others.View image in fullscreenMarlon Brando marches with members of the Congress of Racial Equality to protest an all-white housing area in Torrance, California on 1 January 1963.Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann ArchiveOnce politics enters that relationship, it becomes ungovernable. It can move the parameters of public opinion and discourse in ways that are hard to mediate, so direct is the relationship between the artists and their audience. Which is why the main criterion that renders this activism laudable or not is how much it is blessed by political and economic establishments.Often it is not a problem in itself; sometimes it is even rewarded. Sheeran himselfheadlineda concert for Ukraine. Don Cheadle and George Clooney receivedaccoladesfor their Sudan activism. But when artists’ politics clashes with powerful sponsors, as it did when Gillette Stadium owner Robert KraftremovedMacklemore from the Sheeran lineup, it all becomes less straightforward, so complicated, so bedevilled by nuance that could not possibly be litigated adequately by dilettantes.These collisions are an automatic feature of societies in which politics is failing. The outrage in Palestine is roiling culture because it has been so smothered in politics, because the pain and fury resulting from what the world is witnessing has not been appropriately channelled or responded to by a representative leadership – in fact, it has beenpoliced and criminalised. The spillover into every other part of our lives is inevitable. A healthy political culture should view these spillovers not as crude transgressions into private spaces of consumption, but democracy by other means, because electoral democracy has not squared up to the task.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs long as that remains the case, any demands that politics stay out of – you can insert any industry here – are summoning a world that does not exist, cannot exist and has never existed. In fact, they are asking for a sort of bovine state in which we are shepherded from trough to trough, chewing for momentary satiation on a cultural diet that must remain disconnected from feeling, connection and relation to other human beings. This can be a resonant message in a world in which there is so much duress. But it is an entirely unnatural state that keeps being disrupted by many people looking up from their moments of apportioned relief to be confronted with suffering of such magnitude that its acceptance can only be achieved through a sort of excising of humanity.The problem is not the outspoken artists and entertainers; the problem is what they are speaking about. I wish that the enduring agony of Palestinians were not litigated by the sound and fury and discursive froth of high entertainment, but this is where the politics has brought us. If you want to leave politics out of it, then demand that the politics do the work. Until then, it will be in your music and literature and film, fighting the coercion and bullying that hides behind concern for purity of art, but is really in the business of making you lose your soul.Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsActivismOpinionEd SheeranMacklemoreIsrael-Gaza warCelebritycommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Being in Madness kept some of them out of jail’: how the baggy-trousered nutty boys made a guerrilla cinema classic | Madness | The Guardian
description: From a jail-inspired light sabre fight to the moment a sax-player flew, Take It or Leave It brilliantly captured the band’s grimy origins. Will the film’s return see it finally honoured as a music movie landmark?
Author: Stevie Chick
Headline: From a jail-inspired light sabre fight to the moment a sax-player flew, Take It or Leave It brilliantly captured the band’s grimy origins. Will the film’s return see it finally honoured as a music movie landmark?
Content: ‘Like kids at school showing off’ … Madness filming the music video for Our House in 1982.Photograph: Clare Muller/RedfernsView image in fullscreen‘Like kids at school showing off’ … Madness filming the music video for Our House in 1982.Photograph: Clare Muller/RedfernsMadness‘Being in Madness kept some of them out of jail’: how the baggy-trousered nutty boys made a guerrilla cinema classicFrom a jail-inspired light sabre fight to the moment a sax-player flew, Take It or Leave It brilliantly captured the hit-makers’ grimy origins. Will the film’s return see it finally honoured as a music movie landmark?Stevie ChickMon 21 Sep 2026 09.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 15.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s March 1981 andMadnessare revisiting the haunts of their recent youth with a film crew in tow. In the 18 months since releasing their debut single, The Prince, the group have become the UK’s most beloved hit-makers, their ascent abetted by inventive music videos that have left viewers of Top of the Pops and Tiswas believing a man could fly – while blowing a sax.But this new project is something else. Instead of squandering their newfound wealth on fast cars and country piles, the seven-piece have invested in a semi-fictional big-screen telling of their origin story that tempers their trademark “nuttiness” with a kitchen-sink realism suiting their working-class roots. While Take It or Leave It sank into obscurity soon after release, a new 4K restoration has primed the film for rediscovery as a time-capsule of grimy 70s London, and perhaps cinema’s most honest depiction of the challenges involved in trying to get a band together.The movie was the brainchild of Dave Robinson, honcho of Stiff Records. Back in 1979, Robinson triumphed in the bidding war for Madness, then in their late teens and early 20s. “There was a special connection,” the charismatic Dublin-born mogul says today. “To them I was ‘Uncle Dave’.”View image in fullscreenAll naturals … Madness filming Take It or Leave It in 1981.Photograph: BFIRobinson recognised Madness as more than just prodigiously talented musicians and songwriters. “We were these different characters, jumping around and clowning about, like kids at school showing off,” says keyboardist Mike Barson. “Dave encouraged that.” Uncle Dave intuited this energy would flourish in the embryonic music-video format, hiring Chuck Statler – who’d made memorable clips forDevoand worked quick and cheap – to film Madness’s first promos. Dave took over the reins for 1980’s My Girl, working even quicker and cheaper. “I was also running a record label,” he says, “so we’d have to get the videos done in a day.”But Robinson never compromised his youthful charges’ imaginative approach. Saxophonist Lee Thompson tested the label-owner’s impressive ability to “make things happen” with 1980’s Baggy Trousers. “I told Robbo I wanted to play sax while flying through the air,” says Thompson, who arrived at the shoot to find Robinson had booked a forklift and kirby wire. The resulting stunt became part of the group’s iconography.double quotation markTracking shots were filmed by a cameraman in a trolley or on a bicycleWhen Robinson began work on Take It or Leave It, he says, “people told me it couldn’t be done, that we were mad”. He tapped the band members and manager John “Kelloggs” Kalinowski for £20,000 each (“the price of a fuckin’ two-bedroom in NW5 back then”, says Thompson), covering the rest of the budget himself. “I had planned to shoot it in a week,” he says. But when Robinson arrived on set the first day he was greeted by “50 guys staring at me, eating bacon sandwiches”. Unlike the videos, the movie was “a unionised shoot”, and Robinson sensed this crew would slow him down. “I had to get rid of them. I paid them all off and they never turned up again.”Crew purged, he returned to his “typical smash-and-grab, guerrilla-film-making methods”. Frontman Graham “Suggs” McPherson remembers tracking shots being filmed “by a cameraman in a trolley or on a bicycle”; overhead shots involved “someone hanging off a stepladder”. Robinson rarely sought permission to shoot locations, guitarist Chris Foreman describing their mindset as “do it quick enough and they can’t tell you to stop. By the time some jobsworth comes along, you’ve already finished.” It was a vibe they’d learned as teenage delinquent graffiti artists.Unsurprisingly, Madness took care of the soundtrack, covering Elvis Presley and Fats Domino tracks – often poorly, on purpose, to suggest the roughness of their first incarnations – and performing their own songs during scenes replicating early gigs. They also cut new songs such as Don’t Look Back, a funk track heard during a party scene, and co-wrote the script – what there was of it.View image in fullscreenDelinquent graffiti artists … the film’s smash-and-grab guerrilla-film-making methods harked back to the bands teenage years in Camden.Photograph: BFIBefore production began, Robinson interviewed the group about their early days, boiling his research down to 30 scenes that told the Madness story. On set, the band members would ad-lib these scenes with “great older actors” Robinson had hired to play authority figures. His cast were, he says, “all naturals”. McPherson remembers Robinson screening “Kes, Bronco Bullfrog, Mean Streets and some British kitchen-sink dramas, to get that vibe of just being ourselves”. He also took them to see Raging Bull, Thompson adds, which was “an eye-opener: black and white, grainy, gritty,real. Dave wanted that as our inspiration.”Realism was paramount. Robinson filmed scenes where they’d actually happened: shabby rehearsal rooms; legendary Camden hostelry The Dublin Castle; the Crouch End home of Mike Barson’s mum, where the group first formed. “Dave used cameramen who’d worked on documentaries,” says bassist Mark Bedford, “and the film was close to a documentary – most things had really happened.”“We’d done all these psychedelic videos,” McPherson adds, “but our aim now was to capture the dreary reality of forming a band.” The first 20 minutes of the movie are in black and white, he says, “because Londonfeltfuckin’ black and white in the late 70s”. There’s little of the manic visual invention of their music videos, although a set-piece where Thompson drives a van into a low bridge during brief, ill-fated employment on a building site is a masterpiece of comic pacing. A plan for the streets to turn into marshmallow after a wild night out was nixed due to budget – and a worry this family-friendly band shouldn’t let on that some members enjoyed psychedelics.Nevertheless, Take It or Leave It is a very funny film, much of its comedy coming from Barson. “Mike had a role he could sink his teeth into: the bad guy,” says Foreman. As the sardonic ringleader of this unruly circus, he excoriates band members for bum notes, bad attitudes and, in McPherson’s case, ditching rehearsal to go see his beloved Chelsea FC. Barson’s abrasive manner, which Bedford says was “slightly exaggerated” for the film, sees off McPherson, Thompson and vocalist/trumpeter Cathal Smyth for brief periods, although everyone agrees that without Barson’s “doggedness”, the band would never have made it. “Mike was the engine,” says Bedford.View image in fullscreen‘It’s clear the youthful Madness aren’t Brit School graduates’ … an image from Dave Robinson’s private collection.Photograph: Dave RobinsonThroughout, there is a sense that this beloved pop-cultural institution might easily have never happened, for all the everyday, low-drama reasons so many bands implode: internal ructions, the interminable juggle of creative ambitions and real-life responsibilities – and the eternal struggle to find a decent drummer. When the lineup finally coalesces and the artists formerly known as the North London Invaders rehearse as Madness for the first time, it makes for electrifying cinema.Not least because of the stakes at play. Throughout the film, it’s clear the youthful Madness aren’t Brit School graduates or posh kids slumming it before taking a job at daddy’s firm. Thompson can’t get saxophone lessons because his horn is stolen and its serial number has been rubbed off. Suggs’ chronic truancy and misbehaviour solicit the unwelcome attention of social services, looking to remove him from his mum’s care. One gig ends with an ambush by skinheads in the toilets, the band narrowly escaping a clobbering in their Morris Minors.On the commentary track for an earlier DVD release, Robinson said: “The system didn’t know what to do with young lads who weren’t nasty but were just trying to have a laugh.” Today, he reckons “being in Madness kept some of these lads out of jail”. The film reveals an edge that wasn’t obvious while the group was clowning with Tiswas’s Phantom Flan Flinger, but surfaced on grittier songs like Embarrassment, Overdone and Not Home Today.“I was at a crossroads,” nods Thompson, whose dad had been in prison multiple times. He remembers wondering, “‘Do I stick with the band, or hang around the bus stop sniffing glue?’ The pal who got me my saxophone, he was later stabbed to death in the Music Machine.”Barson’s crossroads moment is depicted in the film, although it’s played as fantasy, he and friend Si Birdsall discovering neon tube-lights, wielding them like light-sabres and evading the coppers. In reality, they actually got caught smashing lightbulbs by transport police and were sentenced to three weeks at Wormwood Scrubs. En route to prison, his police van passed Buckingham Palace, and he saw the bus he used to ride into central London.View image in fullscreenAt a crossroads … the light-sabre scene was inspired by Barson’s arrest and imprisonment for smashing neon lights.Photograph: BFI“I thought, ‘If I was free, I could get on that bus, go home and make myself a cup of tea. But now I’m wondering if they’re going to strip-search us and hose us with disinfectant when we get there.’ I was scared. After that, I pulled back from hanging out with them kids who were into wild, aggressive things and put that energy into music. Years later, in 2012, we played on the roof of Buckingham Palace and the queen waved up at us.”“We were all on a spectrum of petty criminality, growing up in an environment of violence,” says McPherson, “though none of us had that thing where you’ve been beaten into wanting to hurt other people. There was a crossroads where some in our gang were definitely going criminal, and we were the artistic side of that coin. Criminality boils down to: are you prepared to shoot someone? And no, I’m not. I don’t think I had the guts for it. The band was our way out.”Ultimately, the shoot took longer than a week: memories vary, but somewhere between a fortnight and a month. Robinson broke his foot midway through but says: “At the end, we all clapped each other on the back and said, ‘We got away with it!’ We were thinking it’d go on the art film circuit. But it played in one cinema in Camden and that was it. We didn’t get a big campaign from the distributor, which it needed.”Although the Guardian’s Derek Malcolm gave the film a positive review, and a VHS release sold well to the Madness faithful, Take It or Leave It was quickly forgotten. A couple of years later, after theirguest appearances on The Young Ones, that show’s creatives, Ben Elton and Richard Curtis,filmed a pilotfor a proposed Madness sitcom. “The premise was that we ran Britain and had to solve some big problem every week,” remembers Foreman. “ITV were interested, but we were holding out for the BBC. Then Mike left the group, so it came to nothing.”‘We met Princess Margaret and she was paralytic!’ My wild life onboard the Adam and the Ants Antmania rollercoasterRead moreLater, McPherson auditioned for Julien Temple’s Absolute Beginners, but broke his big toe while training with the choreographer. “So that was the beginning and the end of my film career,” he sighs, though he doesn’t really sound very disappointed. “Madness was always my priority,” he explains, “and I’m so glad. If I’d gone into acting, I’d never have achieved everything I did with the band. You can’t have it all.”While he never made another film, Robinson is still active, organising benefit concerts for the children of Ukraine. Madness released their 12th album in 2023 and recently completed a summer tour. The restoration has them reflecting on their movie, and the passage of time. For Barson, four-and-a-half decades have caused reality and near-reality to blur. “When I try to remember what really happened, I get stuck on how it happened in the film,” he says. “The reality has become inaccessible because that film gets in the way.”The film is now a time capsule for a bygone age: the band comment longingly on machines on the tube selling 40p tickets and the ability to park your car wherever you wanted. Other memories are more heartfelt. “Gary Dovey, who was briefly our drummer and played himself in the film, was a good friend of mine,” says Bedford. “He died a few years ago, and it’s amazing to see him on screen, speaking and being himself.”“I was so disappointed with the film when we finished it,” adds McPherson. “I thought it was prosaic and boring. But now – it’s just so charming. We were friends, most of us, before the band started, and we are good friends now. To see our story up on screen makes me very proud. I love those guys. I fuckinglovethem.”Take It or Leave It is in UK and Irish cinemas from 1 October, and on Blu-ray/DVD from 19 October.Explore more on these topicsMadnessSkaPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘My whole identity was wrapped up in Ally McBeal’ – Calista Flockhart on her smash hit 90s comedy rollercoaster | Television | The Guardian
description: ‘In the street or at restaurants, people still come up to me and say, “I became a lawyer because of you.” But I just went to work and said my lines!’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘In the street or at restaurants, people still come up to me and say, “I became a lawyer because of you.” But I just went to work and said my lines!’
Content: ‘When I moved to LA, I was too scared to get on the freeway for a year’ … Calista Flockhart with Jesse L Martin in season one of Ally McBeal.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘When I moved to LA, I was too scared to get on the freeway for a year’ … Calista Flockhart with Jesse L Martin in season one of Ally McBeal.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/Everett/ShutterstockHow we madeTelevision‘My whole identity was wrapped up in Ally McBeal’ – Calista Flockhart on her smash hit 90s comedy rollercoaster‘In the street or at restaurants, people still come up to me and say, “I became a lawyer because of you.” But I just went to work and said my lines!’Interviews by Lee CampbellMon 21 Sep 2026 08.12 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 18.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCalista Flockhart, played Ally McBealI was doing a play in New York, Three Sisters by Chekhov. We regularly got scripts sent to us. One going around was written by David E Kelley. I flew out to Los Angeles to screen test, and I got the part right in the moment. It was a difficult transition as I felt very much settled and happy in New York and I had only been to LA briefly, to shoot The Birdcage. I was such a bad driver that I didn’t get on the freeway there for a year. I was afraid of it.Playing Ally McBeal was exciting and I was up for the challenge, but it was daunting. It was also very collaborative. Everybody fed each other and we all worked it out together. We started shooting in July and were on air in September, so there was this beautiful brief time when it was just ours. I remember that very well. Then, very quickly, it became popular.David is a genius. What I love about his writing is his imagination – there’s no ceiling on it. At first, I thought the dancing baby was really weird. David was so excited about it but I really did not get it. Then, of course, I realised it was quite brilliant. Ally’s biological clock is ticking, and she’s being haunted by some weird, spooky dancing baby. It’s awesome. By nature, I’m a little on the shy side, so I had to find a place in myself to forget about being embarrassed. I just danced crazy and wild because it was sort of reflective of Ally’s inner life.double quotation markWhen Al Green guest starred I had the good fortune of dancing with him. It was magicalIn one episode – Seeing Green – I was having hallucinations ofAl Green. He guest-starred and I had the good fortune of dancing with him. It was filmed very late at night, with rain on the street, and it was so magical. He showed Ally the moves and I tried to do them. Then he flew away and Ally was left standing there alone. It was beautifully written. He is such a kind, sweet soul.In terms of the music, I wouldn’t even say that it was part of the show – the musicwasthe show. The minute you heard Searchin’ My Soul, you wanted to live in this life. I really identified with Vonda Shepard’s music and it was very reflective of what Ally was feeling. It was a way for characters to communicate with each other.At the end of most days shooting, I was emotionally raw – I was pretty much there all day, every day. I was just so totally spent from the rollercoaster of Ally McBeal’s life and where I had to go to get there. In the end, after five seasons, it had sort of run its course and done what it set out to do, but my whole identity was wrapped up in Ally McBeal for five years. My son was about one then and I was really happy to have the time with him, but it was sad to say goodbye to everybody. There’s such a strong bond between us that will never go, even though our lives have gone in many, many different directions.Sometimes at a restaurant or on the street, people come up to me and say: “I became a lawyer because of you.” Then I say: “No, you became a lawyer because of David Kelley.” It had nothing to do with me. I just went to work and said the lines. He had the hard job.Vonda Shepard,musicianI had made two albums, but then I got dropped. I was struggling. I was lugging my keyboard to gigs in the rain, playing in tiny clubs. I have been friends with Michelle Pfeiffer since I was 18, before she was married to David Kelley. The two of them came to see me play one evening, which turned out to be the turning point of my life.About a week later, I got a call from David. The songs that I was playing were from my albumIt’s Good, Eveand they resonated with the character he was writing about, he told me. David wanted me to singTell Him by the Excitersas the theme song, but my manager and I really wanted one of my own songs. So, we played them five of them, including Searchin’ My Soul, and David said: “If you can squeeze that song into one minute, that can be the theme song.” So, we just sped it up and they loved it.‘Such a water-cooler show!’ Jane Krakowski on Ally McBeal – and life as the world’s biggest scene-stealerRead moreOvernight, I went from playing for 30 people to 5,000 people. We won a Golden Globe, we won an Emmy. It changed my life. But I don’t care about being famous – I just want to be able to play music for people who like it and share that with them, and the show gave me that gift.I went on to produce more than 500 songs during its five years. It was more like a musical. It was very fulfilling, watching the music come together. When I was 16, one of my favourite albums was The Belle Album by Al Green. At the end of one track, he laughs. It’s so solidly locked into my memory. We were in the studio with him recording his vocals for an episode and all of a sudden, Al Green sings a take, and he does the laugh. I thought, “Oh, my God, I’ve really made it.”Searchin’ My Soul had the struggle and the challenge and then the breakthrough of the positive ending, the uplifting side of it. The show was a magical experience. I think back on it with such appreciation. You feel that connection and emotion, and it’s genuine.Vonda Shepardtoursthe UKand Irelandfrom 1 October. Her new album,Nine Songs, is out on25 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTelevisionHow we madeDramaTV comedyAl GreenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sense and Sensibility review – Daisy Edgar-Jones leads sober-minded next-gen do-over of Austen romcom | Movies | The Guardian
description: With Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as the Dashwood sisters, this fresh take on a beloved classic is not to be confused with Ang Lee’s
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: With Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as the Dashwood sisters, this fresh take on a beloved classic is not to be confused with Ang Lee’s
Content: Jane again … Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles in Sense and Sensibility.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus FeaturesView image in fullscreenJane again … Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles in Sense and Sensibility.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus FeaturesMoviesReviewSense and Sensibility review – Daisy Edgar-Jones leads sober-minded next-gen do-over of Austen romcomWith Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as the Dashwood sisters, this fresh take on a beloved classic is not to be confused with Ang Lee’sPeter BradshawMon 21 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s no reason for anyone working on a new adaptation of Jane Austen’s Sense and Sensibility to be intimidated bythe celebrated 1995 movieby director Ang Lee and screenwriter Emma Thompson, any more than they should be or overawed by Austen’s original novel. Sacred cows are there to be … not slain, but re-invented. The decision to bring out a next-gen Sense and Sensibility, with a new young cast – as opposed to, say, a new Northanger Abbey ora new spin on the unfinished The Watsons– might bemuse some and at first it bemused me, like hearing about a Love Actually remake starring Millie Bobby Brown. But this turns out to be a more downbeat, ruminative version, happening in much cloudier weather than 30 years ago and without the sugar-rush final wedding scene. The mood is cooler, but interestingly austere, sober and thoughtful. There are also some strange casting decisions.The sisters at the heart of the story, Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, played in 1995 by Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet, are now played byDaisy Edgar-Jonesand Esmé Creed-Miles, and frankly don’t look and sound much like the sisters we thought we knew. They look like young women who knew each other reasonably well at uni and are now in a flatshare in London. It is a story of financial and romantic crisis. Mrs Dashwood and her three daughters, having happily occupied a handsome Sussex estate, are forced to move to humble Barton Cottage in Devon when Mrs Dashwood’s stepson John Dashwood inherits their property and effectively evicted them.Before this can happen, Elinor meets and falls for young Edward Ferrars, a shy and decent young man of a well-to-do family, reticently portrayed byGeorge MacKay. Here, in fact, it should be said that Diana Reid’s script and Georgia Oakley’s direction put into valuably sharper focus something left unstressed in 1995: that Mrs Dashwood (Caitríona Balfe) is pointedly insisting on moving away to the west country rather than endure the indignity of her daughter seeming to be a gold-digger.It is in the wilds of Devon that Elinor broods unhappily on why Edward isn’t proposing marriage, and where the headstrong, romantic Marianne twists her ankle while out for a walk and is carried back to the cottage by dishy dreamboat-cad Mr Willoughby. The latter is played by Frank Dillane with a certain amount of insidious charm, but also a sort of Uriah Heep smirk. And Marianne does not see the integrity and all-round loveliness of the gallant ex-soldier who is poignantly in love with her: Colonel Brandon, heavily and inexplicably played behind hefty facial hair by Norwegian actor Herbert Nordrum.Now, no actor would want to follow Alan Rickman from 1995 in the role of Colonel Brandon. But Nordrum, genuinely great inJoachim Trier’s Oslo-set comedy drama The Worst Person in the World, is just an eccentric, stolid outlier in this context; his line-readings feel unengaged and he doesn’t seem to be that moonstruck by Marianne, or particularly enthused by anything much at all. Of course, some of the film’s (worthwhile) intention is to push against envelopes and stereotypes and I quite enjoyed the gender-challenging casting of Eliot Sumner, icily playing Mr Palmer. But Brandon feels uncomfortable.The scene-stealer is the mischievous, gossipy and forthright Mrs Jennings, marvellously played byFiona Shaw, who brings up the voltage every time she comes on and effectively makes of it a far bigger role than Elizabeth Spriggs in the same part in 1995. Overall, the movie always looks and sounds perfectly good, though some of the sensibility is lacking.Sense and Sensibility is out on 25 September in the UK, 15 October in Australia and 16 October in the US.Explore more on these topicsFilmFilm adaptationsJane AustenRomance filmsDrama filmsDaisy Edgar-JonesGeorge MacKayreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sylvia Plath Stole My Boyfriend: the 95-year-old who has turned her romance with Ted Hughes into a play | Australian theatre | The Guardian
description: The Yorkshire poet had a ‘magic touch’, Liz Hicklin recalls, felt by many women: ‘It was like I was blossoming’
Author: Jenny Valentish
Headline: The Yorkshire poet had a ‘magic touch’, Liz Hicklin recalls, felt by many women: ‘It was like I was blossoming’
