Content: ‘I went around the world trying to recreate Ted Hugheses, but they didn’t match up,’ says Liz Hicklin, pictured with her collaborator, ABC radio presenter Jacinta Parsons.Photograph: Penny Stephens/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I went around the world trying to recreate Ted Hugheses, but they didn’t match up,’ says Liz Hicklin, pictured with her collaborator, ABC radio presenter Jacinta Parsons.Photograph: Penny Stephens/The GuardianAustralian theatreSylvia Plath Stole My Boyfriend: the 95-year-old who has turned her romance with Ted Hughes into a playThe Yorkshire poet had a ‘magic touch’, Liz Hicklin recalls, felt by many women: ‘It was like I was blossoming’Jenny ValentishMon 21 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 19.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiz Hicklin had missed the ferry that could change her life. Pelting rain had made the drive to the Sorrento terminal perilous. Sitting in the car park, watching the boat glide off, she chastised herself.Go home. Don’t be ridiculous. You’re 92.She got on the next ferry.This decision would prove to be a sliding doors moment. As Hicklin, now 95, says: “I really should be knitting” – but instead she debuts her first play at Melbourne fringe festival this October:Sylvia Plath Stole My Boyfriend, about her romantic relationship with a young Ted Hughes.By getting to the Queenscliffe literary festival that day, Hicklin managed to track down the ABC radio presenter Jacinta Parsons. The pair had met fleetingly months before at Clunes Booktown festival, where Parsons, author of A Question of Ageand A Wisdom of Age, hosted a panel about ageing. Hicklin was a spirited audience member (later that day she won a poetry slam) and the two women started talking. Upon being reunited in Queenscliffe, Parsons eventually became Hicklin’s manager.View image in fullscreenHicklin and Hughes read poetry and wrote feverish letters to each otherWhen the three of us meet, we’re surrounded by art and books in Hicklin’s apartment in a residential care home on the Mornington Peninsula. Parsons buzzes in and out, making phone calls. In private, Hicklin says: “Jacinta’s changed my life completely. I’m living life again.” Whenever Parsons sits down, the dynamic switches into a double act.“I’m going to talk about you while I’m looking at your face,” Parsons tells her, cupping Hicklin’s cheek. “Look – you’re so anxious that you’re turning on me like a dog.”At 92, Liz Hicklin embarked on a standup career: ‘I didn’t think about ageing until I was over 90’Read more“You’re an academic and I’m so run of the mill,” Hicklin protests. It’s a recurring theme, as if being self-educated later in life disqualifies her from being taken seriously.While Parsons, as co-director, used Hicklin’s wealth of writing to populate the play, Hicklin is “used to being in control” and worries that there’s too much Plath. “Who’s the drawcard here, Sylvia or me?” she wonders.Hicklin never met Plath, her romantic rival. There’s a hefty compendium of Plath’s poetry sitting on her side table but she doesn’t particularly rate it. She met Hughes, who served as the British poet laureate for 14 years, when studying nursing in Cambridge. They read poetry to each other in local pubs, writing feverish letters whenever apart.“It was like I was blossoming, she says. “I’d get on the bus to Hebden Bridge and immediately feel different, as though they felt things more deeply in Yorkshire. It was his magic touch – that he touched many women with, as we learned.”Amid their romance Hicklin took the opportunity to travel (“a woman’s got to keep her options open”) first to Canada, then Australia. “I went around the world trying to recreate Ted Hugheses but they didn’t match up,” she says.The pair kept writing to each other, with Hughes describing his own travels. “His whole life was trying to conjure up a living that would give him time to write,” Hicklin says. “One idea was to run a boarding house. His uncle Walt ran a trouser factory, so there was that idea … and another was to be a mink farmer.”Eventually, the letters dried up. When Hicklin sent Hughes a Christmas card from Melbourne she received a reply from his mother: “I don’t think you know, dear, that Ted marriedSylvia Plath, a Fulbright Scholar.”Hicklin took to her bed and cried for three days.After Plath’s suicide in 1963, Hicklin was visiting her parents when Hughes and his new partner, Assia Wevill, arranged to visit. “All these years I dreamt of meeting Ted again, I’d hoped I’d be willowy thin,” she says. “He rang the doorbell with Assia, and she was very London literary, shabby chic. I felt very colonial in my eight-months pregnant state, my arms covered in flour.”It was the last time she saw Hughes but she kept his letters and postcards, and two of his unpublished poems, eventually selling the originals to the British Library. Hughes may have called both Hicklin and Plath “Bunny” but it’s possible that only Hicklin got the nickname “Winklepumpkin”.View image in fullscreenHicklin and Parsons at Carlton’s Trades Hall, where the sold-out show will be staged in October.Photograph: Penny Stephens/The Guardian“It was only a short time in my life – of course I’ve milked it,” she says drily. “I’m certainly not like these comedians that seem to talk about nothing. How do they get away with it? But they do.”Sylvia Plath Stole My Boyfriend is an upbeat 50-minute show with a gameshow theme. There’s a voiceover from the Sale of the Century host Pete Smith (now 87 himself) that serves as Hicklin’s inner critic;Plath (played by a co-director, Sarah Sutherland) is the gift-shop showgirl.The play includes other eras of Hicklin’s life, such as raising a family in Melbourne. “We jogged along but I did have an affair,” she says of her marriage. “It was like Mad Men. Our friends were my husband’s work partners, so they weren’t my choice. Our husbands were in advertising, so they were members of clubs, out until midnight. You kept their dinner warm over a pan of hot water. There was nothing to stimulate you on the radio, which was your only companion.”Tragedy also stalked Hicklin, including the suicides of her two daughters. The play asks if we can ever truly make sense of life, even with the wisdom of age.Parsons has taken time off from the ABC to work on a documentary in which Hicklin’s story “becomes the micro in a macro look at ageing”. She’s already made trips to Hicklin and Hughes’ old haunts, even persuading the current resident of The Beacon, Hughes’ former home in West Yorkshire, to let her in. “It’s been pretty fucking surreal, in a way,” Parsons says. “Just walking in someone’s shoes and connecting those pieces of their lives.”For Hicklin, who vividly recalls her walks with Hughes on the Yorkshire Moors – when he would mimic an animal in distress so that owls, stoats and rabbits gathered around him – the videos Parson sent back to her in Melbourne reignited the romance.“I even recognised the window that I’d look through at the shivering sheep,” she says. “It was magical for me.”In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.orgSylvia Plath Stole My Boyfriendis at Trades Hall in Carlton as part of the Melbourne fringe, 15-18 OctoberExplore more on these topicsAustralian theatreComedyTed HughesTheatreSylvia PlathfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Brown men are fearless, funny and sexy’: Salman Toor on clubbing, queerness and New York’s Muslim moment | Art | The Guardian
description: Toor’s electrifying pictures have made him a global star – and he’s even painted Zohran Mamdani. As the artist hits London’s prestigious Courtauld Gallery, he talks about Manet, mullahs and the mayor
Author: Malik Meer
Headline: Toor’s electrifying pictures have made him a global star – and he’s even painted Zohran Mamdani. As the artist hits London’s prestigious Courtauld Gallery, he talks about Manet, mullahs and the mayor
Content: Obsessed with Manet … Toor’s The Bar on East 13th pays tribute to A Bar at the Folies-Bergère.Photograph: Genevieve Hanson/© Salman Toor; Courtesy of the artist, Luhring Augustine, New York, and Thomas Dane GalleryView image in fullscreenObsessed with Manet … Toor’s The Bar on East 13th pays tribute to A Bar at the Folies-Bergère.Photograph: Genevieve Hanson/© Salman Toor; Courtesy of the artist, Luhring Augustine, New York, and Thomas Dane GalleryArtInterview‘Brown men are fearless, funny and sexy’: Salman Toor on clubbing, queerness and New York’s Muslim momentMalik MeerToor’s electrifying pictures have made him a global star – and he’s even painted Zohran Mamdani. As the artist hits London’s prestigious Courtauld Gallery, he talks about Manet, mullahs and the mayorMon 21 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Salman Toor’s paintings, queer south Asian men hang out in bars, twerk at trippy gatherings and lose themselves in phone screens. Sometimes they huddle in the back of taxis or pillow-fight on beds. In one portrait, a brown man stares apprehensively while facing customs officials. For the 43-year-old Pakistani American artist, it’s crucial that these figures take centre stage, after years of being demonised and erased.“It excites me that the cuteness and sexiness of brown protagonists can become familiar,” says Toor when we meet at his sun-drenched Brooklyn studio, a few weeks before his first solo show in Europe. “Their stories are not a gay side story in a family saga. It’s the main story. And everyone else is in the background.”Over the last decade, Toor has been helping to redraw the narratives around immigrants, desire, power and sex. His artwork – rich, figurative oil paintings that echo and subvert European old masters and Indian Mughal miniatures – has confirmed his status as an“international art star”(the New Yorker) and“one of the most fascinating painters of his generation”(the New York Times). Solo museum exhibitions in New York, Baltimore and Beijing have earned universal praise, while in November 2022, his painting Four Friends sold for $1.2m at Sotheby’s. Time recently included him in itsmost influential art people list.View image in fullscreenSignature style … Three Friends in a Cab.Photograph: Farzad Owrang/© Salman Toor; Courtesy of the artist, Luhring Augustine, New York, and Thomas Dane GalleryNext month, London’s Courtauld Gallery presents Someone Like You, a greatest hits of Toor’s paintings and drawings that he selected with the curator Elena Crippa. As it’s home to many of his favourite baroque and impressionist artists, he couldn’t be more thrilled. The Courtauld was one of the galleries he visited on his first trip to London from Pakistan. “It’s the most exciting thing that could happen,” he says, looking genuinely humbled.Dressed in black parachute trousers, a grey sleeveless T-shirt and chunky fashion trainers, Toor is friendly and eager to talk about his art, armed with a printout of images from the show. Like the themes in his work, our conversation moves from pop culture (no, this show is “absolutely not named after an Adele song”) to global politics (he regularly questions his “westernisation”) to family relationships (good, but they’d like to see fewer “willies” in his paintings).double quotation markI came out through painting – it was exciting because I felt freeAs an art student, Toor searched for inspiration at the Courtauld during his many “obsessive” periods. “I was looking at a lot of Rubens and Van Dyck,” he explains. He became particularly obsessed with Édouard Manet’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère. “I stood in front of it and I thought, ‘Oh my God, this has all the solutions to my problems’,” he laughs. In his 2019 painting The Bar on East 13th, Toor pays tribute to Manet’s masterpiece, relocating it to New York’s East Village, where hipster queer couples make out and a brown barman wearing nail polish and braided hair takes the place of the melancholy French barmaid and partying bourgeoisie.Looking at that image now, Toor has mixed feelings: “I had just come out through painting so it was exciting because I felt free. It was a time of well-deserved self-love. But I also felt in danger: I was getting a lot of negative, threatening messages online. I’m from a country which is very conservative. Those are very specific feelings from that time.”Toor was born in Lahore, Pakistan, into a middle-class Muslim family. To avoid his sporty schoolmates, the young artist sought refuge in the art department of the city’s elite Aitchison College and honed his talent. He moved to the US in 2002 to study art in Columbus, Ohio, where he felt isolated until he moved into a hippy commune with“the dreadlocked, blue-haired art kids”. In 2009, he graduated with a master’s in fine arts from New York’s Pratt Institute.View image in fullscreenWalls covered in sketches and ideas … Toor in his studio.Photograph: Sambit BiswasWithin a few years, Toor landed on his signature style: emerald green compositions with explicit gay themes based on his and his friends’ experiences navigating culture and belonging in New York City. In previous interviews, he’s explained that he chose green because it is simultaneously glamorous and poisonous. Today, Toor adds that it has an “atmospheric aspect that you can go deeper inside, an outdoor or nocturnal forest-like place beckoning you”. Most of the artworks in Someone Like You were produced in the last seven years, during which Toor gained US citizenship. “They’re images about immigration and people on the verge of … the threshold of the free world or whatever.” He pauses, reflecting on the reality of US politics. “Or maybe not.”Toor is excited to be in London for the exhibition. He has fond memories of visiting friends in the city in the early 00s, going to Soho bars and the trashy pop club G-A-Y before taking a night bus home to Streatham – “shades on, getting a doner kebab,” he says. “We were just kids. London was a city that opened me up to gay nightlife and art history.”The city also provides a setting in one image. Cross Street grew out of a scene he glimpsed from the window of a favourite London restaurant: Tayyabs in Whitechapel. It shows a group of buff skaters hanging by a street sign as a mullah passes by. Toor was struck by “the proximity of two kinds of people” and wanted to capture the different threads of masculinity that were intimidating to him growing up: the school bullies on one hand and the religious figure on the other.View image in fullscreenBuff skaters … Toor’s painting Cross Street grew out of a scene he glimpsed from a London restaurant.Photograph: Salman Toor; Courtesy of the artist, Luhring Augustine, New York, and Thomas Dane GalleryRight now, Toor lives in New York with his partner, the musicianAli Sethi, in a thrilling moment for the city’s south Asian and Middle Eastern communities. Across politics, culture and arts, New York is witnessing a historic surge of energy and creativity that’s been given a confidence boost by the election of mayor Zohran Mamdani. Earlier this year, the Guardian profiled many ofMuslim New York’sartists, organisers and thinkers while New York magazine devoted a special issue to mark the shifting sands of “Habibi City”.“It’s Mamdani’s New York,” Toor beams. “What I love about this city is that there’s a wonderful connection of artists and creative people who are part of our circle.” As a first-generation immigrant he’s excited to see new worlds unfolding around him, the classicNew York story, concrete jungle where dreams are made: “People are brilliant at finding new solutions to being from traditional backgrounds, and choosing and shedding things to be part of the future.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNot long after Mamdani won the Democratic nomination for mayor,a portrait by Toor of the future leadersurfaced on Instagram. Toor was asked by his friend, the film director Mira Nair, Zohran’s mother, to paint the family in 2007. “The group portrait didn’t come out that well. Mira has it locked up and I hope it remains in storage,” he laughs. “But I knew this [individual portrait of Zohran] was good. She was thrilled and it’s in their home. I saw it there recently.” How does he feel about the image now? “It’s more delicate and smaller than I remember. It’s more finely painted than I thought – at the time it was my idea of rough. Maybe I’ve become freer or grungy.”View image in fullscreenDelicate … Toor’s early portrait of Mamdani.Illustration: Salman Toor; Courtesy of the artist, Luhring Augustine, New York, and Thomas Dane GalleryHe won’t be drawn on Mamdani’s first nine months in office but he recently curated the low key exhibition In a Free State, with his friend, the Israeli American artist Doron Langberg. It was an attempt to deal with the global political horrors that left him creatively crippled and unable to paint figures for a five-month period. Showcasing their friends and others, including many Middle Eastern artists, it aimed to“visualise and contend with a chaotic and alienating time”. Toor says also he wanted to address the cynicism people have about art and politics.‘We weren’t shy. We were queers in leather!’ Sunil Gupta on his momentous photographs of gay lifeRead moreAfter Someone Like You opens, Toor will return to his artwork. The studio walls are covered with sketches and ideas; unfinished pieces include an experiment in painting an erect penis, a large image of workmen fixing a phallic air vent and some attempts at drawing dogs. There is also a portrait ofMahmoud Khalil, the Columbia University student who was detained for more than three months and became the face of the Trump administration’s crackdown on pro-Palestine speech. Toor was inspired to capture him after seeing Khalil give a powerful speech, he says, returning to the theme of the “brown protagonist”.Earlier in the interview we discussed the rise of a new generation of US politicians, including the Michigan senate candidate,Abdul El-Sayed. “The great thing about the new brown men that are so visible now is that they’re fearless,” he says. “They’re funny and they’re sexy. I would love to see the west deal with that.”Judging by thehysterical reactionto El-Sayed’s recent win and thebad faith attackson Zohran Mamdani, they don’t seem to be dealing with it very well, I suggest.“We’ll see,” he says firmly. “They should get used to it.”Salman Toor: Someone Like You is at the Courtauld, London, 2 October to 10 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArtNew YorkZohran MamdaniPaintingExhibitionsRace & religionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Love and respect’ or ‘a cash grab’? The furious battle over the final album by the Fall | Music | The Guardian
description: Creators of Post Script, made with vocals by the late Mark E Smith, defend it as ‘a great, positive record’, but fiancee describes it as ‘ethically wrong’
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: Creators of Post Script, made with vocals by the late Mark E Smith, defend it as ‘a great, positive record’, but fiancee describes it as ‘ethically wrong’
Content: ‘Is it the Fall? Well, Mark is the Fall, so yes, these are Fall songs’ … Mark E Smith in 2007.Photograph: Everynight Images/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Is it the Fall? Well, Mark is the Fall, so yes, these are Fall songs’ … Mark E Smith in 2007.Photograph: Everynight Images/AlamyMusic‘Love and respect’ or ‘a cash grab’? The furious battle over the final album by the FallCreators of Post Script, made with vocals by the late Mark E Smith, defend it as ‘a great, positive record’, but fiancee describes it as ‘ethically wrong’Dave SimpsonMon 21 Sep 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 08.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe fiancee and last manager of the lateMark E Smith, frontman of the Fall, has hit out against the release of an album being marketed as the band’s final official album, calling it “ethically wrong” and a “cash grab”.When Post Script was first announced in June, several media reports assumed the nine-track album contained recordings that the final Fall lineup were working on before the singer’s death, in January 2018. However, it subsequently emerged that it contains unused studio vocals recorded between 2001 and 2014, to which longtime Fall associates Ed Blaney and Simon “Ding” Archer have posthumously added music.Pamela Vander said: “They’re selling it as ‘the final album’ so people will think Mark made it on his deathbed, but none of it [vocally] was made after New Facts Emerge [2017]. I have Mark’s actual last recordings – he was working on a cover of Madonna’s Material Girl – but by the time of his death he had made the decision that New Facts Emerge was the final album, made by the longest-lasting lineup of the Fall, who were with Mark for 10 years. So I don’t think anyone else should override a decision he made when he was alive.”A digital single, 30 Degrees, was released in June. The album is set for release by Cog Sinister on 2 October on CD, black vinyl, limited edition white vinyl and digital formats, with the approval of Smith’s estate. However, Vander said: “Mark’s life was complicated and Mark was very disorganised when it came to any sort of protection for his legacy. I was the manager and I’m not even sure who owns the name ‘the Fall’. It’s a cash grab, just a collection of some shit from the cutting room floor. I wouldn’t have minded if it was being released as ‘the Mark E Smith archive’ or something, but there’s something ethically wrong with releasing it as the Fall.”The situation is further complicated by the various parties’ long relationships with Smith. Blaney played in the Fall in the early 2000s, going on to be tour manager, manager and friend and their collaborations included the 2008 album Smith and Blaney. Archer, the group’s bassist in 2003-4, subsequently produced or engineered eight of the last nine Fall albums.View image in fullscreen‘Mark loved fronting the Fall’ … the band on Mark E Smith’s 50th birthday in 2007.Photograph: John Bentley/AlamyBlaney responded: “Making this record was intended as a fitting tribute to Mark/the Fall because the vocals were there waiting to be put to good use. Mark also trusted Ding whenever he worked with him, so the foundation was there. [In the studio] we felt Mark’s presence: things happened that had Mark’s hallmark all over them.“Words like ‘cashing in’ make me laugh. It was about love and respect for Mark: he was the Fall, and Mark’s vocals were recorded as the Fall, hence it’s being released as the Fall. Mark sounds great and it’s a great, positive record.”When approached for comment by the Guardian, Rob Ayling, director of Cog Sinister, said “the album speaks for itself”, and Archer declined to answer questions. He previously posted on Facebook: “I recorded most of Mark’s vocal takes for 12 years. We would regularly throw down Mark’s freshest ideas to whatever backing he deemed fit at the time: a drone, a drum beat or a cappella, or down the corridor to test the acoustics. Some of these ideas went to the band for development and some were dropped. Others went into the vault with phrases like ‘put that in the safe’ or ‘you can do what you like with that one, cock’. I’d never had the time to check the safe but Post Script provided an opportunity for these loose ends to be tied up. Ed and I found some gems that just needed fleshing out and arranging.“Neither of us are attempting to be the last lineup. The word ‘final’ in the original statement was meant to indicate it will be the last LP of unheard studio recordings. Is it the Fall? Well, Mark is the Fall, so yes, these are Fall songs. If you’re not convinced, don’t buy it.”View image in fullscreenMark E Smith and Pamela Vander.Photograph: Pamela VanderVander was in a relationship with Smith for the last three years of his life, painted the cover of New Facts Emerge, is named in his will (along with his three sisters) and became his carer when he was dying from lung and kidney cancer.LA fans, Mark E Smith’s sisters and Frank Skinner doing the quiz: inside the totally wired festival on the FallRead moreShe said: “He was my soulmate and I’ve not had another boyfriend since he passed. Mark loved fronting the Fall and it was his decision to keep performing until the very end. That man would have died on stage and been happy doing that. He wasn’t embarrassed or scared to go on stage in a wheelchair. To see someone going under physically like that – not being able to use his legs and such – but remain so sharp mentally to the very end was quite a thing to witness. After Salford Royal [hospital] let him go home, in the end it was just me and Mark in the house. When he passed it was almost supernatural. Rain suddenly started crashing down, like a monsoon. It messed me up for ages.”Having initially kept her counsel because “I’d not been in that [Fall] world for years”, she said she decided to speak out against the new release because “it’s been eating me up. I feel it’s still my job to stand up for Mark.”Explore more on these topicsMusicMark E SmithThe FallIndiePop and rockMusic industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Heart of the action: why organ couriers are cinema’s new heroes | Movies | The Guardian
description: Whether its a nod to frontline Covid heroes or a return to biology in a world of digital noise, there’s a rich vein of new films featuring organ deliveries, including Runner and the latest Resident Evil
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Whether its a nod to frontline Covid heroes or a return to biology in a world of digital noise, there’s a rich vein of new films featuring organ deliveries, including Runner and the latest Resident Evil
Content: A life or death mission … Owen Wilson and Alan Ritchson in Runner.Photograph: Runner Productions/PAView image in fullscreenA life or death mission … Owen Wilson and Alan Ritchson in Runner.Photograph: Runner Productions/PAMoviesHeart of the action: why organ couriers are cinema’s new heroesWhether its a nod to frontline Covid heroes or a return to biology in a world of digital noise, there’s a rich vein of new films featuring organ deliveries, including Runner and the latest Resident EvilJonathan WellsMon 21 Sep 2026 05.23 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHollywood loves a ticking clock – especially when there’s a delivery involved. For decades, dangerous cargo has been entrusted to certain types of action hero: spies, soldiers, hitmen, Jason Statham.Lately, however, Hollywood seems interested in a different kind of hero – not to mention a different kind of cargo. Forget your nuclear launch codes, stolen diamonds and mysterious briefcases, for human organs are the new MacGuffins du jour, and the medical professionals charged with getting them to the ICU have become unlikely action heroes.TakeRunner, directed by Scott Waugh, which stars Alan “Reacher” Ritchson as a delivery driver caught in a race against time, and Owen Wilson as an organ courier carrying a liver with a life-or-death deadline. “If she doesn’t get this today,” Wilson says of the girl awaiting the transplant, “she’s not going to make it.”It’s action movie gold. And using an organ as a plot device is smart because suspense is built into the biology: it’s a ticking clock in a cooler. It also unlocks a whole new melange of medical action scenarios: ambulance car chases, surgical scissor knife-fights, hospital shootouts. (Runner, naturally, has the full bloody bingo card.)Co-writer Miles Hubley says he and writing partner Tommy White wanted “a device that wasn’t just about money”, adding: “Neither of us had ever seen a movie where the precious cargo everyone wants was a fragile, life-saving piece of tissue.”View image in fullscreenHe stole my heart … Jason Statham in 2009’s Crank 2: High Voltage.Photograph: Lionsgate/Sportsphoto/AllstarWaugh agrees: an organ gives the film “emotional urgency”. “It’s the idea of a protagonist being driven not by revenge or saving the world, but simply by an obligation to deliver something on time,” he says. “You’ve got a deadline and someone whose life depends on you arriving.”Films such as bike-courier thrillerPremium Rushand the Safdie brothers’Uncut Gemshave set pulses racing using similar time-sensitive tactics, while Statham’s The Transporter built a whole franchise from the idea of a courier up against it. But the medical slant ups the ante even further: organs make the stakes more visceral, more personal.Crank 2: High Voltage understood this. Also starring Statham, it took the organ-chase motif one step further: his character was tasked with tracking down his own stolen heart. Repo Men flipped the script again, with Jude Law on the run to avoid having his artificial heart reclaimed. Organ drama is a rich vein, as it were.double quotation markThere’s something about how physical, vital and undeniably real an organ is ... It’s profoundly humanBut making the medical couriers the good guys is a new twist for 2026. Usually, characters in the organ game are on the shady side, whether in dramas such as Dirty Pretty Things or full-blown horror movies like The Harvest. A new horror, out a week after Runner, transplants this trope, giving theResident Evilfranchise a new protagonist: Austin Abrams’ medical courier.“This could be some eight-year-old boy’s heart or someone’s mom’s brain,” Abrams says in the film. But it’s also more than that. He’s carrying what everyone else is losing – their hope and humanity – in a medical bag. In fact, so important is this particular MacGuffin that US cinema chain Regal has turned it into anovelty popcorn bucket, fake bloodstains and all.View image in fullscreenIn the bag … Austin Abrams in Resident Evil.Photograph: CTMG/PABut why now? Why are medical couriers suddenly getting their action-hero moment? Perhaps it’s the pandemic, and we’re finally giving frontline workers their due. Of course you could go toe-to-toe with the cartel or endure an apocalyptic mutant zombie virus – you fought off Covid! Sure, it’s not much of a thank you, but getting the baddie-busting big-screen treatment beats 50% off at Pret and the odd round of applause.Hubley, too, says he wanted “grounded heroes, who you could imagine bumping into at the grocery store”. And an organ courier brings another dimension to that everyman appeal. “In a world with so much abstract digital noise, there’s something about how physical, vital and undeniably real an organ is. It’s a living thing that can’t be copied, faked or altered. It decays. It can’t be sent over email, or stored on a hard drive. It’s profoundly human.”Resident Evil review – Zach Cregger’s rebooted action horror is a wild rollercoaster rideRead moreNext year, Heartless will put another organ in the delivery bag. Jason Isaacs stars, while The Transporter Refuelled’s Camille Delamarre directs. Delamarre, too, sees a post-pandemic connection. “We’re more conscious of how fragile and irreplaceable the human body is,” says the director. “For me, an organ is the ultimate cargo because it’s not really cargo at all: it’s someone’s life. With a heart, you don’t need to explain the danger. Everyone in the cinema has one beating inside them.”And then there’s the symbolism. “A heart works on two levels. It’s literally keeping someone alive, but it’s also the universal symbol of life, love and mortality. You immediately understand why it matters,” he adds.That’s not to say Runner’s liver doesn’t land. Nor does the spoiler lurking in Resident Evil’s medical bag. The human body, after all, has plenty of organs left for Hollywood to parcel out. And who wouldn’t want to watch Tom Cruise fly a couple of kidneys through a tornado, or Statham hotfoot it across London with a bag full of gallbladders? Heartless may tell us whether this is a passing fad or a new action-movie staple, but if Hollywood’s latest organ harvest is anything to go by, the most compelling clock doesn’t tick any more – it beats.Explore more on these topicsFilmAction and adventure filmsDrama filmsThrillersResident EvilOrgan donationHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Celebrity, sex and motherhood misery: the 10 best books by Rachel Cusk … ranked! | Books | The Guardian
description: From an abstract portrait of an actor who might be Natalie Portman to a groundbreaking work of autofiction, we rate the best from the coolly controversial author
Author: John Self
Headline: From an abstract portrait of an actor who might be Natalie Portman to a groundbreaking work of autofiction, we rate the best from the coolly controversial author
Content: Breaking free of conventional fiction … Rachel Cusk.Photograph: Enric Fontcuberta/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBreaking free of conventional fiction … Rachel Cusk.Photograph: Enric Fontcuberta/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockRankedBooksCelebrity, sex and motherhood misery: the 10 best books by Rachel Cusk … ranked!From an abstract portrait of an actor who might be Natalie Portman to a groundbreaking work of autofiction, we rate the best from the coolly controversial authorJohn SelfMon 21 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreen10Life of M(2026)In Cusk’s headline-grabbing latest, a writer invents the biography of a film star who sounds very like Natalie Portman. Set in the now standard late-Cusk sans serif typeface (no frivolous flourishes!), Life of M serves up observations on fame in a light fictional coating. “To always be playing a part is to have no home.” Having made her name as a devilishly good creator of brainy social comedies, Cusk’s pivot to wintry autofiction since the Outline trilogy appears to have reached its logical conclusion in this flat, abstracted portrait of empty celebrity. The New York Times called it “rarefied, cosmopolitan, self-serious”.Sample line:“Everything I did or said in her company was false. It was as if I was acting, while M came across as authentic and real.”View image in fullscreen9The Lucky Ones(2003)A collection of stories about diverse characters who are linked by the influence of a newspaper columnist. They start weakly – Cusk struggles to embody a working-class female prisoner – but improve once she turns her caustic eye to ski trips and lawyers. The short form enables Cusk to show a narrative strength we don’t always see.Sample line:“Jane and Thomas were ironing out their lives in preparation for parenthood, starching and folding and putting away their youth, their excitement, their spontaneity.”View image in fullscreen8Saving Agnes(1993)After a cracking first line (“The house, like the party, was subsiding”), Cusk’s cheerfully comic debut tickles the reader throughout, as Agnes Day looks for love in contemporary London. Published to acclaim (and a Whitbread award) when Cusk was 26, it has a young writer’s weakness for using elaborate locutions as a shortcut to comedy, but there’s energy on every page, and her phrasing is always perfect: Agnes’s friend Merlin has “a salary for which Elizabeth Bennet would have left Darcy’s dinner burning in the oven”.Sample line:“Like a mirror he gave back nothing but what was already there; smash it and he would be gone, leaving her with nothing but a rearranged face and a few years of bad luck.”View image in fullscreen7The Temporary(1995)Cusk’s sparky second novel is a romantic dramedy. Two Londoners – publishing temp Francine and posh Ralph – bond over a dried-out risotto “like a dish of planetary matter brought back by an alien”. Francine’s house moves frustrate her mother (“You’ve quite ruined my new address book, what with all the crossings-out”); then Ralph wants to move on too. “I thought she understood it was just a temporary thing.” The story builds to an impressively messy climax, with Cusk switching between viewpoints and building tension.Sample line: “‘I’m something of an intellectual myself,’ Neil had said, straightening a tie across which autonomous golf clubs roamed.”View image in fullscreen6Second Place(2021)A writer, M, invites the devilish painter L to live in her home, and some chewy stranger-in-our-midst stuff ensues, upending family life and giving the opportunity for some classic Cuskian observations. “I need to get at the truth of a thing and dig and dig until it is dragged painfully to light.” There’s drama – as L humiliates M and her husband – and comedy, as M’s daughter’s boyfriend reads everyone his terrible novel-in-progress. Inspired by DH Lawrence’s stay in New Mexico in the 1920s, Second Place is a curious novel, and it’s the weirdness that makes it interesting.Sample line:“I’ve been criticised all my life – it’s how I’ve come to know that I’m there.”View image in fullscreen5A Life’s Work(2001)Cusk’s memoir of “all that love and terror and strangeness” of becoming a mother. It’s a book of scorched-earth candour: Cusk acknowledges her own misery at the drudgery of early motherhood and curses the asininity of childcare books. It was of course controversial, not for its writing – few could fault that – but for daring to challenge a Pollyanna-ish portrayal of parenthood. Cusk was unabashed: “This is not a childcare manual, ladies. In these pages you have to think for yourselves.”Sample line: “When I found myself pregnant again when Albertine was six months old I greeted my old cell with the cheerless acceptance of the convict intercepted at large.”View image in fullscreen4Arlington Park(2006)This novel’s Joycean opening settles down to an exquisitely written social comedy. The story of five young mothers, it feels at times like a fictional extension of A Life’s Work: each resents the confinements of motherhood. Perhaps this is what gives the novel its jaundiced eye; not just snobbish (“Mandy Clapp – it was the name on the badge of someone working at a supermarket checkout”) but misanthropic: everyone gets it. “She’d get pretty damned jumpy if her husband’s salary didn’t come rolling in like a Pacific breaker every month, or if people stopped thinking she looked like Felicity Kendal.” But it’s brilliantly funny.Sample line: “It was funny that she had ended up as a teacher, back at school. It made it seem that she wasn’t bright or gifted or exceptional at all. She was merely good at going to school.”View image in fullscreen3In the Fold(2005)This novel is a perfect amalgam of the qualities of early Cusk: funny, cynical, rigorous and linguistically precise. Its narrative of characters who are socially and materially conformist but terrified of appearing conventional centres on a man who falls in with a wealthy family. But the upheavals of the plot – things collapse and break – are less important than the sinuous sentences and streams of dialogue. Hidden here, though, we can perhaps see early evidence of Cusk’s desire to break free of conventional fiction. As one character has it: “Better to be broken than to be a slave of method!”Sample line:“[The schoolboys] make a list of the mothers they’d most like to sleep with. This is the first time she hasn’t made it. It’s soembarrassingfor her.”2The Country Life(1997)longest novel is the blackest of all her early comedies, the humour as often situational as verbal. Stella Benson abandons her job and boyfriend to become an au pair for a rural family’s disabled son. She’s not there long before strange, sinister things start to happen. She defaces the gardens by vomiting pink luncheon meat over them. She discovers a book titled The Runaway Bride by Stella Benson. This is a novel of broad and deep character insight, of social awareness – and of unexpected sexual awakening.Sample line: “I am normally a slow and careful eater, having been schooled by my mother in the many social atrocities it is possible unwittingly to commit during the ingestion of food.”View image in fullscreen1The Outline trilogy(2014-18)“I had no desire to prove that one book was better than another,” says Faye, the narrator. Well, we do! Outline’s revolution took Cusk’s art to a new place, wholly rejecting traditional character and description, and defining writer Faye – who bears similarities to Cusk – in relation to the people she meets on a trip to Athens. “I was beginning to see my own fears and desires manifested outside myself.” There are stories aplenty, but the overall tone is spare and cool, making something entirely original from the wreckage of Cusk’s need to dispose of her old ways. Two sequels followed – Transit and Kudos – but it was the first book that really shook things up. Critics argued that while it offered “few of the standard expected rewards of fiction”, it was nonetheless “a triumph of attitude and daring”.Sample line: “But what other people thought was no longer of any help to me. Those thoughts only existed within certain structures, and I had definitively left those structures.”Explore more on these topicsBooksRankedRachel CuskFictionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Presley Gerber, son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber, dies aged 27 | Celebrity | The Guardian
description: The model, who struggled with addiction and prescription medication dependency, died at a rehab facility
Author: Emma Joyce
Headline: The model, who struggled with addiction and prescription medication dependency, died at a rehab facility
Content: Presley Gerber, son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber, has died at a rehab facility. He was 27.Photograph: Frazer Harrison/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPresley Gerber, son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber, has died at a rehab facility. He was 27.Photograph: Frazer Harrison/Getty ImagesCelebrityPresley Gerber, son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber, dies aged 27The model, who struggled with addiction and prescription medication dependency, died at a rehab facilityEmma JoyceMon 21 Sep 2026 00.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 02.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePresley Gerber, son of supermodel Cindy Crawford and businessman Rande Gerber, has died aged 27.According to the Los Angeles county medical examiner, the former model died on Sunday 20 September at a rehab facility. The cause of death has not been disclosed.Presley, who was the eldest child of the celebrity couple, and brother of model Kaia Gerber, had previously spoken of his mental health and long-term addiction struggles.The death was confirmed by Allie Jenkins, a representative for Crawford and Rande Gerber. “The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time,” Jenkins said in an email.Presley was born in California in 1999. He was signed by IMG Models at age 15, making his runway debut in 2016 for Moschino’s Resort show in Los Angeles. He worked with brands including Celine, Calvin Klein, Dolce & Gabbana and Pepsi.In 2019, Presley was arrested for driving under the influence. He was sentenced to three years’ probation and ordered to complete a DUI program, as well as two days of community service.In recent years, the former model had spoken out about his depression and addiction, sharing posts about his recovery on his Instagram. In a since deleted post from December 2025, Presley spoke of several depressant medications he was taking to treat his panic attacks.“[Mental health] is an issue,” said Presley on podcast Studio 22 in 2023. “It is such a big part of my life. It’s a 24/7 job, and there’s so much to it.”He went on to say he hoped sharing his story would help others suffering with mental health concerns. “That’s really what I want to do: help people, whether you’re depressed, you’re struggling with something that is having a negative effect on your body. I mean it could be anything, and there’s no judgment.”In a social media post on 3 July, Cindy Crawford shared a photo of her son as a young boy with a caption that read, “I’m so proud of the man you’ve become, but I’ll always remember you as my little boy! Love you”.His sister Kaia spoke about her brother’s “decade-long struggle with drug addiction” in the September 2026 issue ofVogue.“When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone,” said Kaia in the interview. “I think that’s also why I started to self-identify as the easy one and never wanted to ask for help. Because it felt like too much to have two children who were needing.”In the US, call or textMental Health Americaat 988 or chat 988lifeline.org. You can also reach Crisis Text Line by texting MHA to 741741. In the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393 andChildlineon 0800 1111. In Australia, support is available atBeyond Blueon 1300 22 4636,Lifelineon 13 11 14, and atMensLineon 1300 789 978Explore more on these topicsCelebrityMental healthDepressionnewsShareReuse this content

title: John Farnham tribute: Céline Dion, Chris Martin and Hugh Jackman honour ‘living legend’ at livestreamed concert | John Farnham | The Guardian
description: Though the man of the hour is unable to attend, fans flock to Rod Laver Arena and cinemas nationwide to celebrate the songs of an Australian icon
Author: Caitlin Cassidy
Headline: Though the man of the hour is unable to attend, fans flock to Rod Laver Arena and cinemas nationwide to celebrate the songs of an Australian icon
Content: Céline Dion appears via videolink at the John Farnham tribute concert at Rod Laver Arena.Photograph: Martin PhilbeyView image in fullscreenCéline Dion appears via videolink at the John Farnham tribute concert at Rod Laver Arena.Photograph: Martin PhilbeyJohn FarnhamJohn Farnham tribute: Céline Dion, Chris Martin and Hugh Jackman honour ‘living legend’ at livestreamed concertThough the man of the hour is unable to attend, fans flock to Rod Laver Arena and cinemas nationwide to celebrate the songs of an Australian iconCaitlin CassidySun 20 Sep 2026 22.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 23.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt a Sydney shopping centre on a balmy Sunday evening, hundreds of people gathered to watch a concert that, according to its host, Richard Wilkins, would set a new livestreaming record for Australian cinemas.Experiencing a Rod Laver Arena event with popcorn in a cinema chair was unusual in itself – but so too was the fact that its hero,John Farnham, would not be performing, or even in attendance.At the sold-out tribute concert in Melbourne more than 120 artists and musicians celebrated the man of the hour.Céline Dion, Hugh Jackman and Chris Martin made special appearances via live telecasts, while Keith Urban, Human Nature, Tina Arena, Jimmy Barnes, Vanessa Amorosi and Jessica Mauboy belted out Farnham songs on stage.View image in fullscreenJimmy and Jane Barnes on the bagpipes on Sunday.Photograph: Martin PhilbeyFarnham’s absence was confirmed by his family on Saturday evening, who said he required 24-hour nursing care and would have to watch the tribute, titled “the celebration concert” for a “living legend”, at home.Céline Dion sings You’re the Voice live from Paris at John Farnham tribute concert – videoHis absence loomed as a large, poignant reminder of the evening’s cause: raising money for Head and Neck Cancer Australia, the charity that supported Farnham during his oral cancer battlein 2022.The 77-year-old’s surgeries mean he can no longer sing in public. His last live performance was at a bushfire benefit concert in February 2020.View image in fullscreenHuman Nature on stage. They sang Every Time You Cry and Simple Life, as well as the opening medley.Photograph: Martin Philbey“John’s health has deteriorated in recent months,” the family said on social media. “He now requires continuous oxygen support and uses a wheelchair for mobility.“We have kept these matters private while our family has adjusted to John’s changing needs. However, we now feel it is important that John’s fans and supporters understand his circumstances and why he cannot be there this weekend.”It was a strange way to watch a concert. The back two rows of the “xtremescreen” cinema had recliner seats, so many in the audience, including myself, were essentially lying down for its duration.John Farnham’s 20 best songsRead moreBefore it began, the screen displayed a countdown timer backed to crowd noise and soft pop hits.As a rendition of Love Is in the Air began to play with three minutes on the clock, an elderly man sitting next to me turned and asked excitedly, “You’ll be singing?”“Oh yes,” I laughed with a hint of fear.Farnham was Australian of the year in 1987 after the astronomical success of Whispering Jack, which remains the highest-selling album by a domestic artist in Australia. In addition towinning 21 Aria awards, he’s the only Australian artist to have a No 1 record on local charts across five consecutive decades.Many in the Sydney crowd were retirees but there were also teenagers, mother-and-daughter duos and young couples. At some points, cinemagoers tapped their feet, while at others, the brave among us launched into soft cheers.Before the screening, Hoyts emailed ticket-holders warning that a “large number of guests” were expected, urging them to arrive 30 minutes early to manage delays.All was handed smoothly and the cinema was a notably full. More than one Farnham T-shirt was spotted and some carried programs they’d bought for $35.View image in fullscreenJessica Mauboy joins the stirring opening rendition of Age of Reason.Photograph: Martin PhilbeyAt risk of losing my citizenship rights, I am not a Farnham fan, yet I found myself moved to tears during a stirring opening rendition of Age of Reason by Mauboy and Mahalia Barnes.“Is kindness an ancient skill buried by our blindness?” they sang, and I thought: “Yes! Exactly. What about the age of reason?”I found myself crying again when Dion –now on tour in Paris, her first full-length concert since being diagnosed with the incurable neurological disorder stiff person syndrome– was beamed into the arena via video to perform You’re the Voice, which she recalled singing with Farnham eight years ago.The sad irony of a man who has inspired generations for his voice losing it in old age was not lost on me, nor was the weirdness of watching a screen that showed people watching Dion on another screen.It was, undoubtedly, a celebration, not only of Farnham but of the nation’s culture, one that is diverse and inclusive and warm and a little bit silly.View image in fullscreenHans leads the crowd to sing Sadie, the Cleaning Lady.Photograph: Martin PhilbeyThere was a queer cabaret star, Hans, leading the crowd to sing Sadie, the Cleaning Lady. There was Hugh Jackman, making fun of his own obsession with Farnham.The final song was always going to be another go at You’re the Voice, with Mitch Tambo performing the opening lines in Gamilaraay and other performers flocking to the stage: Jimmy Barnes and Amorosi and Arena and Farnham’s son Rob. I cried again, as did the woman to my right, as they all hugged each other.I was thinking of Farnham sitting at home, watching the world pay tribute to him in a way few see while they’re still alive. And I was thinking of a line Chris Martin sang in a song he wrote for his remote performance that evening:double quotation markOne day we’ll all be gone but the thing about John Farnham songs is they’ll be living on.Explore more on these topicsJohn FarnhamAustralian musicCéline DionMelbourneCancerPop and rockHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Michael Gove finally gets to play prime minister in The Wargame | Television | The Guardian
description: Gove and Nicola Sturgeon join a simulated cabinet facing an escalating crisis. Plus: Stacey Dooley investigates ‘heightmaxxing’. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Gove and Nicola Sturgeon join a simulated cabinet facing an escalating crisis. Plus: Stacey Dooley investigates ‘heightmaxxing’. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Battle hardened … Michael Gove and Nicola Sturgeon are among the contenders of The Wargame.Photograph: Justin Downing/SkyView image in fullscreenBattle hardened … Michael Gove and Nicola Sturgeon are among the contenders of The Wargame.Photograph: Justin Downing/SkyTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Michael Gove finally gets to play prime minister in The WargameGove and Nicola Sturgeon join a simulated cabinet facing an escalating crisis. Plus: Stacey Dooley investigates ‘heightmaxxing’. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hollie Richardson,Hannah VerdierandGraeme VirtueMon 21 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Wargame9pm, Sky OneUsing political figures from our recent past, this docudrama maps out a British response to an escalating pattern of Russian aggression. Alongside Michael Gove (who gets to cosplay being prime minister at last), politicos including Harriet Harman andNicola Sturgeontake their places round the cabinet table. Credible commitment to the concept is essential to make the drama elements work, and all manage it reasonably well – particularly the unnamed Potus with Russian sympathies …Phil HarrisonClickbait Clinic With Stacey Dooley8.30pm, BBC OneLeg-lengthening surgery. If you can stomach it, hardyStacey Dooleyinvites us to watch the process of a procedure (breaking both legs, inserting screws) to kick off this new series. She’s looking into various health and wellness trends going viral on social media – this one being “heightmaxxing”.Hollie RichardsonFinding Britain’s Slave Traders With David Olusoga9pm, BBC TwoIf anyone doubted the violence and moral corruption underpinning Britain’s imperial past, this two-part documentary will set them straight.David Olusogainvestigates the register of British slave traders, which illuminates the links between the history of modern institutions (including the royal family) and the trade in human misery. Bleak but important.PH999: What Happened Next9pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenBrutal … 999: What Happened Next on Channel 4.Photograph: Channel 4There are some brutal “it could happen to you” stories in tonight’s episode, which traces the aftermath of emergency calls. A woman getting ready for a Christmas night out is stabbed in her own home and a gang stages a series of burglaries in an affluent area.Hannah VerdierColin from Accounts10pm, BBC TwoGordon (Patrick Brammall) and Ashley (Harriet Dyer) have split up from their very attractive partners – but that doesn’t mean they’re ready to get back together. In fact, Ashley brings a date to a sex party, which Gordon ends up at too. It unravels into another hilarious night of excruciating events.HRLucy Letby: Scapegoat?10pm, Channel 5After being found guilty of killing babies in her care, the UK’s most notorious neonatal nurse was jailed for life in 2023. But in the three years since Letby’s sentencing, the prosecution’s clinical and statistical evidence has been repeatedly challenged. This one-off documentary re-examines key points in a highly emotive case.Graeme VirtueExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightStacey DooleyDavid OlusogafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Seasons review – Portuguese pastoral offers poetic excavation of myth and mapping | Movies | The Guardian
description: The rugged roads and lush vegetation of southern Portugal are showcased in this weaving-together of disparate threads of history and landscape
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: The rugged roads and lush vegetation of southern Portugal are showcased in this weaving-together of disparate threads of history and landscape
Content: A form of a cinematic excavation … The Seasons.Photograph: PR ImageView image in fullscreenA form of a cinematic excavation … The Seasons.Photograph: PR ImageMoviesReviewThe Seasons review – Portuguese pastoral offers poetic excavation of myth and mappingThe rugged roads and lush vegetation of southern Portugal are showcased in this weaving-together of disparate threads of history and landscapePhuong LeMon 21 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a sea of doomsday ecological documentaries, Maureen Fazendeiro’s pastoral marvel is a sight for sore eyes. A solo debut feature for the Lisbon-based French director, this hybrid film studies the historical and geographical contours of Alentejo, a rural region in southernPortugal. The opening is set to a jaunty soundtrack of energetic percussion beats and twinkling organ notes, taking in the resplendent vistas of the landscape, with its rugged roads and lush vegetation. We see, too, a small archaeological tool hunt for ancient relics beneath layers of golden dust. Mirroring these acts of care and attention, Fazendeiro’s film takes the form of a cinematic excavation, fusing present-day tableaux with archival materials, folkloric legends with historical records.The abundant use of tracking shots not only takes in the wondrous biodiversity of Alentejo but also facilitates a fluid movement between separate epochs. Observational scenes of green hills, boundless blue skies and roaming livestock are overlaid with narrated excerpts from second world war-era letters written by German archaeologists Georg and Vera Leisner. Credited with producing the first inventory of megalithic monuments in Alentejo, the pair imbues their wartime correspondence with the joy of discovery and the sadness of exile.Elsewhere, history is preserved in oral tradition. One scene observes a circle of elders, in which a woman laments the rise of fascism and the fall of socialism in song, wistful melodies that reminds us of the years of António de Oliveira Salazar’s dictatorship. Another striking sequence takes a leap of imagination by re-staging a 17th-century myth. In weaving together these disparate threads of narrative, Fazendeiro’s sumptuous film offers an alternative form of geographical mapping, in which a landscape can be read like a text or a poem, to be preserved and passed on to future generations.The Seasons isat the ICA, London, from 25 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsPortugalEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Legend of the White Dragon review – Power Rangers alumni back for more in low-budget superhero retread | Movies | The Guardian
description: Simple but emphatic martial arts and a couple of classy cameos are all that give this blandly modern action film a fighting chance
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Simple but emphatic martial arts and a couple of classy cameos are all that give this blandly modern action film a fighting chance
Content: Cobbled together … Legend of the White Dragon.Photograph: Signature EntertainmentView image in fullscreenCobbled together … Legend of the White Dragon.Photograph: Signature EntertainmentMoviesReviewLegend of the White Dragon review – Power Rangers alumni back for more in low-budget superhero retreadSimple but emphatic martial arts and a couple of classy cameos are all that give this blandly modern action film a fighting chancePhil HoadMon 21 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDespite featuring a clutch of Power Rangers graduates, includingJason David Frank, who died in 2022, this crowdfunded effort is beholden to a more recent action tradition. It feels like it’s been cobbled together by ticking tropes off the modern superhero bingo card: Dark Knight-esque pariah hero, Gotham-style civic pantomime with the mayor, police and media, Iron Man helmet-cams, a sprig of eastern mysticism in the initiation sequence, western fighters appropriating said eastern mysticism … the list goes on.After a dustoff with his nemesis Ashtagor that levelled downtown Virtuo City, the superhero White Dragon (Frank) has been held responsible for the catastrophe and forced into exile. With the death count – 1,263 – tattooed in red above his right ear, and the crystal that was the source of his power shattered in two, he is now plain old Erik Reed. It’s not only the authorities who are bent on finding him: the pharma mogul Jai Katua (Aaron Schoenke), who lost his pregnant wife, wants payback. If Katua spending his time on solo katana sessions in his billionaire superlab wasn’t already a mental health red flag, accepting one of the crystal halves and a revenge mandate from Ashtagor should definitely merit an intervention.Considering the presumably teeny budget, Legend of the White Dragon manages a fair approximation of the lacquered hi-tech blockbuster look, and calls in a couple of classy cameos:Michael Madsen, giving the lore a gravitas boost, and Mark Dacascos, who can do kung fu monk blindfolded. The many martial arts sequences are simple but emphatic, in the Power Rangers style. But Schoenke, directing with his father, Sean, unbalances his own film by the simple fact that his own character – a kind of disintegrating, evil Bruce Wayne – is far more interesting than the protagonist.The limp Frank is an energy vacuum, typical of a general acting level that makes Marvel look like Merchant Ivory. Not that the sappy interludes between the fisticuffs, focusing on his sins-of-the-father issues and Katua’s ragebait memories of his former family idyll, help. There’s too little here that might lead the superhero genre into offbeat indie pastures, like Chronicle did back in 2012; only Andrew Bachelor’s supercomputer URI, as ifJARVIShad been reprogrammed as Chris Rock, hints at the possibilities, sassily repeating “scanning” as the bland superhero crew waits for intel.Legend of the White Dragon is available on digital platforms on 28 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmScience fiction and fantasy filmsSuperhero moviesMichael MadsenAction and adventure filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Nish Kumar: Angry Humour from a Really Nice Guy review – enraged and extremely funny | Comedy | The Guardian
description: There is real skill in making us laugh about things that are depressing. And the gags come thick and fast in the ex-Mash Report host’s touring show
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: There is real skill in making us laugh about things that are depressing. And the gags come thick and fast in the ex-Mash Report host’s touring show
Content: Deeply principled joke maker … Nish Kumar at Hackney Empire.Photograph: Paul GilbeyView image in fullscreenDeeply principled joke maker … Nish Kumar at Hackney Empire.Photograph: Paul GilbeyComedyReviewNish Kumar: Angry Humour from a Really Nice Guy review – enraged and extremely funnyHackney Empire, LondonThere is real skill in making us laugh about things that are depressing. And the gags come thick and fast in the ex-Mash Report host’s touring showAnya RyanMon 21 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNish Kumar is angry. And why shouldn’t he be? The world is one big, damning catastrophe. So here the ex-Mash Report host is, in his trademark linguistically dextrous, mile-a-minute style, to run us through the current affairs and colonial-history hellscape. Yes, we get Donald Trump jokes. And yes, there’s more than one mention of how the internet has corrupted us all. But, God, does it feel good to hear someone, clearly enraged, scream the things this Hackney audience is, more than likely, also thinking.He’s the UK’s leading lefty comedian – and for good reason. There is real skill in making us laugh about things that are, broadly, very depressing. Of course, Kumar knows he is preaching to the converted; he states plainly that his audience are a bunch of non-heckling, hand-raising “geeks” who are already on board with his views. Part of the show grapples with that discomfort; he believes passionately in standup as an art form – and it has made him big money – but for the first time, he’s wondered whether now is the right time for his usual political satire. Should we really be laughing when things are, well, this bad?‘I should not be allowed to do interviews’: Nish Kumar on courting controversy and clashing with comicsRead moreIt is a concern you feel could genuinely keep Kumar – and his mother – awake at night. Still, he serves up gags impressively thick and fast. At 41, his conversations with his peers centre largely around their workout routines. But even then, Kumar’s mind wanders to how the actions of the British empire have changed the genetic makeup of south Asian bodies – making it harder for him to lose weight. One by one, he goes through the generations from boomers to gen alphas and speaks of their individual virtues and failings. Some of his most vicious bile is reserved for Jimmy Carr and others who appeared at last autumn’sRiyadh comedy festival.We get a little insight into Kumar’s personal life, too – musings on his 14-year relationship with his partner and fellow comedian Amy Annette may not quite fit the tone of the rest of the show, but are a sweet, reflective addition. And a chat with one “weird little” 13-year-old fan in the crowd is enough to swell your heart and make you believe in the power of comedy to change things. This is Kumar at his very best: a deeply principled joke maker, ready to set society’s wrongs alight.Touring until 27 NovemberExplore more on these topicsComedyNish KumarreviewsShareReuse this content

title: How much is being close to your favorite artist worth? Superfans are reshaping the concert industry | Culture | The Guardian
description: Some admit to spending thousands of dollars for barricade spots and other VIP perks at concerts, which is slowly becoming common
Author: Rosalind Adams
Headline: Some admit to spending thousands of dollars for barricade spots and other VIP perks at concerts, which is slowly becoming common
Content: Fans wearing themed outfits sit and stand while waiting in line to be admitted to the Harry Styles Love On Tour 2022 concert at Madison Square Garden in New York City on 22 August 2022.Photograph: Alexi Rosenfeld/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFans wearing themed outfits sit and stand while waiting in line to be admitted to the Harry Styles Love On Tour 2022 concert at Madison Square Garden in New York City on 22 August 2022.Photograph: Alexi Rosenfeld/Getty ImagesCultureHow much is being close to your favorite artist worth? Superfans are reshaping the concert industrySome admit to spending thousands of dollars for barricade spots and other VIP perks at concerts, which is slowly becoming commonRosalind AdamsMon 21 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenHarry Stylesannounced a fall residency at Madison Square Garden, 43-year-old Tara Bess knew she had to be there. She didn’t want to spend hours camping for a prime spot in the general admission area, so Bess bought a VIP ticket for $1,400 from a resale ticket site, which allowed her to enter the arena early and secure a spot at the barricade.“When you’re up close, you can see him closing his eyes and almost meditating to the music,” Bess said. “You can hear the click of equipment on stage, you just feel very connected to the performance.”After seeing the show from the VIP area earlier this month, she took her sister to see it a second time for a more modest price. To afford the trip from her home in Florida, Bess worked a second job as an Uber driver and saved up for nine months. Bess is part of a growing number of fans who are shelling out for VIP tickets or other perks in order to secure prime concert seats and increase their chances of interacting with their favorite artists.Fans are paying thousands of dollars not just to see their favorite artists live, but to get closer to the performance and have a more exclusive experience.“It’s become more of a norm when you really want to get close to an artist,” said Eddie Meehan, the CEO of Please & Thank You, a VIP events company that’s worked with artists including Robyn and Audrey Hobert. “The growth of it, especially post-Covid, has been astronomical.”Even artists who have traditionally shied away from charging fans for extras have started offering premium tickets to meet demand, said Randy Nichols, a longtime artist manager. Ultimately, the experience is up to the artist and can include exclusive merchandise, meet-and-greets or access to the soundcheck.“Fans want to show their love and their loyalty and get to have that interaction and are more than happy to spend the money,” Nichols said. Typically, a higher percentage of a VIP ticket goes back to the artist than a standard ticket. Those earnings can be a welcome boost for artists as revenue from album sales have declined in the streaming era.The live music industry is noticing the opportunity. Superfans spend 80% more on music each month than casual fans, according toLuminate, a music data company. A 2025 Goldman Sachs report estimated that appealing to superfans could earn the industry an additional $4bn per year.View image in fullscreenFans watch Olivia Rodrigo perform on the Daytime Stage at the 2021 iHeartRadio music festival at Area15 in Las Vegas on 18 September 2021.Photograph: Denise Truscello/Getty Images for iHeartMediaFans who don’t purchase VIP tickets still have a chance to make it to the barricade of a general admission area by showing up early. Some venues discourage fans from camping overnight or may announce that lines won’t be honored until the morning of a show. Some venues have started offering fans the option to skip the entrance line for an additional fee, similar to theme parks. At some concerts, this means the first rows are filled with people who have paid more to be there.Despite the demand, the trend is more typical of larger, corporate-owned venues, said Stephen Parker, the executive director of the National Independent Venue Association. Many venues are wary of charging for these extras at a general admission show.“That egalitarian access for everyone is something that venues have worked really hard to preserve, and ultimately sometimes that’s not compatible with the VIP experience,” he said.The extras can rankle fanbases as competition for the best spots of a show has led to concertgoers who don’t pay for VIP tickets to show up earlier and earlier. Music subreddits are frequentlyfloodedwithpostsasking what time fans need to arrive to get a spot at the barricade. While the answer varies, a two-hour concert can easily extend into an all-day affair to secure a spot in the front.In a June interview with the UK radio station Kiss FM, Olivia Rodrigo described the extreme lengths some fans go to in order to hold their spots at the barricade. “I’ve been to certain concerts and certain festivals where people wear diapers so they can be front row of the show and that’s been an experience that I have smelled,” she said.Bess admitted that she avoided drinking water all day before the Harry Styles show, worried about losing her spot once the show got started. But the crowd ended up being easygoing. “I was definitely expecting a much more aggressive environment but it wasn’t that at all,” she said.Still, for longtime fans who have built a connection with an artist through following their career, paying for VIP is a way to continue supporting the artist.Kesha was on stage during her Freedom Tour last month when she spotted a fan at the front of the crowd holding up a sign saying she had a tooth to give the pop star.“I’m gonna have to get these teeth really fast,” Kesha said, pausing the show. She carefully descended down the steps of the stage in a pair of towering gold boots to grab the package. “I collect human teeth, it’s not weird!” she told the crowd.The tooth belonged to Holly Fisher, who lives in North Carolina and has been a fan of Kesha since high school. After her dentist scheduled an appointment to have a tooth pulled this summer, she knew immediately that she wanted to give it to Kesha. Fisher paid $475 for a VIP ticket, which included access to a soundcheck and early entry to the venue. When the doors opened, Fisher was first through the entrance and grabbed the spot at the center of the barricade with her friends directly in front of the stage.View image in fullscreenHolly Fisher (second from the left) with friends at barricade for Kesha’s concert.Photograph: Courtesy Holly FisherBeing in the front row was a way for Fisher to celebrate Kesha after following her from her early rise to her legal disputes with her former manager, Dr Luke, and now into her new chapter as an independent artist.“It really was this full circle moment for the people who had been there since the beginning,” said Fisher. “Like holy shit, she did it, she made it out alive. I’m just so happy for her.”As videos of concerts flood social media, a premium ticket is a way to have a more unique experience than just being in the building, said Amber Harms, who flew to Chicago to see two BTS shows on their summer tour. Harms became a fan of theK-popgroup while its members were serving their mandatory military service in South Korea.“A lot of that connection or that ability to connect with them in an actual real world environment, wasn’t something available to me at the time that I got into the fandom,” she said.On the second night, she shelled out $3,400 on a resale ticket site for two seats in the front row. While she called the resale prices “ridiculous”, the experience was worth it.“It’s wonderful to be at the concert, but if you can actually be five feet away from them, it’s even better,” said Harms. When one of the members splashed the crowd with a bottle of water and then tossed it into the crowd, Harms’s mother was close enough to snag it as a souvenir.“We were screaming like overexcited pterodactyls,” she said.Explore more on these topicsCultureHarry StylesTicket pricesMusic industryPop and rockBTSK-popfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What do you think of the MPs’ inquiry into UK Eurovision song contest failure? I give it nul points | Laura Snapes | The Guardian
description: There are obvious reasons why the UK flops and flops again, but that isn’t the point. This annual debacle is now part of our national identity, says deputy music editor Laura Snapes
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: There are obvious reasons why the UK flops and flops again, but that isn’t the point. This annual debacle is now part of our national identity, says deputy music editor Laura Snapes
Content: The UK's Eurovision 2026 entry, Look Mum No Computer, on stage in Vienna, Austria, 8 May 2026.Photograph: BBC/EBU/PAView image in fullscreenThe UK's Eurovision 2026 entry, Look Mum No Computer, on stage in Vienna, Austria, 8 May 2026.Photograph: BBC/EBU/PAOpinionEurovisionWhat do you think of the MPs’ inquiry into UK Eurovision song contest failure? I give it nul pointsLaura SnapesThere are obvious reasons why the UK flops and flops again, but that isn’t the point. This annual debacle is now part of our national identityMon 21 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 07.39 EDTShareGiven that Britain’s politics are quite a sizeable reason that we do so badly in Eurovision: here’s something that will definitely, absolutely, categorically help us do better in the competition … interference from MPs.Digital, culture, media and sport committee chair Caroline Dinenage has announced thatMPs will scrutinise the UK’s reliable failure in the competitionto see where we’re going wrong, with a hearing to be held over the coming months. The answers surely don’t take that long to work out.“We want to get to the bottom of who chooses our entrant,” Dinenage said. Currently that’s the BBC, with the assistance of a label or management company. Is our embarrassing misfortune down to “bad song choice, weak performance or something else”, she asked. Can you hear three red cherries dinging? Our songs are embarrassing, the humdrum performances indicative of a nation who think we’re too good for Eurovision high camp, and the “something else” is the lingering whiff of Brexit.View image in fullscreenBonnie Tyler at the 2013 Eurovision in Malmo Arena, Sweden.Photograph: Scanpix Scanpix/ReutersDinenage’s statement concluded by fretting about why we continually come last, or as good as, when as a nation we have “world-class songwriters and musicians”? Let me help there: that’s because no world-class British songwriter or musician would enter Eurovision at this point. No matter how good the song, our reputation as the dunce of the competition is fixed in perpetuity. We’ve tried wacky. We’ve tried the electro-swing beloved of the continent. We’ve tried oldies, besmirching Bonnie and Engelbert’s good names.Nada. At this point, I doubt that even Paul McCartney could pluck victory from the pyro-belching jaws of defeat. No self-respecting artist is going to sacrifice their beautiful creation to those cruel, gnashing European heathens.But!they wail.What about pluckySam Ryder, whofinished secondin2022?Space Man is quite a good song, I’ll grant you that. In summer 2022, at a very trying time in my life, it caught me unawares and made me cry. Improbably, later that day, I actually saw Ryder himself at a service station en route to the south-west and thanked him, very earnestly, for writing it, and got a warm fist bump in return. But Space Man also came second that year because of the UK’s staunch support for Ukraine after Russia invaded months earlier. Fair play, said Europe. You can have that one.(Just a thought: if it turns out that supporting nations experiencing destruction of human life and habitat by aggressive neighbours is one route to Eurovision success, maybe that is something that our politicians could consider doing a great deal more of.)View image in fullscreenSam Ryder at Eurovision 2022 in Turin, Italy.Photograph: Jussi Nukari/REX/ShutterstockRyder was appointed our saviour by Tap management, who look after artists includingLana Del Rey. Apparently capable of delivering victory for our beleaguered nation, they held on to the mantle for 2023 and sentMae Mullerto the competition. She finished second from bottom. In 2024, we pivoted and tried An Actual Popstar People Like,Olly Alexanderformerly of Years & Years, with a song co-written and produced by cutting-edge Charli xcx collaborators. What could possibly go wrong? He finished 18th out of 25.There is no reliable pipeline to Eurovision success available to the UK. The public can’t be trusted: in 2019, the last time the UK voted on our entrant, we sent a winsome young lad called Michael Rice,who had a mere 11 pointsto declareat customs on the way back from the contest in Tel Aviv. Perversely, I would quite like to see what musician British MPs – a group exactly not renowned for their music taste – would send to the competition on our behalf, but I’m not sure it would set back the rot.If anything, they should have some dignity and extract us from the competition: as one of its major funders, the UK gets a pass to the final every year without having to compete for a spot. If a football club finished bottom of the Premier League every year but was artificially kept in because of money, we would burn their ground down. Only relegated to the qualifiers may we rebuild.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenOlly Alexander at Eurovision 2024 in Malmo Arena in Sweden.Photograph: Corinne Cumming/EBU/PAMPs’ concern, while endearing, is also misplaced. Being crap at Eurovision is part of our national identity.
