(If indeed you’re still watching it:thousands have boycottedthe broadcast owing to Israel’s continued inclusion, including our principled Irish neighbours, another reason Britain may struggle to find credible competitors.) Sure, yes, we are very good at pop music – only fellow competitors Sweden have us licked in that regard – but complaining that those talents don’t work properly in this context comes across as sour grapes, like a medal-winning sprinter moaning that they lost the dads’ race at their kid’s sports day.As a competition, Eurovision is less Champions League – statistically proving who’s the best – than it is a kind of musical Crufts, upping the gaiety of nations with competitive displays of ridiculousness. It’s not about naming who’s Best At Pop. Britain’s failure doesn’t matter. If we must try to remedy this, I have two solutions. Pop music is soft power, and this battered country has no softer power than Mr Blobby. Let’s return an old cricketer to the crease for his first musical release in 23 years. If our rotund hero loses – UNLIKELY – he can just destroy the studio.Or, if the government insist on getting involved, here’s a thought. You may have heard that our new PM doesn’t just like the Smiths,he freaking loves the Smiths. He’s got a gold disc of The Queen Is Dead on the wall at the new No 10 North office. He recently jammed to Rusholme Ruffians on the frontline in Kyiv. He saw them live back in the day. Only he can call for the one referendum that will get hearts and minds back on Britain’s side: to forcibly reunite the band and send them to the competition. Morrissey performing live to 130 million viewers worldwide – what could possibly go wrong?Laura Snapes is the Guardian’s deputy music editorExplore more on these topicsEurovisionOpinionBritish identity and societycommentShareReuse this content

title: Bluebeard’s Castle/Oedipus Rex review – gory, gruesome and gripping double bill  | Opera | The Guardian
description: Joe Hill-Gibbins’ claustrophobic staging of Bartók’s opera of dark symbolism is paired with his brand new production of Stravinsky’s psychological drama
Author: Rian Evans
Headline: Joe Hill-Gibbins’ claustrophobic staging of Bartók’s opera of dark symbolism is paired with his brand new production of Stravinsky’s psychological drama
Content: Powerful  … Christine Rice as Judith and Nathan Berg as Bluebeard in Welsh National Opera’s Bluebeard’s Castle.Photograph: Dafydd OwenView image in fullscreenPowerful  … Christine Rice as Judith and Nathan Berg as Bluebeard in Welsh National Opera’s Bluebeard’s Castle.Photograph: Dafydd OwenOperaReviewBluebeard’s Castle/Oedipus Rex review – gory, gruesome and gripping double billWales Millennium Centre, CardiffJoe Hill-Gibbins’ claustrophobic staging of Bartók’s opera of dark symbolism is paired with his brand new production of Stravinsky’s psychological drama, with Peter Hoare superb as the tragic heroRian EvansMon 21 Sep 2026 09.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 10.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWelsh National Operamight be marking its 80th year, but any feelgood factor is decidedly absent from their season-opener. Bartók’s only opera and Stravinsky’s opera-oratorio form a challenging double-bill: serial murders, patricide and incest, blood and more blood, but gripping performances made this a powerful experience.Béla Balázs’s libretto for Bluebeard’s Castle transformed the Perrault fairytale and its happy ending into an intense psychological drama: the castle with its weeping walls and seven locked doors a metaphor for the secret inner workings of the male psyche, and Judith, Bluebeard’s new wife, his fourth, the archetypal woman, too curious for her own good.View image in fullscreenIntimacy as palpable as the unfolding horror … Nathan Berg as Bluebeard.Photograph: Dafydd OwenIn this stagingfirst seen at English National Opera in 2024, director Joe Hill-Gibbins tightens the focus even more sharply so that the castle doors and its keys are also metaphorical, with LJ Parkinson’s Bard – the shamanicregös(narrator) of Hungarian tradition – offering the signature contents of the hidden rooms. Cutlery for weaponry, treasury gold thrown about in sweeping gestures, bouquets of flowers, all are tailored – both to the intricacies of the score and to the setting of the single long table – to mirror the emotional wrangling as, one by one, Judith demands that the doors be opened. The feat ofChristine Rice’s expressive Judith andNathan Berg’s implacable Bluebeard is to create an intimacy as palpable as the unfolding horror.By way of preface to Bartók’s dark symbolism, and in a departure from the ENO version, the women of the WNO chorus, ghostly presences in white, intoned the antiphon O Rubor Sanguinis and the responsory Rex Noster Promptus Est of Hildegard von Bingen, redolent of the blood of martyrdom and of innocents. Their emergence as the final door is opened identifies them as Bluebeard’s previous wives in their wedding finery, 14 all told. But here again, this production departs from the norm, since Judith does not join them – she is condemned instead to live an eternal hell with Bluebeard. His final utterance, “darkness”, with its tritone, the devil’s interval, spells the impossibility of redemption.View image in fullscreenIn total vocal command … Stephen Richardson (Creon & Messenger) and Peter Hoare (Oedipus) in Oedipus Rex.Photograph: Dafydd OwenHill-Gibbins’s Oedipus Rex is new and, using the full width of the Millennium Centre stage and a formidable 35-strong male chorus embodying the force of the Theban populace, lends a scale that fulfils Stravinsky’s aim of a classical monumentality, reinforced by the Latin translation of Jean Cocteau’s original text. The crushing weight of fate is always present, everything stark black, save for a huge half-globe of light – its dazzle sometimes rendering the surtitles invisible – the bright glamour of Rice’s impassioned Jocasta and the blood-red suit ofPeter Hoare’s Oedipus. Hoare, in total vocal command, conveyed convincingly the gradual disintegration of kingly mien, slow to realise the awful truth that he did indeed kill his father and marry his mother, finally inflicting on himself the ultimate dark of blindness.For all the ritualistic element, nothing was static, with arguably too much running around and crawling, and some of Parkinson’s narration was under-projected. But, bound by the authoritative conducting ofLidiya Yankovskaya, who brought Bartók’s eloquence to the fore, and found playful moments as well as grave solemnity in the Stravinsky, this was strong stuff.At the Wales Millennium Centre, Cardiff, 25 September, then touring to Llandudno, Oxford and Plymouth.Explore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicWelsh National OperareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Silent Hill: Townfall review – shame and suffering on the Scottish coast | Games | The Guardian
description: Tragedy, and an apocalyptic fog, befall a fishing community. It is up to outsider Simon to offer some kind of closure
Author: Lewis Gordon
Headline: Tragedy, and an apocalyptic fog, befall a fishing community. It is up to outsider Simon to offer some kind of closure
Content: Slow-burning … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Screen BurnView image in fullscreenSlow-burning … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Screen BurnGamesReviewSilent Hill: Townfall review – shame and suffering on the Scottish coastPlayStation 5 (version played), PC; Screen BurnTragedy, and an apocalyptic fog, befall a fishing community. It is up to outsider Simon to offer some kind of closureLewis GordonMon 21 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 12.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou spend a considerable portion of Silent Hill: Townfall in a kind of foetal position, cowering behind objects that will be eerily familiar to anyone who lived in the UK during the 1990s. Cars seem to be modelled on the era’s boxy Volkswagen Golfs; logos adorning phone boxes should narrowly escape the attention of copyright lawyers at BT Group. (For millennials, the deja vu will likely intensify the horror, as if stepping back into a childhood nightmare.) Simon, the nerdy, unassuming star of the game, pokes his head around corners to catch a glimpse of the demonic entities that wish to maim him, before shrinking back down again with a downwards motion of the analogue stick. In such moments, it’s easy to imagine him wrapping his arms around his knees, clasping his eyes shut and wishing himself away from this place.The game’s setting, St Amelia, is based on the fishing communities of the East Neuk of Fife. The terror lurking here is wonderfully specific: absent lairds, island poverty, an oil-drilling corporation. Anguished beasts lumber down quaint streets lined with sandstone houses and fluttering bunting. Thisvenerable horror seriesmay have shifted to Scotland, yet we remain firmly in classic Silent Hill territory – weather and all. St Amelia finds itself suffused in supernatural fog and the vast majority of its inhabitants have vanished following some kind of mass tragedy. The artful, evocative presentation is such that you can almost taste the in-game air, the briny seaside tang diluted by rainy mist.Visually, this scuzzy, grotty take on Silent Hill from Glasgow studio Screen Burn leans on bold juxtapositions of colour, shadow, and ominous silhouettes. Sometimes the stricken town is bathed in blood-red moonlight; often, pitch-black interiors are illuminated by harsh white torchlight. The arresting imagery brings to mind found-footage horror films such asRecand the spine-tingling camcorder sections of UK classic,The Descent. Simon soon finds a portable television with strange, arcane power: it receives odd, elliptical messages from a nurse called Zoe, and tracks nearby monsters whose outline appears in scratchy low resolution on its small screen.The action is slow-burning and absorbing: Simon lopes about town, hiding from depraved monsters and occasionally bludgeoning them to death with a pipe. To enter some buildings, he has to make an incision with a scalpel in a fleshy door opening as thick, fresh blood oozes out. Gradually, Simon’s reason for visiting St Amelia in the first place becomes clear: guilt. But he’s not the only one racked with it. Zoe, voiced with terrific glassy distance by Kezia Burrows, has her own hangups. The third playable character in this triple-threat portrait of shame and suffering is alpha male Richard, the CEO of an energy company that professed to bring prosperity to the island.There were times when I was so locked in that the hours seemed to pass by in the blink of an eye, as if time had gone wonky just like in St Amelia. One memorable stretch takes place in a municipal-style high-rise building. Armed with a shotgun, and attempting to avoid the game’s nippiest, nastiest enemies, I ascended and descended each floor, as if playing a brutal, Ballardian take onThe Raid. I have never felt such dread at the prospect of entering an open-plan office, knowing what lurked among mouldering office furniture and knackered desktop PCs.View image in fullscreenShrouded in fog … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Screen Burn InteractiveEvery element – scavenging for items, creeping between bins, running at full pelt when all else fails – pulls you deeper into Townfall. Its design broadly adheres todiegetic principles, in that most information is conveyed to you within the game: to view the map, for example, Simon physically pulls it out – the action never pauses. To save your progress, you must find a telephone in St Amelia, manually pick up the receiver, and then dial a number.Puzzles function similarly. You snoop through emails, install floppy disks, and pocket important bits of paper, usually in an effort to gain a key code. These puzzles, though relayed via grounded, dated real-world tech, follow a serendipitous dream logic; even getting stuck feels coherent within the game’s uncanny psychogeographic claustrophobia. (That is, until it doesn’t. Close to the game’s conclusion, one esoteric puzzle about deciphering industrial symbols killed my progress, and my bafflement, frustration and rage had less to do with Townfall’s hallucinatory horror and more to do with its obtuseness.)skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNot even a fiendishly illegible puzzle could derail Townfall. This is a taut, smart tale, less about psychosexual terror than psychosocial dread. What’s most surprising is where the game’s sympathies lie: not with Simon, nurse Zoe, or bullyboy Richard, but the people of St Amelia. Their memorial in the centre of town is one of the game’s clearest images, unobscured by fog, though we’re never privy to the exact events that lead to their deaths. Townfall seems to understand that some things should remain shrouded in fog. The fate of St Amelia naturally festers in our imagination. How very Silent Hill.Silent Hill: Townfall is released 24 September; £44.99Explore more on these topicsGamesSilent HillreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Roman Sands RE:Build review – marooned in a crumbling vaporwave dream | Games | The Guardian
description: The latest work from the team behind Paratopic is part compulsive time-loop management sim, part eerie subterranean adventure
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The latest work from the team behind Paratopic is part compulsive time-loop management sim, part eerie subterranean adventure
Content: Tantalising escape route … Roman Sands RE:Build.Photograph: Arbitrary MetricView image in fullscreenTantalising escape route … Roman Sands RE:Build.Photograph: Arbitrary MetricGamesReviewRoman Sands RE:Build review – marooned in a crumbling vaporwave dreamPC, Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox; Arbitrary MetricThe latest work from the team behind Paratopic is part compulsive time-loop management sim, part eerie subterranean adventureDiego Nicolás ArgüelloMon 21 Sep 2026 04.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 04.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFetch the chair from storage. Deliver a message that causes disgust. Clean vomit in the afternoon and pour another glass in the evening. In Roman Sands RE:Build, you provide concierge service to delirious, broken people who couldn’t care less about the sweat on your forehead and the bags under your eyes.In this reimagining of the 2019 visual novel Roman Sands, crafted by the team behind the Americana horror road trip Paratopic, you’re trapped in a beach resort and tethered in a time loop. The task is deceivingly simple: fulfil menial directives from four gluttonous individuals, unlock tools and items to open more rooms and then do it all over again.The loop is as monotonous as it sounds – and that’s the point. The visuals and sound work collide in flamboyantvaporwave-inspired story exposition. Reward animations are exaggerated to feed your lizard brain with dopamine, satirising the reward loops that make other games feel like a visit to a casino – somemore maliciouslythan others. There’s gig economy commentary to boot.Over time, I familiarised myself with everybody’s routine and needs. I was effective to the point of becoming uncomfortable about how entranced I was, squeezing every possible score multiplier out of every day so that I could spend fake money on stuff I didn’t need from agachaponmachine.View image in fullscreenChilling in the spa in Roman Sands RE:Build.Photograph: Arbitrary MetricBut this is only one half of Roman Sands RE:Build. Completing a series of (often obtuse) puzzles in the resort opens the cracks of the reality you’re trapped in, showing a tantalising escape route. In Act 2, the compulsive time-management is dimmed down in tone and rhythm.Here it’s just you, your dead cow and a familiar voice on the radio, in the bowels of a subterranean research station. A parasite threatens to dismantle an already decaying refuge. Stuck in yet another loop, you must locate spare parts to fix an increasingly demanding machine, all while managing your oxygen level and completing small puzzles with barely enough light to read your PDA. It’s a stark contrast to the luxury resort, yet both acts have you navigating spaces where the walls (and their captives) are barely holding together.Unfortunately this thematic cohesion is not matched by Roman Sands’ technical cohesion. The game froze multiple times, some button prompts didn’t appear until I restarted and occasionally a puzzle’s visual language was totally inscrutable, leaving me running in circles, unsure of how to progress. These problems frustrated me no end.I’m glad I got to see the story through, however, with its not-so-subtle homages to the likes of Danganronpa and Evangelion. It remains one step away from its mysteries and doesn’t take them to extreme lengths. There’s a profound and alluring melancholy etched into this work, a broken and messy world that’s strange enough to foster questions, but smart enough not to provide every answer.Roman Sands RE:Build is out now; £14.99Explore more on these topicsGamesSimulation gamesIndie gamesAdventure gamesPCPuzzle gamesGame playreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Our culture is rich and we need our own space’: the fight to build a permanent centre for Deaf people | Architecture | The Guardian
description: In the UK, 18 million people are hard of hearing – yet there is no dedicated centre for the Deaf community. Now urban planner and activist Amanprit Arnold has made it her mission
Author: Alice Fisher
Headline: In the UK, 18 million people are hard of hearing – yet there is no dedicated centre for the Deaf community. Now urban planner and activist Amanprit Arnold has made it her mission
Content: ‘Being in an environment that’s built for you is so important’ … Amanprit Arnold speaks at an urban planning eventView image in fullscreen‘Being in an environment that’s built for you is so important’ … Amanprit Arnold speaks at an urban planning eventArchitecture‘Our culture is rich and we need our own space’: the fight to build a permanent centre for Deaf peopleIn the UK, 18 million people are hard of hearing – yet there is no dedicated centre for the Deaf community. Now urban planner and activist Amanprit Arnold has made it her missionAlice FisherMon 21 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMeeting outdoors became second nature for most of us over this long, hot summer, but Amanprit Arnold doesn’t get the luxury of choice. She’s sitting at a terrace table when we meet at a cafe because she’s a member of the Deaf community (Deaf with a capital D denotes membership of a unique cultural and linguistic minority).“Nowhere inLondonis specifically designed for me,” says Arnold, who was born deaf and used hearing aids before getting cochlear implants at 21. “Inside a cafe, the acoustics can be so bad. It’s much easier for me to hear out here.”Despite there being18 million people with hearing issues in the UK, deaf people can often be made to feel like outsiders (even when they’re not sitting outside). Mainstream representation has grown thanks to actorRose Ayling-Ellislifting the glitterball trophy on Strictly Come Dancing in 2021 and Fury on the Gladiators reboot. Critically acclaimed films such asSound of MetalandCoda– which won the best picture Oscar in 2022 – showcased the talents of deaf actors and writers, and the mesmerising skills of sign language interpreters at rap performances regularly go viral. But this has not led to a dedicated centre for the Deaf arts anywhere in the UK.View image in fullscreenSign of the times … an image by the Deaf Architecture Front.Photograph: Deaf Architecture FrontArnold wants to change that. She has started the DeafCity Hub campaign to create or adapt a building using deaf-friendly architectural guidelines calledDeafSpace principlesto provide, at last, a co-working and cultural space for her community.double quotation markWe have a really strong cultural identity element and we need somewhere to celebrate thatWhile there are cafes and clubs that bring deaf people together socially around the UK, Arnold sees the DeafCity Hub as a national centre as well as a meeting place. This month, the project has landed a year-long “meanwhile” space (a building awaiting redevelopment) through a partnership with Westminster city council and the Oxford Street Development Corporation, which gives her the chance to prove a place like this is needed.“There is greater visibility of deaf people in the media,” says Arnold, “but when it comes to property and place-making for them, there’s nothing. We have a really strong cultural identity element and we need somewhere to celebrate that, somewhere made for us.”Arnold’s career is in urban planning and strategy, but there’s activism in her background, too. (“In my family, that’s what we do,” she says with a smile.) Her father was race relations director for Birmingham city council in the 1990s andher grandfather was a trade unionist and antiracism campaigner. Arnold’s design agency,Disability Urbanism, specialises in accessibility, helping city planners and real estate developers create welcoming environments for people with disabilities.View image in fullscreenFizzled out … a poster from the 1980s promoting the IDCCShe sees DeafCity Hub as a revival of a 1986 plan for an International Deaf Cultural Centre in London that fizzled out. The 1980s were a heady time for activists, especially in the US, where there were Deaf civil rights protests, the first Oscar for a deaf actor (Marlee Matlinfor 1986’s Children of a Lesser God) and the establishment ofGallaudet University, specifically for deaf people, and the appointment of the university’s first deaf president.In the UK, the BBC launched See Hear, a current affairs programme for deaf people, and TV subtitle provision improved. The British Sign Language Act only received royal assent in 2022, legally recognising BSL as a British language of England, Scotland and Wales, and you still can’t take a GCSE in it (the expected launch date for this qualification is 2028).“Most communities have their own spaces,” says Arnold. “I know that if I go to Soho I’ll be in an LGBTQ+ community space, for example. I think creating DeafCity Hub as a deaf-owned and deaf-led arts space would assert that our culture is also rich.”Being able to access spoken language culture would also be on the DeafCity Hub agenda, as signers often find this difficult. “Theatres and cinemas will have an accessibility page on their websites, but performances with interpreters are rare,” Arnold continues. “You have to go to one specific show – and that’s normally set for noon on a Tuesday when most of us are at work.”Arnold has the 1980s material for the International Deaf Cultural Centre, from plans and optimistic posters to the original architect’s blueprints – which feature a Deaf history archive, a theatre and exhibition space, a bar, a quiet room and even a hostel. Looking through them, she recalls a quote that’s connected to the formation of Gallaudet University and has become a mantra for many activists: “We travel the world to learn about cultures and people. We go into their country to visit them. We now have a country.”The International Deaf Cultural Centre plans are not designed to the DeafSpace guidelines – this is the goal for DeafCity Hub. “Sign language is not just spoken word translated into hands: it’s a rich, spatial language rooted in visual geography, 3D space and facial syntax,” says Arnold. It needs space.View image in fullscreenPleasant and spacious … The London College of Fashion’s East Bank campus, designed by Allies & Morrison, is one of the few public buildings that adhere to DeafSpace principlesPhotograph: Simon MengesDeafSpace principles include features such as wide corridors and staircases that allow people to walk abreast while talking in BSL; natural light and soft colours to guard against eye strain; strategic use of glass and mirrors to improve sightlines; and rooms that accommodate circular seating so large groups can easily see each other’s hands and faces as they sign. If you’ve ever been to the London College of Fashion’sEast Bankcampus, you’ll have experienced the pleasant, spacious feel of DeafSpace, as it’s one of the few public buildings designed to these ideals.Arnold would also like Deaf sector charities to have a home at DeafCity Hub, using boardrooms without rectangular tables, in part to demonstrate how simple changes can make a big difference to her community. “Being in an environment that’s built for you is so important. I went to deaf school as a teenager and that meant I had a wonderful secondary school experience. I was opened up to Deaf culture and I want to be able to share what that was like with other deaf people.”Arnold’s positive experience is harder for deaf kids to access today. There are only22 deaf schools in the UK, down from 75 in the early 1980s. This is partly due to funding cuts and local government policy, but it’s also due to the uptake of cochlear implants, electrical devices that relay sound to the brain, enabling speech development. Arnold feels that the possibility of medical eradication makes it even more important to preserve Deaf culture.Disability by David Turner review – a revelatory new historyRead more“Deaf Gain is a celebrated term in our community, where we frame ourselves as contributors to society. People think it’s important to protect endangered ecosystems and oral dialects, so why would we treat a thriving visual culture and spatial language as something to be eliminated?”Arnold is delighted to have her meanwhile space, but for DeafCity Hub to secure a permanent home, they’ll need funding and a developer partner. If all goes well, she’d like the London space to act as a pilot for an international network of hubs – and for that to work she needs investment. “We need to design and shape accessibility and inclusivity from the start. A meanwhile space won’t be perfect, but it will act as an incubator to develop this idea further.”She has a lot to prove in the next 12 months but she’s ready for it. She gathers her plans and her blueprints from the cafe table, plans for somewhere she can finally call her own.TheDeafCity Hubcampaign launches on 21 September, before theInternational Day of Sign Languageson 23 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsArchitectureDeafness and hearing lossDisabilityHealthActivismCommunitiesLondonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Coco Khan and Nish Kumar take on England flags: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Bestselling book The Good Immigrant launches a series of thoughtful explorations of race – starting with the hosts of Pod Save the UK. Plus, a look at an outrageous heist
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Bestselling book The Good Immigrant launches a series of thoughtful explorations of race – starting with the hosts of Pod Save the UK. Plus, a look at an outrageous heist
Content: Coco Khan and Nish Kumar, who appear in The Good Immigrant: The Official PodcastPhotograph: Lucy North/PAView image in fullscreenCoco Khan and Nish Kumar, who appear in The Good Immigrant: The Official PodcastPhotograph: Lucy North/PABest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioCoco Khan and Nish Kumar take on England flags: best podcasts of the weekBestselling book The Good Immigrant launches a series of thoughtful explorations of race – starting with the hosts of Pod Save the UK. Plus, a look at an outrageous heistHannah J DaviesMon 21 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekThe Good Immigrant: The Official PodcastLaunching alongside a 10th-anniversary edition of the essay collection by writers of colour, thispodcastsees its editor, Nikesh Shukla, reconvene with the book’s contributors. A series of thoughtful conversations about what has changed and what’s stayed the same when it comes to race in the UK starts with Nish Kumar and Coco Khan on England flags, and why humour is essential to their political podcasting.Hannah J DaviesWidely available, episodes weeklyStill CountingThelatest seriesfrom Pod Save doyens Crooked Media is a winning reunion of journalists Nate Silver, Clare Malone and Galen Druke of defunct US site FiveThirtyEight. It’s data-heavy but far from dry, with an opening episode that looks at the darker implications of the Charlie Kirk killing and how voters really feel about Trump.HJDWidely available, episodes weeklyHappy Hour With Ina GartenView image in fullscreenCooking and chatting … Ina Garten.Photograph: NBC/Nathan Congleton/Getty ImagesBetter known as TV’s Barefoot Contessa, Ina Garten has long been the cookery world’s leading fancy aunt and devoted spouse. Her new Vox show is an unapologetically fun and frothyinterview seriesrecorded at her New York home, kicking off with Kate McKinnon on SNL, Meryl Streep and French faux pas.HJDWidely available, episodes weeklyThe JourneyThe New Yorker and In the Dark dissect the bizarre and headline-grabbing story of a Los Angeles couple who collected dozens of children, born to multiple surrogate mothers. Was this “human trafficking for babies” or even maybe a misguided pronatalist plan? Ava Kofmaninvestigatessensitively, following a feature she published earlier this year.HJDWidely available, episodes weeklyRough DiamondIn 1965, David Knight was convicted of stealing the world’s largest uncut diamond, though he maintained his innocence. However, after his release, Knight stole a priceless Vermeer. In this series, Josie Long learns more about the man behind the audacious stories via his letters and recordings – and by speaking to his nephew.Hollie RichardsonWidely available, from Wednesday 23 SeptemberWhat are you listening to this week? title: Three countries, one hike: an Alpine adventure in Austria, Slovenia and Italy | Austria holidays | The Guardian
description: The Alpe Adria loop is an eight-day walking trail that crisscrosses borders, taking in dramatic peaks, glorious meadows and charming places to stay
Author: Sarah Baxter
Headline: The Alpe Adria loop is an eight-day walking trail that crisscrosses borders, taking in dramatic peaks, glorious meadows and charming places to stay
Content: The Italian mountain village of Valbruna has a view of Jôf Fuart, one of the Julian Alps’ most imposing peaks.Photograph: Nicola Simeoni/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Italian mountain village of Valbruna has a view of Jôf Fuart, one of the Julian Alps’ most imposing peaks.Photograph: Nicola Simeoni/AlamyAustria holidaysThree countries, one hike: an Alpine adventure in Austria, Slovenia and ItalyThe Alpe Adria loop is an eight-day walking trail that crisscrosses borders, taking in dramatic peaks, glorious meadows and charming places to staySarah BaxterMon 21 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 02.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Achtung! Staatsgrenze!” OK, the signpost marking the “state border” didn’t have exclamation marks but, with its no-nonsense Prussian font, it did feel quite shouty. The only thing was, no one on the Feistritzer Alm – a peaceful sweep of Alpine pasture at the meeting of Austria and Italy – was paying any attention to it at all.Hikers hiked straight past. Mountain bikers used it to prop up their cycles. Cows grazed willy-nilly. And the patrons of the Schutzhütte Oisternig enjoyed their cold beers regardless of which country they were in. While official boundaries may have changed in these parts over the centuries, the magnificence of the mountains has not.View image in fullscreenMy husband and I had woken that morning in Austria, in the Carinthian village of Feistritz. After breakfast at the oldGasthof Alte Post, we’d bought a loaf from thebäckerei, climbed past the 15th-century church as its bells called worshippers for prayers and continued up through pine forest to these high Alpine meadows – and into Italy.We were hiking theAlpe Adria, a long-distance trail jointly developed by Austria, Slovenia and Italy that runs from the foot of Grossglockner (Austria’s highest mountain at 3,798 metres) to the Adriatic coast. At 750km (466 miles), the full trail is too long for most people’s summer holidays. But a 135km (84 mile) loop – moderate-graded, doable in a week, with walking days of 15-24km (9-15 miles) – has been created where the three nations meet, to offer a multicultural taster. It’s an appealing idea; hikers love circuiting multiple countries – just look at the numbers crowding the Tour du Mont Blanc these days. While the Alpe Adria loop isn’t quite as dramatic as that, it does offer a much quieter alternative.View image in fullscreenThe writer near the Vratca Pass.We started our journey by catching an early Eurostar to Amsterdam, where there was time for canals, beer and crispybitterballenbefore boarding the Nightjet sleeper to Salzburg. In our adjoining capsule-like cabins, we watched the Netherlands segue into Germany, and woke at dawn to pasture, pines and peaks. On the final train from Salzburg to Villach, where we were beginning the loop, the Alps pressed closer, drawing us in.Now, on the Feistritzer Alm, a day and a half into the walk, Austria was behind us (for the time being) and Italy beckoned, beautifully. Just around the hill from the Schutzhütte Oisternig sat the chapel of Our Lady of the Snows (or the Chiesa Madonna della Neve/Almkapelle Maria Schnee, depending on your linguistic preferences); beyond spread deep-green foothills and the jagged Julian Alps, sawing into a hot-blue sky.double quotation markAfter a magical ascent, I sat on the terrace and stared at the peaks, transfixedFrom here, the rest of the day was all downhill, a drop through blessed shade and butterflies, on paths weaving through the pines and peeping out to the peaks, to end in the village of Valbruna, at theValbruna Inn. We had a wonderful room, and spent time on our balcony, gazing past the geraniums to the sheer Jôf Fuart range, which reaches up to 2,666 metres.We also spent time in the hotel’s Julius Kugy Library, a cosy den of books on alpinism, named after a writer-mountaineer legend. Born in 1858 to a Slovenian family in Gorizia – then part of the Austrian empire, now in Italy – Kugy is credited with opening up the Julian Alps. He never lost his reverence for nature, always encouraging others to explore with respect, curiosity and awe. I picked up one of his books and read from his introduction: “[This] tries to describe the mountains as a source of happiness, because such they were in my life.”I couldn’t have agreed more and, with great happiness, we continued the next morning, following the Alpe Adria from Valbruna, across the Saisera River and up through fir and spruce to theSanctuary of Monte Lussari, a ridge-top pilgrim church and hamlet, where the Virgin Mary is said to have appeared in 1360. I was less moved by the miracle, or the shops selling branded tote bags, liqueurs and slippers, than by the mountains scattered far and wide. We lingered to enjoy the view, then descended via alpenrose and ambling goats to Tarvisio, finding a different kind of happiness in the town’s gelaterias. Then, later that evening, we sat with cold beers on our balcony at theHotel Nevada, watching as a storm crashed through, briefly erasing every mountain.View image in fullscreenThe village of Monte Lussari.Photograph: Marco Lissoni/AlamyThe next day brought more joy as the trail took us along the woodland-weavingSentiero del Orsoand then via a busy cycle path to the Fusine lakes. These twin glacial bowls are so arrestingly blue-green you’d think they’d been AI-ed if you weren’t standing right there. We found a quiet spot to picnic, listening to the whinnying of little grebes and staring beyond the dazzling water to the afternoon’s challenge via the rocks ahead: the haul up toRifugio Zacchi.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Alpe Adria loop usually ends each day in a valley bottom, where there are plenty of inns. But not tonight. Zacchi sits at 1,380 metres, tight-hugged by the intimidating peaks that mark the Slovenian border. After a muggy, magical ascent through forest to the refuge, I sat on the terrace, drinking a superb Aperol spritz, and stared at them, transfixed; a few booms of thunder rippled, just in case the power of nature had been in doubt.View image in fullscreenThe blue-green Fusine lakes.Photograph: Liubomir Paut-Fluerasu/AlamyThe food at Zacchi was excellent – venison ragù, chargrilled peppers, potato-pancake-likefrico, made with local montasio cheese. Also excellent was the fact that, in a stroke of luck, we had a dorm to ourselves. We woke, refreshed and ready for the next border hop.The most striking route would have been over the forbidding-looking Vratca Pass. The Alpe Adria took us there, for views east into Triglav national park, but didn’t cross. Instead, the trail backtracked down on the Italian side to follow a path through the verdant Sava Valley to the outdoorsy town of Kranjska Gora.It was a pleasant entrance into Slovenia; however, our exit was spectacular. To get back to Austria the next day, we had to cross the Karavanke Alps and conquer the highest point of our route, the 1,842-metre Schwarzkogel. It was an unrelenting climb, at first amid pasture and shingle roofs, with sublime views to the Julian peaks, then deep in forest serenaded by thrushes, streams trickling to our side.As we neared the top, we could see south across Slovenia’s surging summits, north across Carinthia’s electric-blue lakes and low hills. Squat white marker-stones began to appear too, strung along the ridge’s spine – an international border marked more casually than most front gardens. We slalomed between the posts, enjoying both the freedom of movement and the majesty of nature. For millennia the Alps have been physical and cultural barriers. The Alpe Adria is a bringing together; a source of mountain happiness.The trip was provided by Walks Worldwide; the eight-day, self-guidedAlpe Adria Tri-Country Trekis from£895 B&B.Accommodation in London was provided byGenerator(rooms from £75, dormbeds from £11)Explore more on these topicsAustria holidaysSlovenia holidaysItaly holidaysWalking holidaysEurope holidaysWalkingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jamie Oliver’s recipes for fish pie pasta bake and tomato and feta lentils | Jamie Oliver | The Guardian
description: Sometimes cooking is about celebration or indulgence, but there are other times when you just need a speedy but delicious midweek meal
Author: Jamie Oliver
Headline: Sometimes cooking is about celebration or indulgence, but there are other times when you just need a speedy but delicious midweek meal
Content: Jamie Oliver’s fIsh pie pasta bake.Photograph: David Loftus/Jamie Oliver Enterprises LtdView image in fullscreenJamie Oliver’s fIsh pie pasta bake.Photograph: David Loftus/Jamie Oliver Enterprises LtdQuick and easyJamie OliverJamie Oliver’s recipes for fish pie pasta bake and tomato and feta lentilsSometimes cooking is about celebration or indulgence, but there are other times when you just need a speedy but delicious midweek mealJamie OliverMon 21 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 09.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOf course, the act of cooking can be many things – joy, ritual, nourishment, comfort, celebration, indulgence – but this fish pie pasta bake and tomato and feta lentils are strictly about speed. Because, in reality, these are exactly the kind of recipes we all need in our repertoire, ready to whip out on a Wednesday night.Fish pie pasta bake (pictured top)Prep5 minCook20 minServes4320g frozen spinach1 onion(160g)Olive oil300g dried macaroni50g plain flour2 heapedtsp English mustard500ml semi-skimmed milkSalt and black pepper400g frozen fish pie mix, from sustainable sources100gcheddar2 red chicory60g rocketRed-wine vinegarExtra-virgin olive oilTurn on the grill to high. Boil the kettle. Defrost the spinach in a bowl in the microwave. Peel and finely chop the onion, and place in a large ovenproof frying pan on a high heat with one tablespoon of olive oil. Cook, stirring regularly, for five minutes, or until soft. Cook the pasta in a pan of boiling salted water for eight minutes, until al dente, then drain, reserving a mugful of the starchy cooking water.Stir the flour and mustard into the onions, then gradually stir in the milk. Add the spinach to the pan, water and all, then season. Stir in the fish chunks and simmer for five minutes on a medium heat, then stir in the drained pasta, along with a splash of the reserved water, if needed. Coarsely grate and mix in half the cheese, grating the rest over the top. Carefully transfer to the highest shelf of the grill for a few minutes, until golden and bubbling.Meanwhile, finely slice the chicory bases and separate the leaves, toss with the rocket and a tablespoon each of red-wine vinegar and extra-virgin olive oil, then season. Serve with the fish pie pasta bake.Tomato and feta lentilsView image in fullscreenJamie Oliver’s tomato and feta lentils.Photograph: David Loftus/Jamie Oliver Enterprises LtdPrep5 minCook20 minServes44garlic cloves1 fresh redchilliOlive oil500g ripe tomatoes1460g jarroastred peppers½pomegranate30g shelled unsalted pistachios1 bunchdill(20g)4 flatbreads2400g tinslentilsRed-wine vinegarSalt and black pepper100g fetaPeel the garlic and finely slice with the chilli, then put in a shallow casserole pan on a medium-high heat with two tablespoons of olive oil. Cook, stirring regularly, until soft but not coloured. Chop and add the tomatoes. Tip the peppers, juice and all, into a blender, blitz smooth, then pour into the pan. Cook, stirring occasionally, for eight minutes, or until thickened.Meanwhile, hold the pomegranate half cut side down in your palm and bash the back of it so the seeds tumble out into a bowl. Finely chop the pistachios. Pick and chop the dill. Warm the flatbreads.Drain the lentils and add to the pan with a half-tablespoon of red-wine vinegar. Simmer for a final five minutes, then stir through half the pomegranate seeds and half the chopped dill, and season.Scatter over the pistachios and the remaining pomegranate seeds, crumble over the feta, and sprinkle over the remaining dill. Serve with warm flatbreads.These recipes are edited extracts from 20-Minute Meals by Jamie Oliver, published by Penguin Michael Joseph © Jamie Oliver Enterprises Limited (2026, 20MM) at £30. title: Tattie scones and scrambled eggs, toasted bannocks with honey butter and roast plums – Anna Higham’s big breakfast recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Scottish breakfasts are worth getting up for: think eggs and potato cakes in a freshly baked roll, or toasted barley bread laced with sticky plums and honey butter
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Scottish breakfasts are worth getting up for: think eggs and potato cakes in a freshly baked roll, or toasted barley bread laced with sticky plums and honey butter
Content: Anna Higham’s morning rolls filled with tattie scones and scrambled eggs.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.View image in fullscreenAnna Higham’s morning rolls filled with tattie scones and scrambled eggs.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.FoodTattie scones and scrambled eggs, toasted bannocks with honey butter and roast plums – Anna Higham’s big breakfast recipesScottish breakfasts are worth getting up for: think eggs and potato cakes in a freshly baked roll, or toasted barley bread laced with sticky plums and honey butterAnna HighamMon 21 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 06.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve long wanted a space to cook the food that really excites me, andClementine, which opens its doors in north London next month, is exactly that. These two recipes capture what the cafe is all about. This is food that feels both considered and completely unfussy: crisp morning rolls stuffed with folded scrambled eggs and tattie scones, and griddled barley bannocks served warm with salted honey butter and roast plums. Breakfasts worth getting out of bed for.Morning rolls with tattie scone and scrambled eggsPrep10 minProve9 hr+Cook1 hr 45 minMakes4For the morning rolls375g strong white stone-ground bread flour, plus extra for dusting4g sugar4g salt5g dried active yeast40g lard, or vegetable shortening210g cold waterFor the tattie scones1kg maris piper potatoes165g strong stone-ground flour,plus extra for dusting1½ tsp fine salt1 tsp baking powder60g melted unsalted butterFor the eggs2 tbsp salted butter6 eggs1 tbsp creme fraicheSalt and black pepperRed or brown sauce,to serveFirst, make the morning rolls. Combine the dry ingredients in a bowl, then rub in the lard. Add the water, mix to form a rough dough, then cover with a damp tea towel and leave to rest for 10 minutes.Knead the dough until it feels smooth, springy and has good stretch – about 10 minutes in a mixer on medium speed, 25 minutes by hand. Transfer the dough to a lightly oiled container, cover with a damp tea towel and leave for about an hour to double in size.Turn out the dough on to a well-floured surface, roll it into a rectangle, then divide into 12 equal pieces of about 120g each. Pinch the four corners of one piece of dough into the centre, then flip over. Allow the dough to stick slightly to the worktop and, with a cupped hand, work it into a tight ball. Now use a dough scraper to release it from the bench, then transfer to a lined, high-sided baking tray. Repeat with the remaining pieces of dough, spacing them evenly apart. Sprinkle each with a little flour, cover with a damp cloth and refrigerate overnight.Heat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/475F/gas 9, then bake the rolls for 25-30 minutes, until dark and “well fired” on top; remove and leave to cool slightly.Meanwhile, peel and cut the potatoes into chunks, boil in well-salted water until tender, then drain and mash (or use a potato ricer). Mix in the remaining tattie scone ingredients to make a dough, then divide in two.Put a frying pan on a medium heat. Cut out a 10cm circle of baking paper, flour it well and put one block of the potato dough on top. Roll this into an even 10cm round, score it into quarters, then flip into the hot pan. Cook for three to five minutes, until it puffs up and colours on the bottom, then flip and cook for a minute or two, until coloured on the other side. Transfer to a rack while you roll and cook the remaining dough.Melt a tablespoon of butter in the same frying pan on a medium heat. Whisk the eggs, creme fraiche, salt and pepper, then pour into the hot pan and leave the bottom to set, much as you would an omelette. Use a spatula to push the set egg into the centre, cook until the mix is 75% set, then fold over and take off the heat.Put the remaining tablespoon of butter in a hot pan and, once foaming, fry the tattie scones until golden brown with crisp edges, flipping once halfway. Divide the tattie scones along the score lines, then split the buns and fill with two tattie scones and the eggs. The choice of red or brown sauce is entirely your own.Barley bannocks with honey butter and roast plumsView image in fullscreenAnna Higham’s barley bannocks with honey butter and roast plums.Prep10 minCook1 hrServes6For the bannocks200g barley flour100g plain flour2 tsp bicarbonate of soda1 tsp baking powder1 generous pinch salt60g cold butter300ml buttermilkFor the honey butter100g salted cultured butter, at room temperature30g local runny honeyFor the roast plums6 red or purple plums1 tbsp light brown sugar1 tsp red-wine vinegarMix all the dry ingredients for the bannocks in a large bowl. Grate in the butter, toss it through to coat, then add the buttermilk, holding back 50ml or so in case your flour doesn’t need all of it. Mix gently to a soft dough, then divide into three portions.Roll each portion into a roughly 2½cm-thick disc, then cut each disc into quarters. Put a heavy skillet or griddle pan on a medium heat, then, working in batches, cook the bannocks for about five minutes on each side. Wrap in a tea towel and keep in a warm oven while you cook the rest. (Bannocks freeze very well, so, if need be, freeze any leftovers, ready to warm up whenever you need a wholesome treat.)In a small bowl, whisk all the honey butter ingredients until smooth and light.Wash, halve and stone the plums, keeping the stones. Mix the light brown sugar, vinegar and two tablespoons of water. Crack open the plum stones by wrapping them in a tea towel and smashing with a rolling pin, then remove the kernels and add to the sugar mix. Toss the plums in this mixture, then transfer to a roasting tin and bake at 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7 for 10-15 minutes, until slightly caramelised and starting to collapse.Split open the warm bannocks, add a generous amount of the honey butter and spoon the roast plums on top.Anna Higham is the owner ofQuincebakery andClementine, both in north London.Explore more on these topicsFoodBreakfastBreadBritish food and drinkEggsBakingFruitrecipesShareReuse this content
